patch_review.observation: The fix wraps the template parameter Description value in Django's HTML escaping helper where the stack form builds its parameter fields, so the text used as field help text is rendered as plain text. This matches the card's cause (unescaped template description used as help_text) and its prevention (escape at the point the value becomes a form field attribute). The same one-line change is applied across the branch backports.

patterns.title: Untrusted input in JSON error messages for the IPython /api/contents path enabled XSS
patterns.cause: IPython 3.x before 3.2 allowed remote attackers to inject script or HTML through JSON error messages involving /api/contents. The diffs show error paths that serialized messages without explicitly setting a JSON content type, supporting a response-type weakness that could let data be interpreted as HTML. API responses already had a content security policy restricting framing, but lacked the default resource restriction added by the fix. The sources do not establish the exact payload or browser interaction.
preconditions: The deployment runs IPython 3.x before 3.2.
An attacker can influence content in a JSON error response involving /api/contents.
A victim's browser interprets the attacker-influenced response content as active HTML or script.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade IPython to version 3.2 or later. Follow the fix by explicitly setting the application/json content type in both HTTP-error and unexpected-exception branches of json_errors. The broader diff introduces APIHandler, whose finish method sets the JSON content type, and migrates multiple API handlers to it. Its default content security policy adds a deny-all default resource policy while retaining framing and reporting directives. As general hardening, treat request-derived error text as untrusted data and avoid inserting it into pages as markup.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify the payload field, prove that the URL path was echoed, specify authentication requirements, or establish direct navigation to a crafted link as the trigger. They do not show the framework's default response media type. Broader handler changes do not prove exploitation of every migrated endpoint. The stated affected range is IPython 3.x before 3.2; other branches are unspecified. Configured headers can override the default content security policy. The changes do not sanitize message text or establish safety for clients that insert it as markup, and they do not guarantee coverage of every response path.

fixtures.scenario: An IPython 3.1 notebook server receives a request to a path under /api/contents that triggers an error. The JSON error message includes attacker-supplied text, and a victim's browser handles that text as web script or HTML.
An IPython 3.2 or later server handles the same request. The error message content is neutralized, so attacker-supplied text is not interpreted as web script or HTML in the victim's browser.

citations.quote: inject arbitrary web script or HTML via vectors involving JSON error messages and the /api/contents path
Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in IPython 3.x before 3.2
Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation in IPython

patch_review.observation: The fix sets an explicit JSON content type in the error paths of the JSON error decorator, both for HTTP errors and for unhandled exceptions. It also adds a common API handler base class that forces the JSON content type on finish and appends a default-src none policy to the content security policy. All the services handlers (contents, kernels, sessions, config, clusters and others) are moved onto that base class.

patterns.title: IPython before 3.2: XSS through JSON error messages on the /api/notebooks path
patterns.cause: IPython before 3.2 allowed remote attackers to inject script or HTML through vectors involving JSON error messages and /api/notebooks. The diffs show JSON error responses were not reliably labeled with a JSON content type. This could allow attacker-influenced error text to be interpreted as HTML; the sources do not establish the exact browser execution path.
preconditions: The deployment runs IPython earlier than 3.2.
An attacker can influence content in a JSON error response through a vector involving /api/notebooks.
A victim's browser encounters the error content in a context that permits injected HTML or script to take effect.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to IPython 3.2 or later. The fixes explicitly set the application/json content type in HTTP error and unexpected exception responses. The broader fix introduces APIHandler, migrates API handlers to it, and sets the JSON content type in its finish method. Its default Content-Security-Policy adds a deny-all fallback for content sources while retaining same-origin framing and violation reporting. As general hardening, minimize untrusted text in error messages and apply context-appropriate output encoding when rendering it as HTML.
patterns.limitations: The advisory and diffs do not identify the exact triggering request, establish that a crafted path supplies the payload, require a logged-in victim, or distinguish direct browser interpretation from client-side rendering. The shown fixes change response headers without sanitizing message text, so unsafe client-side HTML insertion remains a separate concern. Custom header settings can override the default Content-Security-Policy, and its content-source fallback does not block every browser capability.

fixtures.scenario: An IPython 3.1 notebook server receives a request on the /api/notebooks path with markup in the part of the request that the server echoes back in a JSON error message. A user's browser then processes that message and the markup is treated as active content.
The same request is sent to IPython 3.2 or later, or to a service that escapes echoed text for its output context. The markup is neutralized and is displayed as plain text, so no script runs.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via vectors involving JSON error messages and the /api/notebooks path.
Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation in IPython

patch_review.observation: The fix sets an explicit JSON content type on the error paths of the JSON error-handling decorator, so error bodies that echo request input are no longer rendered as HTML. It also adds an API base handler that forces a JSON content type when finishing a response and appends a CSP that blocks all content sources by default, then moves all the API handlers onto it. This matches the card's cause and its prevention.

patterns.title: Django 1.8.x URLValidator ReDoS causing CPU exhaustion before 1.8.3
patterns.cause: In Django 1.8.x before 1.8.3, URLValidator's domain label expression used nested repetitions with overlapping character classes, allowing excessive backtracking on failing matches. The added regression cases use a domain-like host followed by a space or a space and a letter. Remote attackers could cause denial of service through excessive CPU consumption.
preconditions: The application runs Django 1.8.x before 1.8.3.
The application uses URLValidator directly or through functionality that relies on it.
Remotely influenced input reaches the validator; the added tests illustrate trailing-junk inputs but do not establish all attack requirements.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade affected Django 1.8.x installations to 1.8.3 or a release containing the fix. The fix simplifies each repeated dotted label to one character-class repetition, with lookahead and lookbehind assertions excluding leading and trailing hyphens; the outer repetition remains. Add regression cases for rejection of hosts followed by trailing junk, as the patch does. As general hardening, avoid ambiguous nested repetitions, assess rejection performance, and consider limiting URL input length before validation.
patterns.limitations: The advisory leaves attack vectors unspecified. The diff supports the backtracking mechanism but provides no measured complexity or timing results. Its regression cases assert rejection, without a timing threshold or proof that all slow inputs are eliminated. The shown fix changes only the domain label expression and adds no total input length bound; it establishes no safety guarantee for other expressions or validators. No safe input cap or broader affected-version range is established.

fixtures.scenario: A public web form on Django 1.8.2 checks a user-submitted link field with URLValidator. A remote client submits crafted values that tie up server CPU and slow or block other requests.
The same form runs on Django 1.8.3 or later. The deployment inventory confirms that no environment still uses an earlier 1.8.x release for URL validation.

citations.quote: validators.URLValidator in Django 1.8.x before 1.8.3 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (CPU consumption) via unspecified vectors.
Django ReDoS in validators.URLValidator

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the domain label pattern in the URL validator, which had a repetition nested inside another repetition over overlapping character classes, with a single repetition over one character class. Lookahead and lookbehind assertions now keep labels from starting or ending with a hyphen. The added tests feed a valid-looking host followed by trailing junk to confirm it is rejected quickly. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Folder names rendered unescaped in the Jupyter and IPython Notebook file browser enable XSS
patterns.cause: The notebook file browser builds web page content that includes a folder name without properly neutralizing it. A folder name containing script or HTML is therefore interpreted by the browser as active markup instead of being shown as text. The affected releases are IPython Notebook before 3.2.2 and Jupyter Notebook 4.0.x before 4.0.5.
preconditions: The server runs IPython Notebook before 3.2.2 or Jupyter Notebook 4.0.x before 4.0.5.
A folder exists whose name contains attacker-chosen script or HTML.
A user opens the file browser view that lists that folder name.
patterns.prevention: Treat every folder name as untrusted data wherever the file browser puts it into a page. Neutralize the name for the context it is placed in, so the browser shows it as plain text and never parses it as markup or script. Prefer a text-only insertion mechanism or the framework's automatic escaping over hand-built markup. Upgrade to IPython Notebook 3.2.2 or later, or Jupyter Notebook 4.0.5 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say the flaw is in the file browser in notebook/notebookapp.py and is triggered via a folder name. They do not describe the exact rendering path, the escaping context, or how a hostile folder name gets created. They also note the issue was first reported as CSRF, which may be inaccurate. This card therefore gives general direction only and no details of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A shared notebook server contains a folder whose name includes an HTML script payload. A user opens the file browser, the folder name is placed into the page as markup, and the payload runs in the user's browser session.
The same folder name is listed in the file browser, but it is neutralized for its page context. The browser shows the literal characters as text, and no script runs.

citations.quote: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the file browser in notebook/notebookapp.py in IPython Notebook before 3.2.2
allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via a folder name.
Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation in Jupyter Notebook

patch_review.observation: The fix changes how the server builds its Jinja template environment in the notebook app settings setup. Autoescaping is now on by default, and any user-supplied environment options are merged on top. As a result, values such as a folder name that are rendered through templates are escaped and shown as text rather than parsed as markup.

patterns.title: Plone URL checking accepts crafted URLs containing script markup, leading to XSS
patterns.cause: Plone's URL checking infrastructure includes a method that decides whether a URL is valid and located in the Plone site. It can be given a specially crafted URL that carries HTML, such as a script tag opener or a javascript scheme, in plain or percent-encoded form. The URL is not rejected, so cross-site scripting can be achieved.
preconditions: A vulnerable Plone release is in use: 3.3.0 through 3.3.6, 4.0.0 through 4.0.10, 4.1.0 through 4.1.6, 4.2.0 through 4.2.7, 4.3.x before 4.3.7, or 5.0rc1.
An attacker can supply a URL value to the Plone URL checking method.
The URL contains a script tag opener or a javascript scheme, either literal or percent-encoded.
patterns.prevention: Treat any URL passed to the validity and in-site check as untrusted data. Reject a URL as invalid if it contains a script tag opener or a javascript scheme, in both literal and percent-encoded forms, before reporting it as a valid in-site URL. Upgrade to a Plone release that includes the upstream fix; 4.3.7 is the first fixed 4.3.x release named in the advisory data.
patterns.limitations: The sources name the vulnerable method only generically and list the four trigger patterns. They do not describe the exact fix, the entry points that reach the method, how the payload is rendered, or the fixed versions for the 3.3, 4.0, 4.1, 4.2 and 5.0 lines. A denylist of known patterns may not cover every encoding variant, and the sources do not say whether other markup is also affected.

fixtures.scenario: A request passes a URL containing a percent-encoded script tag opener, or a javascript scheme, to the Plone URL checking method on an affected version. The method does not reject it, and the script content can run in a visitor's browser.

The same request, with a URL containing a script tag opener or a javascript scheme in literal or percent-encoded form, is rejected as invalid by the URL check on a fixed Plone version. No script content is accepted as a valid in-site URL.

citations.quote: Plone's URL checking infrastructure includes a method for checking if URLs valid and located in the Plone site.
By passing HTML into a specially crafted url containing
Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in Plone 3.3.0 through 3.3.6, 4.0.0 through 4.0.10, 4.1.0 through 4.1.6, 4.2.0 through 4.2.7, 4.3.x before 4.3.7, and 5.0rc1.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds an early check in the portal URL validity method (isURLInPortal) in the URL tool. After the URL is trimmed, it returns false if the URL contains a script tag opener or a javascript scheme, in literal or percent-encoded form. New tests confirm that such URLs are no longer reported as in the portal.

patterns.title: Shell metacharacters in a font name reach command execution in Pygments image formatter
patterns.cause: The FontManager._get_nix_font_path function in formatters/img.py in Pygments 1.2.2 through 2.0.2 lets shell metacharacters in a font name lead to execution of arbitrary commands. The font name is untrusted input, and the affected code does not keep it from being interpreted as shell syntax.
preconditions: The application runs Pygments 1.2.2 through 2.0.2.
The image formatter's font handling on a Unix-like system is used (the function name suggests this, but the sources do not say so explicitly).
An attacker can influence the font name that is passed to the formatter.
patterns.prevention: Treat the font name as data and never as part of a command line. An implementation should avoid building a shell command string from the font name. If an external program must be consulted, pass the name as a separate, literal argument with no shell interpretation. It should also reject or constrain font names that contain unexpected characters. Upgrading to a Pygments release newer than 2.0.2 is the direct remedy implied by the affected version range. Do not let untrusted users choose font names.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only the affected function, the affected version range, and the attack vector of shell metacharacters in a font name. They do not describe the exact vulnerable call, which external program is involved, which release first fixed the issue, or how the upstream change works. The prevention guidance is therefore a general direction and not a description of the upstream fix. The sources also do not say how an attacker typically supplies the font name.

fixtures.scenario: A web service uses Pygments 2.0.2 to render code as images. It accepts a font name from a request parameter and passes it to the image formatter. A user submits a font name containing shell metacharacters followed by an extra command, and that command runs on the server.

The same service uses a Pygments version newer than 2.0.2, or only accepts font names from a fixed server-side list. A font name containing shell metacharacters is rejected or treated as a literal name that matches no font, and no extra command runs.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands via shell metacharacters in a font name.
The FontManager._get_nix_font_path function in formatters/img.py in Pygments 1.2.2 through 2.0.2

patterns.title: Unescaped exception messages in the Werkzeug debugger page enable XSS
patterns.cause: In Werkzeug before 0.11.11, render_full in debug/tbtools.py inserted the plain-text traceback into the HTML debugger page without HTML escaping. The separate exception and exception type fields were already escaped. The unescaped traceback provided an exception-message injection vector through which remote attackers could inject arbitrary web script or HTML.
preconditions: Werkzeug earlier than 0.11.11 is in use, directly or through Flask or another product.
The Werkzeug debugger renders its full HTML error page through render_full.
A remote attacker can influence an exception message included in the unescaped traceback.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Werkzeug to 0.11.11 or later. The shown fix HTML-escapes the plain-text traceback before inserting it into the full debugger page. As general hardening, apply context-appropriate output encoding to every derived representation of untrusted data in error pages, and do not expose the interactive debugger to untrusted users.
patterns.limitations: The shown diffs change only the plain-text traceback substitution in render_full. A separate plaintext_cs field retains its existing hyphen normalization, but the supplied sources do not establish its purpose, rendering context or safety. They do not establish the safety of other fields or debugger pages, or describe how attackers influence exception messages or any additional deployment prerequisites.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs on Werkzeug 0.10 with the debugger enabled. A request makes the application raise an exception whose message includes attacker-supplied markup. The debugger error page inserts that message without encoding, so the markup runs in the browser of whoever views the page.
The same application runs on Werkzeug 0.11.11 or later. The same exception is raised, and the message is shown in the debugger page as inert text instead of executing as script or HTML.

citations.quote: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the render_full function in debug/tbtools.py in the debugger in Pallets Werkzeug before 0.11.11
allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via a field that contains an exception message.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the full debugger page rendering so the plain-text traceback is HTML-escaped before it goes into the page template. The separate plain-text copy field used for sharing is left as it was. This matches the card's cause, prevention, and stated limitation.

patterns.title: Windows path traversal in Radicale filesystem storage backend via crafted request path
patterns.cause: The filesystem storage backend in Radicale before 1.1 on Windows lets a crafted request path reach files outside what the server is meant to serve. The advisory's example is a path that begins with a drive-letter-style component, /c:/file/ignore.
preconditions: Radicale before version 1.1 is in use
The server runs on Windows
The filesystem storage backend is in use
A remote attacker can send requests with a chosen path
patterns.prevention: Do not trust the request path when choosing a file location. Before any read or write, check that the final filesystem location is still inside the configured storage area, and reject request paths that point elsewhere, including drive-letter-style paths like the advisory's example. Upgrade to Radicale 1.1 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources give only a one-line description and one example path. They do not explain the exact parsing or path-joining flaw, list other path forms that may be affected, or say how the upstream fix works. The checks above are a general direction, not a description of the actual patch. Whether non-Windows systems are affected is not stated beyond the Windows scope.

fixtures.scenario: A Radicale server before 1.1 on Windows uses the filesystem storage backend. A remote client requests the path /c:/file/ignore, and the server reads or writes a file outside its intended storage area.

A Radicale server at version 1.1 or later, or an implementation that confirms the final location stays inside the storage area, receives the path /c:/file/ignore and rejects it without touching any file outside that area.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to read or write to arbitrary files via a crafted path, as demonstrated by /c:/file/ignore.
The filesystem storage backend in Radicale before 1.1 on Windows

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that converts a request path into a filesystem path one component at a time. It rejects empty components, components with a drive prefix, components containing path separators, and current or parent directory names, and raises an error otherwise. All storage backends now use this helper instead of joining the request path onto the storage folder directly, and request paths are also sanitized earlier in the request handling.

patterns.title: Redirect target check in is_safe_url accepts URLs with basic authentication
patterns.cause: Before the fix, is_safe_url replaced backslashes with forward slashes before validating the URL. The diff explains that Chrome treats backslashes as slashes in paths, but they can also occur in basic authentication credentials. Normalization could make a URL appear to target the trusted host while its unmodified credentials-bearing form identifies an attacker-controlled host after the at sign. The advisory reports arbitrary-site redirects, phishing, and possible XSS.
preconditions: The application runs Django before 1.8.10, or a 1.9.x release before 1.9.3.
The application relies on is_safe_url to validate a redirect target.
An attacker can influence the redirect target used by the application.
The demonstrated attack combines a backslash and an at sign so normalization changes how the URL's host and credentials are interpreted.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 1.8.10, 1.9.3 or a later fixed release. The fix requires the existing safety checks to pass for both the original URL and the form with backslashes replaced by forward slashes. This avoids trusting only the normalized interpretation. As general hardening, use a fixed local fallback when redirect validation fails.
patterns.limitations: The fix does not ban all embedded credentials: a test permits them when the supplied host argument includes the matching credentials and hostname. Tests also preserve at signs in paths and query values. The sources do not establish coverage of all browser parsing differences, identify application views or input parameters that expose the issue, or explain the possible XSS mechanism.

fixtures.scenario: An application takes a user-supplied redirect target and checks it with is_safe_url on Django 1.9.2. An attacker supplies a URL like http://mysite.example.com\@attacker.com, the check passes, and the victim is sent to the attacker's site.

The application runs Django 1.9.3 or later, or 1.8.10 or later, and still validates the redirect target. A URL containing basic authentication is not trusted, and the user is sent to a default local page.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to redirect users to arbitrary web sites and conduct phishing attacks
via a URL containing basic authentication, as demonstrated by `http://mysite.example.com\@attacker.com`.
Django before 1.8.10 and 1.9.x before 1.9.3

patch_review.observation: The fix stops is_safe_url from judging only a backslash-normalized copy of the URL. It moves the checks into a helper function and requires both the original URL and the backslash-to-slash version to be safe for the expected host. The new tests cover URLs where a backslash precedes an at sign and the real host is external, while URLs whose credentials match the expected host stay allowed.

patterns.title: Authenticated users injecting AngularJS templates through Horizon dashboard forms (CVE-2016-4428)
patterns.cause: Horizon allows remote authenticated users to inject an AngularJS template through a dashboard form, leading to arbitrary script or HTML execution in the browser (CWE-79). The diff identifies user-supplied text interpreted by AngularJS as the weakness: ordinary Django HTML escaping does not neutralize Horizon's custom AngularJS interpolation delimiters.
preconditions: The deployment runs Horizon 8.0.1 or earlier, or 9.0.0 through 9.0.1, without the upstream fix.
The attacker is a remote authenticated user who can submit text through a dashboard form.
The submitted text reaches a page region processed by AngularJS, where its interpolation delimiters can take effect.
patterns.prevention: Apply the upstream fix or upgrade to a Horizon release containing it. The fix wraps Django's escape function, preserves its normal HTML escaping, and then replaces Horizon's opening and closing AngularJS interpolation delimiters with sequences AngularJS does not interpret as those delimiters. The monkeypatch_escape function installs this replacement globally early in both application and test settings. As general hardening, avoid placing untrusted data in AngularJS-compiled regions where possible.
patterns.limitations: The replacement protects output that passes through the patched Django escape function and targets Horizon's configured delimiters. The diff does not establish coverage of every template or output path, including safe-marked values or client-side insertion, or prove that installation precedes all escaping. The sources do not identify a specific vulnerable form, field, or template, establish whether injection is stored or reflected, or give the first fixed release number.

fixtures.scenario: A user with a valid Horizon login enters text containing an AngularJS template into a dashboard form field. The page that later displays the value lets AngularJS process it, so attacker-chosen script or HTML runs in the browser of whoever views that page.

A user enters the same template-like text into the same form field. The page shows it as literal text, AngularJS does not evaluate it, and no script or HTML from the input runs in any viewer's browser.

citations.quote: allows remote authenticated users to inject arbitrary web script or HTML by injecting an AngularJS template in a dashboard form.
OpenStack Dashboard (Horizon) 8.0.1 and earlier and 9.0.0 through 9.0.1

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a wrapper around Django's HTML escape function that, after normal escaping, replaces the AngularJS interpolation delimiters with harmless sequences. It installs the wrapper by monkeypatching at the very start of the dashboard settings module (and the test settings), so all server-rendered templates are covered.

patterns.title: Admin related-object popup callback inserting data through Element.innerHTML (Django XSS)
patterns.cause: The dismissChangeRelatedObjectPopup function in the Django admin script RelatedObjectLookups.js made unsafe use of Element.innerHTML. Markup in data handled by that function could be interpreted as HTML or script by the browser instead of being treated as plain text.
preconditions: The application runs Django before 1.8.14, a 1.9.x release before 1.9.8, or a 1.10.x release before 1.10rc1.
The Django admin is in use and serves the RelatedObjectLookups.js script.
Attacker-influenced data reaches the Element.innerHTML usage inside dismissChangeRelatedObjectPopup.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 1.8.14, 1.9.8, 1.10rc1 or later, which address this issue. In any custom admin JavaScript derived from this file, do not build page content from data by assigning it to Element.innerHTML. Write such data into the page in a way that the browser treats as text, not markup.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which input an attacker controls, how the popup flow is triggered, or what the upstream change does. They also do not describe any workaround other than moving to fixed releases. The text-insertion guidance above is a general direction and is not taken from the advisory wording.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs Django 1.9.7 with the admin enabled. Data containing HTML markup reaches the related-object popup dismissal handling, and the script places it into the page through Element.innerHTML, so the browser runs the injected script in the admin user's session.
A site runs Django 1.9.8 or later, or a project with customized admin scripts that avoid Element.innerHTML for data. The same markup-bearing data is shown as inert text and no script runs.

citations.quote: allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via vectors involving unsafe usage of Element.innerHTML.
Django before 1.8.14, 1.9.x before 1.9.8, and 1.10.x before 1.10rc1

patch_review.observation: The fix changes dismissChangeRelatedObjectPopup so the updated object's display string is written into the select option as plain text, not parsed as HTML. The same switch to plain-text assignment is applied to two toggle helpers in the debug view template. The tests confirm that a name containing markup now appears literally in the select option.

patterns.title: Unsanitized fact variables from the Ansible controller allow command execution on clients
patterns.cause: Ansible before 2.2.0 insufficiently sanitized fact variables. The advisory says an attacker able to create special variables on the controller could execute arbitrary commands on clients as the user Ansible runs as. The diff addresses module-returned facts whose names overlap Ansible control variables by filtering them in the _parse_returned_data function. This supports a risk of facts influencing execution settings, but does not show the later variable merge or command-execution path.
preconditions: The deployment runs Ansible before 2.2.0, the advisory's affected range.
The attacker can create special variables on the controller, as stated in the advisory.
For the path addressed by the diff, a parsed module result contains a fact dictionary with names matching the filtered control-variable names or patterns.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade out of the advisory's affected range to a release containing this fix. When parsing module results, remove facts matching entries in the magic-variable mapping, names beginning with the Ansible prefix followed by a discovered connection-plugin name and an underscore, or names beginning with the Ansible prefix and ending with the interpreter suffix. Preserve the explicit exception for names beginning with the Ansible SSH host-key prefix. In similar designs, prevent untrusted facts from overriding execution settings.
patterns.limitations: The diff filters only fact dictionaries in parsed module results; it does not show protections for other fields or sources. Coverage depends on the magic-variable mapping, discovered connection plugins and interpreter-name pattern. The SSH host-key exception does not establish that every preserved value is harmless. The sources do not establish that control of a managed host is required or sufficient, show the later merge and execution path, or independently confirm which release first shipped this commit.

fixtures.scenario: A controller running Ansible before 2.2.0 sends fact variables to a client. An attacker who can create a special variable on the controller supplies a crafted value, and the client runs arbitrary commands as the user Ansible runs as.

The controller and clients run Ansible 2.2.0 or later, and fact variables received from the controller are sanitized. A crafted variable value is handled as data and no arbitrary command runs on the client.

citations.quote: Ansible before version 2.2.0 fails to properly sanitize fact variables sent from the Ansible controller.
An attacker with the ability to create special variables on the controller could execute arbitrary commands on Ansible clients as the user Ansible runs as.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the parsing of module results so that any returned fact is dropped if its name matches a reserved control variable. That covers the magic variable names for connection and privilege escalation, names prefixed with a connection plugin name, and interpreter settings. SSH host key facts are kept. A new option on the plugin loader's listing function returns only plugin paths, so the connection plugin names can be enumerated without loading them. This matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Open redirect through the came_from parameter after Plone login
patterns.cause: After a login-required visit, Plone sends the user to the login form with a came_from parameter holding the previous URL, then redirects back to it after login. Plone already used a same-site check to block most malicious values. A few more ways of tricking that check into accepting a malicious link were found, so a crafted came_from value could still send an authenticated user to an attacker's site.
preconditions: The application redirects to a came_from style URL taken from the request after a successful login.
The only protection is a same-site check on that URL, and the check can be fooled by crafted links.
An attacker can get a user to click a specially crafted link that leads to the login form.
The deployment runs an affected Plone version (2.5 through 5.1rc1) without the hotfix.
patterns.prevention: Treat the came_from value as untrusted input. Before redirecting, confirm that it points to a page on the same Plone site, using a same-site check that is hardened against crafted links. Apply the vendor hotfix or upgrade past the affected versions. Where the check cannot be trusted, fall back to a fixed default landing page rather than the supplied value.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe which crafted link forms bypassed the original check or how the hotfix changes the check, so this card cannot list specific bypass patterns. They also do not say whether other redirect parameters are affected. They name only Plone 2.5 through 5.1rc1 as affected.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens a link to the Plone login form whose came_from value is crafted so the same-site check accepts it, although it points to an attacker's site. The user logs in and is redirected to the attacker's page, which looks like the original site.

The same crafted link is used against a site with the hardened same-site check. The came_from value is rejected, so the user lands on a page inside the Plone site after login and is not sent to the attacker's site.

citations.quote: Plone 2.5-5.1rc1 sends you to the login form with a 'came_from' parameter set to the previous url.
You would login, and get redirected to the site of the attacker, letting you think that you are still on the original Plone site.
But a few more ways of tricking Plone into accepting a malicious link were discovered, and fixed with this hotfix.

patch_review.observation: The fix hardens the same-site URL check used for redirects after login. It now rejects any absolute URL whose scheme is not http or https (such as mailto and data), and it also checks the HTML-entity-decoded form of the URL, rejecting the link if the decoded form is not in the portal. The existing blacklist of bad substrings is only refactored into a shared list, and tests cover double-slash and backslash forms.

patterns.title: Stored XSS via user-controlled profile home page link
patterns.cause: The advisory describes a member setting JavaScript in the home_page profile property, which executed when a visitor clicked the home page link on the author page. The diff shows that isURLInPortal checked known bad substrings but lacked an explicit scheme allowlist and HTML character reference decoding. It could accept non-web schemes such as data and mailto as portal URLs. The diff does not establish how this helper connects to the reported profile XSS.
preconditions: A site member can set the home_page property of their profile.
The author page renders the malicious value as the home page link target.
A visitor clicks that link.
patterns.prevention: Update isURLInPortal to reject any explicit scheme other than http or https while retaining existing portal membership checks and the bad-substring blacklist. Decode HTML character references and recursively validate the decoded value when it differs, rejecting the original if that check fails. Keep regression tests for rejected mailto, data and entity-encoded inputs, accepted portal URLs, and rejected external URLs with leading slashes. As general hardening, validate user-controlled link and redirect targets consistently and apply context-appropriate output escaping when rendering them.
patterns.limitations: The diffs show the helper and tests, not its callers or the author-page rendering and profile-save paths. They do not establish exploitation through redirects, return addresses, or other profile fields, or show that every non-web scheme executes script. Entity encoding is addressed by the fix but is not stated as necessary for the advisory's attack. Consistent caller validation and output escaping are general hardening, not changes demonstrated by these diffs.

fixtures.scenario: A member sets the profile home page to a javascript scheme value. A visitor opens the author page and clicks the home page link, and the script runs in the visitor's session.
A member sets the home page to a javascript scheme value. It is rejected or neutralized, so the author page shows no active link and clicking never runs script. A normal https address still works.

citations.quote: A member of the Plone site could set javascript in the `home_page` property of their profile
have this executed when a visitor click the home page link on the author page.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the portal URL check so that any absolute URL with a scheme other than http or https is rejected, which covers data, mailto and ftp. It also decodes HTML character references and re-validates the decoded value, so entity-encoded payloads can no longer slip past the substring blacklist. The blacklist is kept as an extra layer, and tests cover mailto, data, entity-encoded and double-slash inputs.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS in certain Apache Airflow 404 pages
patterns.cause: The variables view uses a form name from the URL path to select a template. Its exception handler returned a formatted 404 response containing the unescaped form name. A crafted path could therefore reflect attacker-controlled HTML into the error page and execute script in the victim's browser.
preconditions: The victim can reach an Airflow web UI containing the vulnerable variables error handler.
The victim opens a crafted variables URL containing malicious markup in the form name, and processing reaches the error handler.
The browser permits the reflected payload to execute. The advisories report that Chrome blocked the attempt while Firefox and other browsers did not.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Apache Airflow to 1.9.0 or later, as the advisories recommend. The upstream fix uses Jinja2's escape function on the form name before inserting it into the formatted 404 response. It also adds a regression test that requests a variables path containing an injected image tag and checks for a 404 response without the raw injected tag. As general hardening, review other responses that interpolate request data into HTML and apply appropriate output escaping.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish the full affected version range or authentication requirements. The shown fix covers this variables error response; it does not establish whether other response paths are vulnerable. The regression test checks status and absence of one raw payload, not browser execution or all payload variants. The browser behavior is reported by the advisories and is not a current compatibility guarantee or an application defense.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow deployment older than 1.9.0 is used with Firefox. A user follows a crafted link that triggers an affected 404 page, and the browser does not block the reflected script.
The deployment runs Airflow 1.9.0 or above. The same crafted link to a not-found page no longer yields an XSS, and reviewers also confirm that error pages encode any request-derived text.

citations.quote: It was noticed an XSS in certain 404 pages that could be exploited to perform an XSS attack.
Firefox and other browsers don't, and are vulnerable to this attack.
The fix for this is to upgrade to Apache Airflow 1.9.0 or above.

patch_review.observation: The fix escapes the form name taken from the URL path in the variables view before it is placed into the 404 error string returned when the template cannot be loaded. A regression test requests a path with an injected image tag and checks for a 404 response that does not contain the raw markup. This matches the card's cause, prevention and stated limitations.

patterns.title: Minion ID validation must reject directory traversal in Salt master authentication
patterns.cause: Salt's minion id validation was vulnerable to directory traversal. A remote minion could present a crafted minion ID and authenticate to a master even though its credentials were incorrect. The validation did not stop an identifier supplied by an untrusted peer from being treated as more than a plain name.
preconditions: A Salt master running a release before 2016.11.7, or a 2017.7.x release before 2017.7.1
The master accepts connection attempts from remote minions that supply their own minion ID
The attacker can send a crafted minion ID to the master
patterns.prevention: Treat a minion ID as untrusted input and validate it strictly before the master uses it for authentication decisions. Accept only a plain identifier and reject any value that could traverse directories. Upgrade to Salt 2016.11.7, 2017.7.1 or later, which address the flaw. In your own code that takes peer-supplied identifiers, apply the same rule: validate the identifier first, and do not let it select or alter a location outside the intended storage area.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that minion id validation was vulnerable to directory traversal and that a crafted ID let a minion with incorrect credentials authenticate. They do not describe which files or directories were reached, the exact characters involved, or how the validation was changed. The exact checks to apply are therefore not specified here. Version coverage comes only from the advisory ranges.

fixtures.scenario: A remote minion connects to a vulnerable master with wrong credentials and a minion ID built to include directory traversal elements. The master's validation lets it pass, and the minion is authenticated.

The same minion connects to a patched master. The master's validation rejects the crafted ID because it is not a plain identifier, and the minion is not authenticated. A minion with a plain ID and correct credentials still authenticates normally.

citations.quote: Directory traversal vulnerability in minion id validation in SaltStack Salt before 2016.11.7 and 2017.7.x before 2017.7.1
allows remote minions with incorrect credentials to authenticate to a master via a crafted minion ID.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that rejects minion IDs containing a parent-directory sequence followed by a path separator. The master's id validation function now requires both the existing path-cleaning check and this new check to pass. This matches the card's account of a peer-supplied ID being treated as more than a plain name, and its advice to validate strictly and reject traversal.

patterns.title: Disabled autoescaping in Django technical 500 debug page enables XSS
patterns.cause: In Django 1.10.x before 1.10.8 and 1.11.x before 1.11.5, HTML autoescaping was turned off for one portion of the template that renders the technical 500 debug page. Content rendered in that portion was not HTML-escaped, so under the right circumstances it allowed a cross-site scripting attack.
preconditions: Django 1.10.x earlier than 1.10.8, or Django 1.11.x earlier than 1.11.5, is in use.
Debug mode is enabled, which makes the technical 500 debug page accessible.
The 'right circumstances' named in the advisories are met; the sources do not say what they are.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 1.10.8, 1.11.5, or later. When writing or reviewing error-page and debug templates, keep autoescaping enabled for every region that renders dynamic data, and do not switch it off for a portion of a template unless the content is known to be safe. Do not run production sites with debug mode enabled, since that is what exposes the technical 500 page.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify which portion of the template lost autoescaping, which data reached it, or how an attacker would supply that data, so this card cannot describe the exploit path. They also say most production sites should be unaffected because debug mode should be off there. They do not describe the upstream changes, so this card gives only the general direction of the fix.

fixtures.scenario: A project runs Django 1.11.4 with debug mode enabled. An error produces the technical 500 page, and a portion of that page's template renders with autoescaping disabled, so content that should have been HTML-escaped is emitted raw into the page.

A project runs Django 1.11.5 or later, or 1.10.8 or later, where autoescaping is no longer disabled in that portion of the debug page template. Production also keeps debug mode off, so the technical 500 page is not reachable.

citations.quote: HTML autoescaping was disabled in a portion of the template for the technical 500 debug page.
Given the right circumstances, this allowed a cross-site scripting attack.
This vulnerability shouldn't affect most production sites

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the block that disabled autoescaping around the traceback section of the technical 500 template, so frame data such as filenames, functions, source lines and variables is escaped again by default. It also forces escaping on the chained exception text (the cause or context message shown between frames), since that text could otherwise be treated as already safe and emitted raw. The tests check that a safe-marked exception message and a plain one are both escaped in the HTML view and left as-is in the plain-text view.

patterns.title: Incomplete minion ID validation allows directory traversal and authentication bypass on a Salt master
patterns.cause: The Salt master validated the minion ID supplied by a remote minion, but the validation was incomplete and a crafted minion ID could still perform directory traversal. A minion with incorrect credentials could then authenticate to the master. The advisory says this was an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-12791.
preconditions: A Salt master accepts a minion ID chosen by a remote minion.
The master runs a release before 2016.3.8, 2016.11.8 (2016.11.x line), or 2017.7.2 (2017.7.x line).
The minion ID validation does not fully reject crafted IDs, for example because an earlier fix for CVE-2017-12791 covered only some cases.
patterns.prevention: Treat the minion ID as untrusted input and validate it strictly before it is used for authentication or anywhere else. Accept only a conservative set of identifier characters and reject anything that could be read as a path component. When an earlier traversal fix exists, review it for gaps and test it against varied crafted IDs, not only the original exploit string. Upgrade to a release that contains the corrected validation.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which crafted ID forms bypass the earlier fix. They do not say which files or directories the ID reaches, or exactly how traversal leads to authentication. This card therefore gives only general guidance on validating the ID and cannot list specific rejected patterns. Backported fixes in other branches or distribution packages are not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A remote minion with incorrect credentials connects to a master on an affected version and presents a crafted minion ID. The incomplete validation lets the ID through and the minion authenticates to the master.
The master runs a fixed release with complete minion ID validation. The same crafted ID is rejected, so a minion with incorrect credentials cannot authenticate.

citations.quote: Directory traversal vulnerability in minion id validation in SaltStack Salt before 2016.3.8, 2016.11.x before 2016.11.8, and 2017.7.x before 2017.7.2
allows remote minions with incorrect credentials to authenticate to a master via a crafted minion ID.
this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-12791.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the weak check that only rejected a parent-directory sequence followed by the OS path separator. The ID validation function now rejects any ID containing a forward slash, a backslash, or a NUL byte before the existing path-cleaning check, and a test covers both separators. This matches the card's account of incomplete minion ID validation and its advice to reject anything readable as a path component.

patterns.title: Mistune XSS via newline in link scheme and crafted email autolinks
patterns.cause: Mistune 0.7.4 checked dangerous URL schemes against a lowercased URL with selected leading and trailing characters stripped. An embedded newline could bypass that prefix check and allow XSS. The autolink function used escape instead of escape_link, omitting scheme filtering and the quote escaping used for link targets. The advisory also identifies crafted email addresses as an XSS vector, but does not establish that they work by carrying a script scheme.
preconditions: The application renders attacker-controlled Markdown with Mistune 0.7.4.
The input reaches vulnerable link or autolink handling.
The resulting HTML is rendered in a browser without additional protection that prevents the XSS.
patterns.prevention: Use a release containing the fix. For the blacklist comparison, remove all characters except ASCII letters, digits, slashes and colons from the lowercased, trimmed URL. Reject matching blocked prefixes; otherwise escape the original URL with quote escaping enabled and smart ampersand handling disabled. Route autolink targets and displayed text through escape_link, including email input before adding the mailto prefix. As general hardening, consider a safe-scheme allowlist and final HTML sanitization.
patterns.limitations: The sources identify 0.7.4 as affected but give no complete affected range or fixed release number. They do not provide the crafted email payload or establish browser behavior for every removed character. The filter remains blacklist-based, and the full blacklist is not shown. Normalization affects only comparison; accepted URLs retain their original characters when escaped. The shown entity test expects an escaped ampersand, so it does not support claiming that character entities bypass the fix. The diff does not establish coverage of every href-producing path.

fixtures.scenario: A web app renders user comments with Mistune 0.7.4. A comment has a link whose target splits the word javascript across two lines. The output keeps the link and a click may run script in the viewer's browser.
The same app uses a release that is not 0.7.4 and sanitizes the final HTML. The split-scheme link and a crafted email autolink are neutralized or escaped, so no script runs when a viewer clicks.

citations.quote: mistune.py in Mistune 0.7.4 allows XSS via an unexpected newline
or a crafted email address, related to the escape and autolink functions.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the link sanitizer so that, before comparing against the blocked scheme list, it strips every character other than letters, digits, slash and colon from the lowercased URL. This defeats schemes split by a newline or other stray characters. It also makes the autolink renderer call the link sanitizer instead of only HTML-escaping, so autolinks and email autolinks are subject to the same scheme filter. This matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Directory traversal through the static file route in Sanic before 0.5.1
patterns.cause: Sanic before 0.5.1 allowed arbitrary file reads through directory traversal. The advisories demonstrate it with a request path containing the substring /static/..%2f, so a crafted URL under the static route could reach files outside the intended directory.
preconditions: The application runs Sanic before version 0.5.1.
The application serves files through a static route such as /static.
An attacker can send a request path containing an encoded traversal sequence such as ..%2f.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Sanic 0.5.1 or later. In any code that maps URL paths to files, treat the request path as untrusted, including percent-encoded separators. Resolve the final file location to its canonical form and confirm it stays inside the configured static directory before opening it. Reject the request if it does not. Add a regression test that sends a path like /static/..%2f and expects a rejection.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that versions before 0.5.1 allow arbitrary file reads and give one example substring. They do not describe the internal root cause, how the fix works, or whether other encodings or routes were affected. The canonicalize-and-confine approach is a general defensive direction, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs Sanic 0.5.0 with a static route. A client requests a path beginning with /static/..%2f followed by the name of a file outside the static directory, and the server returns that file's contents.

A service runs Sanic 0.5.1 or later. The same request containing /static/..%2f is rejected or does not return any file outside the static directory, while normal requests for files inside the directory still work.

citations.quote: Sanic before 0.5.1 allows reading arbitrary files with directory traversal, as demonstrated by the /static/..%2f substring.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the static file handler so the joined path is percent-decoded and then converted to an absolute, normalized path. It then checks that the result still begins with the configured root directory, and raises a file-not-found error if it does not. This closes the encoded traversal (..%2f) that previously escaped the static directory, which matches the card's cause and its canonicalize-and-confine prevention.

patterns.title: Unescaped key argument in Mistune _keyify enables XSS
patterns.cause: In Mistune before 0.8.1, the _keyify function in mistune.py does not escape its key argument. Attacker-influenced text that reaches this argument can carry web script or HTML into the output.
preconditions: The application uses Mistune before version 0.8.1.
Attacker-controlled content can reach the key argument handled by the _keyify function.
The generated output is delivered to users as HTML, for example in a web page.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Mistune 0.8.1 or later. In any code that handles key values like this, treat the key as untrusted data and escape it for the HTML context before it is placed in output. Do not rely on the key being harmless. Where practical, also sanitize or restrict the final rendered HTML for untrusted input.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which Markdown constructs supply the key argument, where the key appears in the output, or what payloads work. They also do not describe the exact upstream change, so this card gives only the general direction of escaping the key. Whether other Mistune code paths have similar gaps is not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A site renders user-submitted Markdown with a Mistune release older than 0.8.1. A submission supplies a key containing HTML or script markup, the unescaped key reaches the page, and the markup runs in a visitor's browser.
The same site runs Mistune 0.8.1 or later, so the key argument is escaped. The same submission appears as inert text and no script or HTML from the key is interpreted by the browser.

citations.quote: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the _keyify function in mistune.py in Mistune before 0.8.1
allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML by leveraging failure to escape the

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the _keyify function so the lowercased key is HTML-escaped, with quote escaping turned on, before the existing normalization step runs. This matches the card's cause (the key was not escaped) and its prevention (escape the key for HTML and upgrade to 0.8.1). The version bump and the line-wrapping change to the inline HTML pattern are not part of the fix.

patterns.title: Avoid arbitrary code execution from yaml.load() on untrusted YAML in PyYAML before 5.1
patterns.cause: In PyYAML before 5.1, the yaml.load() API could execute arbitrary code when it parsed untrusted YAML. Applications that deserialize YAML strings with this general-purpose loader, instead of the safe loading API, let attacker-controlled input trigger code execution (CWE-502).
preconditions: The application uses a PyYAML version older than 5.1.
The application calls the yaml.load() API.
The YAML input comes from an untrusted source.
The safe loading function, yaml.safe_load, is not used.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to PyYAML 5.1 or later, which contains the patch for this CVE. Version 4.1 was intended to carry the fix but was yanked because of breaking changes, so do not rely on it. Parse untrusted YAML with yaml.safe_load rather than yaml.load(). Treat the 5.1 deprecation of load() as a prompt to review every call site. Do not use the UnsafeLoader, which was introduced only for backward compatibility with the old load() behavior, for data that is not fully trusted.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which YAML constructs or tags enable code execution, so this card cannot list specific payload types. They do not describe the default behavior of load() in 5.1 beyond its deprecation, or the exact safety properties of UnsafeLoader. They give no guidance on trust boundaries for YAML that is considered trusted. Applications that depend on legacy load() behavior may need migration work, and the sources do not detail it.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs PyYAML 5.0 and parses YAML configuration or documents uploaded by external users with the yaml.load() API. A crafted document causes arbitrary code to run in the service process.

A service runs PyYAML 5.1 or later and parses externally supplied YAML only with yaml.safe_load. Any remaining uses of the legacy load behavior via UnsafeLoader are limited to fully trusted, internally controlled files.

citations.quote: In PyYAML before 5.1, the yaml.load() API could execute arbitrary code if used with untrusted data.
The load() function has been deprecated in version 5.1 and the 'UnsafeLoader' has been introduced for backward compatibility with the function.
PyYAML insecurely deserializes YAML strings leading to arbitrary code execution

patch_review.observation: The change makes the default loader used by the general load and load_all functions build only basic YAML types, so safe loading becomes the default. The old full-power loader is renamed to a danger-named loader with explicit danger_load functions that are documented as able to execute code on untrusted input. This matches the card's cause (the general-purpose loader running code from untrusted YAML) and its advice to use safe loading.

patterns.title: Cross-site scripting in the MoinMoin GUI editor link dialogue
patterns.cause: The link dialog of the MoinMoin GUI editor, implemented by the fckdialog action's link_dialog function, inserts the pagename request parameter unescaped into the value attribute of the Page Name input. Attacker-controlled input can break out of that attribute and inject script or HTML. This request-to-response path supports reflected cross-site scripting.
preconditions: The wiki runs MoinMoin before 1.9.10 without the fix.
The GUI editor's link dialog is reachable and renders attacker-controlled pagename input in a victim's browser.
The attacker can supply the pagename request parameter.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to MoinMoin 1.9.10 or later, or apply the upstream fix. The fix uses wikiutil.escape on the supplied page name and inserts the escaped result into the Page Name input's value attribute. As general hardening, review other dialog templates for raw request values and use escaping appropriate to each HTML output context.
patterns.limitations: The diff fixes the pagename value in the Page Name input; it does not establish whether other parameters or dialogs are vulnerable. The sources do not specify authentication requirements, the attack delivery method, or required victim interaction. The implementation of wikiutil.escape is not included in the supplied diff.

fixtures.scenario: A wiki runs a MoinMoin release older than 1.9.10. A user opens the GUI editor and uses the link dialogue. Attacker-influenced input is handled there and can result in script or HTML running in the victim's browser.
A wiki runs MoinMoin 1.9.10 or later. The GUI editor link dialogue is used in the same way, and the affected version range no longer applies.

citations.quote: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the link dialogue in GUI editor in MoinMoin before 1.9.10
allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via unspecified vectors.

patch_review.observation: The fix computes an HTML-escaped copy of the pagename request value in the link dialog function and uses that escaped copy in the value attribute of the Page Name input, instead of the raw value. This closes the reflected cross-site scripting path described by the card.

patterns.title: Glance v1 copy_from URL enables masked internal port scanning (SSRF)
patterns.cause: Glance Image Service API v1 image creation accepted a user-supplied URL through the copy-from header without enforcing a separate copy_from authorization check in the create path. This enabled masked port scans of internal or loopback services and enumeration of internal network details, with connections appearing to originate from Glance.
preconditions: Glance before Newton with Image Service API v1 enabled, as described by the advisory
The attacker can submit an otherwise permitted image creation request containing a copy-from source URL
The create path does not enforce the dedicated copy_from policy rule
Glance can reach the network destinations being probed
patterns.prevention: In the create function, detect copy-from requests using Controller._copy_from and enforce the dedicated copy_from policy rule before reserving the image. Denied requests receive HTTP 403; the added tests also verify successful creation when the rule permits access. As general hardening, restrict this capability to trusted roles or deny it entirely, disable API v1 where unnecessary, and consider network egress controls and destination filtering.
patterns.limitations: The shown fix adds authorization enforcement, not destination validation. It does not establish whether other URL restrictions exist, so it cannot prove that every URL or internal address remains reachable by authorized users. Protection depends on the effective copy_from policy; its defaults are not shown. The sources do not specify exact patched releases, the response details used for enumeration, or handling of redirects and DNS rebinding.

fixtures.scenario: An attacker creates an image through API v1 with a copy_from value of http://localhost:22. Glance connects from its own host, and the response lets the attacker infer whether that internal port is open.
The service checks the copy_from target against an allowlist and rejects loopback and internal destinations before connecting, so the attacker gets no signal about internal ports.

citations.quote: The 'copy_from' feature in the Image Service API v1 allowed an attacker to perform masked network port scans.
it is possible to create images with a URL such as 'http://localhost:22'.
the scan would appear to originate from the Glance Image service.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check in the v1 image create path: when the request uses the copy-from source, the service now enforces a dedicated copy_from policy rule before reserving the image, returning forbidden if denied. Tests cover both the denied and allowed cases. The target URL itself is not inspected.

patterns.title: Open redirect via numeric URLs accepted by Django is_safe_url
patterns.cause: The redirect safety check django.utils.http.is_safe_url() treated some numeric URLs as safe when they were not. User-supplied on-success redirect targets could therefore send users to an unintended destination. A URL that passed the check and was placed in a link could also lead to XSS.
preconditions: Django 1.10 before 1.10.7, 1.9 before 1.9.13, or 1.8 before 1.8.18 is in use
The application takes a post-action redirect target from user input
The application relies on is_safe_url() to decide whether that target is safe
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 1.10.7, 1.9.13, 1.8.18 or later. Treat any user-supplied redirect target as untrusted and pass it through the safe-URL check before redirecting. Do not place a value into a link just because it passed the check; keep output escaping in place. Fall back to a fixed internal default when the check rejects a target.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which numeric URL forms were wrongly accepted, so this card cannot list exact bypass inputs. They also do not describe how the fix changed the check. Fixed versions are known only for the 1.8, 1.9 and 1.10 branches; other branches are not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A login view on an unpatched Django 1.10.6 reads a next parameter from the request. It passes the check in is_safe_url() and redirects there. An attacker supplies a numeric URL the check wrongly accepts.
The same view runs on Django 1.10.7 or later. It validates the next parameter with the patched is_safe_url() and redirects to a fixed internal default page when validation fails.

citations.quote: considered some numeric URLs "safe" when they shouldn't be
they could suffer from an XSS attack

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the standard library URL parser in the safe-URL check with a vendored copy of the parsing functions that includes an upstream CPython correction. Before, a scheme followed only by digits (such as http: plus a long number) was not recognized as a scheme, so the URL looked like a harmless relative path while browsers treat it as an external host. The added tests block these scheme-plus-number URLs and still allow a relative path that merely contains such text.

patterns.title: Open redirect through the Django static serve view in unpatched releases
patterns.cause: The django.views.static.serve view rebuilt the requested path component by component and redirected to the rebuilt value when it was nonempty and differed from the normalized input. This request-derived redirect allowed a maliciously crafted URL to redirect to another domain. The fix removes the redirect and component rebuilding, retains URL decoding, path normalization and leading-slash removal, and uses safe_join to resolve the path against the document root.
preconditions: The site runs Django 1.10 before 1.10.7, 1.9 before 1.9.13, or 1.8 before 1.8.18.
The site handles the crafted request through django.views.static.serve.
For a victim to be redirected, they must request the crafted URL.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 1.10.7 or later in the 1.10 series, 1.9.13 or later in the 1.9 series, or 1.8.18 or later in the 1.8 series. The fix removes the path-cleaning redirect and uses safe_join with the document root and normalized path. As general hardening, validate any required redirect targets to keep them on the intended host, and add regression checks that crafted requests cannot cause an external redirect.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify an exploit URL or establish that repeated leading slashes alone trigger the issue, nor do they specify the browser interpretation involved. They do not include safe_join's implementation or establish exactly which paths are rejected. The changed index test supports a dot-slash prefix in the root directory heading. The supplied excerpts do not establish development-only usage or reduced production exposure. Releases outside the listed ranges and other application redirects are not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A site on Django 1.10.6 serves files through the django.views.static.serve() view. A user opens a crafted link to the site and is redirected to an unrelated external domain.
The same site is upgraded to Django 1.10.7 or later. The same crafted link no longer sends the user to another domain.

citations.quote: A maliciously crafted URL to a Django (1.10 before 1.10.7, 1.9 before 1.9.13, and 1.8 before 1.8.18) site
could redirect to any other domain, aka an open redirect vulnerability.

patch_review.observation: The patch, applied to three release branches, removes the redirect in the static serve view that was built from the cleaned request path, which allowed an open redirect with crafted leading slashes. It now normalizes the path, strips leading slashes, and resolves it against the document root with safe_join, which rejects escapes from the root. A test change shows the directory index heading for the root now begins with a dot-slash prefix, as the card notes.

patterns.title: Open redirect in Django CommonMiddleware on unpatched 1.11.x and 2.0.x releases
patterns.cause: CommonMiddleware's append-slash redirect path was not escaped when it began with two slashes. With APPEND_SLASH enabled and a URL pattern accepting the slash-appended path, the redirect target could become a scheme-relative URL that browsers interpret as another host, causing an open redirect (CWE-601).
preconditions: The application runs Django 1.11.x before 1.11.15 or Django 2.0.x before 2.0.8.
CommonMiddleware is enabled with APPEND_SLASH turned on.
A URL pattern accepts the path beginning with two slashes after a trailing slash is added, and the request triggers an append-slash redirect.
A crafted request path beginning with two slashes followed by an attacker-controlled host reaches the middleware.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 1.11.15 or later on the 1.11 line, or 2.0.8 or later on the 2.0 line. The fix calls escape_leading_slashes from get_full_path_with_slash to percent-encode the second leading slash, preventing interpretation as a scheme-relative URL. URL reversing also uses this helper in place of its existing inline escaping. As general hardening, custom redirects derived from request paths can apply equivalent escaping or validate that the target is a safe local URL.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish the APPEND_SLASH default, a required victim-delivery method, or affected versions outside the 1.11 and 2.0 lines. Anchoring URL patterns alone does not prevent this issue: the regression test uses an anchored pattern that accepts the problematic path. The demonstrated fix covers append-slash redirects and refactors existing URL-reversing protection; it does not establish the safety of custom redirects.

fixtures.scenario: A web application runs Django 2.0.7 with CommonMiddleware enabled in its middleware settings. It falls in the affected range and is exposed to the open redirect.
A web application runs Django 2.0.8 or later, or 1.11.15 or later, with CommonMiddleware enabled. It is outside the affected ranges named in the advisories.

citations.quote: in Django 1.11.x before 1.11.15 and 2.0.x before 2.0.8 has an Open Redirect.
django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware in Django 1.11.x before 1.11.15 and 2.0.x before 2.0.8 has an Open Redirect.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that rewrites a URL starting with two slashes so the second slash is percent-encoded. CommonMiddleware's append-slash path now passes its redirect target through this helper, and URL reversing reuses it in place of its own inline check. This matches the card's cause, its prevention, and the affected branches.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS via crafted URL in Flask-Admin 1.5.2 helpers module
patterns.cause: Flask-Admin 1.5.2 has reflected XSS via a crafted URL in helpers.py. Before the fix, is_safe_url parsed targets after trimming only leading and trailing whitespace. The diff addresses parser/browser interpretation differences involving whitespace-obfuscated javascript schemes, backslashes interpreted as forward slashes, and excess leading slashes with or without a scheme. These differences could undermine URL safety checks. The tests reject obfuscated script URLs and disguised external-host URLs; they do not demonstrate an application-level open redirect.
preconditions: The application runs Flask-Admin 1.5.2; the supplied sources do not establish an earlier affected version range.
An attacker supplies a crafted URL that reaches is_safe_url.
A victim encounters the crafted URL through the affected application flow; the exact parameter, view, and browser interaction are not shown.
patterns.prevention: Use a Flask-Admin release containing this fix; the supplied sources do not identify its version. The fix normalizes targets before parsing: it converts backslashes to forward slashes, removes whitespace and selected control characters, and reduces excess leading slashes to two, including after an optional scheme. It retains the existing scheme restriction to http and https when a scheme is present; tests retain acceptance of relative paths and rejection of a different host. As general hardening, prefer relative redirect paths or an allowlist of targets, and validate request-derived URLs before using them as links or redirect destinations.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify a fixed release, affected versions beyond 1.5.2, a return parameter, or the call site that renders or redirects to the target. They establish reflected XSS but do not establish a separate open-redirect vulnerability. The change covers validation through is_safe_url, not independent URL handling. Its normalization removes selected control characters, not all, and the supplied tests do not prove compatibility with every browser or future parsing behavior. Output escaping alone is not URL-scheme validation; this is general hardening context, not the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: An administrator of an application running Flask-Admin 1.5.2 follows a link in a message. The link is a crafted URL aimed at the helpers.py code path, and the response reflects attacker-influenced content that the browser treats as active content.

The application runs a Flask-Admin release that includes the fix for CVE-2018-16516. Custom views escape any URL-derived values on output, so a crafted URL is shown as inert text and does not run in the administrator's browser.

citations.quote: helpers.py in Flask-Admin 1.5.2 has Reflected XSS via a crafted URL.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the URL safety check so it normalizes the target the way browsers do before parsing. It turns backslashes into forward slashes, strips all whitespace and control characters (not just leading and trailing ones), and collapses extra slashes after the scheme. The existing scheme and host checks then run on the normalized value, which closes the script-scheme and external-host bypasses described in the card.

patterns.title: Untrusted notebook XSS through nbconvert responses served without a Content Security Policy
patterns.cause: In Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.1, NbconvertFileHandler and NbconvertPostHandler can serve converted active content, including HTML or SVG, under the notebook server's origin without an effective Content Security Policy restriction preventing this XSS. JavaScript in output from an untrusted notebook can consequently execute with access to the server API.
preconditions: The deployment runs Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.1.
An untrusted notebook produces converted content containing executable JavaScript.
A browser renders that content from an nbconvert endpoint under the notebook server's origin without effective sandbox confinement.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Jupyter Notebook 5.7.1 or later. The fix extends the inherited Content Security Policy in both NbconvertFileHandler and NbconvertPostHandler with a sandbox directive that permits scripts but does not preserve same-origin privileges. This confines converted JavaScript to a unique origin to prevent interaction with the notebook server. As general hardening, apply comparable isolation to other endpoints serving user-controlled active content.
patterns.limitations: The diff changes only the two named nbconvert handlers; it does not establish whether other handlers need changes. HTML and SVG are cited examples, not an exhaustive affected-format list. The inherited policy and browser compatibility are not shown. The new sandbox directive permits scripts, but other policy restrictions may still block execution. The sources do not establish that sandboxed content is harmless or that all forms of server communication are prevented.

fixtures.scenario: A user asks the server to convert a notebook from an untrusted source that embeds JavaScript. The nbconvert endpoint returns the result with no Content Security Policy. The browser treats the response as same-origin with the notebook server, so the script can reach the server API.

A user asks the server to convert the same untrusted notebook. The nbconvert endpoint returns the result with a Content Security Policy that stops the embedded script from executing with server API access. The converted document is delivered without exposing the server API.

citations.quote: nbconvert endpoints can execute JavaScript with access to the server API.
NbconvertFileHandler and NbconvertPostHandler do not set a Content Security Policy to prevent this.
Jupyter Notebook before 5.7.1 allows XSS via an untrusted notebook because nbconvert responses are considered to have the same origin as the notebook server.

patch_review.observation: The fix overrides the content security policy property in both nbconvert handlers (file and post) so the inherited policy is extended with a sandbox directive that permits scripts.
