An attacker overwrites that fact with text containing shell metacharacters and a second command. The shell runs the injected command on the controller.

A playbook uses the pipe lookup plugin, and every fact or variable in the command string is first escaped with the quote plugin. When an attacker overwrites the fact with shell metacharacters, the shell treats the whole value as one literal argument and no extra command runs.

citations.quote: A flaw was found in the pipe lookup plugin of ansible.
the variable is not escaped by quote plugin
An attacker could take advantage and run arbitrary commands by overwriting the ansible facts.

patch_review.observation: The upstream change only updates documentation and examples for the pipe lookup plugin. It states that the plugin intentionally runs its command through a shell, warns that unsanitized user or variable input is a security risk, and recommends passing such input through the quote filter, with the example updated to match. This is the same cause (shell enabled, unescaped values) and the same prevention (escape with the quote filter) that the card describes.

patterns.title: Fetch module lets an intercepted or injected path choose the destination on the controller
patterns.cause: When the Ansible Engine fetch module is used, an attacker who intercepts the module can inject a new path and choose a new destination path on the controller node. The advisory text does not say which value is trusted wrongly, so the exact mechanism is not described in the sources.
preconditions: The fetch module is used to copy files from a managed host to the controller node.
An attacker is able to intercept the module and inject a new path.
The Ansible Engine version is in the 2.7.x, 2.8.x or 2.9.x branches, which are believed to be vulnerable.
patterns.prevention: Do not let a path that comes back from the module or the remote side decide where a file is written on the controller. Derive the controller destination from values the controller itself controls. Before writing, resolve the final destination to its canonical form and confirm it stays inside the intended destination directory, rejecting anything that falls outside. Also move to an Ansible release that includes the upstream fix for CVE-2020-1735.
patterns.limitations: The sources are short and do not describe the vulnerable code path, the exact injected field, the fixed versions, or the upstream fix. The prevention direction here is general path-confinement guidance and is not a description of the actual patch. The sources also do not say how an attacker gains the ability to intercept the module.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook runs the fetch module against a managed host. An attacker who intercepts the module injects a new path, and the file is written to a destination of the attacker's choosing on the controller node, outside the directory the playbook author intended.

A playbook runs the fetch module and the controller computes the destination from its own configured destination directory. It resolves the final path and refuses to write if the result is outside that directory, so an injected path cannot redirect the file.

citations.quote: An attacker could intercept the module, inject a new path, and then choose a new destination path on the controller node.
All versions in 2.7.x, 2.8.x and 2.9.x branches are believed to be vulnerable.

patterns.title: Zip extraction in win_unzip writing outside the destination folder
patterns.cause: The Extract-Zip function in the Ansible win_unzip module combined archive entry names with the destination without normalizing the resulting paths or checking containment. Entries containing relative parent-directory segments could therefore escape the destination, causing directories and files to be created outside it.
preconditions: Ansible 2.7.17 and prior, 2.8.9 and prior, or 2.9.6 and prior is in use, as stated in the advisory.
A ZIP archive is extracted on a Windows host through the win_unzip module's Extract-Zip function.
The archive is attacker-crafted and contains entry paths that resolve outside the destination, such as relative parent-directory traversal.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a release containing the fix; the advisory identifies Ansible 2.10 as fixed. Treat archive entry names as untrusted input. Combine each entry name with the destination and normalize the resulting full path. Append a directory separator to the destination and normalize its full path, then require the target to begin with that destination prefix. Fail extraction on a mismatch before creating directories or writing that entry. Parent-directory segments that normalize to a location inside the destination remain allowed, as the added tests demonstrate.
patterns.limitations: The case-sensitive prefix check relies on path normalization and the destination separator; the sources do not test differences between string comparison and filesystem case handling. The shown change targets Extract-Zip; coverage of other archive formats or modules is not established. Absolute-path and other filesystem edge cases are not demonstrated. Extraction fails at the first rejected entry; earlier entries may already have been written, and no rollback is shown. Backports to the 2.7, 2.8, and 2.9 lines are not specified.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook uses win_unzip on a Windows host to extract an archive from an untrusted source. One entry in the archive has a path that climbs out of the destination folder. The extraction writes that file to a location outside the destination because no containment check is made.

The same playbook runs on Ansible 2.10 or later. An entry whose path would land outside the destination folder is not written there, and only files that belong to the destination folder are extracted.

citations.quote: the extracted file(s) are not checked if they belong to the destination folder
An attacker could take advantage of this flaw by crafting an archive anywhere in the file system, using a path traversal.
This issue is fixed in 2.10.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check in the Extract-Zip function of win_unzip. For each entry it builds the full normalized target path and the full normalized destination path with a trailing separator, and fails the module if the target does not start with the destination. The check runs before any directory or file is created, and new tests use archives with parent-directory segments in entry names.

patterns.title: Stale persistent domain definition after live migration exposes destination host devices
patterns.cause: Live migration did not update the persistent domain XML of the guest. After a soft reboot, the guest could reach destination host devices whose paths matched host devices that its old definition referenced on the source host. Those paths can map to different Cinder volumes on the destination.
preconditions: The instance has previously undergone live migration
A user performs a soft reboot of that instance
The deployment allows host-based connections, such as root and ephemeral devices
Device paths on the destination host match paths referenced on the source host but map to different volumes
patterns.prevention: Make sure the persistent domain definition is brought in line with the destination host as part of live migration, so a later soft reboot does not reuse device references from the source host. Run a Nova release that includes the fix (19.3.1, 20.3.1 or later). Treat device paths as host-specific and never assume they refer to the same backing volume on another host.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, so the exact fields updated during migration are not stated. Despite the XXE and CWE-611 labels, the sources describe a stale-definition problem, not XML external entity parsing. Fixed versions are inferred from the affected-version ranges. Deployments without host-based connections are stated as unaffected.

fixtures.scenario: A guest is live migrated, then soft rebooted. Its persistent definition still names device paths from the source host, and on the destination those paths map to other volumes.
After live migration the persistent definition is updated for the destination host, so a soft reboot only reaches the devices intended for this guest.

citations.quote: OpenStack Nova Live migration fails to update persistent domain XML
By performing a soft reboot of an instance that has previously undergone live migration, a user may gain access to destination host devices
Only deployments allowing host-based connections (for instance, root and ephemeral devices) are affected.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes live migration pass the updated destination domain XML to libvirt as the persistent definition as well, so the destination stores the rewritten definition instead of a stale copy from the source host. In the driver this is limited to libvirt 1.3.4 or newer, where that migration parameter exists. This matches the card's cause (stale persistent definition reused after a soft reboot) and its prevention.

patterns.title: Attacker-selected backend module via facts when the use parameter is omitted in Ansible package and service modules
patterns.cause: When the package or service module is used without the 'use' parameter, the module that actually runs is chosen from the Ansible facts file. If an earlier task was run with a malicious user, that user can influence the facts and so select the module that is sent. The advisory titles this an argument injection (CWE-88).
preconditions: The package or service module is used in a task.
The 'use' parameter is not specified in that task.
A previous task was executed with a malicious user who can affect the facts file.
Ansible Engine 2.7.x, 2.8.x or 2.9.x, all believed vulnerable.
patterns.prevention: Specify the 'use' parameter explicitly on package and service tasks so the backend module is not picked from facts. More generally, treat the facts file as untrusted input that an earlier task or user may have written, and do not let it alone decide which module is dispatched. Move to a release that contains the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which Ansible version contains the fix or how the fix works. They do not describe the exact payload or what the selected module can do. They do not say whether setting the 'use' parameter fully removes the risk in every configuration. The facts-handling guidance above is a general hardening direction, not a statement from the advisories. Only 2.7.x, 2.8.x and 2.9.x are named, and they are described as believed vulnerable.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook runs the package module without the 'use' parameter. An earlier task was run with a malicious user, who left facts that name a module of their choosing. The later task then runs the module the attacker selected.
The same playbook sets the 'use' parameter explicitly on the package task, so the backend module is fixed by the playbook author and not taken from the facts file.

citations.quote: A flaw was found in Ansible Engine when the module package or service is used and the parameter 'use' is not specified.
the module sent can be selected by the attacker using the ansible facts file.
Argument Injection in Ansible

patch_review.observation: The fix adds an allowlist of known package manager modules to the package action plugin and of known service manager modules to the service action plugin. When the use parameter is omitted and the module name comes from the pkg_mgr or service_mgr facts, a name outside the list now fails with an error that suggests setting use. This matches the card's cause, where an attacker-influenced facts value selects the dispatched module, and its prevention of setting use explicitly and not trusting facts alone.

patterns.title: SSRF in the Charts and Query View of the old Apache Airflow UI
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow versions prior to 1.10.13, the Charts and Query View of the old Flask-admin based UI were vulnerable to server-side request forgery (CWE-918). The sources do not describe the code path or the mechanism.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version prior to 1.10.13 is deployed
The old Flask-admin based UI is the interface in use
The Charts and Query View of that UI are part of the deployment
patterns.prevention: Run Apache Airflow 1.10.13 or later, which is the first version the sources identify as not affected. The sources give no details of the fix, so no implementation-level guidance is given beyond the version boundary.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief and give no attack vector, required privileges, request parameters, or affected internal targets. They do not say whether any configuration or workaround reduces exposure short of upgrading. They also do not describe how the fix works. This card covers only the version boundary and the named UI components.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs apache-airflow at a version earlier than 1.10.13 and exposes the Charts and Query View of the old Flask-admin based UI.
A deployment runs apache-airflow at version 1.10.13 or later, which is not listed as affected for the Charts and Query View issue.

citations.quote: In Apache Airflow versions prior to 1.10.13, the Charts and Query View of the old (Flask-admin based) UI were vulnerable for SSRF attack.

patterns.title: Incomplete fix leaves the origin parameter open to XSS in Apache Airflow endpoints
patterns.cause: Airflow's origin parameter on endpoints such as /trigger was vulnerable to XSS because the fix for CVE-2020-13944 in 1.10.13 was incomplete. Scheme and host checks in get_safe_url were insufficient. Response tests show origin rendered in a quoted JavaScript string within a button's inline click handler. The diffs initially remove single quotes and re-encode queries, then remove quote stripping while preserving blank query values. A later change rejects semicolon-bearing relative URLs and filters semicolon-bearing query values, addressing parsing differences across Python versions.
preconditions: The deployment runs an affected Apache Airflow version; the advisories disagree on the affected range.
An endpoint such as /trigger accepts an attacker-controlled origin parameter that reaches the vulnerable rendering path.
patterns.prevention: Apply the shared get_safe_url changes: send empty values to the home page; retain scheme and host restrictions; parse queries while preserving blank values and re-encode them. Reject relative URLs containing a semicolon after percent-decoding and fall back to the home page. Remove query arguments whose parsed values contain a semicolon before re-encoding. The final shown approach does not strip single quotes. Upgrade to a release containing the fixes; GHSA identifies 1.10.15 as the affected-range boundary. As general hardening, use encoding appropriate to the JavaScript and HTML attribute contexts where the value is rendered.
patterns.limitations: GHSA says versions before 1.10.15 are affected, while PYSEC and the CVE record say before 1.10.13 despite describing that release's fix as incomplete. The diffs do not establish which releases contain each change. Rendering context is supported by response-test expectations, but the template itself is not included. The sources do not establish exact victim interaction, authentication requirements, or the complete affected endpoint list. Context-specific output encoding is general hardening, not a demonstrated patch change.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs an Airflow version that includes only the 1.10.13 fix. A request to the trigger endpoint carries an attacker-chosen origin value, and the application still treats that value as trustworthy, so the XSS remains exploitable.

A deployment runs Airflow 1.10.15 or later. The origin value on the trigger endpoint and on other endpoints that accept it is handled as untrusted data, and a test with attacker-chosen origin values confirms that none of them lead to script execution.

citations.quote: This is same as CVE-2020-13944 but the implemented fix in Airflow 1.10.13 did not fix the issue completely.
This issue affects Apache Airflow versions prior to 1.10.15.
Apache Airflow cross-site scripting due to incomplete fix for CVE-2020-13944

patch_review.observation: The diffs harden the shared URL-safety helper in several steps. First it re-encodes the query and strips single quotes. Next it returns the home page for empty input and drops the quote stripping. Finally it sends relative URLs containing a semicolon (checked after percent-decoding) to the home page and drops query arguments whose values contain a semicolon. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Flask-CORS resource matching on non-canonical paths allows ../ traversal
patterns.cause: In Flask-CORS before 3.0.9, resource matching does not ensure canonical pathnames; the advisories report that this allows ../ traversal to access private resources. The diff shows cors_after_request previously passed the framework-provided request path directly to try_match. The fix applies unquote_plus before matching resource patterns, changing which CORS rules can match. It does not establish that the supplied path is the raw URL or that decoding reproduces the router's interpretation.
preconditions: The application uses Flask-CORS before 3.0.9.
The extension matches the request path against configured CORS resource patterns.
A non-canonical request pathname reaches resource matching; the advisories identify ../ traversal, but the supplied sources do not establish the exact encoding or routing prerequisites.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Flask-CORS to 3.0.9 or later. The upstream fix applies unquote_plus to the framework-provided request path in cors_after_request before try_match checks resource patterns. This decodes percent escapes and converts plus signs to spaces. As general hardening, test private routes with non-canonical and encoded path spellings to check that the intended CORS policy applies.
patterns.limitations: The diff does not explicitly resolve dot-dot segments or demonstrate complete canonicalization. It does not establish how decoding aligns with routing, including plus-to-space conversion, or provide a traversal reproduction. The exact affected CORS settings, exposed data, and additional attacker prerequisites are unspecified. Custom path matching outside the extension is not covered.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs Flask-CORS older than 3.0.9 and has private routes. A client sends a request whose path includes ../ segments that resolve to a private route. Resource matching does not canonicalize the path, so the private resource is accessed.

An application runs Flask-CORS 3.0.9 or later. Request paths containing ../ segments are put in canonical form before resource matching, so the request is treated as the private route it resolves to and is not reached through a differently matched rule.

citations.quote: It allows ../ directory traversal to access private resources because resource matching does not ensure that pathnames are in a canonical format.
An issue was discovered in Flask-CORS (aka CORS Middleware for Flask) before 3.0.9.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the after-request handler in the extension so the request path is percent-decoded (including plus-to-space) before it is compared with the configured CORS resource patterns. This makes matching use a canonical form of the path instead of the raw spelling. The other changes are CI, test and example updates.

patterns.title: Directory traversal in the MoinMoin cache action leading to remote code execution
patterns.cause: The cache action in action/cache.py in MoinMoin through 1.9.10 accepts a crafted HTTP request that makes it reach files outside the location it is meant to serve. The request is not confined to the intended directory. Combined with attachment upload, this gives an attacker remote code execution.
preconditions: MoinMoin version 1.9.10 or earlier is running.
The cache action is reachable by HTTP request.
The attacker can upload attachments to the wiki, for example through write permission and the AttachFile action.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to MoinMoin 1.9.11 or later, which contains the fixes. Any code that maps a request-supplied name to a file path should keep the resulting path inside its intended directory. The advisory says a workaround is not advised, but disabling the cache action or the AttachFile action might be possible. It also says to grant write permission, which includes uploading attachments, only to trusted users.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the vulnerable request parameter, the exact traversal technique, or how the upload leads to code execution. They do not describe the code-level fix. The workarounds are described only as possibly effective and are not recommended over upgrading. Versions are stated only as 1.9.10 and earlier being affected and 1.9.11 being patched.

fixtures.scenario: A wiki runs MoinMoin 1.9.10 with the cache action and attachment uploads enabled. A user with write permission uploads an attachment, then sends a crafted HTTP request to the cache action that traverses directories, which can lead to remote code execution.
A wiki runs MoinMoin 1.9.11 or later. Write permission is limited to trusted users, and the same crafted request to the cache action does not escape the intended directory.

citations.quote: The cache action in action/cache.py in MoinMoin through 1.9.10 allows directory traversal through a crafted HTTP request.
An attacker who can upload attachments to the wiki can use this to achieve remote code execution.
MoinMoin Wiki 1.9.11 has the necessary fixes and also contains other important fixes.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a strict check on the key request value in the cache action. The key must be a text string that parses as hexadecimal and is exactly 40 characters long, like the keys the key function generates. Otherwise the request gets a 404 and neither the get nor the remove handler runs, so an attacker-controlled name can no longer be turned into a file path outside the cache directory.

patterns.title: Jupyter Notebook open redirect through crafted server links (CVE-2020-26215)
patterns.cause: TrailingSlashHandler built its redirect target by removing trailing slashes from the raw request URI while leaving leading slashes intact. A crafted path beginning with two slashes followed by an external hostname could therefore produce a protocol-relative redirect target, sending the browser to an attacker-chosen website.
preconditions: The notebook server runs a Jupyter Notebook version earlier than 6.1.5.

The attacker crafts a link to a notebook server with repeated leading slashes followed by an external hostname and a trailing slash. The advisory says such links can only reasonably be made for known server hosts.
A user follows the crafted link, and TrailingSlashHandler processes the request.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade notebook to version 6.1.5 or later. In TrailingSlashHandler, separate the path from the query string, strip leading and trailing slashes from the path, prepend exactly one slash, and reattach the unchanged query portion. Interior slashes are not collapsed. Add regression tests for ordinary trailing slashes, repeated boundary slashes, an external hostname after two leading slashes, and query preservation. The supplied tests check a 302 response and the exact Location value including the configured URL prefix.
patterns.limitations: The supplied diff changes TrailingSlashHandler and adds tests for four redirect cases. It does not establish the safety of other redirect routes or whether the same normalization is appropriate for other handlers. The tests inspect redirect responses without following them; they do not demonstrate browser navigation.

fixtures.scenario: A notebook server runs a version before 6.1.5. An attacker crafts a link that begins with the known address of that server. A user opens it believing it is safe and ends up on a spoofed server on the public internet.

The notebook server runs version 6.1.5 or later. A link of the same crafted style that begins with the server address is not expected to send the user to a different website, because the issue is patched in that release.

citations.quote: a maliciously crafted link to a notebook server could redirect the browser to a different website.
A link to your notebook server may appear safe, but ultimately redirect to a spoofed server on the public internet.
The issue is patched in version 6.1.5.

patch_review.observation: The trailing-slash redirect handler used to strip only trailing slashes from the raw request URI, so a path starting with two slashes and a hostname became a protocol-relative Location value. The fix splits off the query string, trims both leading and trailing slashes from the path, prepends exactly one slash, and reattaches the query. Tests cover repeated leading slashes and a query string.

patterns.title: Open redirect via crafted links to Jupyter Server before 1.0.6
patterns.cause: In Jupyter Server before 1.0.6, TrailingSlashHandler derived its redirect location from the request path by removing only trailing slashes. A crafted path beginning with two slashes, followed by an external host name and a trailing slash, could produce a protocol-relative redirect that sent the browser to an attacker-chosen website.
preconditions: The server runs Jupyter Server older than 1.0.6.
A crafted link reaches TrailingSlashHandler with repeated leading slashes, an external host name, and a trailing slash.
A user opens the link and the browser follows the redirect.
The advisory says such links can only reasonably be made for known Jupyter server hosts; it does not establish host knowledge as an absolute technical prerequisite.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to jupyter_server 1.0.6 or later; the advisory identifies 1.0.6 as the patched release. The fix takes the path portion of the request URI before the first question mark, strips leading and trailing slashes, prepends exactly one slash, and preserves the query portion. This prevents the demonstrated repeated-leading-slash input from becoming a protocol-relative redirect. As general hardening, treat request-derived redirect targets as untrusted and validate their destinations.
patterns.limitations: The advisory broadly describes all Jupyter servers as technically affected. The supplied diff covers TrailingSlashHandler and does not establish the behavior or validation needs of other redirect paths or parameters. It does not establish whether authentication is required or prove protection against every cross-origin redirect form. The added tests document expected redirect locations, including query preservation, but end with an unconditional failure and therefore do not demonstrate a passing test suite.

fixtures.scenario: A server running a version older than 1.0.6 is reachable at a known host. An attacker sends a link that looks like it points to that server, but following it redirects the browser to a spoofed server on the public internet.
The server runs jupyter_server 1.0.6 or later. A link to it that carries an off-site destination does not send the browser to an attacker-controlled website.

citations.quote: a maliciously crafted link to a jupyter server could redirect the browser to a different website
A link to your jupyter server may appear safe, but ultimately redirect to a spoofed server on the public internet.
jupyter_server 1.0.6

patch_review.observation: The trailing-slash handler used to rebuild its redirect from the request path by trimming only trailing slashes, so a path like two leading slashes plus a host name and a final slash became a protocol-relative redirect to another origin. The fix takes the request URI, strips both leading and trailing slashes, adds back exactly one leading slash, and keeps the query string. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Open redirect in Jupyter Server links sends browsers to a spoofed site
patterns.cause: In Jupyter Server before 1.1.1, the login handler's _redirect_safe helper checked redirect targets with a string-prefix comparison against base_url. At the root, a double-slash target naming an external host could pass that check. The fix adds URL parsing and encodes backslashes because some browsers, specifically Chrome according to the diff comment, can interpret them as forward slashes. The supplied tests exercise the next parameter during login.
preconditions: An affected Jupyter Server version before 1.1.1 is running.
The server has no base_url prefix, the affected configuration identified by the advisory.
The attacker crafts a link for a known Jupyter Server host with an external redirect target.
A user opens the crafted link and reaches the redirect behavior; the supplied tests exercise this through a login submission.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade jupyter-server to 1.1.1 or later. The fix percent-encodes backslashes and parses the redirect target. Targets with a network location, or whose parsed path with an appended slash fails the base_url prefix check, require an exception: a target with a network location must pass the configured allowed-origin check. That check uses the lowercased scheme and network location. Rejected targets use the fallback, which defaults to base_url. If upgrading is unavailable, the advisory recommends running under a URL prefix through base_url. As general hardening, validate redirect targets structurally rather than relying only on raw string prefixes.
patterns.limitations: The diff shows the login helper and tests with a non-root base_url; it does not establish coverage of other redirect paths or prove successful login is required for every exploit. Backslash encoding is supported, but a standalone double-backslash exploit against the old root prefix check is not demonstrated. The advisory gives a URL prefix workaround without quantifying its reliability. It reports the same vulnerability patched in notebook 5.7.8 without that patch's details. The commit also changes the password-setting config filename from jupyter_server_config.json to jupyter_notebook_config.json, a separate change from redirect validation.

fixtures.scenario: A Jupyter Server older than 1.1.1 runs at the root path with no base_url prefix. An attacker sends a user a link that appears to point at the known server host. After the user opens it, the server redirects the browser to a spoofed server on the public internet.

The server is upgraded to 1.1.1 or later. Alternatively, an older server runs under a url prefix as the advisory's workaround. A link to the server host then does not send the browser to an outside site.

citations.quote: an open redirect vulnerability could cause the jupyter server to redirect the browser to a different malicious website.
All jupyter servers running without a base_url prefix are technically affected
A link to your jupyter server may *appear* safe, but ultimately redirect to a spoofed server on the public internet.
This is fixed in jupyter_server 1.1.1.

patch_review.observation: The fix in the login redirect helper replaces backslashes with their percent-encoded form, parses the next value as a URL, and rejects any value with a network location unless it passes the allowed-origin checks. It also requires the parsed path to sit under the base URL, so root-mounted servers no longer accept double-slash or double-backslash hosts. The same commit changes the config file name used on password change, which the card correctly calls out as unrelated.

patterns.title: Sanitizer and browser parse HTML differently in the lxml clean module (CVE-2020-27783)
patterns.cause: The lxml HTML cleaner could preserve tag and event handler content as text inside a style element, while a browser could interpret the output differently and execute attacker-controlled HTML or JavaScript. The diff demonstrates a style element inside a math element. Existing checks covered CSS tricks and a noscript pattern but missed this case. Separately, style-element import removal used the original text, discarding the result of CSS expression removal.
preconditions: An attacker can supply untrusted HTML to an application using the lxml HTML cleaner.
For the demonstrated bypass, cleaning retains a style element containing markup-like text inside a math element.
The cleaned output is rendered in a browser context where the parsing difference enables execution.
patterns.prevention: Use an lxml release containing the upstream fix. The fix extends the shared style-content check to detect tag-like text and event-handler-like patterns. Suspicious style-element content is replaced with a neutral CSS comment; suspicious inline style attributes are removed. It also makes style-element import removal operate on the result of expression removal. As general hardening, remove style elements when unnecessary and use a content security policy that blocks inline script execution.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify affected or fixed releases or establish all exploitable browser and markup contexts. The math example does not establish that every foreign-content container behaves alike or that math is required for every exploit. The added check is a heuristic, not general browser-parser equivalence; it may reject legitimate style text resembling the matched patterns. The regression test verifies cleaned output, not browser execution. The defense-in-depth recommendations are general hardening, not changes shown in the diff.

fixtures.scenario: A web application passes user-submitted HTML through the lxml clean module and inserts the result into a page. An attacker submits markup that the sanitizer parses as harmless but a browser parses differently, so script runs in the visitor's browser.

The same application uses a patched lxml release and also tests its sanitizer against inputs that parsers handle differently. The sanitizer and the browser agree on how the markup is structured, so no script from the attacker's input executes.

citations.quote: The module's parser didn't properly imitate browsers, which caused different behaviors between the sanitizer and the user's page.
A remote attacker could exploit this flaw to run arbitrary HTML/JS code.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check in the sneaky-JavaScript detection that flags style content containing tag-like text or inline event handler patterns, so a style element inside a math element is replaced with a neutral placeholder. It also corrects the import-rule removal step to work on the output of the earlier expression removal instead of the original text.

patterns.title: Open redirect via unvalidated next parameter in Horizon workflow forms
patterns.cause: Horizon accepted a next parameter from the request and used it as a redirect target without validating it. An attacker could supply a malicious URL in that parameter, and Horizon would automatically redirect the user to it.
preconditions: The application reads a redirect destination from a next request parameter
The supplied destination is not validated before it is used for a redirect
An attacker can get a user to follow a link carrying a crafted next value
The affected workflow form is in a Horizon version before 15.3.2, 16.x before 16.2.1, 17.x, 18.x before 18.3.3, 18.4.x, or 18.5.x
patterns.prevention: Validate the next parameter before redirecting. Accept only destinations that are known to be safe, such as relative paths within the application or hosts the deployment explicitly trusts. If the value fails validation, ignore it and redirect to a fixed default page. Apply the same check everywhere a user-supplied redirect target is consumed, including workflow forms. Upgrade to a fixed Horizon release.
patterns.limitations: The sources only say that the next parameter lacked validation and that this allowed redirection to a malicious URL. They do not describe the exact code paths, which forms or views are affected beyond workflow forms, or the specific validation the fix uses. They do not say how the affected version ranges map to individual fixes. The exact allowlist or validation rules are therefore left to the implementer.

fixtures.scenario: A user receives a link to a Horizon workflow form with the next parameter set to an external attacker-controlled URL. After the user completes the form, Horizon redirects the browser to that external URL without checking it.

A user opens the same link with an external URL in the next parameter. Horizon validates the value, finds that it is not a safe destination, discards it, and redirects to the default in-application page.

citations.quote: There is a lack of validation of the "next" parameter
would allow someone to supply a malicious URL in Horizon that can cause an automatic redirect to the provided malicious URL.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the get_context_data method of the Horizon workflow view. It no longer passes the next request parameter straight into the redirect context. It now checks the value with Django's safe-URL helper against the current request host and drops it when it is not safe. This matches the card's cause (unvalidated next value used as a redirect target) and its prevention (validate, restrict to safe destinations, ignore failing values).

patterns.title: Mutation XSS in bleach.clean when noscript and a raw-text tag are both allowed
patterns.cause: Bleach's parser defaulted to scripting disabled, creating a mismatch with the expected scripting-enabled browser context for noscript. When bleach.clean allowed noscript together with a listed raw tag, this mismatch enabled mutation XSS. The regression tests use nested noscript and raw tags followed by an image with an event handler, and require that image markup to be escaped. The fix changes the parser's default to scripting enabled so noscript is parsed for the expected browser context.
preconditions: The application calls bleach.clean on untrusted input using an affected Bleach release.
The allowed tags include noscript.
The allowed tags also include at least one of title, textarea, script, style, noembed, noframes, iframe or xmp.
The sanitized output is rendered in a browser with scripting enabled, the context targeted by the fix.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a patched release; the GHSA identifies 3.1.1 as patched. If upgrading is not possible, review bleach.clean allowed-tag lists and remove combinations of noscript with any listed raw tag. As general hardening, align sanitizer parsing with the browser's rendering context. A strong Content-Security-Policy that excludes unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval from script-src can additionally mitigate risk, but does not replace the fix or tag-list workaround.
patterns.limitations: The GHSA names 3.1.1 as patched, while the PYSEC and CVE texts say before 3.11; the supplied sources do not resolve that discrepancy or establish a precise affected-version range. The diff tests every listed raw tag but does not establish other affected combinations. It checks sanitized strings rather than browser execution and does not establish the claimed attribute-like hiding mechanism. The list groups RCDATA and raw-text handling under raw tags. CSP mitigates risk without removing the flaw.

fixtures.scenario: A web application sanitizes user comments with bleach.clean on an old bleach release. Its allowed tags list contains noscript and style, so the unsafe combination is permitted and a crafted comment can produce a mutation XSS.

The application runs bleach 3.1.1 or later, and its allowed tags list does not combine noscript with any of the listed raw tags. The page also sends a strict Content-Security-Policy as defense in depth.

citations.quote: a mutation XSS affects users calling bleach.clean with noscript and a raw tag in the allowed/whitelisted tags option.
will also help mitigate the risk.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the default of the parser's scripting setting in the custom parser's parse method from off to on, so noscript content is parsed as raw text the way a scripting-enabled browser does. The added tests allow noscript together with each raw-text tag (title, textarea, script, style, noembed, noframes, iframe, xmp) and check that a trailing image with an event handler stays escaped. This matches the card's cause, preconditions and prevention.

patterns.title: Open redirect via aiohttp normalize_path_middleware before 3.7.4
patterns.cause: The normalize_path_middleware middleware in aiohttp did not consistently collapse leading slashes in candidate redirect paths. A target beginning with multiple slashes followed by a hostname could be interpreted by a browser as a protocol-relative URL to another website, causing an open redirect (CWE-601).
preconditions: The application runs aiohttp older than version 3.7.4.
The application uses normalize_path_middleware.
A candidate path resolves to a route, causing the middleware to issue a redirect.
A user follows a crafted link that causes the middleware to produce a redirect target with multiple leading slashes and an external hostname.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade aiohttp to version 3.7.4 or later. The fix collapses each candidate path's leading run of multiple slashes to one before checking route resolution and issuing a redirect. Regression tests verify a local redirect target with slash appending, slash removal, and neither option enabled. If upgrading is not possible, avoid normalize_path_middleware. As general hardening, other redirect code should validate user-supplied targets and reject or normalize multiple leading slashes to prevent network-path redirects.
patterns.limitations: The change protects candidate paths processed by this middleware; it does not establish the safety of other redirect code. The supplied diff does not show the complete candidate-generation logic or establish every exploitable input and configuration. Its tests demonstrate fixed behavior, not that all tested configurations were previously exploitable. Compatibility effects for applications intentionally using double-slash routes are not established.

fixtures.scenario: A web service runs aiohttp 3.7.3 with normalize_path_middleware enabled. An attacker sends a victim a crafted link to the service, and the victim's browser is redirected to a different website.

The same service runs aiohttp 3.7.4 or later, or runs an older version with normalize_path_middleware removed. The crafted link no longer sends the browser to a different website through this middleware.

citations.quote: A maliciously crafted link to an aiohttp-based web-server could redirect the browser to a different website.
This security problem has been fixed in v3.7.4.
If upgrading is not an option for you, a workaround can be to avoid using

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a step inside the candidate-path loop of the normalize_path_middleware that collapses any leading run of slashes into a single slash before the path is checked against the routes and used for the redirect. As a result, a request such as one starting with two slashes and a host name now redirects to a local absolute path instead of a protocol-relative location. The new test covers the append, remove and merge-only modes and checks that the Location header is a local path.

patterns.title: Mutation XSS in bleach.clean() when SVG or MathML, paragraph or break, and raw-text tags are allowed with comments kept
patterns.cause: In Bleach before 3.3.0, bleach.clean returned retained HTML comment content without escaping it. With the specified allowed-tag combination, browser reparsing and namespace breakout can make markup hidden in that content active, causing mutation XSS. The diff explains that namespace-breaking tags can eject following elements from svg or math; style itself does not cause that breakout. Regression cases combine bare p or br end tags, style, and comment content containing an image with an event handler.
preconditions: The allowed tags include svg or math.
The allowed tags include p or br; the regression cases use bare end tags for these elements.
The allowed tags include at least one of style, title, noscript, script, textarea, noframes, iframe, or xmp.
The strip_comments option is explicitly turned off. It is on by default, and none of the listed tags are in the default allowed tags.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Bleach 3.3.0 or later. The fix escapes ampersands, angle brackets, and both kinds of quotes in retained comment content to address this mutation XSS. As a workaround, keep comment stripping on, exclude both svg and math, exclude both p and br, or exclude all eight elements in the third precondition. A strong Content-Security-Policy whose script-src excludes unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval can also mitigate the risk.
patterns.limitations: The change escapes comment content only when comments are kept; stripping comments remains the default. Output that relied on raw markup inside retained comments will differ. The added tests check sanitized output for style with both namespaces and both end tags; they do not demonstrate browser execution or every element listed in the advisory. The fix does not establish safety against every possible reparsing issue. Content-Security-Policy is a mitigation, not a fix.

fixtures.scenario: An app runs bleach.clean() on user content with svg, p, and style allowed and comment stripping turned off, on a Bleach release older than 3.3.0. Crafted markup can trigger a mutation XSS.
The same app upgrades to Bleach 3.3.0 or later, or stops allowing svg and math, or leaves comment stripping at its default of on, so the risky combination no longer exists.

citations.quote: Users are encouraged to upgrade to bleach v3.3.0 or greater.
bleach v3.3.0 introduces a breaking change to escape HTML comments by default.
none of the above tags are in the default allowed tags and strip_comments defaults to True.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the sanitizer's handling of comment tokens: when comments are kept, the comment text is now escaped for ampersands, angle brackets and quotes before it is returned. The new tests show that a p or br end tag inside svg or math, followed by a style element holding a comment, no longer lets the comment text close the element and become live markup. This matches the card's cause, preconditions and prevention.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through SVG profile picture upload in CKAN
patterns.cause: CKAN 2.9.0 to 2.9.3 allowed low privileged users to upload profile pictures containing malicious SVG scripts, causing stored XSS when a victim opened the picture. The diffs add content-based upload type validation that was missing from the shown uploader path. They also add checks to user and group or organization creation paths, but do not establish those additional image fields as exploitation vectors.
preconditions: The application runs CKAN 2.9.0 to 2.9.3.
A low privileged application user uploads a profile picture containing malicious SVG scripts.
A victim opens the malicious profile picture in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Use the content-based validation added by verify_type before the uploader writes the file. Configure the per-object user and group upload allowlists to reject unwanted detected MIME types, including SVG; an image category alone does not exclude SVG detected as an image. When both category and exact MIME type allowlists are configured, the upload must satisfy both. Validate file bytes rather than relying on extensions or client-supplied types. As general hardening, consider a restrictive content security policy or download-only serving for uploads.
patterns.limitations: The added allowlist enforcement is opt-in: neither list restricts uploads when both are empty. Detection examines only the first 1024 bytes; an exact MIME allowlist is not a guarantee of script-free content. The shown changes do not sanitize SVG or alter file serving, and leave ResourceUpload unchanged. They do not establish complete coverage of all upload paths, exploitation through group or organization images, the first fixed release, or the precise serving and origin conditions for execution. Missing configuration is a limitation of the added protection, not an advisory-established prerequisite for the original vulnerability.

fixtures.scenario: A low privileged user uploads an SVG file containing a script as their profile picture. Another user opens that picture, and the script executes in the second user's browser.

A low privileged user tries to upload an SVG file containing a script as their profile picture. The application either refuses the file or stops its script from running, so nothing executes in the browser of a user who opens the picture.

citations.quote: versions 2.9.0 to 2.9.3 are affected by a stored XSS vulnerability via SVG file upload
This allows low privileged application users to store malicious scripts in their profile picture.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a verify_type step to the uploader. It reads the first 1024 bytes of the upload, detects the real mimetype with libmagic, and raises a validation error if it is not in the configured per-object-type (user or group) mimetype or broad type allowlists. It is opt-in, so with no configuration all uploads are still accepted, and it is called before the file is saved. The card's cause, prevention and limitations match this behavior.

patterns.title: Open redirect through a URL shortener that accepts unchecked external URLs
patterns.cause: The URL shortener functionality did not check user input for open redirects. This let a user create a short URL that pointed to an external, potentially malicious URL, even though the short link appeared to belong to the trusted application.
preconditions: The application offers a URL shortener feature that creates short links from user-supplied input
The user-supplied target is not checked to confirm it is an internal destination, so an external URL is accepted
A victim can be convinced to click the resulting short link, for example one presented as a dashboard link
patterns.prevention: Check every user-supplied target before the shortener stores it or redirects to it. Accept only destinations that belong to the application itself, and reject any URL that points to an external host. Apply the same check at the point where the short link is created, so a malicious external URL is never stored in the first place.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say how the upstream fix validates URLs, which URL forms were abused, or whether the check runs at creation time, at redirect time, or both. They give no detail on handling of relative paths, scheme-relative URLs, or encoded input. Affected versions are stated as up to and including 1.0.1 in some sources and as prior to 1.1.0 in others. The sources do not describe any impact beyond tricking a user into clicking a link.

fixtures.scenario: A malicious user submits an external URL to the shortener. The application creates a short link for it without checking the destination. The link is presented as a dashboard link, and a victim who clicks it is taken to the external site.

A user submits an external URL to the shortener. The application checks the input, finds that it does not point to an internal destination, and refuses to create the short link. A user who submits a destination inside the application gets a working short link.

citations.quote: By not checking user input for open redirects the URL shortener functionality would allow for a malicious user to create a short URL
Apache Superset up to and including 1.0.1 allowed for the creation of an external URL that could be malicious.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a validation helper that accepts only targets beginning with the application's own dashboard or explore path prefixes. It is applied when a short link is created, where anything else gets a 400 response, and again when a stored short link is followed, where an invalid target sends the user to the home page. This matches the card's cause and its advice to check at both creation and redirect time and to allow only internal destinations.

patterns.title: Unsafe handling of the origin parameter on Airflow endpoints such as trigger leads to reflected XSS
patterns.cause: The origin parameter passed to some Apache Airflow endpoints, such as the trigger endpoint, was vulnerable to cross-site scripting. This was a repeat of CVE-2020-13944 and CVE-2020-17515, because the earlier fix did not fully close the issue.
preconditions: Apache Airflow 1.x release older than 1.10.15, or Airflow 2.0.0 or 2.0.1.
An endpoint such as the trigger endpoint accepts an origin parameter supplied in the request.
A user's browser can be induced to send a request carrying an attacker-chosen origin value.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Airflow 1.10.15 or 2.0.2, which the advisories name as the fixed releases. Also move to the latest patch release of the installed Python minor version, as the advisories recommend. In your own code, treat the origin request parameter as untrusted data on every endpoint that accepts it, not only the endpoints named in earlier advisories. After fixing a reported XSS, re-check the whole class of inputs, since a partial fix left this issue open.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say how the origin value was used (for example, where it was placed in a page or a redirect). They do not list every affected endpoint beyond the trigger example, and they do not describe the code change in the fix. Concrete validation or encoding guidance therefore cannot be drawn from them. The Python update advice is tied to a separate CVE, CVE-2021-23336, and its relation to this XSS is not explained.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 2.0.1 deployment exposes the trigger endpoint. A user opens a link whose origin parameter holds attacker-chosen content, and the deployment does not treat that value as untrusted.
The deployment runs Airflow 2.0.2 or 1.10.15 or later. The origin parameter is handled as untrusted input on the trigger endpoint and on other endpoints that accept it.

citations.quote: parameter passed to some of the endpoints like '/trigger' was vulnerable to XSS exploit.
the implemented fix did not fix the issue completely.
Update to Airflow 1.10.15 or 2.0.2.

patterns.title: lxml Cleaner leaves formaction attribute when forms and safe_attrs_only are disabled
patterns.cause: The lxml HTML Cleaner uses a known list of link attributes for URL checking, but HTML5 formaction was missing. With safe_attrs_only and forms both disabled, JavaScript URLs in formaction could bypass sanitization. The attribute overrides the form action, allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary JavaScript when users interact with incorrectly sanitized HTML. The regression test covers input and button elements.
preconditions: The application sanitizes attacker-supplied HTML with the lxml HTML Cleaner
Both forms and safe_attrs_only are disabled
The installed lxml version is earlier than 4.6.3
Users interact with the incorrectly sanitized HTML output
patterns.prevention: Upgrade lxml to version 4.6.3 or later. The fix adds formaction to the known link attributes; the regression test verifies that JavaScript URLs in formaction are replaced with empty values. Avoid disabling both forms and safe_attrs_only for untrusted HTML. As general hardening, prefer an explicit attribute allowlist rather than relying solely on a list of known URL-bearing attributes.
patterns.limitations: The supplied test verifies empty formaction values on input and button elements under the stated configuration, not every dangerous URL scheme or configuration. The sources do not establish the default Cleaner settings, the exact browser interaction required for exploitation, or whether other unlisted URL-bearing attributes have the same weakness. They do not establish that enabling either option alone is sufficient.

fixtures.scenario: A web app cleans user-submitted HTML with an lxml Cleaner older than 4.6.3 that has safe_attrs_only and forms both disabled. The submitted markup keeps a formaction attribute, and a user who interacts with the page may run attacker JS.

A web app cleans user-submitted HTML with lxml 4.6.3 or later. Even if safe_attrs_only and forms are disabled, the Cleaner handles the formaction attribute, so the output no longer lets it bypass the sanitizer.

citations.quote: When disabling the safe_attrs_only and forms arguments, the Cleaner class does not remove the formaction attribute allowing for JS to bypass the sanitizer.
A remote attacker could exploit this flaw to run arbitrary JS code on users who interact with incorrectly sanitized HTML.
This issue is patched in lxml 4.6.3.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds the HTML5 formaction attribute to the list of link attributes in the lxml HTML defs module, so the Cleaner now checks its value for dangerous URL schemes. The added test shows that with forms and safe_attrs_only disabled, a javascript: value on input and button elements is emptied rather than passed through, and the version is bumped to 4.6.3.

patterns.title: Missing server-side link protocol validation in Wagtail rich text fields allows javascript: URLs
patterns.cause: When saving a rich text field in the admin interface, Wagtail did not apply server-side checks to ensure that link URLs use a valid protocol. The server accepted whatever URL the submitted data contained, so a crafted POST request could store links with javascript: URLs containing arbitrary code (CWE-79).
preconditions: The site runs an affected Wagtail version, earlier than 2.11.7 on the 2.11 LTS branch or 2.12.4 on the 2.12 branch.
The attacker is a user with access to the Wagtail admin interface.
The attacker submits a hand-crafted POST request that saves rich text content with a link whose URL uses an unsafe protocol such as javascript:.
patterns.prevention: Do not rely on the editor user interface to restrict link URLs. When rich text is saved, validate every link URL on the server and accept only valid protocols, so content with javascript: URLs is never stored or published. The advisory workaround does this by passing external link URLs through Wagtail's whitelist URL check when converting editor content to the database format. The permanent remedy is to upgrade to Wagtail 2.11.7 or 2.12.4 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not list which protocols count as valid, do not describe how already-stored content is handled, and do not describe the internals of the official fix. Exposure is limited to users with Wagtail admin access; the advisory says ordinary site visitors cannot exploit it. Sites that cannot upgrade should follow the workaround in the GitHub advisory, but the sources do not say whether it covers every rich text entry path.

fixtures.scenario: An editor with admin access sends a crafted POST request that saves a rich text field containing a link whose URL starts with javascript: and carries script code. The server stores and publishes it without checking the protocol, so the script can run when someone follows the link.

The same crafted POST request is sent, but the server checks each link URL for a valid protocol when saving the rich text. The javascript: link is not accepted as valid link content, and only links with valid protocols are stored.

citations.quote: Wagtail does not apply server-side checks to ensure that link URLs use a valid protocol
The vulnerability is not exploitable by an ordinary site visitor without access to the Wagtail admin.
Patched versions have been released as Wagtail 2.11.7 (for the LTS 2.11 branch) and Wagtail 2.12.4 (for the current 2.12 branch).

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the link conversion in the contentstate converter so that external link URLs go through the whitelist URL check when editor content is converted to the database format. A javascript: URL is dropped, leaving an anchor with no href, while http and local paths are kept. This matches the card's cause (no server-side protocol validation on saved rich text) and its prevention (validate link URLs on the server rather than trusting the editor UI).

patterns.title: Indirect access to untrusted modules through allowed modules in through-the-web TAL expressions
patterns.cause: Zope Page Template path traversal did not reject underscore-prefixed path elements, allowing indirect access to untrusted modules through modules permitted in TAL expressions. The diff tests traversal from random through its private itertools reference to the repeat callable, illustrating the module restriction bypass. It also adds rejection tests for traversal to a context object's special class attribute.
preconditions: An affected Zope version before 4.6 in the 4.x line or before 5.2 in the 5.x line.
The site allows untrusted users to add or edit Zope Page Templates through the web.
The user can author TAL path expressions; template creation and editing require the Manager role by default, but permissions can be granted otherwise.
For the illustrated module bypass, an allowed module exposes an underscore-prefixed reference to another module.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Zope 4.6 or 5.2 or later. The fix adds name checks to the traversal routines in both the classic and Chameleon-based expression engines. Each checked path element beginning with an underscore raises NotFound, except the single underscore name, which remains accepted with a deprecation warning announcing removal in Zope 6. This blocks the illustrated private-module traversal route. As general hardening, apply equivalent checks consistently across template traversal engines. As a workaround, use Zope's user/role permissions to restrict through-the-web Page Template creation and editing to trusted users, and do not assign the Manager role to untrusted users.
patterns.limitations: The shown checks reject underscore-prefixed attribute and dictionary-key traversal, except the single underscore; affected path lookups can therefore raise NotFound. The diff announces removal of the single underscore exception in Zope 6 but does not verify that removal occurred. It changes path traversal routines without establishing coverage of every TAL access route or exposure beyond through-the-web Page Templates. The Chameleon HTML underscore-traversal test is skipped because its required random-module context is unavailable. The advisory names remote code execution but gives no exploit details. The workaround limits access without removing the flaw.

fixtures.scenario: A Zope 4.5 site grants template add/edit permission through the web to a group of semi-trusted users. One of them writes a TAL expression that starts from a module permitted for direct use and reaches an untrusted module that is blocked for direct import, gaining file system access.

The site runs Zope 5.2 or 4.6 or later, and template add/edit permission through the web is limited to trusted administrators. Expressions cannot reach blocked modules through allowed ones, and untrusted users do not hold the Manager role.

citations.quote: some of the untrusted modules are available indirectly through Python modules that are available for direct use.
Only sites that allow untrusted users to add/edit Zope Page Templates through the web are at risk.
The problem has been fixed in Zope 5.2 and 4.6.
Untrusted users should not be assigned the Zope Manager role and adding/editing Zope Page Templates through the web should be restricted to trusted users only.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check to the path traversal step in both the classic expression engine (boboAwareZopeTraverse) and the Chameleon-based engine. Any path element starting with an underscore now raises NotFound, so names like the class attribute or private module references such as an itertools attribute of random cannot be reached. The bare single underscore name still works but emits a deprecation warning, and the new tests cover these cases. This matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Untrusted modules reachable through TAL expression traversal in through-the-web Zope Page Templates
patterns.cause: In through-the-web Page Templates, path expressions on objects without Zope traversal support, including Python modules, used traversePathElement without applying Zope security policy. Restrictions on directly available modules did not prevent indirect access to disallowed module attributes. The regression tests cover access directly through a module, through an intermediary variable, and through a dictionary holding the module. The advisory describes remote code execution through TAL expression traversal.
preconditions: The site runs a Zope release affected by the traversal flaw; the supplied sources do not establish a complete affected version range.
Untrusted users can add or edit Zope Page Templates through the web.
Template editing requires the Manager role by default, but sites can grant access through other permission configurations.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a fixed Zope release. Both traversal implementations add current security manager validation after resolving non-traversable objects in restricted traversal, except for the single underscore compatibility case. Other underscore-prefixed names are rejected. Unauthorized validation exceptions become NotFound to reduce information disclosure. Traversable objects use restrictedTraverse in restricted mode. Use permitted module attributes; the bundled template now accesses the explicitly allowed getSecurityManager directly through AccessControl. Restrict template editing to trusted users using standard roles and permissions, and do not grant untrusted users Manager. As general hardening, enforce security policy in custom restricted traversal.
patterns.limitations: The class-based implementation skips these checks for non-traversable objects when configured for unrestricted traversal; the diff does not establish who can select that mode. A single underscore also bypasses explicit validation with a deprecation warning. Denied module accesses in the tests raise NotFound, but some underscore cases permit LocationError, so failure behavior is not uniform. The sources do not prove elimination of all information leaks or demonstrate an execution payload. They name 4.6.1 as fixed but disagree on 5.x: 5.21 versus 5.2.1; verify release information. The advisory limits risk to sites allowing untrusted template editors.

fixtures.scenario: A Zope site on an unpatched version lets a less-trusted user edit Page Templates through the web. That user writes a TAL expression that starts from an allowed module and traverses onward to a module that is not meant to be usable, such as one giving file system access.
The site runs a patched Zope release, and only trusted administrators hold the permission to add or edit Page Templates through the web. Untrusted users cannot author TAL expressions.

citations.quote: But some of the untrusted modules are available indirectly through Python modules that are available for direct use.
Only sites that allow untrusted users to add/edit Zope Page Templates through the web are at risk.
Most Python modules are not available for using in TAL expressions that you can add through-the-web, for example in Zope Page Templates.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds an explicit security manager validation after each traversal step on objects that are not Zope traversable, because the generic traversal helper applies no security policy. Failed checks are turned into not found errors, underscore-prefixed names remain blocked apart from the single underscore name kept for compatibility, and traversal modes other than restricted are left unvalidated. This matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Unsanitized form action attribute in untrusted notebook HTML enables code execution on load
patterns.cause: JupyterLab did not sanitize the action attribute of html form elements in notebook content. This made it possible to trigger form validation outside of the form itself, so an untrusted notebook could execute code when it was opened. The advisories classify the issue as XSS leading to remote code execution.
preconditions: The user runs an affected JupyterLab version, meaning one older than the patched releases 3.1.4, 3.0.17, 2.3.2, 2.2.10 or 1.2.21.
The user opens an untrusted notebook, since the attack requires user action.
The notebook contains html with a form element whose action attribute is not sanitized.
patterns.prevention: Treat all notebook-supplied html as untrusted. When rendering it, sanitize the action attribute of form elements so that attacker-chosen values are removed or restricted rather than passed through. Do not allow form behavior in untrusted content to be triggered from outside the form. Also restrict form submissions with a Content Security Policy, as the advisory's OWASP reference suggests. Upgrade to a patched release for your version line.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact mechanism by which the form validation leads to code execution, nor which attribute values are dangerous. They do not say whether the classic notebook package is affected or which notebook version fixes it, and the patched versions listed are JupyterLab releases. They do not specify the sanitization rules or the Content Security Policy directives to use. The Content Security Policy point rests only on the advisory's OWASP reference title. Exploitation still requires the user to open the notebook.

fixtures.scenario: A user on an affected JupyterLab version opens a notebook from an unknown source. Its html output contains a form whose action attribute is passed through unsanitized, so form validation is triggered outside the form and code runs on load.

A user opens the same notebook in a patched JupyterLab release, or in a deployment that sanitizes the form action attribute of untrusted html and restricts form submissions. The form action is neutralized and no code runs on load.

citations.quote: Untrusted notebook can execute code on load. This is a remote code execution, but requires user action to open a notebook.
Using this it is possible to trigger the form validation outside of the form itself.
Patched in the following versions: 3.1.4, 3.0.17, 2.3.2, 2.2.10, 1.2.21.
OWASP Page on Restricting Form Submissions

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the action attribute from the list of attributes the sanitizer permits on form elements, so action is now stripped from untrusted notebook HTML. This matches the card's cause (the action attribute passed through unsanitized) and its main prevention (remove or restrict it). The Content Security Policy advice goes beyond the diff, but the card's limitations section flags it as resting only on the advisory's reference.

patterns.title: Sanitizer bypass in untrusted notebook HTML output leads to XSS and code execution on load
patterns.cause: Jupyter Notebook relied on a deprecated version of Google Caja to sanitize user input. A public Caja bypass let crafted HTML in a notebook output evade sanitization and run script when the notebook was opened. The script could then use Jupyter APIs to execute code.
preconditions: The victim runs a Notebook version older than the patched releases 5.7.11 or 6.4.1
The victim opens a malicious ipynb document, which is the required user action
Untrusted notebook content is sanitized with the deprecated Caja library
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Notebook to 5.7.11 or 6.4.1 or later. Do not treat a deprecated, bypassable sanitizer as the only barrier for HTML in untrusted notebooks. Treat all content in a notebook from an unknown source as attacker-controlled, and follow the injection prevention rules in the OWASP cheat sheet that the advisory references.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch works, which Caja bypass was used beyond the public example, or which versions before the fixes are affected. They do not cover other notebook front ends or other XSS paths. The advisory states that the attack needs user action to open the notebook.

fixtures.scenario: A user on an unpatched Notebook opens an ipynb file from an unknown sender. A code cell holds a display output with crafted HTML that bypasses the Caja sanitizer, so script runs on load and can call Jupyter APIs.
The user runs Notebook 5.7.11 or 6.4.1 or later and opens the same file. The crafted HTML output no longer runs script on load.

citations.quote: Jupyter Notebook uses a deprecated version of Google Caja to sanitize user inputs.
A public Caja bypass can be used to trigger an XSS when a victim opens a malicious ipynb document in Jupyter Notebook.
Untrusted notebook can execute code on load.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the deprecated Google Caja sanitizer from the build, package data and the security module. The sanitize function now delegates to the maintained JupyterLab sanitizer, which is bundled with webpack, and CSS styles are stripped unless CSS is allowed. This matches the card's cause, a bypassable deprecated sanitizer applied to untrusted notebook HTML, and its advice to upgrade rather than rely on that sanitizer.

patterns.title: Open redirect through crafted URLs in Flask-AppBuilder OAuth (CVE-2021-32805)
patterns.cause: The oauth_authorized callback in Flask-AppBuilder took the first next destination from OAuth state and redirected to it without validating the destination. An attacker could share a crafted URL on the trusted application's domain that redirected a user to a malicious site. This is an open redirect (CWE-601) caused by missing redirect-target validation.
preconditions: The application uses Flask-AppBuilder with OAuth authentication enabled.
The application runs an affected version; the advisory identifies 3.2.2 or above as the upgrade remedy.
A user follows an attacker-supplied crafted application URL, and the OAuth callback reaches the redirect with an external next destination in accepted state.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Flask-AppBuilder to 3.2.2 or above. The fix defaults to the application index and uses the first next destination from state only when its parsed network location exactly matches the current request host. Otherwise, it retains the index destination. As an advisory stop-gap, filter incoming HTTP traffic whose next parameter names a different domain. As general hardening, validate post-login redirect destinations against the application's own host or an explicit allow list.
patterns.limitations: The comparison uses the parsed network location, including any port or user information, rather than only the hostname; it does not check the scheme. Relative paths fall back to the index. The sources do not establish the earliest affected version, the complete crafted-login sequence, or whether non-OAuth flows are affected. State signature validation is present; the diff does not establish that attackers can forge state. Unknown-provider rejection is separate callback hardening in the same diff, not evidence of release scope. The traffic filter's coverage of other URL shapes is unspecified.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs a Flask-AppBuilder version older than 3.2.2 with OAuth login enabled. An attacker sends a victim a link on the application's own trusted domain whose next parameter names an external attacker-controlled site. The victim follows it and lands on the malicious site.

The application runs Flask-AppBuilder 3.2.2 or above. Alternatively, a gateway in front of an older version drops requests whose next parameter names a domain different from the application's own, so a crafted link no longer sends the user off-site.

citations.quote: an attacker can share a carefully crafted URL with a trusted domain for an application built with Flask-AppBuilder
Install Flask-AppBuilder 3.2.2 or above

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the OAuth callback so the next destination taken from the signed state is parsed and followed only when its host equals the current request host. Otherwise it logs a warning and redirects to the application index page. The same change also rejects unknown providers in the callback, which is separate hardening.

patterns.title: Template injection in Ansible via facts placed in multi-line YAML strings
patterns.cause: Ansible's do_template lost a result's unsafe marking when appending trailing newlines to match the source. This could leave previously unsafe data as an ordinary string, allowing embedded template syntax to be evaluated on later use. The advisory describes controller template injection through facts used in multi-line YAML strings, including facts that do not routinely contain special template characters, with command injection and sensitive information disclosure affecting confidentiality and integrity. The regression test demonstrates the unsafe-value case with a folded YAML scalar.
preconditions: Rendering uses an unsafe-marked value and marks the rendering context unsafe.
Trailing-newline preservation appends newlines because the source has more trailing newlines than the rendered result; the test exercises this with a folded YAML scalar.
The result is subsequently used where embedded template syntax can be evaluated.
Exploitation would require attacker-influenced template syntax to reach the affected value; the sources do not specify how attackers obtain that influence.
patterns.prevention: Use an Ansible release containing the supplied fix. In do_template, retain the rendering context's unsafe status and use wrap_var to restore unsafe wrapping after trailing newlines are appended when that context was unsafe. Keep regression coverage that renders an unsafe value through both a folded multi-line scalar and a single-line template, then checks that the embedded syntax remains literal, allowing for the added trailing newline.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify affected or fixed release versions, attacker access requirements, or a complete command-injection exploit. Multi-line YAML alone does not establish that newline padding occurs; the source must have more trailing newlines than the rendered result. The diff addresses this specific unsafe-status loss and does not establish the behavior of other string conversions or playbooks that deliberately re-template untrusted data.

fixtures.scenario: A playbook writes a template in a multi-line YAML string and inserts a fact value. A managed host reports a fact containing template syntax, and the controller evaluates it as template code, running attacker-chosen commands.
A playbook uses fact values only as plain data. Template syntax inside a fact is not evaluated, and the controller runs an Ansible version containing the upstream fix.

citations.quote: A flaw was found in Ansible, where a user's controller is vulnerable to template injection.
This issue can occur through facts used in the template if the user is trying to put templates in multi-line YAML strings
This flaw allows attackers to perform command injection, which discloses sensitive information.

patch_review.observation: The fix records whether the rendering context was unsafe in a local flag, and after the trailing-newline padding step appends newlines to the result, it wraps the result as unsafe again. Before, the padding produced a plain string that lost the unsafe marking. A regression playbook renders an unsafe value inside a folded multi-line string and checks that no templating occurred.

patterns.title: Regular expression denial of service in the NLTK comparative sentences corpus reader
