patterns.cause: The KEYWORD pattern in nltk/corpus/reader/comparative_sents.py extracts a trailing parenthesized group with no opening parenthesis inside it. Its negative lookahead contains a greedy any-character repeat, causing repeated scans of the remaining text at candidate opening parentheses. A long run of opening parentheses can therefore cause quadratic matching work. The advisory identifies attacker-supplied input to the reader's _read_comparison_block function as a way to cause excessive CPU consumption.
preconditions: The application uses the NLTK comparative sentences reader's _read_comparison_block function.
An attacker can supply input that reaches the vulnerable keyword pattern, such as text containing many opening parentheses.
The installed code retains the vulnerable KEYWORD pattern rather than the upstream replacement.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade nltk to a release containing the upstream fix. The fix replaces the lookahead and greedy capture with a negated character class that excludes opening parentheses, followed by a closing parenthesis and an end anchor. This avoids repeated lookahead scans while preserving the intended extraction for single-line input. Retain the upstream regression test comparing matching times on short and long runs of opening parentheses. As general hardening, prefer delimiter-excluding character classes where appropriate, cap untrusted line length, and bound parsing time.
patterns.limitations: The supplied sources give no affected or fixed version numbers and do not show the reader's full call path or establish that it applies KEYWORD to every line. The regression test uses 4,000 and 40,000 repeated opening parentheses, compares median timings, reports roughly 80-fold growth before the fix, and accepts growth below 30-fold afterward. This supports reduced slowdown, not a universal linear-time guarantee. The change adds no input-size bound. Size and time limits are general hardening. Other reader patterns are outside this change's scope.

fixtures.scenario: A web service accepts user-uploaded text files and passes their contents to the NLTK comparative sentences reader. An attacker uploads a crafted file, and the call to _read_comparison_block() uses excessive CPU, so other requests are delayed or time out.

The service runs a patched nltk release and loads the comparative sentences corpus only from trusted, bundled files. Any user-supplied text is size-limited and parsed in a worker with a timeout, so a slow parse is stopped without affecting other requests.

citations.quote: The nltk package is vulnerable to ReDoS (regular expression denial of service).
may cause an application to consume an excessive amount of CPU.
nltk is vulnerable to Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the keyword pattern in the comparative sentences reader. The old pattern used a negative lookahead with a greedy any-character repeat after each opening parenthesis. The new pattern uses a negated character class that excludes the opening parenthesis, which removes the repeated scan-and-backtrack work. A doctest also compares matching time on short and long adversarial inputs, as the card suggests.

patterns.title: Inefficient regular expressions in nltk RegexpTaggers allow ReDoS
patterns.cause: The cardinal number rules in RegexpTaggers used by get_pos_tagger and malt_regex_tagger contained an unescaped dot in the optional decimal part. This wildcard can consume a digit, allowing the two digit runs to match overlapping portions of the input. The pattern structure permits excessive backtracking on long digit sequences followed by a character that forces failure, consistent with the reported ReDoS. The fix escapes the dot so it requires a literal decimal point.
preconditions: The application uses an nltk implementation containing the old cardinal number rule.
Input reaches that rule through get_pos_tagger, malt_regex_tagger, the modified demo taggers, or a tagger reusing the old pattern.
For attacker-triggered denial of service, an attacker must be able to influence tokens evaluated by the rule; the sources do not establish a specific exposure path.
patterns.prevention: Use an nltk release containing the upstream fix. Update reused copies of the affected cardinal number rule to require a literal decimal point; the diff also updates demo taggers and documentation examples. As general hardening, review custom regular expressions for overlapping repetitions and unintended wildcards, and treat externally supplied tagger input as untrusted.
patterns.limitations: The sources provide no affected or fixed version numbers, attack benchmarks, input-length thresholds, or deployment prerequisites. The failing-input explanation follows from the pattern structure rather than a supplied exploit or timing test; exponential or catastrophic behavior is not established. The security change addresses the cardinal number rule and does not establish the safety of other custom patterns. Tokens previously accepted through a non-dot separator no longer match this rule, which can change tagging results; updated doctest results also show behavioral changes.

fixtures.scenario: A web service runs an affected nltk release and calls get_pos_tagger on text submitted by anonymous users. A crafted submission makes the regex-based tagger consume excessive CPU time, and the service becomes unresponsive to other requests.

The same service runs an nltk release that includes the upstream fix for CVE-2021-3842. Any custom RegexpTagger rules it adds have been reviewed for inefficient regular expression complexity, so tagging untrusted text does not cause a CPU exhaustion.

citations.quote: NLTK is vulnerable to REDoS in some RegexpTaggers used in the functions
nltk is vulnerable to Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity

patch_review.observation: The fix escapes the dot in the optional decimal part of the cardinal number pattern, so it matches only a literal decimal point. It is applied in malt_regex_tagger, in get_pos_tagger in the glue module, and in the demo and docstring examples. The other edits only update doctest expectations that shifted slightly because tokens wrongly accepted as numbers are no longer tagged that way.

patterns.title: Directory traversal in Babel Locale loading leads to code execution
patterns.cause: In Babel before 2.9.1, Babel.Locale could be made to load arbitrary locale .dat files through directory traversal. These files contain serialized Python objects, so loading an attacker-chosen file can lead to code execution.
preconditions: The application uses a Babel version before 2.9.1.
An attacker can influence which locale Babel.Locale loads.
A .dat file containing serialized Python objects, chosen by the attacker, is reachable by the traversal.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Babel to 2.9.1 or later. In an implementation of locale loading, treat the locale identifier as untrusted input. Make sure it can only select files inside the intended locale data directory, and never let it resolve to a path outside that directory. Reject identifiers that contain path separators or parent directory references before any file is opened. Do not deserialize data files that come from outside the trusted locale data set.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state the vulnerable version range and the general impact. They do not describe the exact vulnerable code path, how locale names reach the file loader, or how the upstream fix works. The validation guidance above is a general direction and not a description of the upstream change. The sources also do not say whether other Babel entry points are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A web application runs Babel before 2.9.1 and passes a user-supplied locale string to Babel.Locale. The string contains traversal sequences that point at a locale .dat file outside the locale data directory. Babel loads the file, and the serialized Python objects in it can run code.

The application runs Babel 2.9.1 or later and only passes locale identifiers that it has checked against the locales it expects. A request with traversal sequences in the locale value is rejected and no file outside the locale data directory is loaded.

citations.quote: Babel.Locale in Babel before 2.9.1 allows attackers to load arbitrary locale .dat files (containing serialized Python objects) via directory traversal, leading to code execution.
allows attackers to load arbitrary locale .dat files (containing serialized Python objects) via directory traversal

patch_review.observation: The fix reduces the locale identifier to its final path component in both the loading function and a new filename-resolution helper, so a name with parent directory references can no longer reach files outside the locale data directory. It also rejects Windows reserved device names on that platform, and tests cover traversal through exists, load and Locale construction.

patterns.title: lxml HTML Cleaner lets crafted script and SVG data URI script through
patterns.cause: The HTML Cleaner in lxml.html, used to sanitize untrusted markup, failed to remove certain crafted script content. It also let script content through when it was inside SVG files embedded using data URIs. Markup that the application treats as cleaned can therefore still carry executable script (cross-site scripting).
preconditions: The application uses the HTML Cleaner in lxml.html to sanitize untrusted HTML.
The installed lxml version is older than 4.6.5.
The cleaned output is used in a security relevant context, such as being rendered to other users in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade lxml to version 4.6.5 or later anywhere the HTML Cleaner handles untrusted input. Until the upgrade is deployed, do not treat Cleaner output from older versions as safe to render in a security relevant context. The sources list no workarounds, so the upgrade is the only remediation they support. After upgrading, confirm the deployed environment, including any pinned or vendored copies, actually resolves to the patched version.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe which crafted script patterns were missed or how the patch changes the Cleaner, so this card cannot say what input to filter or test for beyond SVG content in data URIs. They state there are no known workarounds, so no interim mitigation is documented. They say nothing about versions or code paths outside the HTML Cleaner, and they do not say whether upgrading alone is enough defense for every use of cleaned output.

fixtures.scenario: A web application accepts user-submitted HTML, passes it through the lxml.html Cleaner on lxml 4.4, and shows the result to other users. An attacker submits an SVG file embedded as a data URI, or other crafted script content, and the Cleaner leaves the script in the output.
The same application runs lxml 4.6.5 or later, verified in the deployed environment, so the Cleaner no longer lets the crafted script content or the SVG data URI script pass through.

citations.quote: The HTML Cleaner in lxml.html lets certain crafted script content pass through, as well as script content in SVG files embedded using data URIs.
Users that employ the HTML cleaner in a security relevant context should upgrade to lxml 4.6.5.
There are no known workarounds available.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the Cleaner's style check reject any stylesheet containing an import rule. This blocks obfuscated forms that become a real import after a keyword is stripped out. It also changes the data URL scheme check so image data URIs with SVG or XML media types are treated as unsafe and removed, while ordinary raster image data URIs stay allowed. The release bump to 4.6.5 matches the card's patched version.

patterns.title: Unrestricted file paths in Gradio static file serving expose host files
patterns.cause: In gradio versions before 2.5.0, file paths requested through the interface were not restricted. Static files were served in a way that let a remote user who received a shared Gradio link read arbitrary files on the host, limited only by operating system permissions.
preconditions: Running a gradio version prior to 2.5.0
The interface is publicly shared through a generated Gradio link while the link is active
The attacker knows the exact file name or relative file path on the host
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to gradio 2.5.0 or later. In similar file-serving code, restrict requested paths to an intended directory: resolve the requested path to its canonical absolute form, then confirm it lies inside the allowed base directory before opening it. Reject anything outside that directory. Add regression tests for traversal attempts so the check is not reverted.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact vulnerable code path, the endpoint involved, or the mechanics of the patch, so the canonicalization guidance is a general direction and not a description of the upstream fix. Access was read-only, and no evidence of exploitation is reported.

fixtures.scenario: A user shares a public link from an older gradio release. A remote visitor requests a path pointing outside the served folder, and the server returns that host file because paths are unrestricted.
A patched gradio release or a similar server resolves each requested path, checks it is inside the allowed base directory, and refuses requests that resolve elsewhere.

citations.quote: File paths are not restricted and users who receive a Gradio link can access any files on the host computer
An attacker would be able to view the contents of a file on the computer if they knew the exact relative filepath.
Paths are opened in read only mode. The problem has been patched in gradio 2.5.0.

patch_review.observation: The change is in the file-serving route. It drops the filename-sanitizing step and instead joins the requested path to the working directory with a safe join helper, for both the encrypted-example branch and the plain send-file branch. This confines requested paths to the base directory and rejects anything that escapes it, which matches the card's cause and its prevention of restricting paths to an allowed directory.

patterns.title: Untrusted origin query argument on the Trigger DAG with config screen leads to XSS in Apache Airflow
patterns.cause: The Trigger DAG with config template inserted the user-controlled origin query argument into a JavaScript string in the Cancel button's inline event handler. HTML escaping alone does not protect this JavaScript context, allowing a crafted value to escape the string and execute script.
preconditions: Apache Airflow 2.2.3 or earlier is in use.
A user can reach the Trigger DAG with config page.
A crafted origin query argument reaches the template and is rendered in the Cancel button's inline JavaScript handler.
patterns.prevention: Replace the Cancel button's inline JavaScript navigation with an ordinary link whose href contains the HTML-escaped origin value. Preserve the existing fallback behavior: the shown tests expect a JavaScript URL and an external HTTP URL to resolve to /home. Add a regression test checking that a markup-bearing origin appears escaped in the Cancel link. Upgrade to a release confirmed to include this fix. As general hardening, review similar request-derived values in inline JavaScript contexts.
patterns.limitations: The shown template change affects only the Cancel control. The sources do not establish required authentication, a specific attacker delivery method, or the first fixed release. The tests demonstrate fallback expectations for specific URL inputs but do not show the validation implementation or prove comprehensive scheme and host filtering. HTML escaping in an href alone does not prevent dangerous URL schemes, and the response assertion checks for expected escaped content rather than proving that no unsafe content exists elsewhere.

fixtures.scenario: A user follows a crafted link to the Trigger DAG with config screen in Airflow 2.2.3 or earlier. The origin query argument in the link carries attacker-chosen content, and the screen handles it in a way that lets script run in the user's browser session.
The same link is opened, but the screen treats the origin query argument as untrusted data and does not let its content be interpreted as markup or script, so no attacker-controlled script runs.

citations.quote: screen was susceptible to XSS attacks via the
This issue affects Apache Airflow versions 2.2.3 and below.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the Cancel button, which put the origin value inside an inline JavaScript click handler, with an ordinary link element whose href is filled by the autoescaping template. The updated tests submit a markup-bearing origin and expect the HTML-escaped form in the response, while script-scheme and external-host values still fall back to the home page. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Open redirect in archivy web application redirects
patterns.cause: Archivy before the fixed release was vulnerable to open redirect (CWE-601), meaning the application could send users to a destination that was not confined to the application itself. The sources do not say which endpoint or parameter was affected.
preconditions: The application issues HTTP redirects to a target that can be influenced by the request
The target is not restricted to a trusted set of destinations before the redirect is sent
A victim follows a link that points at the legitimate application but leads to an attacker-chosen destination
patterns.prevention: Do not redirect to a caller-supplied destination as-is. Prefer fixed, server-side redirect targets or a short allow-list of known internal destinations. If a caller-supplied target is unavoidable, validate it before use and accept only relative paths on the same site, rejecting any value that names another host or scheme. Upgrade archivy to a release that includes the fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that archivy is vulnerable to open redirect. They do not name the affected route, parameter or validation flaw, so the cause and the validation guidance above are the general CWE-601 pattern rather than confirmed details of this bug. The advisories disagree on the fixed version: one says prior to 1.7.1 and the others say prior to 1.7.0. Check the upstream release notes before choosing a version.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens a link to the archivy site that carries a destination value pointing to an external host. After the action completes, the application redirects the browser to that external host without checking it, so the user lands on an attacker-controlled page.

The same link carries a destination value. The application accepts it only if it is a relative path inside the site or is on a fixed allow-list. An external host is rejected and the user is sent to a default internal page instead.

citations.quote: archivy prior to version 1.7.1 is vulnerable to open redirect.
Open Redirect in GitHub repository archivy/archivy prior to 1.7.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix targets the login route, which redirected to the next query parameter after a successful login without any check. A new helper resolves the target against the host URL and allows it only if the scheme is http or https and the host matches the current site; otherwise the user is sent to the home page. The card's general guidance (do not redirect to a caller-supplied target as-is, validate it and reject other hosts or schemes) matches this, though the card does not name the login next parameter that the diff shows.

patterns.title: DOM-based XSS on the OctoPrint login endpoint before version 1.8.0
patterns.cause: OctoPrint before 1.8.0 has DOM-based XSS in the login endpoint. The diff shows that the login view previously accepted the redirect query parameter without checking its URL scheme or network location, allowing values such as javascript: URLs. The advisory reports JavaScript injection that may lead to account takeover in a phishing scenario; the browser-side execution path is not shown.
preconditions: The deployment runs OctoPrint prior to 1.8.0.
The login endpoint is reachable by the victim's browser.
An attacker influences the redirect query parameter in a login request involving the victim, consistent with the advisory's phishing scenario; the required interaction is not specified.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to OctoPrint 1.8.0 or later. Following the shown fix, validate the supplied redirect target in the server-side login view using urlparse. Reject values with a nonempty scheme or network location, log a warning, and replace them with the default index URL constructed from the application's script root and index route. This rejects scheme-bearing and scheme-relative URLs without introducing a destination allowlist.
patterns.limitations: The diff does not show how the redirect value reaches or is consumed by the front end, the exact DOM sink, or whether opening a link alone triggers execution. The validation checks only the parsed scheme and network location; it does not restrict the parsed path or establish that every accepted value is safe under browser URL parsing. Authentication state, cookies, and content security policy effects are unspecified. Rejected values may reflect misconfiguration or an attack attempt.

fixtures.scenario: An administrator running OctoPrint prior to 1.8.0 follows a link crafted by an attacker to the login page. Injected javascript runs in the page, and the attacker may use it to take over the account in a phishing scenario.

The same administrator opens a crafted link to the login page of an OctoPrint instance at 1.8.0 or later. The advisory lists no javascript injection for that version, so the attacker-supplied content is not expected to execute.

citations.quote: The login endpoint allows for javascript injection which may lead to account takeover in a phishing scenario.
Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - DOM in GitHub repository octoprint/octoprint prior to 1.8.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix parses the redirect query parameter in the login view with a URL parser. If the value has a scheme or a network location, it logs a warning and falls back to the default index location. This matches the card's cause (an unvalidated redirect target used as a navigation target) and its prevention (accept only relative same-origin paths, fall back to a default, log rejections).

patterns.title: OctoPrint Stream URL value can execute an XSS payload (CVE-2022-1432)
patterns.cause: In OctoPrint before 1.8.0, the webcam Stream URL allowed XSS. The shown stream-type detection lacked scheme validation, although it performed a limited format check. In the settings Test action's MJPEG branch, the URL was concatenated into an image element's HTML, exposing an injection point for crafted input. The sources do not establish a specific working payload.
preconditions: OctoPrint is a version prior to 1.8.0.
A malicious value is supplied through the webcam Stream URL.
For the preview injection point shown, a user invokes the settings Test action and the value reaches the MJPEG preview branch.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade OctoPrint to 1.8.0 or later. The fix adds validateWebcamUrl to check accepted URL prefixes and parse the URL: HTTP, HTTPS and WebRTC absolute URLs, protocol-relative URLs and host-relative paths. determineWebcamStreamType rejects invalid URLs and uses the parsed protocol and pathname to classify streams. The settings UI flags invalid values and disables Test for them; the Test handler catches classification errors and avoids the shown preview branches. As general hardening, avoid concatenating untrusted values into HTML; use safe DOM attribute APIs or context-appropriate escaping.
patterns.limitations: The changes shown are client-side. The MJPEG preview still concatenates the original URL into HTML without added escaping, so URL validation alone does not establish that every accepted value is safe for that context. The sources do not establish attacker access requirements, how malicious values reach the setting, whether exploitation requires persistence, or server-side enforcement. They also do not establish that Test is the only affected rendering path.

fixtures.scenario: An OctoPrint instance older than 1.8.0 has a Stream URL value containing an XSS payload, and the payload executes.
An OctoPrint instance at version 1.8.0 or later is configured with the same kind of Stream URL value, and the value does not result in script execution.

citations.quote: The Stream URL of octoprint application allowing a xss payload to execute.
Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Generic in GitHub repository octoprint/octoprint prior to 1.8.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a strict client-side check on the webcam Stream URL. Only http, https and webrtc URLs, or protocol-relative and host-relative paths, are accepted, and they are parsed with the URL parser. Stream type detection now throws on invalid input, the settings page marks an invalid URL as an error, and the Test button is disabled, so a script-capable or malformed value is never rendered into the preview markup. The preview code still builds markup by concatenation, as the card's limitations point out.

patterns.title: Unencoded context output from the Django debug template tag leads to XSS
patterns.cause: The debug template tag in Django 2.2 before 2.2.27, 3.2 before 3.2.12, and 4.0 before 4.0.2 does not properly encode the current context when it renders it. Context values that contain markup can therefore reach the page unescaped, which may lead to cross-site scripting (CWE-79).
preconditions: The application runs Django 2.2 before 2.2.27, 3.2 before 3.2.12, or 4.0 before 4.0.2.
A rendered template uses the debug template tag.
The current template context holds values that contain HTML-significant characters, for example values influenced by users.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 2.2.27, 3.2.12, 4.0.2 or later within the matching release line. The general principle is that any dump of the template context must be HTML-encoded before it is written into a page, so that values are shown as text and never interpreted as markup. Until the upgrade is applied, avoid rendering the debug tag in templates that are served to users.
patterns.limitations: The advisories are brief. They do not say which context values are attacker-controllable, whether a particular setting such as DEBUG is needed for the tag to produce output, or how the upstream change implements the encoding. The advice to avoid the tag until upgrade is a conservative workaround inferred from the description, not stated in the sources. Only the three listed release lines are named as affected.

fixtures.scenario: A site on Django 3.2.11 includes the debug template tag in a page template. A context value contains script markup supplied by a user, and the tag writes it into the response without proper encoding, so the browser may execute it.
The same site runs Django 3.2.12 or later, or its templates do not use the debug tag. Context values that contain markup are shown as inert text and no script runs.

citations.quote: does not properly encode the current context. This may lead to XSS.
Django 2.2 before 2.2.27, 3.2 before 3.2.12, and 4.0 before 4.0.2

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the debug tag's render method in all three release lines so that the formatted output of each context value and of the loaded modules mapping is HTML-escaped before it is joined into the page. It also makes the tag return nothing unless the DEBUG setting is on. The card's cause (unencoded context output) and its prevention (upgrade, and encode any context dump) match the escaping change. The DEBUG gate is an extra hardening step that the card leaves as an open question.

patterns.title: Spaces in temporary pathnames can lead to unintended file deletion in Pillow before 9.0.1
patterns.cause: In Pillow before 9.0.1, the affected ImageShow show_file methods for macOS and Unix passed the image pathname through an unquoted shell variable when launching a viewer and removing the image. Spaces could split that pathname into separate arguments, causing the forced removal command to target files other than the temporary image. The advisory describes this as path traversal.
preconditions: The application uses Pillow older than 9.0.1.
The application reaches an affected ImageShow viewer path on macOS or Unix that uses the vulnerable shell-based show_file method.
The temporary image pathname contains spaces.
For unintended deletion through pathname splitting, the resulting arguments identify other files that the process has permission to delete.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Pillow 9.0.1 or later. The fix replaces the affected shell-based show_file methods with viewer launches using argument lists and cleanup using Python's os.remove on the original pathname. The final supplied diff shares a cleanup helper that waits 20 seconds for the macOS Preview and XDG viewers; other shown viewer methods remove the file immediately after launching. As general hardening, pass paths as separate arguments without a shell, target the original path during cleanup, and quote paths wherever shell commands remain.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish the attacker's required control or how a problematic pathname is introduced; control of the temporary directory is not a demonstrated prerequisite. The diffs show ImageShow changes, not a review of every Pillow path-handling operation. Shell-based command construction remains in the shown code with quoted paths, so the fix does not eliminate all shell use. The fixed cleanup delay is visible, but the sources do not establish that it is sufficient for every viewer or demonstrate a timing failure.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs Pillow before 9.0.1 and works with a temporary pathname that contains a space. The space is mishandled, and a file other than the intended temporary file is deleted.
An application runs Pillow 9.0.1 or later. Temporary pathnames containing spaces are handled as single complete paths, so cleanup removes only the intended temporary file.

citations.quote: Pillow before 9.0.1 allows attackers to delete files because spaces in temporary pathnames are mishandled.
Path traversal in Pillow

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the shell-string launches in the macOS viewer and the Unix viewer classes, where the path was fed through an unquoted shell variable and then removed with a forced shell remove. It now starts viewers with argument lists and deletes the file from Python, either right away or from a small helper process after a delay. This matches the card's cause, prevention and delay trade-off.

patterns.title: Open redirect on the Flask-AppBuilder database authentication login page
patterns.cause: Flask-AppBuilder versions below 3.4.5 have an open redirect vulnerability in database authentication login (CWE-601). After successful authentication, a nonempty next query parameter was passed to redirect without destination validation, allowing an attacker-supplied external destination. The diff replaces this pattern in multiple login handlers with get_safe_redirect. It also replaces the OAuth callback's existing network-location comparison with the shared check.
preconditions: The application runs Flask-AppBuilder below version 3.4.5.
The application exposes the database authentication login page.
An attacker-supplied external destination reaches the next query parameter on a successful login request; a crafted login link is a possible delivery method.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Flask-AppBuilder to 3.4.5 or later. The new is_safe_redirect_url function resolves the target against the request's host URL for validation, allowing only http or https with an exactly matching network location, including any port. The get_safe_redirect function returns the original target when accepted; empty or rejected targets produce a warning and fall back to the application index. Relative targets can pass this check. As general hardening, custom redirect handlers can apply equivalent validation before redirecting user-supplied targets.
patterns.limitations: The advisories confirm database authentication scope. The supplied diff does not identify the other login handlers as LDAP or OpenID, or establish their affected version ranges. Different network locations are rejected even if trusted, but effects on legitimate single sign-on setups are not documented. Protection of custom views depends on their implementation and is not established here. The advisories report no known workarounds.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs Flask-AppBuilder 3.4.4 with database authentication enabled, so its login page is exposed to the open redirect described in the advisories.
A deployment runs Flask-AppBuilder 3.4.5 or later with database authentication enabled, which is the fixed release named in the advisories.

citations.quote: Flask-AppBuilder contains an open redirect vulnerability when using database authentication login page on versions below 3.4.5.
There are no known workarounds. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 3.4.5 or later.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a shared helper that resolves the requested next target against the current host URL and accepts it only when the scheme is http or https and the host matches the application host. Otherwise it logs a warning and falls back to the index page. The helper is applied in the database, LDAP and OpenID login views and replaces the host-only comparison in the OAuth callback. This matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Catastrophic backtracking in mistune inline markup regular expressions
patterns.cause: In mistune through 2.0.2, support for inline markup is implemented with regular expressions that can involve a high amount of backtracking on certain edge cases. This behavior is commonly called catastrophic backtracking (CWE-1333), so some inputs can make the regex engine consume far more work than their size suggests.
preconditions: The application uses mistune version 2.0.2 or earlier.
Text is parsed with inline markup support, which relies on the affected regular expressions.
The parsed text includes input that hits the edge cases that cause heavy backtracking.
patterns.prevention: Move to a mistune release newer than 2.0.2, since the advisories describe the affected range as through 2.0.2. When writing or reviewing inline markup parsing, avoid regular expressions whose matching work can grow sharply on edge-case input. Where untrusted text is rendered, consider bounding the input size and the time spent parsing it as defense in depth.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the problem only in general terms. They do not name the exact patterns, the triggering inputs, the first fixed version, or the specific change made upstream. They also do not say whether the backtracking cost is polynomial or exponential. The size and time limits suggested above are general hardening and are not described in the sources as fixes for this issue.

fixtures.scenario: A web service renders user-submitted comments with mistune 2.0.2 and inline markup enabled. A comment containing an edge case that triggers heavy backtracking in the inline regular expressions makes the parser use excessive time on that request.

The same service runs a mistune release newer than 2.0.2, and inline markup parsing no longer relies on the regular expressions that backtrack heavily. It also caps the length of submitted comments before parsing.

citations.quote: support of inline markup is implemented by using regular expressions that can involve a high amount of backtracking on certain edge cases
This behavior is commonly named catastrophic backtracking.

patch_review.observation: The upstream commits rewrite the emphasis and strong regular expressions in the inline parser. The old patterns used lazy, overlapping alternatives that could backtrack heavily. The new ones split emphasis into asterisk and underscore rules, with a single shared tokenizing function and tighter matching of escapes and closing markers. This matches the card's cause, which is catastrophic backtracking in inline markup regexes, and its fix direction of upgrading and avoiding backtracking-prone patterns.

patterns.title: Directory traversal through custom component file serving in Streamlit
patterns.cause: The Streamlit server handled URLs for custom components by processing file paths taken from the request and returning the contents of the named file. File operations were not confined to the custom component directory, so a crafted URL could reach files elsewhere on the web server file system. One source also says existing files could be overwritten.
preconditions: The Streamlit app is hosted with custom components in use.
The Streamlit version is older than 1.11.1, the release that resolved the issue.
An attacker can send a crafted URL containing file paths to the Streamlit server.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Streamlit 1.11.1 or later. In any code that serves or writes files based on request paths, restrict every file operation to one designated base directory, here the custom component directory. Make sure a requested path cannot traverse outside that directory, and reject requests that would. As defense in depth, run the web server with low privileges and place it behind a firewall, which reduces the impact of any such exploit. Review custom components before using them.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact path forms an attacker used or the precise check added in the patch, so this card gives only the general direction of confining operations to the component directory. They state there are no workarounds, so upgrading is the only remedy they name. Low privileges and firewalls reduce severity but do not remove the flaw. The sources are inconsistent on impact: the advisory and CVE text mention only reading files, while the PYSEC entry also mentions overwriting files. The sources say Streamlit continued to check for other occurrences of the flaw, so other code paths are not ruled out.

fixtures.scenario: A team hosts a Streamlit app on Streamlit 1.10 that uses a custom component. An outside user sends a request to the component route with a file path that points outside the component directory, and the server returns the contents of a server log or another world readable file.

The same app runs Streamlit 1.11.1 or later, so file operations for custom components are limited to the component directory. The same request with an outside file path does not return the file. The server also runs under a low privilege account behind a firewall.

citations.quote: Users hosting Streamlit app(s) that use custom components are vulnerable to a directory traversal attack
This patch ensures that any file operations are restricted only to the custom component directory and cannot traverse outside of that.
return the contents of that file or overwrite existing files on the web-server
This issue has been resolved in version 1.11.1. Users are advised to upgrade.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the custom component GET handler to resolve the component root and the requested file to their real paths, following symlinks. It then rejects any request whose resolved path is not under the component root, returning a forbidden 403 response. New tests cover an absolute-style path, a parent-directory path, and a symlink pointing outside the root.

patterns.title: Sanic static file serving exposes lateral directories via encoded slash URLs
patterns.cause: The static file handler checked for parent-directory sequences before URL decoding, allowing encoded slashes to evade that check. It then joined the requested URI to the served directory, decoded the joined path and made it absolute. The subsequent string-prefix check could accept a lateral or sibling path whose name shared the root prefix. The advisories describe lateral directory access through app.static using encoded %2F URLs and explicitly state that parent directory traversal is not impacted.
preconditions: The application serves content through app.static.
A request uses encoded %2F slashes with parent-reference segments that evade the check before decoding.
The handler has the vulnerable validation behavior, and the resolved lateral path passes its root string-prefix check.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a listed patched release appropriate to the release line: 20.12.7 or 21.12.2 for the LTS lines, or 22.6.1. The patch decodes the requested URI and strips leading slashes before splitting it into segments. It rejects exact parent-reference segments and segments containing the platform path separator, then joins the validated URI to the served directory and makes the result absolute. It also decodes and makes the root absolute, retaining the final string-prefix check. The advisory reports no known workaround.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish complete affected-version ranges or the extent of exposed lateral directories. The final containment check remains a string-prefix comparison; the patch does not replace it with a component-aware check. Segment separator rejection blocks backslashes on Windows, as the added tests show. Names merely containing two dots are not rejected by the exact parent-segment check; successful serving of a directory ending in two dots is tested only outside Windows. This does not establish universal filesystem support for such names.

fixtures.scenario: An application on an unpatched Sanic release serves a directory with app.static. A client sends a request whose URL contains encoded %2F sequences, and the server returns content from a lateral directory.
The same application runs a patched Sanic release (20.12.7, 21.12.2 or 22.6.1 or later on its line). The same encoded %2F request no longer yields access to lateral directories.

citations.quote: Affected versions of sanic allow access to lateral directories when using
Parent directory traversal is not impacted.
There is no known workaround for this issue.

patch_review.observation: The old handler rejected parent-directory sequences by looking at the raw URI before decoding, so an encoded slash combined with parent segments slipped through. The fix decodes the URI first, splits it into segments, rejects any parent segment or any segment containing the platform separator, then makes the path absolute and checks it against the root. The final containment check is still a string-prefix test, and a test confirms that folder names merely containing two dots stay servable.

patterns.title: Malicious IPv6 redirect URI can cause denial of service in oauthlib URI validation
patterns.cause: The IPv6 address pattern in oauthlib's uri_validate module used nested, unbounded repetition over overlapping colon and hexadecimal character matches. A malicious URI with a long run of colons inside a bracketed host can trigger excessive backtracking during is_absolute_uri validation, causing denial of service. The pattern supports the exponential-backtracking explanation, but the sources do not measure worker occupancy or request throughput.
preconditions: The application uses oauthlib OAuth2.0 provider support or directly calls affected uri_validate functions.
Attacker-controlled URI input reaches an affected validation function, such as through a redirect URI.
The installed code still contains the vulnerable IPv6 pattern. The CVE record describes versions 3.1.1 until 3.2.1 as affected, but the supplied advisories disagree about the fixed release.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to 3.2.2, the fixed release named by the GitHub advisory, or a later release retaining the fix. The patch removes the outer unbounded repetition and bounds the final hexadecimal segment to one through four digits. Retain a regression test for a bracketed run of colons; the added test requires completion within 0.1 seconds. The advisory's interim workaround is to check redirect URIs in the web toolkit before oauthlib and reject those containing a colon, assuming ports and IPv6 are unnecessary. As general hardening, avoid nested quantifiers with overlapping matches, bound component lengths, and cap input length before matching.
patterns.limitations: The sources establish validation DoS, not open redirect exploitation. The CVE and PYSEC records name 3.2.1 as patched and report no known workarounds; GitHub names 3.2.2 and supplies a pre-check. Exact affected boundaries are therefore unclear. Skipped tests label IPv6 edge cases and IPv4-embedded forms unsupported, but use unbracketed hosts; they do not establish rejection or partial matching of valid bracketed IPv6 URIs. Other regexes are unchanged, so this diff does not establish their resistance to backtracking. The timing test is not a general performance guarantee. The colon workaround can reject legitimate URIs, including ordinary scheme separators.

fixtures.scenario: An OAuth2.0 provider built on an affected oauthlib version receives an authorization request whose redirect URI has a bracketed IPv6 host made of a long run of colons. The URI is passed straight into oauthlib's absolute-URI validation, and the web application becomes unresponsive to other users.

The provider runs a fixed oauthlib release (3.2.2 or later). Where it cannot upgrade yet and needs no ports or IPv6 hosts, its web layer rejects any redirect URI containing a colon before oauthlib is called. The same malicious request is refused quickly and the application stays responsive.

citations.quote: Attacker providing malicious redirect uri can cause DoS to oauthlib's web application.
OAuthLib applications using OAuth2.0 provider support or use directly
Issue fixed in 3.2.2 release.
assuming no port or IPv6 is fundamentally required.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the IPv6 address pattern, which had a nested unbounded repetition over colons and hex digits, with a simpler pattern that limits the final group to one to four hex digits. It adds a regression test with a long run of colons inside brackets that checks validation finishes quickly. It also adds tests that mark compressed and IPv4-embedded IPv6 forms as skipped and unsupported.

patterns.title: SSRF in Label Studio Data Import allows arbitrary file access
patterns.cause: Label Studio Community Edition 1.5.0 and earlier has an SSRF flaw in Data Import that lets authenticated users access arbitrary server-local files. The shown URL import path in load_tasks passes user-supplied URLs to tasks_from_url without explicitly rejecting file URLs. It includes a local-address check conditional on SSRF_PROTECTION_ENABLED, but the excerpt does not establish that this was the only guard.
preconditions: Label Studio Community Edition 1.5.0 or earlier is deployed.
The attacker has an authenticated account. Self-registration is enabled by default in these versions, allowing a remote attacker to create one.
The attacker can submit a file URL through the affected URL import path.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to version 1.6.0, which the advisory identifies as fixed. In the shown path, load_tasks trims surrounding whitespace for a case-sensitive check of the lowercase file scheme prefix followed by two slashes, raising a validation error before calling tasks_from_url. General hardening: allow only expected network schemes, parse and compare schemes case-insensitively, keep available local-address protections enabled, and treat all authenticated users, including self-registered users, as untrusted.
patterns.limitations: The diff adds a narrow prefix check in one path, not a general scheme allow-list. Tests cover two lowercase file URLs, including surrounding whitespace; other forms and paths are not established as protected or vulnerable. The existing local-address check remains conditional, and its coverage of private addresses is not shown. The sources do not establish successful import of file contents as task data, access to internal network services, or the risk reduction from disabling self-registration.

fixtures.scenario: A Label Studio 1.5.0 server keeps the default self-registration setting. A remote person creates an account, uses the Data Import module, and reads arbitrary files from the server's file system.
The deployment runs Label Studio 1.6.0 or later. A newly registered user who tries the same import cannot use the Data Import module to read arbitrary files on the system.

citations.quote: allows an authenticated user to access arbitrary files on the system
self-registration is enabled by default in these versions of Label Studio
This issue is fixed in version 1.6.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check in the URL branch of the task-loading function that trims whitespace and, if the URL starts with the file scheme, raises a validation error before any fetch. The existing local-address check is left as is. A test confirms that file URLs, including ones with surrounding whitespace, are rejected.

patterns.title: OS command injection in the Apache Airflow Pinot Provider task execution context
patterns.cause: Before Pinot Provider 4.0.0, PinotAdminHook took its executable path from the connection extra field, falling back to the constructor argument. The path selected the program launched by run_cli through subprocess.Popen. Attacker control of that value could therefore control commands executed in the task execution context without write access to DAG files. The diff addresses controllable executable selection; it does not show shell metacharacter interpretation.
preconditions: Apache Airflow Pinot Provider earlier than 4.0.0 is installed. The advisory also identifies Airflow earlier than 2.3.0 as affected when the provider is installed.
The attacker can influence the executable path consumed by the hook, such as through the connection extra field; the sources do not establish the exact permissions or input channel required.
A task invokes PinotAdminHook.run_cli with the attacker-influenced executable path.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade the Pinot Provider to 4.0.0 or later. Version 4.0.0 requires Airflow 2.3.0 or later, so upgrade older Airflow deployments first; upgrading Airflow alone is insufficient, and the provider must be installed explicitly. The fix ignores the connection extra command path, fixes the executable name to pinot-admin.sh, and rejects nondefault constructor command paths. Ensure pinot-admin.sh is available on the worker's PATH. As general hardening, prevent lower-privileged data from selecting executables, use a fixed executable or a controlled allowlist, and protect PATH and its executable locations from untrusted modification.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not specify attacker roles or how executable-path control is obtained. A nondefault constructor path raises an error, while a connection extra path is ignored. Custom installation directories can still be used through PATH; the fix does not prohibit them. The diff leaves remaining argument construction unchanged and does not establish whether those arguments are safe or vulnerable. The fixed name still relies on PATH resolution.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs Apache Airflow with the Pinot Provider at a version before 4.0.0. A user without write access to DAG files influences a value that a Pinot task turns into an OS command, so the attacker controls the commands the task executes.

A deployment runs Airflow 2.3.0 or later with the Pinot Provider explicitly installed at version 4.0.0 or later. Externally influenced values are not passed unneutralized into OS commands in the task execution context.

citations.quote: allows an attacker to control commands executed in the task execution context, without write access to DAG files
Apache Airflow Pinot Provider 4.0.0 can only be installed for Airflow 2.3.0+
you need to manually install the Pinot Provider version 4.0.0 in order to get rid of the vulnerability

patch_review.observation: The fix stops the Pinot admin hook from reading the command path from the connection extra field. The executable is now fixed to the default admin script name, and the constructor raises an error if a caller passes any other path. This matches the card's cause (a controllable executable path) and its prevention (a fixed program name resolved through PATH).

patterns.title: Unescaped Host header reflected in NameVirtualHost 404 page enables HTML injection
patterns.cause: When the Host header does not match a configured host, twisted.web.vhost.NameVirtualHost returns a NoResource resource. That resource renders the attacker-supplied Host header into the 404 HTML response without escaping it. Markup or script in the header therefore reaches the response body as live HTML.
preconditions: The application uses twisted.web.vhost.NameVirtualHost to serve a Twisted web site.
The Twisted version is 0.9.4 or later and earlier than 22.10.0rc1.
A request arrives whose Host header matches no configured virtual host, so the 404 NoResource path is taken.
The attacker can control the Host header of a request whose response is rendered by a victim or client.
patterns.prevention: Treat the Host header as untrusted input. Any HTML page that echoes it, including error pages, must encode HTML-significant characters first, or must not echo it at all. Upgrade Twisted to 22.10.0rc1 or later, which contains the fix. The advisory lists no workarounds, so upgrading is the documented remedy.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so no implementation detail is given here. The CVE text says exploitation should be very difficult in practice, because modifying the Host header of a normal request implies a privileged position. The sources cover only the NameVirtualHost 404 path and do not say whether other Twisted components echo the Host header.

fixtures.scenario: A site is served through a NameVirtualHost with no matching host entry. A request arrives with a Host header containing an HTML heading element. The 404 body echoes the header value as live markup, so the injected element is interpreted by the browser.

The same request is sent to a site running Twisted 22.10.0rc1 or later, or to a site that encodes HTML-significant characters before echoing the header. The 404 page shows the header only as inert text, and no injected element is parsed.

citations.quote: renders the Host header unescaped into the 404 response allowing HTML and script injection.
In practice this should be very difficult to exploit as being able to modify the Host header
This issue was fixed in version 22.10.0rc1. There are no known workarounds.
first appeared in the 0.9.4 release.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a new pages module whose error pages are built with the template system, so the brief and detail text are HTML-escaped. NameVirtualHost now uses the new not-found page for unknown or missing Host headers. The old ErrorPage, NoResource and ForbiddenResource classes are kept only as deprecated unsafe aliases, still used internally for fixed or already-escaped text.

patterns.title: Regular expression denial of service in Mako Lexer parsing before 1.2.2
patterns.cause: In Mako before 1.2.2, Lexer.match_tag_start uses a repeated attribute group containing lazy quoted-string matches that can consume their own quote delimiters, including across newlines. This permits ambiguous splitting of quote-heavy input and excessive backtracking when a tag cannot be completed, causing regular expression denial of service. The added regression test covers an opening tag with a keyword followed by 3,000 double quotes and no closing delimiter.
preconditions: The installed Mako version is earlier than 1.2.2.
Template text reaches Lexer parsing, directly or through the affected babelplugin or linguaplugin integrations.
For an attacker to trigger the issue, attacker-influenced malformed template text must reach that parsing path; the sources do not establish how that access is obtained.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Mako to 1.2.2 or later, the advisory's fixed-version boundary, including environments using babelplugin or linguaplugin. The diff changes quoted-string matching to exclude each string's own quote delimiter, reducing ambiguous matching in the repeated attribute group. It adds a regression test requiring a syntax error for an unterminated tag with 3,000 double quotes. As general hardening, avoid delimiter-consuming wildcard matches inside repeated lexer groups and restrict parsing of untrusted templates.
patterns.limitations: The diff also explicitly accepts commas between attributes for backward compatibility and tests page tags with and without a comma. Only the tag-start pattern is changed here; the sources do not establish the safety of all lexer patterns or prove that all alternatives are disjoint. The regression test has no timing assertion, so it does not establish a runtime bound. The sources provide no timeout guidance or verified mitigation other than the fix, and do not establish remote reachability.

fixtures.scenario: A service uses a Mako release earlier than 1.2.2 and feeds template text supplied by an outside party into the Lexer class, so a crafted input can make parsing consume excessive time.
The same service runs Mako 1.2.2 or later, and its Lexer, babelplugin and linguaplugin parsing paths use that patched release.

citations.quote: Sqlalchemy mako before 1.2.2 is vulnerable to Regular expression Denial of Service when using the Lexer class to parse.
This also affects babelplugin and linguaplugin.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the quoted-string alternatives in the tag-start pattern of the Lexer from lazy any-character matches to matches that exclude the delimiter quote. This removes the overlap that caused catastrophic backtracking on an unclosed tag followed by many quotes. It also adds a comma alternative so older page tags with a stray comma still parse, and adds a regression test with thousands of quote characters.

patterns.title: Untrusted run_id in Airflow example DAGs enables command execution
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow versions before 2.4.0, the example DAGs let a user who can trigger DAGs from the UI supply a run_id by hand. That value led to arbitrary command execution. The run_id is attacker-controlled input and was not kept apart from command execution.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version earlier than 2.4.0 is running.
The example DAGs are available in the deployment.
The attacker has UI access and can trigger DAGs.
The attacker can type in a run_id value when triggering a DAG manually.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 2.4.0 or later. In any DAG code you write, treat run_id as untrusted user input. Do not let its content become part of command text that a shell or other interpreter will run. Keep it as plain data, and validate or restrict its content before using it in any operation that runs commands.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which example DAG was affected or how run_id reached command execution. They do not describe the upstream change or give workarounds other than the fixed version boundary. This card gives only a general direction and is not a complete audit of how run_id is used elsewhere. The sources do not cover custom DAGs, but any code that handles run_id the same way should be reviewed.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow deployment on a version before 2.4.0 has example DAGs available. A user with UI access triggers one manually and enters a run_id containing command text instead of a normal identifier. The command runs on the Airflow host.
The deployment runs Airflow 2.4.0 or later. A user triggers a DAG with an unusual run_id, and the value is treated only as data, so no command from it is executed.

citations.quote: allows an attacker with UI access who can trigger DAGs, to execute arbitrary commands via manually provided run_id parameter
This issue affects Apache Airflow versions prior to 2.4.0.
Apache Airflow vulnerable to OS Command Injection via example DAGs

patch_review.observation: The fix edits the example bash operator DAG, whose shell command text embedded the templated run_id value. That let a manually supplied run_id be interpreted by the shell. The command now uses the task instance key string instead, so the user-controlled run_id no longer appears in the command text. This matches the card's cause (untrusted run_id reaching command execution) and its prevention (keep run_id out of shell command text).

patterns.title: OS command injection via Apache Airflow Pig Provider before 4.0.0
patterns.cause: PigCliHook read pig_properties from connection extras, split the string on whitespace, and appended the resulting arguments to the Pig command. This exposed a connection-sourced command argument injection path. The advisory reports attacker control of commands in the task execution context without write access to DAG files. The fix removes connection extras as a source of Pig properties.
preconditions: Pig Provider earlier than 4.0.0 is installed. The advisory also covers Airflow earlier than 2.3.0 when Pig Provider is installed.
A task uses PigCliHook with attacker-influenced pig_properties in its connection extras.
The sources do not establish the permissions or entry point needed to influence those extras; the advisory says DAG file write access is unnecessary.
patterns.prevention: Manually install Pig Provider 4.0.0 or later, including on Airflow 2.3.0 or newer. Older Airflow deployments must first upgrade to at least 2.3.0 to install provider 4.0.0. Migrate connection-extra properties to the list-of-strings argument accepted by PigOperator or PigCliHook. The hook rejects truthy legacy extra values and appends the supplied list directly without whitespace splitting. As general hardening, restrict connection editing and use structured argument lists from trusted sources instead of splitting editable configuration strings.
patterns.limitations: The diff removes one argument source without adding sanitization. Pig options remain a whitespace-split string, and PigOperator makes both options and properties templated. Untrusted values reaching these inputs could influence arguments, but the sources do not establish a remaining exploitable vulnerability or attacker access to them. Legacy extras cause an error only when their value is truthy, not merely when the key exists. The exact exploit payload and attacker permissions are unspecified.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs Airflow earlier than 2.3.0 with a Pig Provider earlier than 4.0.0 installed. An attacker without write access to DAG files influences a command executed in the task execution context, and special elements are not neutralized.
A deployment runs Airflow 2.3.0 or later and has manually installed Pig Provider 4.0.0 or later, so the vulnerable provider version is no longer present.

citations.quote: allows an attacker to control commands executed in the task execution context, without write access to DAG files
This issue affects Pig Provider versions prior to 4.0.0.
Pig Provider 4.0.0 can only be installed for Airflow 2.3.0+
you need to manually install the Pig Provider version 4.0.0 in order to get rid of the vulnerability

patch_review.observation: The fix stops the hook from reading a pig properties string from the connection extra and splitting it into command arguments. Now the hook raises an error if that extra is present, and properties come in as a list of strings through the hook or operator argument. The operator also gains templated pig options and properties fields, which matches the card's limitations.

patterns.title: Open redirect in the Apache Airflow webserver confirm endpoint
patterns.cause: Apache Airflow 2.3.0 through 2.3.4 had an open redirect in the webserver's /confirm endpoint (CWE-601). The confirm view read the request's origin parameter directly without applying get_safe_url at that point. The patch routes that value through get_safe_url. The supplied diff does not show its subsequent redirect use.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version is in the range 2.3.0 through 2.3.4.
The webserver's /confirm endpoint is reachable.
A request supplies an attacker-controlled origin value.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to an Airflow release containing the fix. The patch applies get_safe_url to the origin parameter when the confirm view reads it from the request. As general hardening, validate user-supplied return or next destinations against an application-defined allowlist or same-host policy before redirecting.
patterns.limitations: The supplied diff shows only the origin handling change in confirm. It does not include the get_safe_url implementation, so its accepted hosts and schemes, local-URL policy, and fallback behavior cannot be confirmed. The sources do not establish authentication requirements, the required user interaction, downstream redirect behavior, the status of other endpoints, or the first patched version.

fixtures.scenario: An organization runs Apache Airflow 2.3.4 with the webserver reachable by its users. A crafted link to the /confirm endpoint on the trusted Airflow host sends the user's browser to an external site chosen by the link's author.
The organization runs a release newer than 2.3.4 that includes the upstream fix. The same style of link to /confirm does not send the user to an arbitrary external site.

citations.quote: In Apache Airflow 2.3.0 through 2.3.4, there was an open redirect in the webserver's
Apache Airflow contains open redirect

patch_review.observation: The fix wraps the origin query parameter read in the confirm view with the existing safe-URL helper, so an external or untrusted destination is replaced by a safe internal default instead of being used for the later redirect. This matches the card's description of an unvalidated origin parameter and its sanitization-at-read-time prevention.

patterns.title: ReDoS in setuptools package_index when parsing untrusted index HTML
patterns.cause: In setuptools 65.5.0 and earlier, package_index.py uses a vulnerable regular expression on HTML fetched from a package page or a custom PackageIndex page. Crafted HTML can make the match take excessive time, which causes denial of service.
preconditions: setuptools version 65.5.0 or earlier is in use
The package_index code fetches HTML from a PyPI package page or a custom PackageIndex page
An attacker can influence the HTML content, for example through a crafted package or a malicious custom index
patterns.prevention: Upgrade setuptools to 65.5.1 or later, which patches the vulnerable regular expression. Treat HTML fetched from package indexes as untrusted input. Do not run backtracking-prone regular expressions over it without safeguards. Where possible, restrict which index servers a build or install process contacts.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the exact regular expression, the input shape that triggers the slowdown, or how the patch changes the matching logic. They give no measurements of impact. Guidance beyond upgrading and treating fetched HTML as untrusted is therefore general and not confirmed by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A build environment runs setuptools 65.5.0 and fetches a package page from a custom index. The page contains crafted HTML, and the regular expression in package_index.py consumes excessive processing time, so the process stalls.
A build environment runs setuptools 65.5.1 or later and fetches the same crafted page. The patched matching does not cause a denial of service, and the process continues normally.

citations.quote: cause a denial of service by fetching malicious HTML from a PyPI package or custom PackageIndex page
There is a Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) in package_index.py.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the regular expression that finds HTML tags carrying a rel attribute in package_index.py. It caps the whitespace allowed around the equals sign at a small fixed number and stops the value pattern from also matching spaces, which removes the catastrophic backtracking. The timeout-guarded ReDoS test is no longer marked as an expected failure. This agrees with the card's cause (a backtracking-prone regex on fetched index HTML) and its prevention (upgrade and treat fetched HTML as untrusted).

patterns.title: OS command injection in the Apache Airflow Spark Provider (CVE-2022-40954)
patterns.cause: SparkSubmitHook accepted an unchecked executable name or path through its spark binary argument or the effective spark-binary connection extra. The spark-home extra could select the installation directory used to construct the executable path. This allowed configuration to influence executable selection without an allowlist. The advisory identifies this as OS command injection (CWE-78) allowing arbitrary file reads in the task execution context without write access to DAG files.
preconditions: Spark Provider earlier than 4.0.0 is installed. The advisory also identifies Airflow earlier than 2.3.0 with Spark Provider installed as affected.

For the executable-selection route shown in the diff, attacker-controlled input must reach the effective spark binary argument, spark-binary extra, or spark-home extra; the sources do not establish the permissions needed to do so.
A task uses SparkSubmitHook with the affected configuration to construct and execute a command.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Spark Provider to 4.0.0 or later, requiring Airflow 2.3.0 or later; upgrading Airflow alone can leave a vulnerable provider installed, so upgrade the provider explicitly. The fix validates the explicit spark binary argument and effective connection binary against spark-submit and spark2-submit, rejects truthy spark-home extras, and uses PATH lookup for submission and driver-kill commands. Remove spark-home settings and replace unsupported binary selections with an allowed name available on PATH. General hardening: constrain executable selection from user-editable configuration with a fixed allowlist.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not specify the attacker's exact permissions or input-delivery mechanism, and the advisory states arbitrary file read rather than demonstrating unrestricted program execution. The diff adds executable-selection checks, not sanitization of other command arguments; it does not establish their safety or the status of other providers. Custom installation locations can still be exposed through PATH, but custom binary names are rejected when selected. A false or empty spark-home value is not rejected, and an explicit allowed binary can override an unsupported spark-binary extra.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs Airflow 2.2.x with an older Spark Provider installed. An attacker without write access to DAG files can read arbitrary files in the task execution context.
A deployment runs Airflow 2.3.0 or later and has manually installed Spark Provider 4.0.0, so the vulnerable provider version is no longer present.

citations.quote: allows an attacker to read arbtrary files in the task execution context, without write access to DAG files
This issue affects Spark Provider versions prior to 4.0.0.
Note that you need to manually install the Spark Provider version 4.0.0 in order to get rid of the vulnerability

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a fixed allowlist of two spark submit binary names. It rejects any other binary from the connection extra or the constructor argument, and it refuses connections that set the spark-home extra. The binary is now always resolved from the PATH, and the code that built a path from the home directory is removed.

patterns.title: Locale parameter in internationalized URLs interpreted as a regular expression (Django ReDoS)
patterns.cause: In affected Django releases, the locale parameter used by internationalized URLs was treated as a regular expression. Because the value was interpreted as a pattern rather than matched as plain text, it could be used for a potential denial of service attack (CWE-1333, inefficient regular expression complexity).
preconditions: The application runs Django 3.2 before 3.2.16, 4.0 before 4.0.8, or 4.1 before 4.1.2.
The application uses internationalized URLs.
A locale parameter value that an attacker can influence reaches the code that treats it as a regular expression.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 3.2.16, 4.0.8, 4.1.2 or a later release. In any code that builds URL patterns from locale values, do not let a locale value be interpreted as regular expression syntax. Treat it as literal text, either by matching it as a plain string or by escaping it fully before it is combined into a pattern. Where practical, compare it against a fixed list of configured language codes instead of a pattern.
patterns.limitations: The advisories are brief. They do not say which Django component or function was affected, what pattern shape triggers the slowdown, how severe the slowdown is, or how the upstream change works. They do not say whether any input other than the locale parameter is affected. This card does not claim that input length limits or other mitigations are sufficient. The upgrade is the only remedy named by the version ranges in the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A site on Django 4.0.7 serves internationalized URLs. A remote client supplies a crafted locale value, and the framework treats it as a regular expression, so request handling can be slowed enough to deny service to other users.

The same site runs Django 4.0.8 or later, or any code that handles locale values treats them as literal text or checks them against a fixed list of configured languages. A crafted locale value is matched as ordinary text and gets no regular expression interpretation.

citations.quote: internationalized URLs were subject to a potential denial of service attack via the locale parameter, which is treated as a regular expression.
In Django 3.2 before 3.2.16, 4.0 before 4.0.8, and 4.1 before 4.1.2

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the regex property of the locale prefix pattern class in the URL resolvers module, so the language prefix is escaped before it is compiled. The locale string is now matched as literal text rather than as regular expression syntax. A new test shows that a malformed locale value used to raise a regex compile error during URL reversal. The same change is applied on the 3.2, 4.0 and 4.1 branches.

patterns.title: WsgiDAV directory browser can render untrusted data as cross site scripting
patterns.cause: The directory browser used a Jinja2 environment without automatic HTML escaping. Untrusted values displayed in its interface, such as a realm or user name, could therefore be interpreted as markup and cause script execution in a visitor's browser.
preconditions: WsgiDAV directory browsing is enabled.
Attacker-influenced data, such as a realm or user name, is displayed in the directory browser interface.
The installation uses the vulnerable rendering behavior without the escaping fix.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade WsgiDAV to version 4.1.0, which the advisory identifies as patched. The fix uses Jinja2's select_autoescape function to enable automatic escaping for the HTML template, while explicitly preserving extra link markup and the trailer as trusted HTML. Such exceptions require their content to be safe for HTML rendering. Until upgrading, disable the directory browser in the configuration.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish whether directory browsing is enabled by default or give a complete affected version range or field list. The diff does not show how extra link markup and the trailer are constructed, so their safety cannot be verified from it. The advisory says simply uploading a file or folder with a manipulated name is insufficient to exploit this vulnerability. Disabling the directory browser removes that feature.

fixtures.scenario: A WsgiDAV server older than 4.1.0 has directory browsing enabled. Its realm or user name values come from a source that outsiders can influence, and these values are shown in the directory browser page.
The same server runs WsgiDAV 4.1.0 or later, or it has the directory browser disabled in its configuration, so the page that displays those values is not exposed in a vulnerable form.

citations.quote: Implementations using this library with directory browsing enabled may be susceptible to Cross Site Scripting (XSS) attacks.
However if the WsgiDAV library is used in a scenario where untrusted data is displayed in the directory browser's user interface
This issue has been patched, users can upgrade to version 4.1.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix turns on automatic escaping for the Jinja2 environment that renders the directory browser template, using the extension-based autoescape selection, which covers the html template. Two template fields that the code builds as HTML, the extra link markup per row and the trailer, are explicitly marked as trusted so they still render. This matches the card's cause (escaping disabled) and its prevention (enable autoescaping for the whole environment and bypass only for pre-built fragments).

patterns.title: Reflected XSS through the origin query argument on the Airflow Trigger DAG with config screen
patterns.cause: Apache Airflow before 2.4.2 was susceptible to XSS through the origin query argument on the Trigger DAG with config screen. The old get_safe_url function parsed input without first resolving it against the server base URL. It allowed an empty, HTTP, or HTTPS scheme and an empty or server-matching network location, then reconstructed the URL after normalizing its query. The fix addresses unsafe URL interpretation by resolving input before validation; tests cover a leading-space script-style URL and unusual relative forms.
preconditions: Apache Airflow before 2.4.2 is deployed.
A user accesses the Trigger DAG with config screen with an attacker-controlled origin query argument.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade apache-airflow to 2.4.2 or later. Follow the revised get_safe_url behavior: resolve the supplied URL against the request's server base URL, require HTTP or HTTPS and an identical network location, including any port, and return the resolved URL. Return the home page for empty input, failed validation, or a semicolon found after URL decoding. Retain template output encoding, which the rendering tests show is already present; as general hardening, it complements URL validation.
patterns.limitations: The supplied excerpts do not show the template or call site, so the exact link placement and browser execution sequence are not established. Tests show a leading-space script-style input becoming a same-server absolute path, but do not demonstrate exploitation in a browser. Relative URLs become absolute in returned and rendered output; a change to visible link text is not established. The helper changes apply to its callers, but other affected screens, authentication requirements, and reverse-proxy behavior are not documented.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs an Airflow version older than 2.4.2. A user follows a link to the Trigger DAG with config screen whose origin query argument carries attacker-supplied content, and the page handles that value unsafely.
A deployment runs Airflow 2.4.2 or later. The same link is opened, and the origin query argument is not able to inject script into the Trigger DAG with config screen.

citations.quote: In Apache Airflow versions prior to 2.4.2, the "Trigger DAG with config" screen was susceptible to XSS attacks via the
Apache Airflow Cross-site Scripting vulnerability
