patch_review.observation: The fix rewrites the shared URL sanitizer so it no longer trusts the parsed scheme and host of the raw string. It resolves the value against the server's own base URL, accepts only http or https with a host equal to the server's, and otherwise returns the home page. The semicolon rejection stays, and the tests show a leading-space script value becoming a same-host absolute link and relative values becoming absolute.

patterns.title: Open redirect in the Apache Airflow webserver confirm endpoint (CVE-2022-43985)
patterns.cause: Apache Airflow before 2.4.2 had an open redirect in the webserver's confirm endpoint (CWE-601). The diff changes get_safe_url, which parsed user-supplied targets before resolving them against the server base URL. It accepted http, https or an empty scheme, and either the request host or an empty network location. The fix validates the resolved destination instead. Ordinary protocol-relative URLs naming another host were already rejected; the sources do not establish a specific successful bypass payload.
preconditions: Apache Airflow before 2.4.2 is deployed.
The webserver's confirm endpoint is reachable and processes a user-supplied redirect target.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 2.4.2 or later. Follow the get_safe_url fix: resolve the supplied target against the request's server base URL with urljoin, then parse it with urlsplit. Require an http or https scheme and a network location exactly matching that of the server base URL, including any port. Return the resolved absolute URL when accepted; otherwise fall back to the index page. Empty targets and targets containing a semicolon after URL decoding also retain the index-page fallback.
patterns.limitations: The shared helper change does not establish that every caller was vulnerable, and the diff omits confirm endpoint wiring and its parameter name. Authentication requirements, victim interaction and successful browser exploitation are unspecified. Tests show selected backslash-containing and leading-whitespace inputs becoming absolute URLs with same-host paths, not being rejected; browser behavior is not demonstrated. Accepted targets become absolute, while index-page fallbacks can remain relative. The existing semicolon check is described as protection against potential XSS and is unchanged.

fixtures.scenario: An organization runs an Airflow webserver older than 2.4.2 and exposes it to users. Its confirm endpoint is affected by the open redirect described in the advisories.
An organization runs Airflow 2.4.2 or later, which the advisories treat as outside the affected range for this open redirect in the confirm endpoint.

citations.quote: In Apache Airflow versions prior to 2.4.2, there was an open redirect in the webserver's
In Apache Airflow versions prior to 2.4.2, there was an open redirect in the webserver's

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the redirect-safety helper so it no longer accepts a URL just because its raw scheme and host are the server's own or empty. It now resolves the supplied value against the server's base URL, then requires an http or https scheme and the same host, and otherwise falls back to the home page. The tests add protocol-relative, backslash, leading-whitespace and javascript scheme inputs, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Open redirect in the Apache Airflow webserver login endpoint before 2.4.3
patterns.cause: Apache Airflow before 2.4.3 had an open redirect in the webserver login endpoint (CWE-601). The diff shows that Flask-AppBuilder security views used a different redirect helper from Airflow routes. The fix replaces that helper to make URL filtering consistent; the diff does not establish the exact validation defect.
preconditions: The deployment runs Apache Airflow earlier than 2.4.3.
The webserver login endpoint is reachable.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 2.4.3 or later, using the advisory's fixed-version boundary. During appbuilder initialization, the fix replaces the Flask-AppBuilder security views' get_safe_redirect helper with Airflow's get_safe_url function. This aligns redirects using that helper with Airflow's URL filtering.
patterns.limitations: The patch replaces a helper at runtime without modifying or showing the validator's implementation. Protection therefore relies on Airflow's existing validator, whose exact acceptance rules are not shown. The sources do not identify the input parameter, payload forms, required victim interaction, or whether authentication must complete. They do not establish coverage of custom views, previously imported helper references, or every redirect path. The supplied diff contains no tests.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow webserver at a version earlier than 2.4.3 is reachable by users. An attacker shares a crafted link to its login endpoint, and the endpoint can send the user to a different site than the Airflow instance.
The deployment runs Airflow 2.4.3 or later. The login endpoint does not send users to arbitrary external sites, only to destinations the application trusts.

citations.quote: In Apache Airflow versions prior to 2.4.3
there was an open redirect in the webserver's

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a step during appbuilder initialization that replaces the redirect-safety function used by the Flask-AppBuilder security views with Airflow's own safe-URL function. Login redirects from the FAB views therefore go through the same validation as Airflow's other routes. The card's cause, prevention and limitations all match this change.

patterns.title: Open redirect via the success_url parameter in Horizon Web Dashboard
patterns.cause: Horizon Web Dashboard versions 19.4.0 through 20.1.4 are affected by an open redirect (CWE-601) reachable through the success_url parameter. The advisories give no further mechanism, so the likely cause is that a caller-supplied destination is used for a redirect without enough restriction. That reading is an inference from the weakness class, not something the sources state.
preconditions: The deployment runs Horizon Web Dashboard in the affected range, 19.4.0 through 20.1.4.
A request can carry a success_url parameter whose value an outside party can choose or influence.
A user can be induced to follow a link or submit a request that carries that value.
patterns.prevention: Do not send users to a redirect target taken from the success_url parameter unless it has been validated first. Accept only destinations the application trusts, such as relative paths on its own host or an explicit allow list of hosts. Otherwise ignore the supplied value and use a fixed default page. Run the check on the final, fully parsed target, not on the raw string. Upgrading to a Horizon release that includes the vendor fix for the referenced bug is the direct remedy.
patterns.limitations: The sources only name the affected version range and the success_url parameter. They do not say which views or forms use the parameter, how the vulnerable code handles it, what the impact is beyond an open redirect, or which release fixes it. The validation guidance above is general CWE-601 practice, not a description of the upstream change. Check the linked bug report and the vendor release notes before relying on a specific fixed version.

fixtures.scenario: An affected Horizon deployment, in the 19.4.0 through 20.1.4 range, receives a request whose success_url parameter points to an external site chosen by a third party. After the action completes, the user is redirected to that external site.

A Horizon deployment checks the success_url value before redirecting. A value pointing to an external, non-allowed host is rejected and the user lands on a default internal page. A relative path within the application is accepted.

citations.quote: Open Redirect vulnerability in Horizon Web Dashboard 19.4.0 thru 20.1.4 via the success_url parameter.
Open Redirect vulnerability in Horizon Web Dashboard 19.4.0 thru 20.1.4 via the success_url parameter.

patterns.title: XXE in OpenStack Swift S3 API allows arbitrary host file read via crafted XML
patterns.cause: The S3 compatibility layer of OpenStack Swift (s3api and swift3) accepted XML supplied by authenticated users and parsed it in a way that let crafted XML make the service return arbitrary file contents from the host server. The sources classify this as XML external entity injection but do not describe the exact parser or configuration involved.
preconditions: The deployment runs OpenStack Swift before 2.28.1, a 2.29.x release before 2.29.2, or version 2.30.0.
The S3 API is enabled, either through s3api (Rocky or later) or swift3 (Queens and earlier).
The attacker is an authenticated user able to submit crafted XML files to the S3 API.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a fixed Swift release (2.28.1, 2.29.2, or a later version). In general, an implementation that parses XML from API clients should not let that XML cause external resources or local files to be resolved, so that file contents from the host can never appear in a response. Treat all client-supplied XML as untrusted input, including requests from authenticated users.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the vulnerable XML parser, the specific S3 operations or XML elements affected, or the exact hardening used in the fix, so this card gives only general direction. They also do not say whether network-based entity resolution is possible, or whether any workaround exists short of upgrading. The swift3 project is described as no longer actively developed, and the sources do not say whether it receives a fix.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user sends the S3 API an XML document containing an external entity declaration that points to a local file on the Swift host, and the service returns that file content in its response.
The same authenticated user sends the same crafted XML to a patched Swift release, and the service does not resolve the external entity, so no host file contents are returned.

citations.quote: By supplying crafted XML files, an authenticated user may coerce the S3 API into returning arbitrary file contents from the host server
This impacts both s3api deployments (Rocky or later), and swift3 deployments (Queens and earlier, no longer actively developed).
An issue was discovered in OpenStack Swift before 2.28.1, 2.29.x before 2.29.2, and 2.30.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the shared lxml-based XML parser in the s3api etree module so it no longer expands entities and no longer fetches resources over the network. Tests send a document type declaration with an external entity pointing at a local file in several S3 operations (multi-delete, bucket ACL, bucket creation, versioning, multipart completion) and check that file contents never appear in responses. This matches the card's description of XXE leading to host file disclosure and its direction of not letting client XML resolve external resources.

patterns.title: Stored cross-site scripting in pyload-ng before 0.5.0b3.dev42
patterns.cause: The advisories identify stored XSS in pyload-ng before 0.5.0b3.dev42. In the modern and pyplex package views, the Package function concatenates link URLs and names into an anchor's href and content without visible encoding at that point. The fix targets default navigation when the anchor is clicked, consistent with a script-scheme URL risk; the sources do not establish an exact exploit payload.
preconditions: The deployment runs pyload-ng earlier than 0.5.0b3.dev42.
Attacker-controlled content must be stored and later rendered to a user; the sources do not establish the submission route or required privileges.

The changed rendering path is in the modern and pyplex package views. A click is relevant to the navigation path addressed by the fix, but is not established as necessary for every possible injection.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to 0.5.0b3.dev42 or later, the advisory's stated fixed boundary. The upstream fix adds an inline click handler that cancels the anchor's default navigation in both themes, addressing script-scheme execution through that default click action. As general hardening beyond this patch, avoid concatenating untrusted fields into HTML, use safe DOM construction or context-appropriate encoding, and validate URL schemes separately.
patterns.limitations: The diff leaves URL, name, error and other field concatenation unchanged; it adds neither encoding nor URL-scheme validation. It does not show whether upstream validation exists, so remaining exploitable injection points cannot be confirmed. The sources do not establish exact payloads, attacker privileges, whether another user's session is required, or whether affected scope is limited to these two themes. Canceling default clicks does not establish comprehensive stored-XSS protection.

fixtures.scenario: A pyload-ng instance runs a release older than 0.5.0b3.dev42 and is therefore within the affected range for the stored XSS issue.
A pyload-ng instance runs version 0.5.0b3.dev42 or newer, outside the affected range named in the advisories.

citations.quote: Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Stored in GitHub repository pyload/pyload prior to 0.5.0b3.dev42.
Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Stored in GitHub repository pyload/pyload prior to 0.5.0b3.dev42.

patch_review.observation: The fix touches the package link rendering in the modern and pyplex themes. It adds an inline click handler on the generated anchor that cancels default navigation, so a stored script-scheme URL no longer runs when the link is clicked. Encoding of the name and URL is not changed, which the card's limitations section already states.

patterns.title: Remote file existence check via absolute path traversal in mlflow server and mlflow ui
patterns.cause: The file-based Model Registry store lacked the added check rejecting path separators in registered model names. The fix adds that check, and its regression test rejects an absolute-path-like name during a registered-model lookup. The advisory describes an absolute path traversal vulnerability (CWE-36) that lets remote callers check whether arbitrary files exist, including files unrelated to MLflow and remote files accessible to the host. The supplied diff does not show the complete path-resolution or response flow.
preconditions: The deployment hosts the Model Registry through mlflow server or mlflow ui on an affected release; the sources disagree on the fixed version.
An untrusted caller can query the server. The advisory identifies insufficient caller restrictions as the exposure condition; it does not establish that authentication must be absent.
The code path addressed by this diff uses the file-based Model Registry store.
Existence checks concern locations accessible to the host, including remote storage where accessible.
patterns.prevention: Retain the existing model-name validation and additionally reject names containing the platform path separator or its alternate separator when defined. The diff introduces this validation in the file-based registry store, with a regression test exercising registered-model lookup. Upgrade to a patched release; given the conflicting version statements, 2.2.2 or later is the conservative target. Limit access to Model Registry and Tracking servers through a VPC, IP allowlist, authentication or authorization middleware, or another restriction. Scope cloud credentials to files and directories related to MLflow.
patterns.limitations: The advisory names 2.2.1 as patched; the CVE and PYSEC texts describe versions before 2.2.2 as affected. The diff does not establish coverage of every path-producing entry point, other identifiers, or other backends, and separator rejection alone does not prove path containment. Access restrictions and credential scoping reduce exposure rather than remove the flaw. The sources describe existence checks, not file-content disclosure. The advisory says integrations that do not run mlflow server or mlflow ui are unaffected.

fixtures.scenario: A team runs mlflow server on an older version with the Model Registry reachable by any host on a broad network. There is no authentication, and the server uses cloud credentials that can read many buckets. A remote caller can learn whether arbitrary local or remote files exist.

The team runs a patched MLflow release, places the server behind a VPC with an IP allowlist and authentication middleware, and scopes the server's cloud credentials to MLflow artifact locations only. Unrelated files cannot be probed by outsiders.

citations.quote: enables an actor to check the existence of arbitrary files unrelated to MLflow from the host server
Absolute Path Traversal in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.2.2.
This vulnerability has been patched in MLflow 2.2.1, which was released to PyPI on March 2nd, 2023.
restrict the scope of your server's cloud credentials such that it can only access files and directories related to MLflow

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a file-store-specific model name check that runs the original validation and then rejects any name containing the platform path separator or the alternate separator, using a new helper in the file utilities. Because the wrapper replaces the imported validator inside the file store, every entry point that maps a name to a path is covered. The added test confirms that looking up a model by an absolute path name now fails with an invalid-name error.

patterns.title: Path traversal in MLflow server and UI lets remote callers read files outside MLflow storage
patterns.cause: In MLflow versions before 2.2.1, the download and upload handlers for mlflow-artifacts endpoints passed the validate_path_is_safe function itself to the validator instead of the caller-supplied artifact path. This left the request path unchecked by those calls. The advisories describe path traversal involving backslashes that enables remote callers to download arbitrary files unrelated to MLflow, including files in remote locations accessible to the host.
preconditions: The advisory identifies deployments hosting the MLflow Model Registry through mlflow server or mlflow ui with MLflow older than 2.2.1.
The caller can reach the affected artifact download endpoint; the diff also corrects validation in the upload handler.
Access restrictions do not prevent the caller from querying the server; the complete absence of a VPC, IP allowlist, or authentication or authorization middleware is not required.
The host can access the targeted files, whether local or in accessible remote storage.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to MLflow 2.2.1 or later. The fix makes both artifact handlers pass the request's artifact path to validate_path_is_safe. Limit access to Model Registry and Tracking servers with a VPC, an IP allowlist, authentication and authorization middleware, or another access restriction. Scope remote storage credentials to MLflow-related files and directories. As general hardening, ensure validation checks untrusted path input and test path-accepting handlers with traversal payloads, including backslash and encoded forms.
patterns.limitations: The diff shows the incorrect validator argument and its correction, but not the validator implementation or its runtime behavior when given a function. It does not establish arbitrary file writes, coverage of all traversal encodings, or exploitability of every path-accepting handler. Network restrictions and credential scoping reduce exposure but do not repair unpatched code. The advisory reports integrations that do not use mlflow server or mlflow ui, including Databricks Managed MLflow and MLflow on Azure Machine Learning, as unaffected.

fixtures.scenario: An MLflow 2.2.0 instance started with mlflow server is exposed to a wide network with no authentication. A remote caller sends a request whose path value uses backslash and two-dot traversal elements to name a file outside MLflow storage, and the server returns that file.

The same deployment runs MLflow 2.2.1 or later. The server sits inside a VPC with an inbound IP allowlist and uses cloud credentials scoped to MLflow artifact locations only, so a traversal-style request cannot reach unrelated files.

citations.quote: enables an actor to download arbitrary files unrelated to MLflow from the host server, including any files stored in remote locations
Path Traversal: '\..\filename' in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.2.1.
This vulnerability has been patched in MLflow 2.2.1, which was released to PyPI on March 2nd, 2023.
limiting who can access your MLflow Model Registry and MLflow Tracking servers using a cloud VPC, an IP allowlist for inbound requests

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the artifact download and upload handlers in the server so the safety validator receives the caller-supplied artifact path. Before, each handler passed the validator function to itself, so the request path was never checked. This matches the card's cause and its prevention of upgrading and validating the untrusted input directly.

patterns.title: Command injection from improper neutralization in Apache Airflow and the Airflow MySQL Provider
patterns.cause: The advisories classify this as command injection. The diff shows MySqlHook taking local file loading settings from connection extras: local_infile for mysqlclient and allow_local_infile for mysql-connector-python. Those settings could enable the client capability through connection configuration. The fix moves that control to an explicit hook parameter. The sources do not establish the claimed malicious-server file-reading exploit or that connection configuration is necessarily untrusted.
preconditions: The advisories list Apache Airflow before 2.5.1 and Apache Airflow MySQL Provider before 4.0.0 as affected.
The changed code path uses MySqlHook with mysqlclient or mysql-connector-python.
In the old implementation, a truthy local file loading setting in the relevant connection extra caused the hook to request that capability. Exact exploitation prerequisites are not provided.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade affected Airflow installations to 2.5.1 or later and affected MySQL Provider installations to 4.0.0 or later. The fix stops reading the local file loading toggle from connection extras and introduces a local_infile hook parameter that defaults to false. The Hive and Vertica transfer operators enable it when bulk loading is requested. Existing callers relying on extras must use the hook parameter or an operator that supplies it. As general hardening, restrict connection editing and enable local file loading only for trusted servers.
patterns.limitations: The supplied diff covers MySqlHook and the Hive and Vertica transfer operators, not all command construction. It does not establish required attacker privileges, a malicious-server file-reading outcome, or a complete exploit sequence. The hook parameter defaults to false, but the shown code omits the driver option when false rather than explicitly disabling it; effective driver defaults are not established. Bulk loading also requires server support. Connection-editing restrictions and server-trust advice are general hardening, not demonstrated upstream fixes.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs Apache Airflow 2.5.0 together with an Apache Airflow MySQL Provider release older than 4.0.0, so both components fall in the affected ranges.
A deployment runs Apache Airflow 2.5.1 or later together with the Apache Airflow MySQL Provider 4.0.0 or later, so neither component is in an affected range.

citations.quote: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in a Command ('Command Injection') vulnerability in Apache Software Foundation Apache Airflow
This issue affects Apache Airflow: before 2.5.1; Apache Airflow MySQL Provider: before 4.0.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops the MySQL hook from reading the local file loading setting out of connection extras for both the mysqlclient and mysql-connector drivers. Local file loading is now off by default and is enabled only by an explicit hook parameter, which the Hive-to-MySQL and Vertica-to-MySQL operators set only when bulk load is requested. This matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Path traversal through the run_id parameter in Apache Airflow before 2.6.3
patterns.cause: Airflow did not adequately validate user-supplied run_id values. In the trigger view and DAG.create_dagrun, forward slashes produced a deprecation warning but were still allowed. The advisory confirms that manipulating run_id could enable path traversal and unauthorized file access outside the intended directory. The fix replaces those warnings with pattern-based rejection and adds model-level validation.
preconditions: The deployment runs apache-airflow in a version before 2.6.3.
The attacker is an authenticated user.
The attacker can supply or manipulate run_id; the diff shows user input through the DAG trigger view.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to 2.6.3 or later. The fix checks nonempty run_id values in the trigger view, DAG.create_dagrun and DagRun.validate_run_id, rejecting values that match neither the configured pattern nor the built-in pattern. The default configured pattern allows ASCII letters, digits, underscores, periods, tildes, colons, plus signs and hyphens. The separate built-in pattern accepts the timestamp format for scheduled, manual and dataset-triggered run IDs regardless of the custom pattern. As general hardening, validate identifiers that may reach file paths with a strict allowlist at every entry point and avoid custom patterns that admit path separators.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify the consuming file operation, affected files, read/write capabilities or exact permissions beyond authentication and control of run_id. Trigger permission is not established as a universal exploit prerequisite. The diff shows no cleanup of existing stored IDs; model validation also covers run_id attribute changes, so its scope is not limited to creation. A custom pattern replaces the configured default and is an alternative to the built-in format. Permissive or prefix-only custom patterns can weaken protection because matching does not inherently require the entire value to match.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user submits a run_id value crafted to point outside the directory the application intends to use. The application is an Airflow release before 2.6.3, and the resulting file access lands outside the intended directory structure.
The same authenticated user submits the same crafted run_id to an Airflow 2.6.3 or later deployment. Access derived from run_id remains confined to the intended directory structure.

citations.quote: allows an attacker to perform unauthorized file access outside the intended directory structure by manipulating the run_id parameter
it requires an authenticated user to exploit it
It is recommended to upgrade to a version that is not affected

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a configurable allowlist pattern for user-supplied run IDs, with a default that permits only letters, digits and a few safe punctuation characters. It replaces the old warning about forward slashes with a hard rejection in the trigger view, in DAG run creation and in a model-level validator on the run_id field. Internally generated run IDs for scheduled, manual and dataset-triggered runs are matched by a separate built-in format so they are not affected.

patterns.title: Relative path traversal in mlflow versions prior to 2.3.1
patterns.cause: MLflow versions prior to 2.3.1 had relative path traversal in model version source validation. User-controlled source URIs could contain parent-directory references without the added path-resolution check. The fix targets references intended to access local filesystem paths on the tracking server; its tests reject traversal sources using HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, object-store, and mlflow-artifacts schemes.
preconditions: The deployment runs an affected MLflow version prior to 2.3.1.
An attacker can submit a model version creation request and control its source field.
The supplied source contains traversal references in its URI path component and reaches the affected validation path.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade MLflow to version 2.3.1 or later. The fix extends source validation by parsing the URI path, resolving it with filesystem path semantics, converting it to forward-slash form, removing the resolved drive component for Windows, and rejecting the source if the result differs from the original path. The added helper has no scheme filter. Its error requires an absolute path without relative references; tests retain acceptance of valid absolute local and mlflow-artifacts paths.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish authentication requirements, a separate registry-enablement prerequisite, or demonstrated file access and its impact. The comparison checks whether path resolution changes the path; it does not explicitly enforce containment within a designated artifact root and can reject differences beyond parent-directory references. The supplied diff shows model version source validation, but does not establish coverage of other endpoints or encoded and unusual path forms.

fixtures.scenario: An mlflow deployment older than 2.3.1 is exposed to untrusted users, and a path containing relative segments is supplied to it, which falls under the reported relative path traversal weakness.
The deployment runs mlflow 2.3.1 or later, so it is outside the affected range stated in the advisories.

citations.quote: Relative Path Traversal in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.3.1.
Relative path traversal in mlflow

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a validation step to the model version source check. It takes the path component of the source URI, resolves it to a canonical form, and rejects the request with an invalid-parameter error if the result differs from the supplied path, which blocks parent-directory references. The check runs for http, https, ftp, object store and mlflow-artifacts sources, and the new tests confirm that such sources with relative segments are refused while absolute ones are accepted.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through the watch URL field in changedetection.io
patterns.cause: The advisories report stored XSS through the watch URL on the main page. The diff identifies missing URL scheme checks in validation, storage, and the watch link property, allowing dangerous schemes such as javascript to reach link handling. This supports a script-URL attack mechanism, but does not establish how the previous generic URL validator handled every payload. HTML escaping alone does not neutralize a dangerous link scheme.
preconditions: An attacker-controlled payload reaches the URL parameter of Add a new change detection watch and is stored.
The stored URL reaches the main page's vulnerable rendering or link handling.
For the script-link mechanism suggested by the diff, a user activates the unsafe link; the advisories do not specify the interaction required for every payload.
patterns.prevention: Use the shared is_safe_url check in form validation, datastore add_watch, and the watch link property. Its default allowlist permits HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, and file schemes. It removes source: occurrences case-insensitively, trims surrounding whitespace, and matches the configured scheme pattern case-insensitively. Reject unsafe additions and return a DISABLED placeholder from the link property for unsafe stored URLs. Queue quick-add, clone, and API creation results only when creation succeeds; expose form errors and return HTTP 400 for refused API creation. The tests cover edit and quick-add rejection. Retain HTML output encoding as general hardening, and upgrade to a release containing the fix.
patterns.limitations: Sources disagree on the affected range: before 0.40.2 versus before 0.40.1.1; the diff does not resolve the fixed release. The scheme pattern is configurable and can be weakened. File URLs pass the default scheme check but have a separate ALLOW_FILE_URI restriction. No stored-data cleanup is shown; the link guard checks the stored URL before subsequent template processing, so universal harmlessness is not established. The excerpts omit the page template and do not establish all rendering paths, other affected pages or fields, attacker permissions, or a user-tricking prerequisite. DISABLED is a returned value, not proof of a disabled UI control.

fixtures.scenario: A user adds a new watch and enters a URL value containing a crafted script or HTML payload. The value is stored. When anyone opens the main page, the payload is rendered as active content and runs in their browser.

A user adds a new watch and enters the same crafted payload. The application rejects it as an invalid URL, or stores it and encodes it on output. The main page shows it as inert text and no script runs.

citations.quote: Changedetection.io before 0.40.2 was discovered to contain a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the main page.
execute arbitrary web scripts or HTML via a crafted payload injected into the URL parameter
Changedetection.io before v0.40.1.1 was discovered to contain a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the main page.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a central scheme allowlist check (http, https, ftp, file, overridable by an environment setting) that also strips the source: prefix and trims whitespace before matching. It is applied in form validation, the datastore add function, quick add, clone and the API, which now report an error instead of queuing a watch. The watch link property also returns a disabled placeholder for unsafe stored URLs, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Shell command injection through the terminal title helper in IPython on Windows without ctypes
patterns.cause: The IPython terminal title helper, set_term_title in IPython.utils.terminal, can let text passed as the title be run as shell commands. This happens on Windows when ctypes is unavailable. Untrusted text such as a directory name can then become commands executed with the privileges of the current process.
preconditions: The code runs on Windows in a Python environment where ctypes is not available.

set_term_title is called directly, for example by a tool that uses IPython as a library. The ipython binary itself does not reach the vulnerable code, because the ctypes dependency in IPython.utils._process_win32 blocks it.
Attacker-influenced text, such as a directory name the user is induced to enter, reaches the title argument.
An affected IPython release is installed.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade IPython to a patched release. Until then, make sure every call to set_term_title uses only trusted or filtered input. Do not pass attacker-influenced strings such as folder names, paths or user-supplied labels as the title. Library authors who call this helper should treat the title as untrusted data and must not rely on the ctypes dependency to make the vulnerable path unreachable.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch changes the code, so this card does not either. They also do not say exactly how the shell command is built. The advisories disagree on the fixed version: the CVE and PYSEC text say prior to 8.1.0, while the GitHub advisory says prior to 8.10.0. Check the installed version against the GitHub advisory. The sources do not say what filtering is sufficient. The impact is limited to the scope of the current process.

fixtures.scenario: A Windows tool built on IPython as a library runs in an environment without ctypes. It calls set_term_title with the current working directory, and an attacker has created a folder whose name contains shell command text. When the user changes into that folder, the text can run as commands.

The same tool runs on a patched IPython release, or it only calls set_term_title with a fixed trusted title or a value filtered against shell metacharacters. A folder name containing command text is not executed.

citations.quote: Should an attacker get untrusted input to an instance of this function they would be able to inject shell commands as current process
Users are only vulnerable when calling this function in Windows in a Python environment where
Users of ipython as a library are advised to upgrade.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the Windows fallback that built a shell command string from the title and ran it through the system shell when ctypes could not be imported. Windows now always imports ctypes and sets the console title through the Win32 API, so title text never reaches a shell. The card's cause, preconditions and upgrade-first prevention agree with this.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS from URL payloads rendered as-is in hosted Streamlit apps
patterns.cause: Streamlit 0.63.0 through 0.80.0 had reflected XSS through crafted URLs. The component handler wrote request paths and, for read failures, exception text into 404 response bodies. The media handler included the requested absolute path in a 404 HTTP error message. The advisory reports that malicious JavaScript could be rendered as-is and execute in a victim's browser; the diff removes these details from the affected errors.
preconditions: The app runs Streamlit 0.63.0 through 0.80.0 inclusive.
The hosted app is reachable by the victim over a network.
An attacker crafts a URL containing a JavaScript payload that reaches a vulnerable error path.
The victim is tricked into visiting the crafted URL in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Streamlit 0.81.0 or later; the advisory recommends a supported release. The patch replaces component error bodies and the media 404 error message with fixed generic text. It adds server-side logging of component read failures, including the path and exception, and retains existing missing-media logging. As general hardening, avoid reflecting request-controlled paths or exception details in error pages; use context-appropriate escaping when displaying untrusted data and a non-HTML content type for plain-text errors.
patterns.limitations: The diff does not show response content types or how the media HTTP error message reaches a browser, so direct HTML reflection by both routes is not established. It shows changes to these error paths, not an exhaustive assessment of other handlers or all exploit prerequisites. The advisory rates severity as moderate, with a maximum CVSSv3 base score of 5.9, and states that versions before 0.63.0 and after 0.80.0 need no action for this vulnerability.

fixtures.scenario: A team hosts an internal dashboard on a Streamlit release between 0.63.0 and 0.80.0. An attacker sends a colleague a link to the dashboard with a Javascript payload in the URL. The colleague opens it and the server renders the payload as-is, so the script executes in the colleague's browser.

The same dashboard runs Streamlit 0.81.0 or later. The same crafted link is opened, but the patched version does not render the payload as executable script, so nothing runs in the colleague's browser.

citations.quote: An attacker could craft a malicious URL with Javascript payloads to a Streamlit app.
the server would render the malicious javascript payload as-is, leading to XSS.
Version 0.81.0 contains a patch for this vulnerability.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the 404 bodies in the component file handler and the media file route with fixed generic text (not found, read error) instead of echoing the requested path or the exception text. The detailed path and exception are now only logged on the server. This matches the card's cause (request-controlled data reflected into the response body) and its prevention.

patterns.title: Open redirect in Tornado 6.3.1 and earlier via a crafted URL
patterns.cause: The static file handler's validate_absolute_path function issues a permanent redirect to append a trailing slash during directory handling. It built the target from the request path without rejecting two leading slashes. Such a target is a protocol-relative URL: browsers interpret the next segment as a hostname, allowing redirection to an attacker-chosen site and enabling phishing.
preconditions: The application runs Tornado 6.3.1 or earlier and uses the affected static file handler.
The handler's configuration and routing allow a request whose path starts with two slashes and lacks a trailing slash to reach the directory redirect branch.
A remote, unauthenticated attacker crafts a URL that reaches this branch, and a user accesses it.
patterns.prevention: Use a Tornado release containing the supplied fix. In the static file handler's trailing-slash redirect branch, validate_absolute_path rejects request paths starting with two slashes with HTTP 403 before redirecting. As general hardening, reject or safely normalize multiple leading slashes when constructing redirects from request paths, and review custom handlers that redirect using incoming paths.
patterns.limitations: The advisories identify 6.3.1 and earlier as affected, but the supplied sources do not establish the first fixed release. The diff says the vulnerable branch is reachable only under certain configurations; it does not fully specify them. The shown fix guards the static file handler's trailing-slash redirect, not every request or other application redirects.

fixtures.scenario: An application on Tornado 6.3.1 receives a link with a crafted URL, sent by an attacker in a phishing message. A user opens it and is redirected to an attacker-chosen web site.

An application on a Tornado release newer than 6.3.1 receives the same crafted URL. Any redirect destination derived from request input is confirmed to be a trusted site, so the user is never sent to the attacker's site.

citations.quote: Open redirect vulnerability in Tornado versions 6.3.1 and earlier allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to redirect a user to an arbitrary web site
conduct a phishing attack by having user access a specially crafted URL.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check in the static file handler's path validation so that, when it would redirect a directory request to a trailing-slash URL, a request path starting with two slashes is rejected with a 403 error. Such a path would otherwise become a protocol-relative URL and cause an open redirect. The card describes this cause, the narrow configuration needed, and the fix direction correctly.

patterns.title: Stored XSS in Wagtail ModelAdmin parent chooser and document inspect views
patterns.cause: Two Wagtail ModelAdmin admin views displayed attacker-influenced page and document data without safe HTML escaping. The sources describe the workaround as patched HTML escaping, using plain-text breadcrumbs for pages and escaped link markup for documents. A low-privilege editor could store content that ran script when a higher-privileged admin opened these views.
preconditions: Wagtail ModelAdmin is enabled, with Wagtail from version 1.5 and before 4.1.4 or 4.2.2
For pages, ChooseParentView is reachable because pages are managed through ModelAdmin
For documents, the ModelAdmin InspectView is enabled and shows document fields
A limited-permission editor can create pages or documents that a higher-privileged user later views
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Wagtail 4.1.4 or 4.2.2 or later. If upgrade is not possible, disable ModelAdmin for page models, or use a custom ChooseParentView that shows page breadcrumbs as plain text. For documents, disable InspectView, exclude document fields from it, or use a custom view that builds document link markup with escaped values. Treat content written by editors as untrusted in every admin view.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the exact fields that carry the payload, nor describe the upstream fix in detail. They cover only ChooseParentView and InspectView, so other admin views are not assessed. Ordinary site visitors without admin access are stated as not affected. The workaround must be applied to each ModelAdmin class concerned.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs an affected Wagtail with ModelAdmin managing a page model. A limited editor saves a page with script-bearing content. An administrator opens the Choose a parent page view, and the script runs with the administrator's credentials.
The site runs Wagtail 4.1.4 or 4.2.2 or later. The same editor content is shown in the Choose a parent page view and the document Inspect view as inert text, and no script runs for the administrator.

citations.quote: could potentially craft pages and documents that, when viewed by a user with higher privileges, could perform actions with that user's credentials
The vulnerability is not exploitable by an ordinary site visitor without access to the Wagtail admin, and only affects sites with ModelAdmin enabled.
Site owners who are unable to upgrade to the new versions can disable or override the corresponding functionality.
Patched versions have been released as Wagtail 4.1.4 and Wagtail 4.2.2.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the parent chooser form's label method for pages so it no longer marks the joined ancestor titles as safe HTML. It now joins the titles as plain text with a text separator, so the template escapes them, and a test confirms a script in a page title is escaped. This matches the card's page-side cause and its plain-text breadcrumb prevention. The document inspect view fix is not in this diff, so that half of the card cannot be checked here.

patterns.title: Starlette StaticFiles path traversal via character-wise prefix check
patterns.cause: The static file handler decided whether a requested file was inside the served directory by calling os.path.commonprefix(). That function compares paths one character at a time and does not treat its arguments as paths. A dot-dot request that resolves to a sibling whose name begins with the served directory name (for example static1.txt next to static) therefore passes the containment check.
preconditions: The application serves files with StaticFiles from a directory such as static.
A sibling file or directory exists whose name starts with the same characters as the served directory name.
An attacker can send a request path containing dot-dot segments unchanged, for example with curl --path-as-is.
patterns.prevention: Check containment by comparing whole path components, not characters. Resolve the requested path to a normalized absolute form, then use os.path.commonpath() against the served directory, as the advisory recommends, and reject the request if the common path is not the served directory itself. Upgrade Starlette to 0.27.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the fixed version handles symbolic links, Windows path forms, or other normalization edge cases. They do not say whether the check alone is sufficient for every deployment. Only the dot-dot sibling-prefix case is documented. The affected range is stated as 0.13.5 up to, but not including, 0.27.0.

fixtures.scenario: A service mounts a static files handler on a directory named static. A sibling file named static1.txt and a sibling directory named static_disallow exist. A request using a dot-dot path, sent as-is, reaches the sibling and its content is returned.

Same layout, but the containment check compares whole path components after resolving the request path. The dot-dot request resolves outside the static directory and is rejected as not found, while files inside static are still served.

citations.quote: it does not treat the arguments as paths.
Confidentiality is breached: An attacker may obtain files that should not be open to the public.
allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to view files in a web service which was built using Starlette.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the character-wise prefix comparison in the static file lookup with a component-wise common path comparison against the resolved served directory. New tests confirm that dot-dot requests reaching a sibling file or directory whose name begins with the served directory name now return not found.

patterns.title: Stored XSS on the Airflow task instance details page (CVE-2023-29247)
patterns.cause: The task instance details page has stored XSS. Its script reads selected task attributes as serialized HTML through innerHTML, then concatenates that value into HTML for a time element or link and reparses it through innerHTML. The link target is unquoted. This can turn attacker-influenced stored content into active markup or allow attribute injection. Timestamp formatting requires a 32-character value accepted by the date parser; otherwise, the old link check accepts any value containing http.
preconditions: Apache Airflow is earlier than 2.6.0.
An attacker can influence stored content displayed in a task attribute processed by the script; the sources do not establish the write path or required privileges.
A user opens the task instance details page, and the affected value reaches the timestamp or link formatting branch.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Apache Airflow to 2.6.0 or later. The fix replaces HTML string construction in both formatting branches with DOM element creation, attribute setters, and text nodes, preventing the inserted value from being parsed as HTML during that transformation. It also replaces the http substring check with the validator library's isURL function before creating links. As general hardening, consider explicitly restricting allowed URL schemes.
patterns.limitations: The supplied diffs change timestamp and link formatting in the task details script and add the validator dependency. They do not establish the malicious content's write path, required privileges, or whether DAG or task definitions provide that path. They do not show the validator's accepted schemes or demonstrate a remaining unsafe-link bypass. They do not establish the safety of initial rendering or other pages and templates; reviewing those would be general hardening.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow deployment running a version earlier than 2.6.0 shows the task instance details page to operators. Attacker-influenced stored content appears on that page, and the browser treats it as active content when an operator views it.
An Airflow deployment runs version 2.6.0 or later. Stored values on the task instance details page are displayed as plain text, so an operator viewing the page does not trigger script execution.

citations.quote: Task instance details page in the UI is vulnerable to stored cross-site scripting.
This issue affects Apache Airflow before 2.6.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces string-built markup in the task details script with DOM element creation. Attributes are set through the attribute setter and the displayed value is inserted as a text node, for both the time element and the link. A follow-up change swaps the substring test for http with a proper URL validator from the validator package. This matches the card's cause (raw values parsed as HTML, unquoted link target, weak URL check) and its prevention.

patterns.title: Directory traversal through the path parameter of the mlflow get-artifact endpoint
patterns.cause: The advisories attribute arbitrary server-file reads to traversal through the path parameter of get-artifact. The diff adds missing handler-level path validation to get-artifact, artifact listing, and model-version get-artifact before repository use or joining with a proxied artifact destination. It does not establish arbitrary file reads through all three endpoints or the absence of repository-level checks.
preconditions: An attacker can submit a path parameter to the affected get-artifact endpoint.
The server runs an affected mlflow version; the supplied advisories disagree on the affected range.
Artifact path handling allows the supplied path to reach a file outside the intended artifact location that the server can read.
patterns.prevention: Use an mlflow release containing the upstream validation. The fix calls validate_path_is_safe in get-artifact and model-version get-artifact, and in artifact listing when a path is supplied. It checks a POSIX-normalized copy of each nonempty path, rejecting host-platform absolute paths, host-platform separators other than the forward slash, and paths that equal or begin with a parent-directory component after normalization. Rejection produces an invalid-parameter error. Internal parent-directory components that normalize away are allowed. The original path, not the normalized copy, continues downstream. As general hardening, review other path-taking endpoints for equivalent validation needs.
patterns.limitations: Validation is lexical: it does not resolve symbolic links or verify the actual storage location. Confinement therefore also depends on downstream interpretation of the original path; the diff does not establish safety for every repository backend. The sources do not specify authentication requirements or establish equivalent exploitability of artifact listing and model-version get-artifact. One advisory says prior to v2.0.0; the others say up to v2.0.1. Neither the exact affected range nor a fixed release is resolved by the supplied sources.

fixtures.scenario: A client calls the /get-artifact endpoint with a path value that points outside the artifact store, and the server returns the contents of an arbitrary file from its filesystem.

A client calls the /get-artifact endpoint with a path value. The server resolves it to a canonical location and confirms it is inside the artifact root. A value that points elsewhere is rejected and no file content is returned.

citations.quote: A directory traversal vulnerability in the /get-artifact API method of the mlflow platform up to v2.0.1
allows attackers to read arbitrary files on the server via the path parameter.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a shared path validator that normalizes the client-supplied path as a POSIX path and rejects it with an invalid-parameter error if it contains OS-specific alternate separators, is absolute, or escapes upward via a parent-directory reference. It is called in the get-artifact handler, the artifact listing handler, and the model-version get-artifact handler before the path is used or joined to the artifact root.

patterns.title: Prompt-injected arbitrary URL retrieval (SSRF) in Langchain before 0.0.329
patterns.cause: APIChain generates an API URL from a user question and fetches it without a destination check in the shown pre-fix code. Prompt injection can steer this URL, causing server-side requests to arbitrary destinations, including reachable internal APIs, and potentially injecting fetched content into downstream tasks. The advisories describe affected Langchain versions as before 0.0.329; the CVE record says through 0.0.155.
preconditions: The application uses APIChain with the unchecked request behavior shown in the diff.
Attacker-influenced text reaches the question used to generate the API URL.
The service can make a request to the attacker-selected destination.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to 0.0.329 or later according to the advisories, and configure a narrow, nonempty allowlist when creating APIChain. The fix checks exact equality of the parsed scheme and network location, including any port or user information, before the synchronous or asynchronous fetch and raises an error on mismatch. Use full scheme-and-authority entries. Construction rejects an omitted or empty allowlist; explicitly passing None disables this restriction and is discouraged. Treat fetched content as untrusted. As general hardening, consider network egress controls.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not reconcile the affected version ranges, and the diff alone does not establish its release version. The shown changes cover APIChain; protection in other URL-fetching components is not established. The comparison ignores paths, queries, and fragments. No redirect destination or DNS resolution checks are shown, but the request wrapper implementation is absent, so its behavior and the effectiveness of possible bypasses are not established. The allowlist does not establish that fetched content is safe for downstream use.

fixtures.scenario: A service built on a Langchain version before 0.0.329 accepts user text. An attacker embeds an instruction in that text that makes the service retrieve data from an attacker-chosen URL, and the fetched content then flows into later processing steps.
The service runs Langchain 0.0.329 or later. The destination of any retrieval is not decided by prompt text alone, and fetched content is handled as untrusted data before it reaches downstream tasks.

citations.quote: In Langchain before 0.0.329, prompt injection allows an attacker to force the service to retrieve data from an arbitrary URL
potentially injecting content into downstream tasks.
prompt injection allows an attacker to force the service to retrieve data from an arbitrary URL, essentially providing SSRF

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a domain allowlist option to the API chain. Creation now fails if no allowlist is given (an explicit None opts out). Both the sync and async request paths compare the scheme and host of the model-generated URL against the allowlist and raise an error on a mismatch before any request is made.

patterns.title: Crafted input to the LangChain JIRA API wrapper can lead to OS command injection and remote code execution
patterns.cause: In langchain before v0.0.225, the other method of JiraAPIWrapper executed the supplied query as Python code with the wrapper object in scope. Crafted input could therefore execute arbitrary Python code, including operating system commands, with the application's privileges. The advisory classifies this as OS command injection. The old tool prompt explicitly requested Python code as input.
preconditions: The application uses an affected langchain version before v0.0.225.
The other method of JiraAPIWrapper is reachable, potentially through the tool for other Jira API calls.
An attacker can influence the query passed to that method. An agent-mediated attack would require attacker influence over the generated tool input.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade langchain to v0.0.225 or later. The patch replaces Python execution with JSON parsing, then looks up the named Jira client attribute and calls it with supplied positional and keyword arguments. The tool prompt is updated to describe structured input. Treat tool input as data rather than executable Python. As general hardening beyond the patch, restrict callable Jira operations with an explicit allowlist and use a Jira account with only the permissions needed.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish how an attacker reaches the wrapper or whether a particular user prompt can control an agent's tool input. The patched method has no explicit allowlist or public-method restriction; successful calls depend on the selected attribute being callable and accepting the arguments. The added test demonstrates issue creation, but the sources do not establish every reachable operation or its authorization behavior. They do not support ranking residual risk as smaller. The prompt change guides input format; enforcement comes from the implementation.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs langchain at a version before v0.0.225 and exposes the JIRA API wrapper to requests that carry attacker-controlled text. The attacker submits crafted input and arbitrary code runs on the host.

A service runs langchain v0.0.225 or later. Input to the JIRA API wrapper is still treated as untrusted, and the wrapper is only reachable by trusted callers, so crafted input does not lead to code execution.

citations.quote: Langchain before v0.0.225 was discovered to contain a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in the component JiraAPIWrapper (aka the JIRA API wrapper).
This vulnerability allows attackers to execute arbitrary code via crafted input.
Langchain OS Command Injection vulnerability
Langchain 0.0.171 is vulnerable to Arbitrary Code Execution.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the dynamic execution of the query string in the other action of JiraAPIWrapper. It now parses the input as JSON and calls a named method on the Jira client with the supplied positional and keyword arguments. The tool prompt is also changed to ask for a dictionary instead of Python code. The card's cause, prevention and the remaining risk from attribute-based method lookup all match this.

patterns.title: ReDoS in Django EmailValidator and URLValidator via many domain name labels
patterns.cause: EmailValidator and URLValidator lacked an upfront total input length cap. Crafted emails or URLs with a very large number of domain name labels could cause excessive regular expression matching work and potential denial of service. The fix adds length checks before these validators' regular expression matching without changing the patterns.
preconditions: The application uses an affected Django release. The advisory lists Django 3.2 before 3.2.20, 4 before 4.1.10, and 4.2 before 4.2.3.
An attacker can supply an email address or URL with a very large number of domain name labels to EmailValidator or URLValidator.
The crafted input reaches the vulnerable matching path; any earlier input restrictions are insufficient to block it.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a release containing the fix, with stated fixed versions 3.2.20, 4.1.10, and 4.2.3 for their respective series. URLValidator rejects values longer than its maximum length, which defaults to 2048 characters. EmailValidator rejects values longer than 320 characters. These checks precede the validators' regular expression matching. The forms EmailField also defaults to a maximum length of 320. As general hardening, enforce request size and field length limits and avoid passing unbounded input to regular expressions.
patterns.limitations: The patterns remain unchanged; the sources provide no timing measurements or minimum attack size. URLs longer than 2048 characters are rejected by default, even if otherwise valid; overriding the maximum length changes this cap. The sources do not establish that subclasses inheriting the fix require separate limits, or assess copied validators and unrelated patterns. They do not enumerate application call sites or establish automatic validation of model fields. The advisory's wording '4 before 4.1.10' is imprecise and does not support silently narrowing that range to 4.1 alone. Unlisted series are not assessed.

fixtures.scenario: A public signup form validates the email field with EmailValidator on Django 4.2.2. An attacker submits an address whose domain part has a very large number of labels, and the validation work ties up the worker handling the request.
The same signup form runs on Django 4.2.3 or later, which is outside the affected range, so an email with a very large number of domain labels is not subject to this ReDoS.

citations.quote: potential ReDoS (regular expression denial of service) attack via a very large number of domain name labels of emails and URLs.
In Django 3.2 before 3.2.20, 4 before 4.1.10, and 4.2 before 4.2.3

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a length cap before any regular expression runs: the URL validator rejects non-string values and values over 2048 characters, and the email validator rejects values over 320 characters. The forms email field now defaults its maximum length to 320. The regular expressions are left unchanged, and new tests cover a long run of domain labels, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: SQL injection via SQLDatabaseChain in langchain before v0.0.247
patterns.cause: SQLDatabaseChain turns natural language input into SQL and executes model output without enforcing a statement policy. Its optional model-based query checker can rewrite SQL but is not the parser validation added by the diff. Attacker-influenced input can therefore lead to unintended queries and sensitive information disclosure (CWE-89). The code also supports updates, so modification is possible when database permissions allow it. Prompt injection is a plausible mechanism, but the sources do not demonstrate an exploit. The shown fix targets generated SQL validation, not fixed-query string construction.
preconditions: The application executes generated SQL through SQLDatabaseChain, directly or through SQLDatabaseSequentialChain.
A remote attacker can supply input that reaches the chain and influences SQL generation.
The database connection can access sensitive data; broad privileges or write access are not required for disclosure.
No effective control blocks the harmful generated query before execution.
patterns.prevention: Apply the validation approach shown in the diff: use validate_sql to parse generated SQL with SQLFluff, reject parsing failures, and retain SQLValidation's default rejection of non-select statement types. Wildcard selects are allowed by default but can be forbidden; configure unsupported dialects to fail rather than skip validation. Ensure validation covers the SQL actually executed, including query-checker output. Verify that a chosen release contains the intended protection. As general hardening, restrict untrusted access and use a database account limited to required tables and read-only access where appropriate.
patterns.limitations: Statement-type and wildcard checks do not enforce data authorization or prevent prompt injection; permitted selects can still disclose accessible data. Unsupported dialects skip validation with a warning by default. The added check precedes the query-checker branch, so validation of rewritten SQL is not shown. The CVE lists versions before v0.0.247; PYSEC names v0.0.64. Neither diff establishes which release shipped the validator. The later diff removes core SQL chain exports and loads SQLDatabaseChain from langchain_experimental.sql, but does not establish equivalent protection there. Relocation alone is not a security boundary. The sources do not establish exploit reliability or complete containment.

fixtures.scenario: A public web service runs langchain v0.0.64 and passes user-submitted text to SQLDatabaseChain over a database that holds customer records. A remote attacker crafts input that triggers SQL injection and reads data the service was never meant to return.
The service runs langchain v0.0.247 or later, and SQLDatabaseChain uses a database account limited to the minimum data needed. The same crafted input does not expose the sensitive records.

citations.quote: SQL injection vulnerability in langchain before v0.0.247 allows a remote attacker to obtain sensitive information via the SQLDatabaseChain component.
SQL injection vulnerability in langchain v.0.0.64 allows a remote attacker to obtain sensitive information via the SQLDatabaseChain component.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a validation step that parses the model-generated SQL with a SQL parsing library before it is run. By default it rejects anything that fails to parse or is not a select statement, and it offers opt-in switches to forbid wildcard selects and to refuse unsupported dialects. A later commit moves the SQL chain into the experimental package, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Low-privilege role can test database connections through default REST API permission
patterns.cause: The default permission set in Apache Superset up to and including 2.1.0 let the Gamma role use the REST API function that tests database connections. This function was not limited to roles meant to manage databases, so an authorization gap left an outbound-connection feature open to low-privilege users.
preconditions: Apache Superset version 2.1.0 or earlier is deployed.
The attacker holds an authenticated account with the Gamma role.
The default REST API permissions for the Gamma role have not been tightened.
patterns.prevention: Grant any API function that makes the server connect to a configurable database target only to roles that are meant to manage database connections. Do not include it in the default permissions of low-privilege roles such as Gamma. Audit role-to-permission mappings after install and after upgrade, and move to a Superset release newer than 2.1.0 that corrects the default permission. Keep an authorization check on the connection-test endpoint itself, so it does not rely on the user being logged in.
patterns.limitations: The advisories give only a one-sentence description. They do not name the endpoint, the permission name, the fixed release, or the exact network behavior. The server-side request forgery classification comes from the CWE metadata, not from the source text. This card therefore cannot say which internal targets are reachable or what a tester can learn from the responses.

fixtures.scenario: A Superset 2.1.0 instance runs with default role permissions. A user logged in with only the Gamma role calls the REST API to test a database connection, and the request is accepted although the user has no database management duties.

The same instance has the connection-test permission removed from the Gamma role, or runs a release newer than 2.1.0 that corrects the default. The Gamma user's request to test a database connection is denied as unauthorized, and only database-management roles can run it.

citations.quote: An improper default REST API permission for Gamma users in Apache Superset up to and including 2.1.0
allows for an authenticated Gamma user to test database connections.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the route-to-permission mapping so the connection-test and parameter-validation API methods need the write permission on the database resource instead of the read permission. Gamma holds only read access there, so it can no longer reach these outbound-connection functions. This matches the card's account of an authorization gap, where a low-privilege role could use a function meant for roles that manage databases.

patterns.title: Apache Airflow before 2.6.3: crafted input from an authenticated user makes a request hang
patterns.cause: Apache Airflow before 2.6.3 allows an authenticated user to submit crafted input that hangs the current request. The diff points to a regular expression denial of service weakness: partial_subset matches a supplied pattern against DAG task ids using Python's standard regular expression engine, and the fix replaces that engine with RE2. The sources do not demonstrate the exact backtracking behavior or CPU impact.
preconditions: The deployment runs Apache Airflow before 2.6.3.
An authenticated user can submit crafted input to the affected request path.
For the regex path shown in the diff, a supplied pattern reaches partial_subset and is matched against DAG task ids; the request-to-function connection is not shown.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Apache Airflow to 2.6.3 or later. The fix switches regular expression operations in the DAG model module to RE2, adds the google-re2 dependency, and adjusts pattern type references. As general hardening, prefer engines designed to avoid catastrophic backtracking for untrusted patterns and bound pattern length and execution time.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify the endpoint, request parameter, exploit pattern, or exact conditions needed to trigger the hang. They establish a stalled current request, not wider resource exhaustion. The diff changes the DAG model module and a dependency; it does not assess regex use elsewhere or in plugins. It provides no runtime complexity proof or compatibility tests for backreferences, lookarounds, or previously compiled patterns.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow deployment on a version before 2.6.3 accepts input from an authenticated user. That user submits crafted input and the current request hangs.
An Airflow deployment runs version 2.6.3 or later. The same crafted input from an authenticated user does not cause the request to hang.

citations.quote: an authenticated user can use crafted input to make the current request hang
It is recommended to upgrade to a version that is not affected

patch_review.observation: The fix swaps the standard library regex module for the RE2 binding in the DAG model module, so the task id pattern used in partial_subset is matched with a linear-time engine. It also adds the google-re2 package as a required dependency in the packaging configuration.

patterns.title: Airflow test connection feature abused by users with Connection edit privileges
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow before 2.7.0, an authenticated user with Connection edit privileges could access connection information and abuse connection testing to establish harmful connections or cause server denial of service through repeated requests. The patched API and CLI paths lacked the configuration gate introduced by the fix, which makes connection testing opt-in across the UI, API and CLI.
preconditions: Apache Airflow earlier than 2.7.0 is deployed.
The attacker is authenticated and has Connection edit privileges.
Connection testing is accessible to that user.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 2.7.0 or newer. The core test_connection setting defaults to Disabled. Unless it is Enabled, the API returns HTTP 403 and the CLI exits with an error. Disabled disables the UI test button; Hidden hides it and also disables testing. Leave testing disabled unless needed. Before enabling it, review users who can add or edit Connections and ensure they are trusted. Review and narrow permissions for sensitive functionality.
patterns.limitations: The diff adds an opt-in gate, not destination validation or rate limiting; it does not establish whether other controls already exist. Enabling testing retains the documented risk of malicious use. The sources do not establish arbitrary-host access, internal-service probing, precise hook construction behavior, or network prerequisites. Adding this setting in 2.7.0 does not prove testing was universally accessible in every earlier deployment or that permission reduction was the only earlier mitigation.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 2.6 deployment grants Connection edit rights to many users. One user repeatedly submits test connection requests with chosen settings, exhausting the server and making it open unwanted connections.
Airflow 2.7.0 or newer is deployed, and Connection edit rights are limited to a few trusted administrators who have reviewed their access to sensitive functions.

citations.quote: can be exploited by an authenticated user possessing Connection edit privileges
exploit the test connection feature by sending many requests, leading to a denial of service (DoS) condition on the server
administrators are encouraged to review and adjust user permissions to restrict access to sensitive functionalities, reducing the attack surface.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a core configuration option for connection testing that defaults to Disabled. The REST API refuses test requests with a forbidden status, the CLI test command prints a message and exits with an error, and the UI button is disabled or hidden depending on the option value. It is an opt-in gate with a warning to review who can edit Connections, and it adds no destination validation.

patterns.title: Absolute path traversal in mlflow before 2.5.0 (CVE-2023-3765)
patterns.cause: The advisories classify the flaw as an absolute path traversal in the mlflow project. In this class of bug, a caller-supplied path that is already absolute is used to reach files directly, instead of being kept inside an intended base location. The sources do not name the affected function, endpoint, or parameter.
preconditions: The deployment runs mlflow at a version earlier than 2.5.0.
A path value comes from an untrusted party and is used for file access.
The path is not confined to an intended base directory before it is used.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mlflow to version 2.5.0 or later. In any code that accepts file locations from untrusted input, refuse absolute paths. Resolve the final path with a canonicalizing call such as os.path.realpath(). Then confirm the resolved result is still inside the intended base directory before any read or write. Reject the request if it is not.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that this is an absolute path traversal in mlflow prior to 2.5.0. They do not identify the vulnerable component, the entry point, the impact (read, write, or both), or the exact fix. The generic hardening steps above are the standard defense for this weakness class, not a description of the upstream change. Check the mlflow release notes and advisory details before treating any specific code path as affected or fixed.

fixtures.scenario: A service running an mlflow version older than 2.5.0 accepts a file location from a remote user. The user supplies an absolute path that points outside the intended storage area, and the service uses it as given.

A service runs mlflow 2.5.0 or later. Any custom code that handles user-supplied locations rejects absolute paths, resolves the final path, and verifies it lies under the intended base directory before accessing the file.

citations.quote: Absolute Path Traversal in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.5.0.
Absolute Path Traversal in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.5.0.

patterns.title: Command injection in PaddlePaddle fs.py before version 2.5.0
patterns.cause: PaddlePaddle before 2.5.0 has command injection in fs.py. Its mkdirs method interpolated the supplied directory path into a command executed through the operating system shell. The diff also shows this pattern in distributed launch utilities using log directory settings. Shell metacharacters in these paths could be interpreted as commands, enabling arbitrary command execution.
preconditions: An affected PaddlePaddle release earlier than 2.5.0 is installed.
An attacker can influence a directory path supplied to mkdirs or a log directory setting used by the changed launch utilities.
Execution reaches a vulnerable shell-based directory creation call with that path.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to PaddlePaddle 2.5.0 or later, following the advisory's version boundary. The upstream fix replaces shell-based directory creation with the standard library's os.makedirs function, allowing existing directories. These directory creation operations no longer parse paths through a shell. As general hardening, use native library calls or argument-list process invocations without a shell for file operations, and avoid interpolating untrusted values into shell command strings.
patterns.limitations: The advisories identify fs.py; the diff additionally changes directory creation in launch utilities without establishing their affected version ranges separately. The sources do not establish how attackers obtain control of paths or what privileges are required. The diff leaves a shell-based endpoints.log removal call in the fleet launch utilities unchanged, so it does not establish that log directory values never reach a shell elsewhere.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs PaddlePaddle older than 2.5.0 and uses its fs.py functionality with values that an outside party can influence, so an attacker may be able to run arbitrary commands on the host.
The same service runs PaddlePaddle 2.5.0 or later, and any custom code that invokes operating system commands keeps untrusted data out of command interpretation.

citations.quote: PaddlePaddle before 2.5.0 has a command injection in fs.py.
This resulted in the ability to execute arbitrary commands on the operating system.
