patch_review.observation: The fix replaces shell-based directory creation (os.system with an interpolated path) with the standard library recursive directory-creation call in the local filesystem mkdirs method and in several launch utilities that handle the log directory. The path is no longer parsed by a shell, which removes the injection. A shell call that removes the endpoints log file is left unchanged.

patterns.title: Open redirect after login in Jupyter Server via crafted login links
patterns.cause: The login redirect check used a server-side URL parser that interprets extra slashes after a scheme differently from browsers. The parser could report a scheme but no host, leaving the apparent host in the path. If that path passed the server's base-path check, the old logic could accept it without checking its origin. Browsers could instead interpret the first path segment as a host and redirect to an external site.
preconditions: The attacker knows a Jupyter Server address and crafts a login link containing a malicious next redirect value.
The victim follows the link and successfully logs in, or already has an authenticated session.
For the illustrated bypass, extra slashes after the scheme cause the server parser to report no host, while the parsed path passes the base-path check and the browser interprets an external host.
patterns.prevention: Normalize and validate the requested redirect in the login handler's _redirect_safe function. The fix splits at the first colon, when present, strips leading forward slashes from the remainder, and reconstructs a separator with exactly two slashes. It retains existing percent-encoding of backslashes. Treat either a scheme or a host as requiring the existing cross-origin check, and retain the base-path restriction for local paths. Add a regression test rejecting an extra-slash URL whose apparent host contains an encoded at-sign. Upgrade to Jupyter Server 2.7.2, which the advisories identify as containing the fix.
patterns.limitations: The supplied diff covers the login redirect helper and a regression test, not other redirect paths. It does not show the complete cross-origin policy or fallback behavior, or establish protection against every browser/parser discrepancy. The advisories confirm release 2.7.2 contains the fix but do not specify a complete affected-version range or the status of every later release. They report no known workarounds and do not establish consequences beyond redirection.

fixtures.scenario: A user receives a login link for a known Jupyter Server that carries a destination pointing to an external site. The user logs in, or is already logged in, and the server sends the browser to that external site.
A user receives the same kind of login link, but the server accepts only destinations served by the Jupyter Server. The external destination is rejected and the browser lands on a page on the server.

citations.quote: Maliciously crafted login links to known Jupyter Servers can cause successful login or an already logged-in session to be redirected to arbitrary sites
which should be restricted to Jupyter Server-served URLs
There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

patch_review.observation: The fix normalizes the next URL before parsing, collapsing any run of slashes after the scheme separator to exactly two, because the server-side parser and browsers disagree on a scheme followed by three slashes. It also treats a URL as non-local when it has either a scheme or a host, so such URLs go through the cross-origin check. A regression test was added using a scheme with an extra slash and an encoded at-sign in the host part.

patterns.title: Incomplete cross-site credential checks on the jupyter-server files endpoint
patterns.cause: The handler serving the /files/ URLs did not apply proper cross-site credential checks. The earlier upstream patch for CVE-2019-9644 was not applied completely, so part of that vulnerability stayed open. As a result, certain file contents could be exposed to cross-site requests, or files could be accessed when a user opened untrusted files via Open image in new tab.
preconditions: jupyter-server older than release 2.7.2 is in use
The /files/ URLs are served by the default files handler, not the alternative handler the advisory says implements the correct checks
A user can be induced to open untrusted content or an attacker-controlled page while having access to the server
patterns.prevention: Upgrade jupyter-server to 2.7.2 or later. If an upgrade is not possible, set the ContentsManager files handler class option to the FilesHandler class in jupyter_server.files.handlers. It is slower but implements the correct checks. In general, any handler that serves user files, including a performance-oriented replacement for a standard handler, should enforce the same cross-site credential checks as the reference handler. A security patch should also be applied to every handler path that serves the same data, so no variant is left unprotected.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which checks are missing, which request properties are validated, or how the faster default handler differs from FilesHandler. They do not describe a concrete exploit chain or the exact file types affected. This card gives only the general direction and the documented workaround, and it does not cover other endpoints.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment runs a jupyter-server version older than 2.7.2 with the default files handler. A user opens an untrusted file or a cross-site page, and a request to a /files/ URL is served without the proper cross-site credential check, exposing file contents.
A deployment runs jupyter-server 2.7.2 or later, or sets the files handler class option to the FilesHandler class. Cross-site requests to /files/ URLs are subject to the correct credential checks.

citations.quote: Upstream patch for CVE-2019-9644 was not applied completely, leaving part of the vulnerability open.
Improper cross-site credential checks on
which implements the correct checks.
Jupyter Server 2.7.2

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a cross-site request forgery token check at the start of the get method in the authenticated static file handler in base/handlers.py. This is the default handler behind the files URLs, so it had been missing the check that the alternative FilesHandler already enforced. This matches the card's account of an incomplete earlier patch and its advice to upgrade, to use the stricter handler as a workaround, and to protect every handler path that serves the same data.

patterns.title: Unblocked non-multi options in GitPython clone and clone_from allow command injection
patterns.cause: GitPython before 3.1.32 did not block insecure non-multi options in clone and clone_from. The library makes external calls to git without sufficient sanitization of input arguments, so attacker-influenced input such as a crafted remote URL can reach the git command line and lead to remote code execution. The advisory describes this as an incomplete fix for CVE-2022-24439.
preconditions: The application uses GitPython older than 3.1.32.
The application calls clone or clone_from.
An attacker can influence the remote URL or the options passed to the clone call.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade GitPython to 3.1.32 or later. Treat any remote URL or clone option that comes from users or other untrusted input as hostile. Do not let such input choose which git options are passed to clone or clone_from. Allow only a fixed, reviewed set of options and validate the repository URL against an expected form (for example, permitted schemes and hosts) before calling the library.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not list which options are considered insecure, do not describe the exact validation the fixed release performs, and do not give the precise exploit payload. This card therefore cannot say whether an input filter alone is sufficient, and it does not replace upgrading. The sources also do not cover other GitPython entry points beyond clone and clone_from.

fixtures.scenario: A web service lets users submit a repository address and optional clone settings. It passes them straight to clone_from on GitPython 3.1.31. A crafted remote URL or option value is forwarded to git and executes attacker-chosen commands on the server.

The same service runs GitPython 3.1.32 or later. It accepts only a repository URL that matches an allowlist of expected hosts and schemes, and it ignores any user-supplied clone options, so untrusted input cannot add options to the git invocation.

citations.quote: GitPython before 3.1.32 does not block insecure non-multi options in clone and clone_from.
the library makes external calls to git without sufficient sanitization of input arguments
which makes it possible to inject a maliciously crafted remote URL into the clone command

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the clone path check the keyword arguments passed to clone and clone_from against the list of unsafe git clone options, such as upload-pack and config, unless unsafe options are explicitly allowed. Before this, only the multi-options list was checked, so these options could be passed unchecked as plain keyword arguments. The new tests confirm that both clone and clone_from now raise an error for these options.

patterns.title: OS command injection in mlflow versions prior to 2.6.0 (CVE-2023-4033)
patterns.cause: In mlflow's pyfunc backend, predict embedded a derived local model URI, input path, output path and content type in inline Python within a command string for non-local environment execution. This mixed parameter data with executable text, enabling OS command injection. The scoring server's get_cmd function also interpolated the host or combined host and port into command text without shell quoting.
preconditions: The deployment uses mlflow older than 2.6.0, the affected range stated by the advisories.

Exploitation requires influence over a value incorporated into the vulnerable command text, such as a prediction path, content type or serving host; the sources do not establish how an attacker obtains that influence.
The shown prediction path requires a non-local environment manager. The serving command construction is a separate path, with no equivalent prerequisite established by this diff.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mlflow to 2.6.0 or later. The fix replaces inline prediction code with a dedicated script accepting named command-line arguments. It applies shlex.quote to content type and supplied input and output paths before joining the command. For serving, it quotes the combined host and port or host alone on non-Windows systems, and the host on Windows. General hardening: prefer process APIs that pass arguments separately without a shell, avoid embedding untrusted values in executable code, and validate content types against supported values.
patterns.limitations: The diff still joins prediction arguments into command text and does not explicitly quote the script path or derived local model URI. It does not establish whether those omissions are exploitable. Windows serving adds quoting only for the host; POSIX and Windows shell rules differ, and Windows protection is not demonstrated here. The added prediction tests use the local environment manager, so they do not demonstrate protection of the changed non-local path. Attacker access, required privileges, wrapper-service exposure and other command-building components are not established by these sources.

fixtures.scenario: A team runs an mlflow installation whose version is older than 2.6.0, and it is within the range the advisories list as affected by OS command injection.
A team runs mlflow 2.6.0 or later, which is outside the affected range stated in the advisories.

citations.quote: OS Command Injection in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.6.0.
OS Command Injection in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.6.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops the predict path from embedding the model URI, input path, output path and content type in an inline Python code string run through a shell. It adds a small dedicated script that takes these as named command-line arguments, and the user-controlled values are shell-quoted before the command is joined. The scoring server command builder also shell-quotes the host and the host-and-port address, including the Windows branch for the host. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Static view path traversal up one directory through null-byte handling in Python 3.11 path normalization
patterns.cause: On affected Python 3.11 and 3.12 pre-release versions, the path normalization function os.path.normpath truncates its input at the first null byte. A Pyramid static view that serves files from a full filesystem path can then resolve a request to a location one directory above the static root. The only file the sources say could be exposed this way is index.html in the parent directory. The sources do not describe the exact request form that triggers this.
preconditions: Pyramid 2.0.0 or 2.0.1 is in use.
The runtime is an affected Python version: 3.11.0 to 3.11.4, or 3.12.0a1 to 3.12.0rc1.
A static view is configured with a full filesystem path.
An index.html file sits exactly one directory above the static view's filesystem path.
patterns.prevention: Reject any requested path that contains a null byte before it is normalized or joined to the static root, so that truncation during normalization cannot change the resolved location. Run a Python version in which normalization no longer truncates at the first null byte, such as 3.11.5 or later in the 3.11 series, or temporarily use the 3.10 series. Use a Pyramid release that rejects null-byte paths, which is 2.0.2 per the advisory. Treat null bytes in file and directory names as invalid for static serving.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say how the null byte reaches the static view or which request encodings are affected, so a general input-validation review is still advisable. They state that exposure is limited to index.html one level up. They give no further detail on other deployment layouts. Null-byte rejection in Pyramid is described as a precaution and not as the root-cause fix, which the sources place in Python itself. The sources do not say whether other Python versions or other frameworks behave the same way.

fixtures.scenario: A Pyramid 2.0.1 application runs on Python 3.11.4 and serves a static view from an absolute directory. An index.html file exists in that directory's parent. A request containing a null byte in the path is normalized with truncation, and the parent index.html may be served.
The same application uses Pyramid 2.0.2 on Python 3.11.5 or later. Any request path containing a null byte is rejected before normalization, and the parent index.html is never served.

citations.quote: Pyramid now will reject any path that contains a null-byte out of caution.
impacts users of Python 3.11 that are using a Pyramid static view with a full filesystem path
Use a version of Python 3 that is not affected.
returning the behavior to pre-3.11 Python

patch_review.observation: The Pyramid change makes the static view's path-security check treat a null character in any path element as invalid, so the request is refused with not-found. The CPython change makes the path normalization routine keep the full string length instead of cutting at the first null byte, which is the root cause. This matches the card's cause (truncation during normalization letting a dot-dot element escape the static root by one level) and its prevention (reject null bytes, and run a fixed Python or Pyramid release).

patterns.title: Reference names joined to the .git directory can escape it and read arbitrary files
patterns.cause: To resolve some git references, the library reads files from the .git directory. In some places the file name comes from the user. The code joins the base directory with that user-given string and does not check whether the final path is outside the base directory. A name containing parent-directory segments can therefore point at any file on the system.
preconditions: The application passes user-controlled strings as reference or revision names to repository lookups such as commit, tree, or index diff.
The library joins the string to the .git directory path without confirming the result stays inside it.
The installed GitPython version predates 3.1.37.
patterns.prevention: Treat reference names as untrusted. After joining a name to the base directory, confirm the final path is still inside the repository's .git directory before opening it, ideally after resolving symlinks. Also validate that reference names are well formed and reject those containing traversal segments or absolute paths. Upgrade to GitPython 3.1.37 or later. In application code, validate user-supplied revision strings before handing them to the library.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the issue as blind: file contents could not be shown. Impact is limited to things like probing whether a file exists, or a denial of service from reading a large or endless file. The reporter says other code paths may also reach the flaw, and only three were confirmed. The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail. One advisory says the issue was not yet addressed, while the CVE record says it was addressed in 3.1.37.

fixtures.scenario: An application passes a user-supplied revision string with parent-directory segments to a repository commit lookup. The library joins it to the .git directory and reads a file outside that directory.
The application validates the reference name, and the library confirms the resolved path is inside the .git directory before reading. Traversal names are rejected.

citations.quote: That code joins the base directory with a user given string without checking if the final path is located outside the base directory.
This allows an attacker to make GitPython read any file from the system.
This issue has been addressed in version 3.1.37.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops traversal by validating the reference name before any file is read. The first commit rejects any name containing parent-directory segments in the internal reference lookup helper. The follow-up replaces that with a full check against git's reference-name format rules, which also rejects leading slashes, double slashes, control characters, and other malformed names. The fix does not check the resolved path against the .git directory.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through uploaded SVG images in Zope
patterns.cause: Zope has stored XSS involving uploaded SVG images containing malicious code. An attacker must upload an image and trick a user into following a specially crafted link, allowing script execution in the site's context. The affected File and Image serving path lacked the content-type-based attachment handling added by the fix. The advisory states that embedding the SVG as an image tag's source is not vulnerable.
preconditions: An affected, unpatched Zope installation; the advisory identifies fixes in 4.8.10 and 5.8.5.
The site allows untrusted users to upload images.
An attacker uploads an SVG image containing malicious code.
A user is tricked into following a specially crafted link.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a patched Zope release, such as 4.8.10 or 5.8.5. In index_html, the fix adds an attachment Content-Disposition header when a nonempty stored content type is outside the default inline allowlist. The list includes PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, plain text and PDF. The filename comes from the object ID, gains an extension when it has no dot, and is UTF-8 percent-encoded. Environment variables configure the lists and select denylist mode, whose defaults include SVG, HTML and JavaScript types. Keep these active types excluded from inline delivery. Restrict the Add Documents, Images, and Files permission to trusted roles; only Manager holds it by default.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify the crafted URL or establish that any direct object URL suffices, that a victim must be authenticated, or that HTML and JavaScript are confirmed exploit cases. The shown fix covers index_html; other serving paths are not established. Subclasses can override the policy. Empty content types do not force download, and matching uses the stored type exactly. Expanding the allowlist or omitting active types from the denylist can leave them inline; an empty denylist disables this protection. The response body remains unchanged, so the fix does not sanitize SVG content. The sources do not establish behavior after downloading or serving it elsewhere. Permission restrictions limit upload access but do not repair unpatched code.

fixtures.scenario: An unpatched Zope 5.8.4 site lets an untrusted community role upload images. An attacker uploads an SVG file that contains malicious code, then sends a victim a crafted link. The victim follows the link and the code runs in the context of the site.

The site runs Zope 5.8.5 or later, or 4.8.10 or later. The permission to add documents, images, and files is held only by the Manager role, so untrusted users cannot upload an SVG file. SVG images are shown only through image tags that name them as the source.

citations.quote: There is a stored cross site scripting vulnerability for SVG images.
To exploit the vulnerability, an attacker would first need to upload an image, and then trick a user into following a specially crafted link.
All versions of Zope are impacted on sites that allow untrusted users to upload images.
Patches are available in Zope 4.8.10 and 5.8.5.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds an inline allowlist of safe content types, plus an optional denylist mode, both configurable through environment variables and class attributes. The File and Image view method (index_html) now sets an attachment Content-Disposition header with a filename, generated when the id has no extension, for any type not allowed inline. This forces SVG, HTML and JavaScript to download instead of rendering in the site origin, which matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through the unquoted title property in Zope Management Interface breadcrumbs
patterns.cause: The title property, available on most Zope objects, can hold script code. The Zope Management Interface (ZMI) displays it unquoted in the breadcrumbs element, so stored script runs in the browser of anyone who views the affected object.
preconditions: The deployment runs Zope 4 or Zope 5 below the patched releases 4.8.11 and 5.8.6.
Someone can store attacker-chosen text in the title property of a Zope object.
A user views that object in the ZMI, where the breadcrumbs element renders the title without quoting.
patterns.prevention: Treat the title property as untrusted text wherever the ZMI renders it, including the breadcrumbs element. Quote or escape it for the HTML context at output time, so stored markup is shown as plain text and never interpreted. Upgrade to Zope 4.8.11 or 5.8.6 or later, which the advisories name as the patched releases. As a workaround until then, keep editing and viewing of Zope objects in the ZMI limited to Manager users, which the advisory says is the default.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patches change the code, so the exact escaping approach is not covered here. They do not say whether other properties or other ZMI views have the same flaw. They do not say how effective the Manager-only workaround is when a Manager user is the author or the viewer of the malicious title. Only breadcrumbs rendering is named as the affected output.

fixtures.scenario: A user with permission to edit an object sets its title property to text containing script code. An administrator later opens that object in the ZMI on an unpatched Zope 4 or 5 install. The breadcrumbs element prints the title unquoted, so the script runs in the administrator's browser session.

The same title text is stored, but the ZMI quotes the title when it renders the breadcrumbs, or the site runs Zope 4.8.11 or 5.8.6 or later. The administrator sees the text displayed literally and no script runs.

citations.quote: because the title property is displayed unquoted in the breadcrumbs element
The title property, available on most Zope objects, can be used to store script code
Make sure only Manager users can edit and view Zope objects in the Zope Management Interface. This is the default.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the ZMI tabs template so the breadcrumb list element's class attribute, which is built from the object's title or id, is now HTML-quoted. Before, the title value went into the attribute unescaped, so stored markup could break out of the attribute and run script. This matches the card's cause (an unquoted title in the breadcrumbs) and its prevention (escape at output time).

patterns.title: Recursive URL crawling must not pivot from an external server to an internal server
patterns.cause: The advisories identify SSRF (CWE-918) in LangChain before 0.0.317 in RecursiveUrlLoader: crawling can proceed from an external server to an internal server. Separately, the sitemap diff shows that SitemapLoader lacked a default same-site restriction, although optional URL filters existed. Malicious sitemap content could cause requests to other domains, including internal services, and fetched data could leak into downstream systems such as indexes.
preconditions: For the advisory's vulnerability, the application uses RecursiveUrlLoader from LangChain before 0.0.317.
The recursive crawl encounters a link that allows it to proceed from an external server to an internal server.
For the separate sitemap scenario, the application loads attacker-modified sitemap content containing a destination permitted by any configured URL filters.
Requests to internal services require those services to be reachable from the loader's execution environment.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to LangChain 0.0.317 or later for the advisory's recursive-loader issue, and retain the documented default domain restriction. For SitemapLoader, use the shown fix and keep its default restriction enabled: parse_sitemap skips remote sitemap entries whose parsed scheme or network location differs from the sitemap's. Network location includes any port and user information, not just the hostname. Apply permitted URL patterns through filter_urls, including for local sitemaps; these are regular expressions, so escape literal special characters. For remote sitemaps, the domain restriction takes precedence over those patterns. Restrict crawl submissions and generally deny crawlers network access to internal servers.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish the sitemap change's affected versions, release version, or connection to this CVE. The recursive-loader diff adds security documentation and tightens a type annotation; it does not show a new request-validation implementation. The sitemap restriction is optional and bypassed for local files. Same-host sites remain within the documented domain boundary. The shown comparison does not validate resolved IP addresses or enforce a scheme allowlist; overall redirect, DNS, and non-default-scheme handling is not established by these excerpts. Domain restrictions mitigate SSRF but do not eliminate it.

fixtures.scenario: A crawl starts at a page on an external server that links to a host on the internal network. The loader follows that link, so the crawler fetches content from the internal server on behalf of whoever controls the external page.

A crawl starts at a page on an external server that links to a host on the internal network. The loader refuses to proceed from the external server to the internal server, and the internal host is never requested.

citations.quote: LangChain before 0.0.317 allows SSRF via document_loaders/recursive_url_loader.py because crawling can proceed from an external server to an internal server.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a restrict_to_same_domain option to the sitemap loader, on by default. When the sitemap is remote, it skips any listed URL whose scheme and host differ from the sitemap's, and the existing URL pattern filter is applied afterward. The local-file exception, the opt-out, and the shared-host caveat all appear in the documentation changes. The recursive URL loader only gets a security note, since its same-domain default already existed. The card's cause, prevention, and limitations match this.

patterns.title: Stored XSS via uploaded avatar served with a file-extension-derived content type
patterns.cause: Avatar upload validation only confirmed the file could be read as an image and trusted the client-supplied Content-Type. The uploaded file extension was never validated on the server and was saved as given. Avatars were served by Django's built-in serve view, which picks the response Content-Type from the URL extension, so a file named with an html extension was rendered as a web page.
preconditions: An authenticated user can upload an avatar and control its filename and declared mimetype
The server does not validate the uploaded file extension (only client-side checks exist)
Uploaded avatars are served by Django's built-in serve view, which derives Content-Type from the URL extension
A victim visits the crafted avatar URL on the application's origin
patterns.prevention: Validate the file extension on the server side, not only in client-side code, and do not trust user-controlled inputs such as the declared mimetype or filename. Stop serving uploaded avatars through Django's built-in serve view and use a purpose-built controller that sets the content type itself. Optionally store file content in the database instead of the filesystem to reduce other file-related risks.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change beyond saying version 1.9.2 fixes the issue. They do not specify the allowed extension list, the content-type handling details of a replacement controller, or whether additional response headers should be used. Other remediation options are listed only as advice.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user uploads a JPEG whose metadata comment holds script markup, renames it with an html extension, and sends an image mimetype. The server accepts it and serves it by extension as HTML, so a visiting victim runs the script.

The server checks the extension on its own side and rejects an html filename despite the image mimetype. Avatars are returned by a dedicated controller that sets an image content type, so embedded markup is never rendered as a page.

citations.quote: The issue with the Django `serve` view is that it determines the `Content-Type` of the response by the file extension in the URL path.
The only file extension validation is performed on the client-side, which can be easily bypassed.
Validate the file extension on the server side, not in client-side code.

patterns.title: SSRF filter bypass through one-time DNS check, redirects and DNS rebinding in URL import
patterns.cause: The advisory describes URL imports validating a single DNS lookup before the request, allowing HTTP redirects or DNS rebinding to bypass the check. The diff addresses a related weakness in validate_ip: it blocked the unspecified IPv4 address, IPv4 loopback, and three private IPv4 ranges, but omitted link-local, shared address space, other reserved IPv4 blocks, and IPv6 ranges. These omissions could allow access to internal services at otherwise reachable addresses.
preconditions: The server imports an attacker-supplied URL.
SSRF_PROTECTION_ENABLED is enabled, but validation uses the advisory's pre-request lookup or the diff's limited deny list.
The URL leads to an omitted address range, follows an attacker-selected redirect to an internal address, or uses DNS answers that change between validation and the request.
An internal web service or cloud metadata API is reachable from the server at the target address.
patterns.prevention: Validate the actual connected peer's address against the deny list before saving responses, including responses reached through redirects. Expand validate_ip's defaults to cover the listed IPv4 and IPv6 special-use ranges: unspecified, loopback, private, link-local, shared, protocol-assignment, documentation, benchmarking, multicast, reserved, broadcast, translation, tunneling, discard, ORCHIDv2, unique-local and IPv4-mapped ranges. Include internal cloud API ranges. Keep default bans enabled, allow additional operator-specified subnets, warn that disabling defaults is risky, and report the matched blocked range.
patterns.limitations: The advisories report versions before 1.11.0 affected and testing on 1.8.2. This diff expands and configures the deny list; it does not show a new DNS rebinding or redirect fix. Tests use mocked connected-peer addresses and include an existing redirect rejection test, but the request implementation is absent, so validation of every redirect hop is not established. SSRF protection defaults to off. Disabling default bans leaves only operator-specified bans. The sources do not establish exploitability of every omitted range or exhaustive coverage of all special-use or site-specific networks.

fixtures.scenario: A user imports a task file from a URL on an attacker host. The name resolves to a public address during validation, then to 127.0.0.1 when the request is sent, or the host answers with a 301 redirect to an internal server.

The server checks the IP address of the connection it actually makes and applies the deny list to it, including after any redirect, so a rebinding name or a redirect to an internal address is rejected.

citations.quote: The issue here is the SSRF validation is only performed before the request is sent, and does not validate the destination IP address.
Before saving any responses, validate the destination IP address is not in the deny list.
This protection can be bypassed by either using HTTP redirection or performing a DNS rebinding attack.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the validation function's tiny deny list (unspecified address plus four private IPv4 ranges) with a broad list of reserved and special-use IPv4 and IPv6 ranges. It adds settings to keep the defaults on and to let operators add their own banned subnets, and the error now names the blocked range. The card's cause, prevention and limitations match this, and it correctly notes that the diff does not change redirect or DNS rebinding handling.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through unsanitized DAG parameter descriptions in Apache Airflow
patterns.cause: Airflow had stored XSS through DAG parameter descriptions, which the advisory describes as allowing unbounded, unsanitized JavaScript. The trigger view marked HTML descriptions and custom HTML form definitions as safe markup. The shared wrapped_markdown function also allowed raw HTML in descriptions and DAG documentation. A DAG author could supply malicious content that executed in another user's browser when the affected content was displayed.
preconditions: Apache Airflow 2.6.0 through 2.7.3 is in use, as stated by the advisory.
An attacker can author or modify a DAG and control its parameter descriptions, custom HTML form definitions, or Markdown documentation.
The affected rendering path trusts author-supplied HTML or permits raw HTML in Markdown.
Another user views the affected DAG content or trigger form in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Airflow 2.8.0 or newer. Keep the webserver option allow_raw_html_descriptions disabled, its default. The fix makes wrapped_markdown escape raw HTML while retaining Markdown formatting and gates trusted HTML descriptions and custom forms behind that option. With HTML disabled, custom form definitions are removed from prepared form data; legacy HTML descriptions fall back to escaped text when no Markdown description is present. Markdown descriptions take precedence. The UI displays migration and deprecation warnings; migrate descriptions to description_md. Enable raw HTML only when DAG authors are trusted, since it permits potentially unsafe JavaScript.
patterns.limitations: The diff changes trigger-form preparation and the shared Markdown helper; it does not establish exhaustive coverage of all rendering paths or other DAG fields. Disabling raw HTML changes HTML formatting and removes custom widgets from the form, but does not establish that DAG execution breaks. Opting in restores unsafe HTML support. The advisory rules out browser-sandbox escape and additional server-side manipulation beyond the DAG author's existing abilities, not all additional client-side impact: misleading viewers remains possible. No description-size limit is added, and the supplied tests check HTML escaping rather than every possible XSS payload.

fixtures.scenario: A DAG author writes a parameter description that contains script markup. Another user opens the DAG details in the browser. The description is rendered without sanitization, so the script runs in that user's session and can change what they see.

A DAG author writes a parameter description that contains script markup. The application sanitizes or escapes the text and limits its length when it renders it. The viewer sees inert text, and no script runs in the browser.

citations.quote: allows a DAG author to add an unbounded and not-sanitized javascript in the parameter description field of the DAG
This Javascript can be executed on the client side of any of the user who looks at the tasks in the browser sandbox.
Users of Apache Airflow are recommended to upgrade to version 2.8.0 or newer to mitigate the risk associated with this vulnerability

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a webserver option, off by default, that controls raw HTML. The Markdown helper now turns off raw HTML unless the option is on, and the trigger form view only marks legacy HTML descriptions and custom form HTML as safe when it is on. Otherwise it drops the custom form, shows the old HTML description as plain escaped text, and flashes a warning pointing authors to the Markdown description field.

patterns.title: Unvalidated package folder on edit allows writing downloads outside the downloads directory
patterns.cause: pyLoad restricts the folder name when a package is created, so it stays inside the downloads folder. The package edit path in the web UI takes the folder value from the request and stores it with no equivalent restriction. An authenticated user can therefore point a package at any directory on the server filesystem, and the downloaded file is written there. If that directory holds pyLoad event scripts, this can lead to command execution.
preconditions: The attacker is an authenticated web UI user who can create and edit packages.
The package edit handler accepts a folder value from the request and passes it on without the restriction applied at creation.
The attacker can make the server download a file they control, for example from a link to a server they run.
The target directory is writable by the pyLoad process, such as a scripts directory that pyLoad processes and runs.
patterns.prevention: Treat the package folder as untrusted input on every path that sets it, not only at creation. The edit operation must enforce the same rule as package creation: the resulting storage location must stay within the downloads folder. Apply the check in the shared code that stores package data, so no entry point can skip it. Reject or neutralize folder values that name locations outside the downloads root, and verify the final location is inside that root before any file is written.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the missing check on the edit path and a proof of concept that abuses script directories. They do not describe the upstream fix, so the exact validation approach is not specified here. They also do not assess whether the creation-time filter is sufficient on its own. The CVE record only labels the issue as unrestricted file upload, and the sources give no affected-version range beyond 0.5.0. The scripts-based command execution depends on pyLoad settings and on how it processes script directories. This card does not cover hardening of those features.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user creates a package with a valid link, then edits it and sets the folder field to an absolute path of a pyLoad scripts directory. After the package is restarted, the downloaded file is stored in that directory instead of under the downloads folder.

An authenticated user edits a package and submits a folder value naming a location outside the downloads folder. The server rejects or neutralizes the value, and any file the package downloads stays inside the downloads folder.

citations.quote: However, when editing packages there is no prevention in place and a user can just pick any arbitrary directory in the filesystem.
a filter is applied to make sure it can't traverse directories and stays within /downloads.
A web UI user can store files anywhere on the pyLoad server and gain command execution by abusing scripts.
pyLoad 0.5.0 is vulnerable to Unrestricted File Upload.

patch_review.observation: The fix hardens the web UI package edit handler, which previously passed the folder value from the request straight into the package data. It now strips leading path separators and parent-directory sequences from that value. It also adds parent-directory replacement to the folder cleanup used when a package is created. This matches the card's cause, where the edit path lacked the restriction applied at creation, and its direction of enforcing the same rule on edit.

patterns.title: Ray job submission API reachable by remote attackers allows arbitrary code execution
patterns.cause: Ray's job submission API allows remote arbitrary code execution when accessible to untrusted callers. Ray assumes a strictly controlled network, and the diff warns that exposing internal Ray ports to untrusted clients is unsafe. This does not establish that every Ray port executes code. The supplied change adds exposure detection tooling without changing API request handling.
preconditions: A Ray deployment exposes the job submission API; the advisory names versions 2.6.3 and 2.8.0.
An untrusted remote caller can reach and use that API. Public internet exposure is one possible route, but a public IP alone does not establish access.
patterns.prevention: Treat job submission as a code execution interface. Keep Ray inside a strictly controlled network and block untrusted access to its ports with network controls such as firewalls or security groups. Use the added check_open_ports CLI function to check exposure; repeating checks after deployment or network changes is general hardening. It schedules listening-port discovery on each alive node and asks an external service to check internet reachability. Validate reported exposure and, if confirmed, immediately shut down the cluster and remediate it. Within the controlled environment, Ray 2.52.0 and later offer optional token authentication as an additional layer.
patterns.limitations: The checker detects exposure, not attacks, and enforces no access controls. Results reflect the check time and may be false positives or miss exposure. Discovery is limited to recognized processes and accessible connection data; failed node checks are logged and omitted, so a clean summary can be incomplete. By default, port lists go to an external service, which sees the request's source address; no public-address field is sent. The service URL is configurable, and external requests may conflict with local policy. The sources do not establish an SSRF mechanism, the full affected range, the tool's first release, or token authentication's configuration and coverage. The vendor disputes the report on intended-use grounds.

fixtures.scenario: A team runs a Ray cluster and makes the job submission API reachable from a broad or public network with no token authentication. A remote attacker sends a job to the API and gets arbitrary code executed on the cluster.
A team runs Ray inside a strictly controlled network that untrusted hosts cannot reach. They run version 2.52.0 or later with token authentication enabled, so only authorized callers can submit jobs.

citations.quote: Anyscale Ray allows a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the job submission API.
Ray, as stated in its documentation, is not intended for use outside of a strictly controlled network environment.
customers at version 2.52.0 and later can choose to use token authentication.

patch_review.observation: The commit does not change how Ray handles requests. It adds a command line check that finds the listening ports of Ray processes on each alive node, asks an external service (overridable by option) to probe them from the internet, and warns that exposed Ray ports allow arbitrary code execution. The card's cause (Ray assumes a trusted network) and its prevention (network isolation plus this verification command) match the diff.

patterns.title: SQL injection through a user-specified quote in the Superset where_in Jinja macro
patterns.cause: The where_in Jinja macro in Apache Superset lets users specify a quote. Combined with a carefully crafted statement, that user-chosen quote allows SQL injection.
preconditions: Running Apache Superset before 2.1.3, or from 3.0.0 before 3.0.2 (the CVE record says before 2.1.2 for the 2.x line).
Jinja templating is used in queries, and the where_in macro is called.
A user can supply the quote argument together with a crafted statement.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Apache Superset to 2.1.3 or 3.0.2 or later, as the advisories recommend. In any similar templating helper, do not let a caller-chosen quote character decide how values are delimited in generated SQL. Fix the delimiting inside the helper rather than trusting user input.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the internal fix, the exact macro arguments, or any workaround short of upgrading. The CVE record lists 2.1.2 as the last affected 2.x version, while the GitHub and PYSEC advisories say before 2.1.3. This card therefore does not claim whether 2.1.2 is affected.

fixtures.scenario: A Superset 3.0.1 deployment lets users write Jinja queries. A user calls the where_in macro with a custom quote value and a crafted statement, which breaks out of the intended value list and alters the SQL.
The deployment runs Superset 3.0.2 or 2.1.3 or later, where the advisories say the issue is fixed. The same where_in call with a custom quote and crafted statement does not alter the query.

citations.quote: A where_in JINJA macro allows users to specify a quote, which combined with a carefully crafted statement would allow for SQL injection
Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.1.3 or 3.0.2, which fixes the issue.
This issue affects Apache Superset: before 2.1.2, from 3.0.0 before 3.0.2.

patch_review.observation: The fix drops the caller-supplied quote argument from the where_in macro. Values are now rendered by SQLAlchemy as dialect-aware literals through the database dialect, so quoting and escaping are no longer user-controlled. If a quote argument is still passed, it is ignored and a warning comment is appended to the output. This matches the card's cause (user-chosen quote enables injection) and its prevention (do not let the caller pick the delimiter, and fix delimiting inside the helper).

patterns.title: XCom pickle deserialization can be reached even when XCom pickling is disabled
patterns.cause: In Apache Airflow before 2.8.1, XCom deserialization could bypass the setting that disables pickling. With pickling disabled, the deserialize routine first attempted UTF-8 decoding and JSON parsing. On a JSON decoding or Unicode decoding error, it fell back to unpickling the stored bytes. A DAG author able to poison XCom data could therefore trigger unsafe deserialization despite pickling being disabled.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version is earlier than 2.8.1.
XCom pickling is disabled.
The attacker can author a DAG, which the advisory identifies as required, and can poison XCom data with crafted pickle data.
Airflow later deserializes the poisoned value, and UTF-8 decoding or JSON parsing fails, triggering the pickle fallback.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade apache-airflow to 2.8.1 or later. The fix removes the pickle fallback from the disabled-pickling branch, leaving UTF-8 decoding and JSON parsing errors to propagate. Do not rely on the disabled-pickling setting alone on affected versions. As general hardening, enforce deserialization settings on every applicable read path, use a strict data format without falling back to an unsafe deserializer, and restrict who can author DAGs.
patterns.limitations: The updated test confirms that a previously pickled XCom value raises a Unicode decoding error when read with pickling disabled; the sources do not prescribe migration or purging. The shown production change removes this fallback and leaves pickling-enabled behavior unchanged, but does not establish broader security guarantees or assess all deserialization paths. The advisory rates the issue low because exploitation requires a DAG author; alternative attacker roles are not established. Restricting DAG authorship is general hardening, not an upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 2.8.0 deployment has XCom pickling turned off and the operator assumes XComs are therefore safe. A user with DAG authoring rights crafts a task that writes poisoned XCom data, and the data is deserialized later despite the setting.

The deployment runs Airflow 2.8.1 or later with XCom pickling turned off. The same DAG author cannot use the bypass to get poisoned XCom data deserialized, and DAG authoring rights are limited to trusted users.

citations.quote: Apache Airflow, versions before 2.8.1, have a vulnerability that allows a potential attacker to poison the XCom data
This vulnerability is considered low since it requires a DAG author to exploit it.
Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.8.1 or later, which fixes this issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the fallback in the XCom deserialization path used when pickling is disabled. Previously a JSON or Unicode decoding failure led to unpickling the raw bytes; now the value is parsed only as JSON and any failure raises an error. Tests were updated so reading a pickled value with pickling disabled now raises a decoding error.

patterns.title: Symlink in a malicious Ansible role overwrites files outside the extraction path
patterns.cause: During ansible-galaxy role installation from a tar archive, member names were sanitized but symlink targets were not. The supplied exploit archive places a symlink to an outside target before a regular file with the same member name, allowing extraction to write through the link outside the installation directory. The advisory classifies this as absolute path traversal and describes victim execution of a malicious role; the regression test targets installation without running the role.
preconditions: The victim installs an attacker-crafted role archive using the vulnerable ansible-galaxy extraction path; the regression test uses a local tar file.
The archive contains a symlink targeting a location outside the role installation directory whose target escapes the existing name sanitization.
In the demonstrated exploit, a later regular file member has the same name as the symlink, allowing extraction to write through that link.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to an Ansible release containing the fix. The patch applies sanitization to both member names and link targets for regular-file and symlink members. It removes the archive parent directory text, drops empty path components, and drops components that traverse upward, start with a tilde, or contain a dollar sign, warning for the latter three cases before rebuilding the path. As general hardening, install roles only from trusted sources, verify resolved destinations remain inside the installation directory, and refuse file writes through previously extracted symlinks.
patterns.limitations: Affected and fixed versions and remote delivery routes are not established by these sources. The patch filters path components rather than explicitly resolving final destinations or refusing writes through existing symlinks. Its comment warns that filtering can break installation. The regression test expects installation failure and absence of the outside target file, but does not establish that every illegal name causes failure. The shown change covers role installation; it does not establish the safety or vulnerability of other archive handling paths.

fixtures.scenario: A user downloads a role from an untrusted party. The role contains a symlink that points to a file outside the extraction directory. During extraction or execution, a write goes through the symlink and overwrites that outside file.

The same role is processed by an implementation that resolves the real destination of every entry, including symlink targets, and rejects any entry that resolves outside the extraction directory. The outside file is left unchanged and the role is refused.

citations.quote: A symlink can be used to overwrite a file outside of the extraction path.
This flaw allows an attacker to craft a malicious Ansible role and make the victim execute the role.

patch_review.observation: The fix applies the same path-component sanitization that was previously applied only to the member name to the symlink target as well. It drops empty components (which turns absolute paths into relative ones) and components that are parent-directory markers, start with a tilde, or contain a dollar sign, and it warns about each illegal one. A new integration test builds an archive with a symlink and a same-named file and checks that the outside file is not overwritten and the install fails.

patterns.title: Arbitrary file read through the file route of a publicly exposed Gradio app
patterns.cause: Gradio versions before 4.11.0 had a flaw in the file route that allowed file traversal. An attacker who knew the path of a file on the host could read it. Regular browser URLs did not trigger the flaw, but programmatic tools such as curl could, so the server could not rely on the client to keep requests well formed. The same route could also be abused for server-side request forgery.
preconditions: The application runs a gradio version earlier than 4.11.0.
The app is reachable at a public URL, for example created with the share option or hosted on Hugging Face Spaces.
The attacker knows or can guess the path of a file to look for.
The attacker sends requests with a programmatic tool rather than a normal browser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade gradio to 4.11.0 or later, which fixes both the file traversal and the server-side request forgery problems in the file route. In any similar file-serving endpoint, do not assume that clients send well-formed URLs, because a browser can behave differently from a raw HTTP tool. The server should itself check that every requested path refers only to files the application meant to expose, and it should not fetch arbitrary remote locations on behalf of a caller.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact malformed request shape or the mechanics of the upstream fix, so this card gives only the upgrade direction and general guidance. They do not say which files or deployments were actually exposed, and they give no detail on how the request forgery was carried out. Apps that are not publicly reachable are described as less exposed only by implication.

fixtures.scenario: A demo built with a gradio version before 4.11.0 is shared through a public link. A remote user with curl requests a known file path through the file route and receives the contents of a file outside the intended files.
The same demo runs gradio 4.11.0 or later. A raw request for an arbitrary host file through the file route is not served, and the route cannot be used for server-side request forgery.

citations.quote: This was not possible through regular URLs passed into a browser, but it was possible through the use of programmatic tools
an attacker could access arbitrary files on a machine running a Gradio app with a public URL
also contained a vulnerability that made it possible to use it for SSRF attacks
This issue has been patched in version 4.11.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the path containment helper so a relative path is rejected if parent-directory segments appear anywhere in it, not only at the start, which closes traversal through a subdirectory followed by parent segments. It also changes the file route so a URL-like path is recognized by a purely syntactic check instead of a helper that contacted the remote address, which removes the server-side request forgery. Both match the card's cause and its prevention advice.

patterns.title: Command injection in PaddlePaddle get_online_pass_interval (CVE-2023-52310)
patterns.cause: In PaddlePaddle before 2.6.0, get_online_pass_interval in the incubate distributed fleet utilities concatenates its days and hours arguments into shell commands executed through os.popen for expansion. Shell metacharacters in attacker-controlled values can therefore execute arbitrary operating system commands.
preconditions: The application uses PaddlePaddle before 2.6.0.
The deployment calls get_online_pass_interval.
An attacker can influence the days or hours arguments passed to the function.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade PaddlePaddle to 2.6.0 or later, the boundary identified by the advisories. The supplied fix adds assertions intended to reject pipes, semicolons, backslashes, forward slashes and parentheses before the shell calls. As general hardening, replace shell-based expansion with direct string processing where feasible. If an external process is needed, use separate arguments without a shell. If shell use remains necessary, validate against a strict allow-list based on the actual input grammar.
patterns.limitations: The fix retains shell execution. Its checks do not reject backticks, dollar signs, ampersands, redirection characters or newlines. The hours check mistakenly checks the already-processed days list for a closing parenthesis instead of checking hours. Python optimization can disable assertions. These checks therefore do not eliminate the underlying shell-injection risk. The sources do not establish how an attacker reaches the function or gains control of its arguments, and they do not define a complete safe input grammar.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs PaddlePaddle 2.5.x and passes externally supplied values to get_online_pass_interval. A crafted value leads to execution of arbitrary operating system commands.
The service runs PaddlePaddle 2.6.0 or later. Any value that reaches an external process is validated and passed as a separate argument, so it is never interpreted as command text.

citations.quote: PaddlePaddle before 2.6.0 has a command injection in get_online_pass_interval.
This resulted in the ability to execute arbitrary commands on the operating system.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds assertion checks that reject a few shell characters (pipe, semicolon, backslash, slash, and parentheses) in the days and hours arguments before each is passed to a shell echo via os.popen. It does not remove the shell call. The hours check mistakenly tests the days value for a closing parenthesis, which matches the card's limitations.

patterns.title: Command injection in PaddlePaddle _wget_download before version 2.6.0
patterns.cause: PaddlePaddle before 2.6.0 has command injection in _wget_download. The function inserts the url and temporary output path into a wget command string executed through a shell, allowing shell metacharacters in those values to alter command execution. The upstream change adds an assertion that the parsed url scheme is http or https; an unexpected scheme alone does not establish command injection.
preconditions: PaddlePaddle before 2.6.0 is used, according to the advisories.
The application or workflow reaches _wget_download.

Exploitation through the shown command construction requires attacker influence over a value inserted into the shell command, such as the url or output path; the sources do not establish how that influence is obtained.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to PaddlePaddle 2.6.0 or later, which the advisories do not list as affected. The shown upstream change asserts that the parsed url scheme is http or https before constructing the command. As general hardening, enforce scheme validation without relying on assertions and avoid interpolating external values into shell commands: use an argument-list invocation with shell execution disabled or an in-process HTTP client.
patterns.limitations: The diff retains shell execution and unquoted interpolation of the url and temporary output path. An http or https scheme does not neutralize shell metacharacters, and Python assertions can be disabled, so the diff does not demonstrate complete prevention. Exceptions within the new try block are logged and return false instead of propagating; successful calls still return the destination path. The sources do not establish attacker access, caller validation, or whether other helpers are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs PaddlePaddle 2.5.x and uses a feature that calls _wget_download with a value an outside party can influence. The attacker gets arbitrary commands executed on the host operating system.
The same service runs PaddlePaddle 2.6.0 or later, and any value that reaches a download step is handled as data and not as command text. The download does not result in arbitrary command execution.

citations.quote: PaddlePaddle before 2.6.0 has a command injection in _wget_download.
This resulted in the ability to execute arbitrary commands on the operating system.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check at the start of the download helper that parses the url and only accepts the http and https schemes. The whole body is also wrapped so any failure is logged and false is returned instead of an exception being raised. The command is still built as a string and run through a shell, which the card's limitations section correctly notes.

patterns.title: PaddlePaddle command injection in convert_shape_compare (CVE-2023-52314)
patterns.cause: In PaddlePaddle before 2.6.0, the dygraph-to-static helper convert_shape_compare concatenated comparison operator strings into expressions evaluated by Python's eval function, without checking them against a fixed set of operators. Both Paddle Variable or Value inputs and other inputs reached dynamic evaluation. An attacker-controlled operator string reaching evaluation could execute arbitrary Python code in the host process, including operating system commands.
preconditions: PaddlePaddle older than 2.6.0 is installed.
The attacker can control an operator string passed to convert_shape_compare.
The helper is called with arguments that allow the malicious operator string to reach evaluation.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade PaddlePaddle to 2.6.0 or later, following the advisory's affected-version boundary. The supplied fix removes convert_shape_compare and its package-level export. As general hardening, avoid evaluating expressions built from untrusted strings; map supported comparison operators to functions through a fixed allow-list and reject unsupported values.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish how attackers could supply operator strings in a deployment, including whether models or converted code provide such a route. The removed tests demonstrate direct calls, so execution does not inherently require a conversion workflow. The diff does not independently establish which release contains the removal or assess other dynamic evaluation sites. No deployment-specific workaround is documented.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs PaddlePaddle 2.5.x and exercises convert_shape_compare. Under the advisory, an attacker who can influence this path could execute arbitrary commands on the host operating system.
The same service runs PaddlePaddle 2.6.0 or later, which is outside the affected range named by the advisories for convert_shape_compare.

citations.quote: PaddlePaddle before 2.6.0 has a command injection in convert_shape_compare.
This resulted in the ability to execute arbitrary commands on the operating system.

patch_review.observation: The fix deletes the convert_shape_compare helper, its public export from the dy2static package, and its tests. The helper built comparison expressions from operator strings and ran them through Python's dynamic evaluation without validating the operator, so removing it eliminates the code injection path. This matches the card's cause and its upgrade-or-allow-list prevention.

patterns.title: Mercurial revision in pip VCS URL injects options into hg clone
patterns.cause: When pip installed from a Mercurial VCS URL, the revision given in that URL was passed to the hg clone call in a way that let it be read as a command-line option. An attacker-chosen revision could therefore add arbitrary Mercurial configuration options.
preconditions: pip older than version 23.3 is used
The package is installed from a Mercurial VCS URL, meaning one that starts with hg+
The revision part of the URL is controlled or influenced by an untrusted party
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to pip 23.3 or later. In code that builds version-control commands, make sure a user-supplied revision can only be interpreted as a revision value and never as an option to the clone command. Treat revisions in requirement URLs as untrusted input, and review requirement files from third parties before installing hg+ URLs.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so the exact mechanism is not covered here. They also do not say which configuration options are dangerous, or whether other version control systems are affected. They only state that users who do not install from Mercurial are not affected.

fixtures.scenario: A requirements file from an untrusted contributor lists an hg+ URL whose revision text looks like a Mercurial configuration option. pip older than 23.3 passes it to hg clone, which applies the injected configuration.
The same requirements file is installed with pip 23.3 or later, or the project has no hg+ URLs. The revision is not treated as a clone option, and installs from other sources are unaffected.

citations.quote: the specified Mercurial revision could be used to inject arbitrary configuration options to the
Controlling the Mercurial configuration can modify how and which repository is installed.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes how pip builds the Mercurial revision arguments. The flag and the revision are now one combined argument in the equals form, instead of two separate arguments, so an attacker-supplied revision cannot be parsed as its own option. A unit test was updated to match. This agrees with the card's cause and its prevention direction.

patterns.title: Arbitrary file upload via HTTP PUT to an MLflow server (path traversal class)
patterns.cause: The advisory reports arbitrary file writes through HTTP PUT in MLflow. The diff shows that validate_path_is_safe accepted Windows drive-relative paths despite checks for absolute paths and slash-delimited parent-directory segments. These paths refer to a drive's current directory and suggest a path traversal bypass (CWE-22). The fix adds a Windows-only check for a colon in the second character position. The supplied diff does not demonstrate the complete path from an upload request to a write outside the intended root.
preconditions: The server runs on Windows for the drive-relative bypass addressed by the added check.
A client-controlled path reaches validate_path_is_safe and a subsequent file write; the advisory identifies HTTP PUT, but the diff does not show this call chain.
The deployed validator lacks the added Windows second-character colon check; the affected release range is not supplied.
patterns.prevention: Use an MLflow release containing this fix. In validate_path_is_safe, reject paths whose second character is a colon when running on Windows, including drive-relative forms without a separator after the colon. Preserve existing absolute-path and parent-directory checks and rejection of the tested backslash traversal forms. The new check concerns a specific character position, not drive designators anywhere in a path. As general hardening, validate client-supplied paths before use, verify canonical destination containment within the intended root, and restrict access to write endpoints.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify the upload endpoint or parameter, show all validator callers, establish the complete escape mechanism, or specify affected and fixed releases. Windows is explicit in the added condition, but the advisory does not establish that every affected deployment is Windows-only. Authentication requirements and deployment exposure are unspecified. Canonical containment and access restrictions are general hardening, not changes shown by the diff.

fixtures.scenario: A client sends an HTTP PUT request to an MLflow server with a destination that points outside the intended storage area. The server writes the supplied content to that location, so an arbitrary file is placed on the server.

A client sends an HTTP PUT request with a destination that points outside the intended storage area. The server resolves the final path, sees that it is not inside the permitted root, and rejects the request without writing any file.

citations.quote: MLflow allowed arbitrary files to be PUT onto the server.
MLflow allowed arbitrary files to be PUT onto the server.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a Windows-only condition to the artifact path validator in the server handlers. It rejects any path whose second character is a colon, which covers drive-relative forms such as a letter, a colon and a relative name that earlier checks let through. The tests move these drive-relative cases from the accepted list to the rejected list and add one with parent-directory segments.

patterns.title: Unauthenticated arbitrary file overwrite in MLflow server leading to code execution
patterns.cause: The HTTP artifact repository accepted paths from artifact listing responses without validating them before joining them with a requested path or returning them. Absolute paths or parent-directory segments could escape the intended artifact directory when subsequently used for file operations. The advisory reports unauthenticated arbitrary file overwrite on the MLflow server, potentially leading to command execution through files such as shell startup files; the diff does not show the complete exploitation chain.
preconditions: An attacker can reach the affected MLflow operation; the advisory states that authentication is not required.
Exploitation through the listing weakness requires attacker influence over returned artifact paths, but the sources do not explain how that influence is obtained.
File overwrite requires write access by the affected process; command execution additionally depends on the overwritten content later being executed.
patterns.prevention: Use the shared validate_path_is_safe function to validate each returned artifact path in list_artifacts before joining or returning it. The helper converts file URIs for validation and rejects parent-directory segments, Windows or POSIX absolute paths, and platform-recognized alternate separators. The colon-prefix check applies only on Windows. The patch moves the existing server validator into the URI utility module and imports it in server handlers and the HTTP artifact repository. As general hardening, verify final destination containment and minimize process write permissions.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not specify affected versions or show the complete route from unauthenticated input to server-side overwrite. The diff adds validation in HTTP artifact listings and relocates an existing server validator; it does not establish coverage of every upload, download, or other path handler. Validation is lexical and does not resolve symbolic links. Alternate-separator and colon-prefix checks are platform-dependent. Added tests cover a POSIX absolute path and parent-directory traversal.

fixtures.scenario: An MLflow server is exposed on a network with no authentication. An anonymous remote user makes it write a file at a location of their choosing, replacing a user's shell startup file, and gets command execution on the host.

An MLflow server requires authentication for write operations and confines writes to its designated storage area. It runs under an account that cannot modify shell startup files, so an anonymous request cannot overwrite them.

citations.quote: An attacker can overwrite any file on the server hosting MLflow without any authentication.
allows to write / overwrite any file on the file system

patch_review.observation: The fix moves the path safety check into a shared helper in the URI utilities module and calls it on every path returned in the artifact listing response of the HTTP artifact repository. Absolute paths, parent-directory segments, and non-forward-slash separators are rejected with an invalid-path error before the path is joined with the base. A test covers an absolute path and a traversal path.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS from echoing the Content-Type header in MLflow auth server responses
patterns.cause: The MLflow auth server code takes the user-supplied Content-Type header from a POST request and places it directly into a formatted string that is returned to the user. The value is not sanitized or escaped, so attacker-chosen JavaScript in the header can run in the victim's browser.
preconditions: The MLflow server runs with the auth component in mlflow/server/auth/__init__.py handling POST requests.
A response message is built by placing the raw Content-Type header value into a formatted string.
The reflected response is interpreted by a victim's browser in a way that lets injected script execute.
patterns.prevention: Treat every request header, including Content-Type, as untrusted data. Do not insert its raw value into response text. Prefer a fixed error message that does not repeat the header. If the value must be shown, escape or sanitize it for the output context first. Check that the response content type and encoding prevent the browser from treating reflected text as active markup. Add tests that send script-like Content-Type values and confirm the response does not contain them unescaped.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, the affected or patched versions, the specific endpoint or error path, or the response content type returned. The guidance above is general output-handling direction and is not a statement about how MLflow resolved the issue.

fixtures.scenario: A client sends a POST request to the MLflow auth-enabled server with a Content-Type header containing script content. The server builds an error message by formatting the header value into a string and returns it, so the script text appears unescaped in the response a victim's browser renders.

A client sends the same POST request with a script-like Content-Type header. The server replies with a fixed message that does not repeat the header, or with an escaped value, and no script text appears as active content in the response.

citations.quote: An attacker can inject malicious JavaScript code into the Content-Type header, which is then improperly reflected back to the user without adequate sanitization or escaping
the user-supplied Content-Type header is directly injected into a Python formatted string and returned to the user

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the create_user error response, which echoed the raw Content-Type header, with a fixed message listing the accepted types. It also adds a shared check that rejects POST and PUT requests whose Content-Type is missing or not on an allowlist, and applies it to JSON-parsing handlers. The card's cause (reflecting the unsanitized header) and its prevention (use a fixed message, do not echo the header, add tests) match the main change.

patterns.title: Gradio command injection and sensitive information exposure (CVE-2023-6572)
patterns.cause: The changeset-generation GitHub Actions workflow directly interpolated workflow_run repository and branch names into a shell echo command. This lets those values affect shell parsing and can permit command injection if an attacker controls suitable input. The advisories identify command injection and sensitive information exposure, but do not explain their relationship. The fix removes the echo step.
preconditions: The repository uses the affected workflow with the removed echo step still present.
An attacker can influence a repository or branch value interpolated into that step with content the shell interprets as commands.
The affected step executes with the attacker-influenced event data.
patterns.prevention: Apply the upstream workflow change by removing the echo concurrency group step. As general hardening, avoid directly interpolating untrusted event values into shell scripts; pass them through environment variables and reference them as quoted shell variables. Give workflow tokens only the permissions they need.
patterns.limitations: The diff establishes a repository CI injection point, but does not establish elevated privileges, reachable secrets or tokens, or a specific fork pull request attack route. It does not identify exposed information, other affected workflows, affected package versions, or a first fixed release. It also does not establish whether installed gradio applications have related exposure or whether a package upgrade addresses it.

fixtures.scenario: A team hosts a gradio app built from a version older than the fix on main. An unauthorized outside user can reach the app, and the app may allow command injection or leak sensitive information to that user.
A team runs a gradio release that contains the upstream fix. It treats externally supplied values as data rather than command text and does not expose sensitive information to unauthorized users.

citations.quote: Command Injection in GitHub repository gradio-app/gradio prior to main.
Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor in GitHub repository gradio-app/gradio prior to main.

patch_review.observation: The fix deletes a workflow step that echoed the workflow_run head repository name and head branch by interpolating them straight into a shell run script. Those fields are attacker-controlled from a fork, so a crafted branch name could inject commands in a privileged workflow_run job. Removing the step eliminates the injection point, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Deserialization of untrusted data in transformers before 4.36.0
patterns.cause: The advisories describe unsafe deserialization in transformers before 4.36.0, also written as 4.36. The diff shows pickle loading without an explicit trust opt-in gate in the Transformer-XL tokenizer's pretrained vocabulary path, the pickle cache branch of get_lm_corpus, and the RAG legacy index functions _load_passages and _deserialize_index for passages and index metadata. Loading a malicious pickle through these paths can execute arbitrary code (CWE-502).
