preconditions: The application uses an affected transformers release; the advisories identify releases before 4.36.0, also written as 4.36.
Execution reaches a Transformer-XL pretrained vocabulary pickle load, its corpus pickle cache branch, or a RAG legacy index passages or metadata pickle load.
An untrusted or tampered pickle reaches that load. The sources do not establish how an attacker supplies or modifies it.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a release containing the shown fix. It blocks these four pickle loads by default unless the TRUST_REMOTE_CODE environment variable evaluates to true. Leave this opt-in disabled for untrusted or potentially tampered data; enable it only after verifying the pickle data and deciding to trust it. Avoid untrusted pickle artifacts in these Transformer-XL and RAG legacy index paths. As general hardening, prefer formats that do not execute code during deserialization where supported.
patterns.limitations: The gate does not validate pickle contents or make unpickling safe. The same process environment variable controls all four shown gates; coverage of additional guarded paths is not established. The corpus torch.load branch remains unchanged, and the RAG FAISS index read precedes the metadata gate. The diff does not establish library-wide coverage, specific attacker delivery channels, safe-format alternatives, or the first release containing this commit. The advisory version boundary is supplied separately from the diff.

fixtures.scenario: A service pins transformers to a release older than 4.36.0 and passes data obtained from an untrusted outside source into a step that deserializes it.
A service runs transformers 4.36.0 or later and does not pass data from untrusted sources into deserialization steps.

citations.quote: Deserialization of Untrusted Data in GitHub repository huggingface/transformers prior to 4.36.0.
Deserialization of Untrusted Data in GitHub repository huggingface/transformers prior to 4.36.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a guard before each unsafe pickle load in the Transformer-XL tokenizer (the pretrained vocab file and the cached corpus) and in the RAG legacy retriever (the passages file and the index metadata file). Each guard raises an error unless a trust environment variable is set to a true value. The legacy index tests are also removed. This matches the card's cause and its opt-in-gate prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Path traversal in MLflow versions before 2.9.2
patterns.cause: The advisories identify path traversal in MLflow before 2.9.2. The diff concerns filename handling in HTTPDatasetSource.load. URL-derived filenames previously used POSIX basename handling; the fix switches to platform-native basename handling, addressing differing path-separator semantics on Windows. Content-Disposition filenames already passed through the _is_path check before this change, so the diff does not establish that malicious header paths bypassed validation.
preconditions: The deployment runs an MLflow release older than 2.9.2.
A user or workflow loads a dataset through HTTPDatasetSource.

Exploitation would require influence over a filename-producing input; the diff changes URL-derived filename handling and tests crafted response headers, but does not establish the exact exploit prerequisites.
Writing outside the intended directory would require process write permission at the reached location.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to MLflow 2.9.2 or later. The fix centralizes filename extraction in _extract_filename, preserves invalid-parameter rejection of Content-Disposition filenames recognized as paths by _is_path, and uses platform-native basename handling for URL-derived filenames. It retains the fixed dataset_source fallback when extraction returns an empty name. As general hardening, confirm that the resolved destination stays inside the intended download directory before writing.
patterns.limitations: The diff does not show the implementation of _is_path or the final file-writing operation, so it cannot establish rejection of every slash, backslash, or drive-qualified form. Added Windows-only tests expect rejection of two backslash-containing header filenames; they do not demonstrate a pre-fix header-validation bypass or establish that only Windows is affected. Exact exploit prerequisites, authentication requirements, impact, and exposure of other MLflow components are not specified.

fixtures.scenario: A team runs an mlflow release older than 2.9.2 and has not applied the update, so it is within the version range the advisories describe as affected by path traversal.
A team runs mlflow 2.9.2 or later, which is outside the version range the advisories describe as affected.

citations.quote: Path Traversal in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.9.2.

patch_review.observation: The fix moves filename extraction into a single helper that rejects any Content-Disposition filename that looks like a path, and it switches the URL-derived fallback from the POSIX basename to the platform-native basename. A fixed default name is still used when nothing usable is found. It also adds Windows-only tests with backslash and relative-directory filenames that must raise an invalid-parameter error.

patterns.title: Backslash-style parent directory sequences in file names (MLflow before 2.9.2)
patterns.cause: MLflow before 2.9.2 has a path traversal weakness described by the advisories as backslash parent-directory traversal. The diff shows that validate_path_is_safe did not URL-decode input before validation, allowing encoded traversal syntax to evade checks. New tests cover percent-encoded dots and forward slashes in the helper, artifact deletion handler, and HTTP artifact listing. The sources do not demonstrate the downstream decoding and directory escape sequence claimed in the rewritten card.
preconditions: The deployment runs MLflow prior to 2.9.2.
An untrusted path reaches validate_path_is_safe through an affected artifact operation.
For the encoded traversal case addressed by the diff, the path contains percent-encoded traversal syntax.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade MLflow to 2.9.2 or later. The fix URL-decodes paths before existing safety checks and removes the rejected path from error messages. Preserve rejection of parent-directory traversal, absolute paths and fragment markers, with platform-specific handling of drive and UNC paths. Tests also retain rejection of absolute paths containing encoded null bytes, without establishing a separate null-byte check. As general hardening, validate the representation used downstream and resolve the final path to confirm it remains within the allowed base directory.
patterns.limitations: The diff does not establish all affected callers, attacker permissions, downstream decoding behavior, or specific read, write or deletion impact. Artifact deletion tests enable artifact serving; this is not shown to be a universal prerequisite. Existing Windows traversal, drive and UNC tests are relocated, but newly added encoded traversal cases do not establish equivalent Windows coverage. The helper adds one decoding pass; the sources do not establish whether repeated encoding is exploitable or fully handled.

fixtures.scenario: An mlflow installation older than 2.9.2 handles a file name that contains the backslash parent-directory pattern, and the name is not rejected as a traversal attempt.
The installation runs mlflow 2.9.2 or later, and any application code that accepts file names also treats the backslash parent-directory pattern as traversal.

citations.quote: Path Traversal: '\..\filename' in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.9.2.
Path Traversal: '\..\filename' in GitHub repository mlflow/mlflow prior to 2.9.2.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the path safety helper URL-decode the supplied path before running any of its checks, so percent-encoded dots and separators can no longer pass validation and then be decoded into a traversal downstream. It also changes the error message so it no longer echoes the rejected path, and the tests now cover encoded parent-directory sequences.

patterns.title: Command injection in mlflow through a downloaded malicious config
patterns.cause: The render_and_merge_yaml function used a regular, unsandboxed Jinja2 environment for YAML templating. The fix replaces it with a sandboxed environment, indicating a template evaluation weakness. The advisories report full command execution on the victim system after a user downloads a malicious config. The sources do not show the payload or establish the exact execution mechanism.
preconditions: An affected mlflow installation is used; affected versions are not specified.
A user downloads an attacker-crafted config, which the advisories describe as the only required user interaction.
Exploitation through the changed function would require malicious input to reach its template evaluation path; the sources do not explain how the download triggers this.
patterns.prevention: Use Jinja2's SandboxedEnvironment in render_and_merge_yaml to restrict template evaluation, while retaining StrictUndefined handling and the existing filesystem loader. Upgrade to an mlflow release containing this change; the sources do not identify a fixed release. As general hardening, treat externally obtained templates and configs as untrusted and review them before use.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not specify affected or fixed versions, the malicious config format, the triggering workflow, or whether attacker control of context YAML alone is sufficient. The diff shows only the environment change in render_and_merge_yaml. It does not establish server-side execution, demonstrate arbitrary Python evaluation, exclude shell involvement, or prove complete isolation or protection of other template and config paths.

fixtures.scenario: A user downloads a config file supplied by an untrusted party and loads it with a vulnerable mlflow version. Content in the config is carried into command execution, and the attacker gains full command execution on the user's system.

A user loads only configs from trusted sources with a patched mlflow version. Values from the config are validated and never passed to a command interpreter, so a crafted config cannot cause command execution.

citations.quote: with only one user interaction(download a malicious config), attackers can gain full command execution on the victim system.
mlflow Command Injection vulnerability

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the recipe YAML rendering function to build its Jinja2 environment from the sandboxed environment class instead of the plain one, keeping the file system loader, strict undefined handling, and line comment prefix unchanged. This restricts what template expressions can reach, which closes the template injection path to command execution.

patterns.title: MLflow server-side request forgery exposing internal HTTP(s) servers
patterns.cause: MLflow had an SSRF weakness (CWE-918) allowing a malicious user to access internal HTTP(S) servers. The diff addresses redirect following in the shared _get_http_response_with_retries helper, adding environment and per-call controls while retaining redirects by default. This supports redirect following as the mitigation target, but does not establish the exact attacker-controlled input or exploit sequence.
preconditions: A malicious user can interact with an affected MLflow deployment; required permissions are unspecified.
Internal HTTP(S) servers are reachable from the MLflow host.
For a redirect-mediated attack, an attacker-influenced request must encounter a redirect to an internal destination, and the relevant request must allow redirects.
patterns.prevention: Use a release containing the fix and set the MLFLOW_ALLOW_HTTP_REDIRECTS environment variable to false in the server environment to disable redirect following for requests using the modified helper. Explicit per-call settings take precedence over the environment setting and can re-enable redirects. Disabled redirects can return a redirect response to the caller; they do not necessarily raise an exception. As general hardening, restrict MLflow host egress to required services, including restricting access to internal services and cloud metadata endpoints.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify affected or fixed versions, the vulnerable endpoint, attacker permissions, or the exact exploit chain. The change adds no initial-destination validation, so this control alone does not block direct requests to internal hosts. Coverage is limited to requests using the modified helper, and redirects remain enabled by default. Despite the added documentation's exception claim, tests show redirect responses returned without an exception. Effects on specific storage or download flows are not demonstrated. The advisory mentions worst-case remote code execution on AWS but provides no mechanism; metadata access is not established.

fixtures.scenario: An MLflow server runs on a cloud instance with network access to internal HTTP(s) servers. A malicious user makes the server send requests to those internal services, and in the worst case this leads to remote code execution on the host.
The MLflow deployment is upgraded to a fixed release, and its network egress is limited to required services. A request aimed at an internal HTTP(s) server is not served on the user's behalf.

citations.quote: A malicious user could use this issue to access internal HTTP(s) servers
in the worst case (ie: aws instance) it could be abused to get a remote code execution on the victim machine

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a boolean environment variable for allowing HTTP redirects, defaulting to enabled, and makes the shared retrying request helper pass an explicit redirect setting to the session. A per-call keyword can override the environment value. It adds no destination validation or allowlist, and redirects stay on by default.

patterns.title: Deserialization of untrusted data in huggingface transformers before 4.36
patterns.cause: The advisories report untrusted deserialization in transformers before 4.36. The diff shows pickle loading without an explicit trust opt-in at four sites: pretrained vocabulary loading in the deprecated Transformer-XL tokenizer, cached corpus loading in get_lm_corpus, and passages and index metadata loading in the RAG legacy retriever. A malicious pickle reaching one of these loads can execute arbitrary code.
preconditions: The application uses an affected transformers version; the advisories identify versions before 4.36.
Execution reaches one of the four pickle-loading branches for a Transformer-XL vocabulary or cached corpus, or RAG legacy passages or index metadata.
An untrusted party can supply or tamper with the pickle file that is loaded.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to transformers 4.36 or later based on the advisory's affected-version range. The supplied patch adds a default-deny guard before each of the four pickle loads, raising an error unless the TRUST_REMOTE_CODE environment variable is interpreted as true. Leave this opt-in disabled for untrusted data; enable it only after verifying the pickle data's origin and integrity. Avoid untrusted or potentially tampered pickle files. As general hardening, prefer inert data formats where supported.
patterns.limitations: The diff does not establish which release first contains these guards or how an attacker delivers the files. The opt-in does not validate pickle contents or make malicious data safe. Protection shown is limited to four pickle loads; the adjacent torch-based corpus load remains unchanged, and the FAISS index read precedes the metadata guard. No library-wide or checkpoint-loading protection is established. Legacy-index tests are removed, but the reason is unspecified and their removal adds no runtime protection. Support for replacement formats is not established.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs transformers 4.35 and processes serialized data supplied by an outside party, such as a downloaded artifact from an unverified origin, without checking where it came from.
A service runs transformers 4.36 or later, and only loads serialized artifacts from sources it has verified and trusts. Externally supplied data is not passed to deserialization paths.

citations.quote: Deserialization of Untrusted Data in GitHub repository huggingface/transformers prior to 4.36.
Deserialization of Untrusted Data in GitHub repository huggingface/transformers prior to 4.36.

patch_review.observation: The patch adds a guard before each of four unpickling calls: the Transformer-XL tokenizer vocabulary load, the Transformer-XL cached corpus load, the RAG legacy passages load, and the RAG legacy index metadata load. Each guard raises an error unless a trust environment variable is set to a true value. The patch also removes the legacy-index tests, since they would now fail by default.

patterns.title: Recursive URL crawler follows links to other hosts despite the outside-link restriction
patterns.cause: The recursive URL loader's link filter relied on a raw URL prefix when outside links were prevented. A base URL ending at the hostname could therefore admit a different hostname beginning with that text, or the same hostname with an added port. An attacker controlling crawled page content could supply such links and cause unintended fetches. A different scheme alone would not pass the original prefix check.
preconditions: An application uses the recursive URL loader with outside-link prevention enabled and follows links from fetched pages; the advisory demonstrates a crawl depth of two.
The base URL permits an unintended destination to share its full textual prefix, as with a URL ending at the hostname.
An attacker controls a crawled page's content and can insert malicious links.
The installation uses the vulnerable link extraction helper; affected package version ranges are not supplied.
patterns.prevention: Use a langchain installation containing the upstream fix to extract_sub_links. The helper parses URLs, recognizes HTTP and HTTPS absolute links, supplies the current scheme for protocol-relative links, and resolves other links using their parsed paths. With outside-link prevention enabled, it requires exact equality of the parsed network location, including any explicit port, then retains the full base URL prefix check. This rejects lookalike hosts and added ports while retaining scheme and more specific path restrictions.
patterns.limitations: The supplied diff changes the link extraction helper and adds regression tests; it does not establish the scope of all affected callers or other loaders. It contains no redirect, DNS rebinding, or internal-address checks, and the sources do not establish protection against those cases. They provide neither affected version ranges nor a fixed release number for langchain or langchain-core.

fixtures.scenario: A crawler starts at a trusted site with outside links prevented. A page there links to a different host whose name looks similar. The crawler downloads that file anyway.
The same crawl runs on a fixed langchain version. The link to the different host is rejected before any request is sent, and only pages on the intended site are fetched.

citations.quote: the crawler would proceed to download that file as well even though
langchain Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerability

patch_review.observation: The fix to the link extraction helper parses the base URL and each candidate link, and when outside links are prevented it requires the network location (host and port) to match before also requiring the link to start with the full base URL, which keeps the scheme and path restriction. The new test rejects lookalike hosts, other ports and a changed scheme, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Path traversal via remote filename when loading HTTP dataset sources
patterns.cause: When loading a dataset from an HTTP source, a filename from the server's Content-Disposition header was used to build the local destination path without checking for directory components. An attacker-controlled header could supply traversal sequences or an absolute path, allowing writes outside the intended download directory. The shown fix validates this header-derived filename.
preconditions: The application loads a dataset through HTTPDatasetSource; the advisory describes HTTP, and the added test uses HTTPS.
An attacker can influence the Content-Disposition filename returned by the source.
The filename contains path components interpreted by the host operating system and reaches the download path construction without the added validation.
patterns.prevention: Validate the Content-Disposition filename after stripping surrounding quotes. The fix compares it with its basename under the host operating system's path rules and raises an invalid-parameter error if they differ. As general hardening, resolve the final destination and verify containment within the intended download directory before writing. Upgrade to a release containing this validation; the advisories identify version 2.9.0 as fixed.
patterns.limitations: The basename comparison does not reject standalone dot or parent-directory names and follows host-specific path rules. The URL fallback uses POSIX basename and is unchanged; this does not establish its safety on every host, despite the advisories also implicating URL-derived names. The shown validation does not check the caller's destination directory or other dataset source types. The sources do not explain escalation from file write to command execution. Their affected-version claim of 8.2.1 and fixed-version claim of 2.9.0 leave the affected range unclear.

fixtures.scenario: A dataset is loaded from an HTTP URL whose server sends a Content-Disposition filename containing parent-directory sequences or an absolute path. The file is written outside the download directory.
The same dataset load reduces the remote filename to a bare base name, then checks the resolved destination is inside the download directory. A traversal filename is rejected or neutralized.

citations.quote: the filename extracted from the `Content-Disposition` header or the URL path is used to generate the final file path without proper sanitization
This flaw enables an attacker to control the file path fully by utilizing path traversal or absolute path techniques
The issue is fixed in version 2.9.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that treats a name as a path when it differs from its own base name. The load method now uses it on the Content-Disposition filename and raises an invalid-parameter error for absolute paths, relative directories, and parent-directory sequences. The URL-path fallback is left alone, and tests cover the rejected cases.

patterns.title: Filter bypass leads to command injection in the PaddlePaddle wget download helper
patterns.cause: The download helper paddle.utils.download._wget_download in paddlepaddle 2.6.0 was affected by command injection (CWE-78). The advisory describes it as a bypass of a filter, so a filter was present but could be circumvented. The sources do not say what the filter checked or how it was bypassed.
preconditions: The application uses paddlepaddle 2.6.0, the version named in the advisories.
Execution reaches the wget-based download helper paddle.utils.download._wget_download.
The sources do not say which input is attacker-controlled, so whether outside data reaches the helper must be checked per deployment.
patterns.prevention: Do not treat a filter or blocklist as sufficient protection for data that ends up in an operating system command, because this issue was a bypass of such a filter. Keep outside-influenced values out of any command line that a shell interprets. Prefer a native download facility, or pass each argument as a separate element to the process launcher without a shell. Also validate the value strictly against an allow-list of expected forms before use. Upgrade to a release that contains the upstream fix for this CVE.
patterns.limitations: The sources only give the affected function, the version, the weakness class and the fact that a filter was bypassed. They do not describe the vulnerable input, the bypass technique, the first fixed version or the upstream change. The prevention direction is general guidance for this weakness class, not a description of what the maintainers changed.

fixtures.scenario: A service runs paddlepaddle 2.6.0 and passes a value supplied by an outside party to the wget-based download helper. It relies only on the built-in filter to make that value safe.

A service never passes outside-influenced values to the wget-based download helper unchecked. It validates them against a strict allow-list, and its downloads do not go through a shell-interpreted command line.

citations.quote: Command injection in paddle.utils.download._wget_download (bypass filter) in paddlepaddle/paddle 2.6.0
Command injection in paddle.utils.download._wget_download (bypass filter) in paddlepaddle/paddle 2.6.0

patch_review.observation: The fix deletes the wget download helper entirely. That helper built a command string, quoted the URL and file name, and ran it through a shell. The hub caller no longer selects wget for gitee, and only the native httpx-based download method remains. This matches the card's advice to avoid shell-interpreted commands and prefer a native download facility.

patterns.title: Command injection in the IrGraph.draw method of PaddlePaddle 2.6.0
patterns.cause: The advisories identify command injection in IrGraph.draw in PaddlePaddle 2.6.0. Its _convert_to_pdf helper concatenated the dot input path and derived PDF output path into a command string and executed it through a shell. Shell metacharacters in those paths could be interpreted as commands. The fix passes the dot program and its arguments separately without enabling shell execution.
preconditions: The application uses the vulnerable implementation; the advisories identify PaddlePaddle 2.6.0.
An attacker can influence a file path included in the conversion command; the supplied sources do not establish how that control is obtained.
Execution reaches the shell-based dot-to-PDF conversion in IrGraph.draw.
patterns.prevention: Use a PaddlePaddle release containing the shown fix, which passes the dot program and each argument as separate list items without invoking a shell. As general interim hardening, keep untrusted values out of paths used by the vulnerable conversion command.
patterns.limitations: The supplied diff changes only the dot-to-PDF subprocess call. It does not show how the save path and name parameters produce the input path, establish attacker access to those values, or assess other command execution sites. The sources identify 2.6.0 but provide neither a broader affected-version range nor the first fixed release. They also do not establish dot's handling of paths beginning with a dash.

fixtures.scenario: A service running paddlepaddle 2.6.0 calls IrGraph.draw, and a value that an outside party can influence ends up in that call.
A service calls IrGraph.draw only with fixed, developer-chosen values, or runs a release confirmed to contain the vendor fix, and does not build command text from external input.

citations.quote: Command injection in IrGraph.draw in paddlepaddle/paddle 2.6.0
Command injection in IrGraph.draw in paddlepaddle/paddle 2.6.0

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the pdf conversion helper in IrGraph.draw so the dot tool is launched with an argument list and without shell execution. The file paths derived from the save path and name are no longer parsed by a shell, which removes the command injection.

patterns.title: Arbitrary file overwrite via path traversal in PaddlePaddle before 2.6
patterns.cause: The download function in paddle.dataset.common joins the caller-supplied module name to the data home directory without prior validation. The patch adds validation for that name and the optional string save name to restrict path characters and parent-directory traversal. The advisories report arbitrary file overwrite through path traversal in PaddlePaddle before 2.6.
preconditions: The deployment uses PaddlePaddle before 2.6.
Exploitation through these parameters requires attacker influence over the module name or save name passed to download; the sources do not establish how that influence is obtained.
The process has write permission at the destination reached by traversal.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade PaddlePaddle to 2.6 or later, consistent with the advisories' affected-version boundary. The patch restricts module names to letters, digits, underscores, forward slashes and hyphens. It validates string save names with the same characters plus periods, while excluding consecutive periods. As general hardening, resolve destination paths and enforce containment within the intended data directory before writing, and grant the process only the write access it needs.
patterns.limitations: Non-matching names cause a match-result access error rather than an explicit validation rejection in the shown code; outer error handling is unknown. Both patterns permit leading forward slashes, and the shown module-name join can therefore discard the data home directory for an absolute path. No canonical containment check is added. Save-name validation applies only to strings, and its later use is not shown. The diff changes only download; it does not establish coverage of other write paths or an external attack entry point.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs paddlepaddle 2.5. An externally supplied name containing parent-directory segments is joined to an output directory and used for a write, so a file outside that directory is overwritten.

An application runs paddlepaddle 2.6 or later. Any externally supplied name is resolved to a canonical absolute path and rejected unless it lies inside the intended output directory, so no file outside it is written.

citations.quote: Arbitrary File Overwrite Via Path Traversal in paddlepaddle/paddle before 2.6

patch_review.observation: The fix adds regular-expression checks at the start of the download helper. The module name may only contain letters, digits, underscore, hyphen and slash, so it cannot hold dots or parent-directory segments. The save name may also contain dots but not two in a row. Non-matching input causes an unhandled error, and slashes are still allowed, so absolute-looking values are not fully blocked. The card's cause, prevention and limitations match this.

patterns.title: Gradio path traversal: local file include via user-supplied JSON in an API request
patterns.cause: A JSON value supplied by a remote user in an API request was not safely handled, so it could trigger a local file include on the server. The sources do not say which field or code path was affected.
preconditions: A vulnerable version of the gradio package is exposed to remote API requests.
The server accepts a user-supplied JSON value in an API request.
That value can influence which local file the server reads or includes.
patterns.prevention: Treat every JSON value from an API request as untrusted. Do not let such a value choose a local file location directly. Where a request value must refer to a file, resolve it to a canonical absolute path (for example with os.path.realpath()) and accept it only if it falls inside an explicitly allowed directory. Reject anything else. Also upgrade to a gradio release that includes the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that a local file include could be triggered remotely through a user-supplied JSON value. They do not name the vulnerable endpoint, the JSON field, the affected or fixed versions, or the exact validation the fix applies. The canonicalize-and-confine approach above is a general direction, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A remote client sends an API request whose JSON value points at a local file path outside the intended content area, and the server reads or includes that file because it trusts the value.

A remote client sends the same kind of API request, but the server canonicalizes the path from the JSON value, finds it outside the allowed directory, and rejects the request without reading the file.

citations.quote: A local file include could be remotely triggered in Gradio due to a vulnerable user-supplied JSON value in an API request.
Gradio Path Traversal vulnerability

patterns.title: Unneutralized input in generated pages in django CMS (CVE-2024-11319)
patterns.cause: The page_attribute template tag in django-cms stripped tags from page_title values instead of HTML escaping them. This left quotes and incomplete tag fragments insufficiently neutralized, allowing crafted titles to cause cross-site scripting (CWE-79) when rendered in a susceptible HTML context.
preconditions: The deployment runs an affected django-cms release; the advisory lists 3.11.7, 3.11.8, 4.1.2 and 4.1.3.
A template renders page_title through the page_attribute tag.
An attacker can influence the title rendered in a susceptible HTML context; the sources do not establish the required permissions or input route.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a release containing the upstream fix. The fix removes the page_title exception so retrieved attribute values other than datetime instances receive HTML escaping instead of stripping tags from titles. Retain regression tests covering script markup, ampersands, quotes and incomplete tags. As general hardening, use context-appropriate output escaping and review custom templates and tags that mark title values as safe or strip tags manually.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify the first fixed release, establish the status of unlisted versions, or specify attacker privileges, the title input route or the exact exploitable HTML context. The shown change escapes values at output time and contains no stored-title rewrite. Its protection is limited to this tag's output; other output paths and contexts require separate assessment.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs django-cms 4.1.3. Input that a visitor or editor can influence ends up in a generated page without proper neutralization, so a script supplied by an attacker can run in another user's browser.
A site runs a django-cms release that is not in the affected list. Custom page-generation code neutralizes externally influenced input for its output context before it appears in the page.

citations.quote: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (XSS or 'Cross-site Scripting') vulnerability in django CMS Association django-cms allows Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).
This issue affects django-cms: 3.11.7, 3.11.8, 4.1.2, 4.1.3.

patch_review.observation: In the page_attribute tag's value lookup, the page title was handled with tag stripping while other attributes were escaped. The fix removes that special case so every non-date value gets standard HTML escaping. The tests now check that a script payload, an ampersand and a quote-plus-unclosed-tag payload all come out escaped. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Untrusted configuration files deserialized without validation in MobileViTV2 handling (CVE-2024-11392)
patterns.cause: The advisory identifies insufficient validation of user-supplied MobileViTV2 configuration data in Hugging Face Transformers, allowing deserialization of untrusted data and arbitrary code execution as the current user. Separately, the diff explains that model conversion scripts often open insecure legacy formats, including pickle and Torch bin files, and removes those scripts during release preparation.
preconditions: An affected Transformers installation handles malicious user-supplied MobileViTV2 configuration data.
The target interacts with attacker-controlled content by visiting a malicious page or opening a malicious file, as stated in the advisory.
patterns.prevention: Exclude model conversion scripts from release wheels through the upstream release-preparation change. The remove_conversion_scripts function recursively deletes Python files whose names begin with convert from the models directory, and pre_release_work invokes it for both regular and patch releases. Use a release verified to include this change. As general hardening, use trusted conversion inputs, isolate conversion work, and prefer safe formats and restricted loading modes where available.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify affected or fixed versions, the exact unsafe MobileViTV2 call, or the detailed exploit path. They do not establish that running a conversion script is required, that every conversion script is vulnerable, or that the library never needs these scripts at runtime. The diff deletes matching files from the checkout used for release preparation; it does not modify their loading logic or runtime configuration handling. It does not verify the contents of published artifacts or all source checkouts.

fixtures.scenario: A user downloads a MobileViTV2 configuration file from an untrusted source and loads it with Transformers. The configuration handling deserializes its contents without validating them, so a crafted file can run attacker-chosen code as the current user.

A user loads a MobileViTV2 configuration only from a trusted source, using a Transformers release that includes the fix. Content from any untrusted origin is validated as plain data before it is used, so no unvalidated content is deserialized.

citations.quote: The specific flaw exists within the handling of configuration files.
The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data.
User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a step to the pre-release process that deletes every model conversion script under the models directory, so release wheels no longer include code that opens pickle or Torch bin files. The scripts are not made safe and the library's runtime loading is unchanged, which is what the card describes.

patterns.title: Deserialization of untrusted model files in Hugging Face Transformers MaskFormer
patterns.cause: The advisory identifies insufficient validation of user-supplied model data in Transformers MaskFormer, allowing deserialization of untrusted data and code execution as the current user. The diff addresses distribution of model conversion scripts that often open insecure legacy formats, including pickle and Torch bin checkpoints. It does not identify the vulnerable loader or establish that conversion scripts are the only affected path.
preconditions: An affected Transformers installation parses attacker-controlled model data.
User interaction is required; the advisory describes visiting a malicious page or opening a malicious file.
For exposure through conversion tooling, a conversion script must process an untrusted checkpoint; the supplied sources do not establish this as the sole exploitation route.
patterns.prevention: Use a release that incorporates the upstream removal step. The remove_conversion_scripts function deletes Python files whose names begin with convert under the model source directory during pre-release preparation, with the stated intent of excluding conversion scripts from release wheels. Retain this release step and avoid running conversion scripts on untrusted checkpoints. As general hardening, isolate legacy model conversion and run it with minimal privileges.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no affected or fixed version numbers, exact vulnerable loading function, or confirmed serialization format for the MaskFormer exploit. The diff deletes files from the source tree used for release preparation, rather than filtering only built artifacts. It does not modify deserialization implementations or the main model loading path. It does not establish the contents of every source checkout or older release, prove that all conversion scripts are unsafe, or assess safetensors.

fixtures.scenario: A service lets users submit a MaskFormer model file and parses it with an affected Transformers installation without validating its contents. A crafted file leads to deserialization of untrusted data and code execution as the service user.

A service loads MaskFormer model files only from a source the team trusts and controls, on an updated Transformers release. It rejects user-submitted model files and runs the loader with minimal privileges.

citations.quote: The specific flaw exists within the parsing of model files.
The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data.
User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a step to the release preparation script that deletes every model conversion script (files whose names start with convert) under the models directory when a release or patch is prepared. This keeps the legacy loaders, which open pickle and Torch bin files, out of release wheels. It does not change the loaders or the core model loading path, which matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Untrusted Trax model files deserialized without validation in Transformers
patterns.cause: The advisory attributes arbitrary code execution as the current user to insufficient validation of user-supplied Trax model data before deserialization. The diff identifies conversion scripts for older, unsupported model formats as a packaging risk because they often open insecure file types, including pickle and Torch binary model files. It does not identify the specific Trax loader or establish that it uses pickle.
preconditions: An affected Transformers installation processes attacker-controlled Trax model data.
User interaction is required; the advisory describes visiting a malicious page or opening a malicious file.
The data reaches model-file handling that deserializes untrusted input.
patterns.prevention: Exclude conversion scripts from release wheels. The fix adds remove_conversion_scripts and calls it during pre_release_work to recursively delete Python files whose names begin with convert under the models directory. Use a release whose wheels incorporate this removal; the sources do not identify its version. As general hardening, use trusted checkpoint sources, isolate conversion work, and prefer safer serialization formats where supported.
patterns.limitations: The diff removes scripts during release preparation; it does not add validation or repair their loaders. It does not identify the vulnerable Trax function, its serialization format, affected or fixed versions, or how a malicious page reaches model loading. The intended exclusion from release wheels depends on running the updated preparation process. The sources do not establish that every source installation or older release is exposed, or that importing a conversion script triggers deserialization.

fixtures.scenario: An application downloads a Trax model file from an unknown third party and loads it with an affected Transformers version. The file contains attacker-crafted data, so loading it deserializes untrusted content and runs the attacker's code with the current user's privileges.

An application loads Trax model files only from a trusted, verified source, and the loading path validates the file data before deserializing it. The same application runs a Transformers version that includes the maintainers' fix, so a crafted file does not lead to code execution.

citations.quote: The specific flaw exists within the handling of model files.
The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data.
An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current user.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a pre-release step that deletes the model conversion scripts under the models directory, so release wheels no longer contain scripts that open unsafe formats such as pickle or Torch bin files. The card's cause, its prevention (strip the scripts from release builds), and its limitations (source and older releases remain affected) all match this change.

patterns.title: Gradio file parameter lets attackers probe internal ports through distinguishable responses
patterns.cause: The advisory describes SSRF through a client-controlled file value in a GET request: a Location header versus a File not allowed error lets an attacker infer internal port status. The diff shows that the file function used validate_url to decide whether to return an HTTP 302 redirect to the supplied value. It replaces that helper with is_http_url_like. The helper implementations and error path are absent, so the precise network request and success or failure behavior claimed in the rewritten card are not established.
preconditions: The attacker can reach the file route and supply a path or URL value in a GET request.
The request must satisfy the route's login_check dependency; the supplied sources do not establish when authentication is required.
For internal port scanning, the server must have network access to the internal targets being probed.
The attacker can distinguish a Location header from a File not allowed error.
patterns.prevention: Use a gradio release containing the referenced fix, which replaces validate_url with is_http_url_like in the file function's redirect decision. This indicates a shift toward HTTP URL classification rather than reachability-dependent validation, although the helper implementations are not supplied. As general hardening, keep URL classification independent of network reachability and restrict external redirect destinations if arbitrary redirects are unnecessary.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify affected or fixed release versions, show either helper's implementation, or prove that all port-probing behavior is eliminated. The diff retains a redirect to the supplied value when is_http_url_like accepts it, but does not establish the full set of accepted destinations or whether this constitutes a separate exploitable open redirect. The advisory describes SSRF; the supplied family label is open_redirect.

fixtures.scenario: An attacker sends repeated GET requests to a gradio app, changing the file parameter to point at different internal addresses and ports. Some responses carry a Location header and others return a File not allowed error, so the attacker maps which internal ports are open.

The same requests are made, but the app checks the file parameter against what it is meant to serve and refuses all other values. Every refused request gets the same response whether or not the internal port is open, so the attacker learns nothing about the internal network.

citations.quote: By manipulating the 'file' parameter in a GET request, an attacker can discern the status of internal ports
based on the presence of a 'Location' header or a 'File not allowed' error in the response.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the call to a validation helper that made a real network request from the server with a local, string-based check on whether the value looks like an http or https URL. The redirect branch no longer depends on whether the target host or port is reachable, which removes the SSRF probing oracle.

patterns.title: Open redirect via unvalidated next parameter in login flow
patterns.cause: The login functionality of pyload-ng handles the next parameter improperly, so an attacker-supplied value can send users to an arbitrary external site after they interact with the login page.
preconditions: The application exposes a login endpoint that accepts a next parameter indicating where to send the user afterward
The affected version is pyload 0.5.0, before the fix in pyload-ng 0.5.0b3.dev79
A victim can be induced to follow an attacker-crafted login link containing a malicious next value
patterns.prevention: Treat the next parameter as untrusted input. Before redirecting, check that the target is a local path on the same site and not an absolute URL or a URL naming another host. Reject or ignore any value that fails the check and fall back to a fixed default page. Alternatively, map allowed destinations to server-side identifiers instead of accepting raw URLs. Upgrade to pyload-ng 0.5.0b3.dev79 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation the upstream fix applies, which URL forms were accepted by the vulnerable code, or whether other endpoints share the same weakness. The guidance above is general redirect-handling direction and not a description of the upstream change. Whether the redirect happens before or after authentication is not stated.

fixtures.scenario: A phishing email links to the pyload login page with a next parameter pointing to an attacker-controlled external site. The user logs in and the application redirects the browser to that external site, which imitates the real interface.

The login page receives a next parameter pointing to an external site. The application detects that the target is not a local path on the same site, discards it, and redirects the user to the default home page after login.

citations.quote: The vulnerability is due to improper handling of the 'next' parameter in the login functionality.
An attacker can exploit this vulnerability to redirect users to malicious sites, which can be used for phishing or other malicious activities.
The issue is fixed in pyload-ng 0.5.0b3.dev79.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops accepting a raw URL for the post-login destination. The next value is now treated as an application route name, resolved through the router, and any unknown value falls back to the dashboard. The login-required decorator now passes only the endpoint name, and the Referer header is no longer used as a redirect source. The older same-host URL check is dropped, since it could be bypassed.

patterns.title: ReDoS in the Nougat fast tokenizer post-processing of transformers
patterns.cause: In the huggingface/transformers file tokenization_nougat_fast.py, the post_process_single() function runs a regular expression over specially crafted input. The regex can show exponential time complexity under certain conditions, which causes excessive backtracking and very high CPU usage.
preconditions: The application uses transformers version 4.46.3, the affected version named in the advisories.
The application uses the Nougat fast tokenizer code in tokenization_nougat_fast.py.
post_process_single() is called on text that an attacker can craft or influence.
patterns.prevention: Do not run a regular expression that can backtrack exponentially over untrusted or model-generated text. Review the patterns used in post-processing and rewrite any that can backtrack heavily so their running time stays predictable. Upgrade to a transformers release that includes the upstream fix once it is available for your environment. Where possible, keep untrusted text from reaching this post-processing step without checks, and keep a CPU or time limit around it so one request cannot stall the service.
patterns.limitations: The sources name the affected file, function and version, but do not describe the exact regex, the triggering input shape, or how the upstream fix changes the pattern. They also do not list fixed versions or say how the crafted input reaches the function in a given deployment. The mitigations here are general directions, not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A service uses transformers 4.46.3 and passes externally supplied text to the Nougat fast tokenizer post-processing. A crafted input makes the regex in post_process_single() backtrack excessively, so CPU stays pinned and the service becomes unresponsive.

A service uses a transformers release that includes the upstream fix, or a patched post-processing step whose pattern cannot backtrack exponentially. The same crafted input finishes in normal time, and the service keeps handling other requests.

citations.quote: The vulnerability occurs in the post_process_single() function, where a regular expression processes specially crafted input.
The issue stems from the regex exhibiting exponential time complexity under certain conditions, leading to excessive backtracking.
This can result in significantly high CPU usage and potential application downtime

patch_review.observation: The diff changes only the heading-removal pattern in post_process_single in the Nougat fast tokenizer. The old pattern repeated a group that itself contained a repeated alternative, a nested quantifier that backtracks exponentially on long digit or numeral runs. The new pattern removes that nesting by using simple, non-nested repeats, so matching time stays predictable.

patterns.title: SQL injection via prompt injection in the LlamaIndex JSON query engine
patterns.cause: The advisories identify SQL injection through prompt injection in the default_jsonalyzer function of JSONalyzeQueryEngine. Attacker-influenced prompts can steer LLM-generated SQL executed using SQLite, potentially causing arbitrary file creation and denial of service. The diff moves the implementation from core to the experimental package without changing its SQL logic and adds security warnings. Core retains a replacement class that raises a DeprecationWarning exception when instantiated.
preconditions: The application uses a working JSONalyzeQueryEngine implementation with default_jsonalyzer.
An attacker can influence prompt content used to generate SQL.
The engine executes the resulting SQL; the sources do not establish exact filesystem permissions or resource conditions needed for each impact.
patterns.prevention: Use a release containing the core replacement that prevents engine instantiation. The GitHub and PYSEC advisories identify 0.12.3, while the CVE record identifies 0.5.1; confirm the applicable package and release rather than comparing these numbers directly. Moving to the experimental implementation does not harden its SQL execution. Its warning discourages production use and calls for substantial sandboxing or virtual machines. As general hardening, restrict filesystem writes and process resource consumption.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish a complete affected-version range or explicitly map 0.12.3 to llama-index-core. The experimental package is bumped to 0.5.1, but that does not establish a SQL safety fix. Its new jsonalyze initializer imports the core replacement, so successful migration through that export is not demonstrated. Core instantiation raises an exception; importing the replacement alone need not fail. The excerpts do not show SQL validation, exploit statements, file-creation mechanics, or whether attacker-controlled data alone suffices. The advisory title mentions insecure temporary-file permissions without explaining that mechanism. Other engines' affected status is unknown.

fixtures.scenario: A chat application passes user questions to JSONalyzeQueryEngine on an unpatched llama-index. A user embeds instructions in the question, and the generated SQL is altered to create files or exhaust resources on the host.

The application runs a llama-index version that includes the fix, at least 0.12.3. It treats user-derived query text as untrusted and runs the engine in a process with restricted file and resource permissions. The same malicious question does not result in file creation or denial of service.

citations.quote: allows for SQL injection via prompt injection. This can lead to arbitrary file creation and Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks.
The vulnerability affects the latest version and is fixed in version 0.12.3.
The vulnerability affects the latest version and is fixed in version 0.5.1.
LlamaIndex vulnerable to Creation of Temporary File in Directory with Insecure Permissions

patch_review.observation: The fix does not harden the SQL path. It replaces the core JSON query engine with a stub whose constructor raises a deprecation warning, and moves the original logic essentially unchanged (97 percent similarity) into the experimental package. The moved module gets a warning that LLM-generated SQL run on SQLite can create arbitrary files and needs heavy sandboxing, and the experimental package version is bumped to 0.5.1. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Unvalidated file paths in Gradio upload requests allow arbitrary file read
patterns.cause: The UploadButton handling of file upload paths did not properly validate user-supplied input. An attacker who intercepts and modifies the network request to the queue join endpoint can change the file path and make the server read or place files in unintended locations, such as private SSH keys.
preconditions: The Gradio application runs a version older than 4.19.2
The application is reachable by untrusted users, for example through a public link or Hugging Face Spaces
The attacker can intercept and modify the requests the Gradio front end sends to the server
patterns.prevention: Treat every file path that arrives in a client request as untrusted. Do not let the client choose which server-side file is read or where an upload lands. Check the path on the server against the directories the application is meant to expose, and reject anything outside them before any file access. Upgrade Gradio to version 4.19.2 or higher, which contains the fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation flaw, the request fields involved, or how the patch works. They give no detail on which directories are safe or how the check should be written. The claim that remote code execution is possible is stated only as a potential outcome.

fixtures.scenario: A public Gradio app uses an upload button. An attacker edits the request sent to the queue join endpoint so the file path points to a private SSH key on the host, and the server accepts the path and returns the file.
The server treats the submitted path as untrusted and checks it against the allowed locations. A path pointing outside them is rejected, and the app runs Gradio 4.19.2 or higher.

citations.quote: access files on the machine hosting the Gradio application
improper validation of user-supplied input in the UploadButton component
allowing attackers to redirect file uploads to unintended locations on the server
Yes, the problem has been patched in Gradio version 4.19.2 or higher.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check in the input preprocessing path. When a request comes from the network rather than a direct call to the Blocks function, any non-URL file path in the payload must lie inside the configured upload folder, or a ValueError is raised before the file is copied into the cache. A shared helper now provides the upload folder, and an explicit-call flag lets internal calls skip the check. This matches the card's cause (unvalidated client-supplied paths) and its prevention (server-side check against allowed directories, reject anything outside).

patterns.title: ReDoS in Scrapy XML node iteration and open_in_browser from regex-based parsing of untrusted responses
patterns.cause: Scrapy used vulnerable regular expressions to parse response content in two places: the default iternodes node iterator (used by XMLFeedSpider and its subclasses, and by direct calls to scrapy.utils.iterators.xmliter), and, in Scrapy 2.6.0 to 2.11.0, open_in_browser for a response with no base tag. A crafted response makes the regular expression engine do inefficient work, which causes extreme CPU and memory usage and can hang the process.
preconditions: The application uses XMLFeedSpider or a subclass with the default iternodes iterator, or calls scrapy.utils.iterators.xmliter directly.
Alternatively, on Scrapy 2.6.0 to 2.11.0, the application calls open_in_browser on a response that has no base tag.
An attacker can influence the response content that is parsed, for example through a malicious or compromised site or feed being crawled.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Scrapy 2.11.1, or to Scrapy 1.8.4 if on 1.8 or lower and the upgrade to 2.11.1 is not possible. As an interim workaround for XMLFeedSpider, switch the node iterator from the default to the xml or html iterator. For open_in_browser, either review the response content before calling it or define the base tag manually so that the automatic definition is not triggered. In general, avoid parsing untrusted markup with regular expressions that can backtrack heavily, and prefer a real parser or bounded patterns.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the exact vulnerable patterns, the input shapes that trigger them, or the size at which the slowdown becomes severe, so this card cannot describe attack payloads. They do not say whether the xml and html iterators are free of every similar issue, only that switching to them is a listed workaround. The manual review workaround for open_in_browser is vague about what to look for. The sources do not say whether other Scrapy parsing code is affected, nor whether open_in_browser is affected in versions older than 2.6.0 (the advisory only lists 2.6.0 to 2.11.0).

fixtures.scenario: A crawler uses an XMLFeedSpider subclass with the default iternodes iterator to process feeds fetched from third-party servers. One server returns a specially crafted XML body, and the worker spends extreme CPU and memory in node iteration and stops serving other requests.

The same crawler runs Scrapy 2.11.1 or later (or 1.8.4 on the 1.8 line). If it must stay on an older release, the spider is configured to use the xml or html node iterator instead of the default, so the crafted body does not cause runaway resource use.

citations.quote: Handling a malicious response could cause extreme CPU and memory usage during the parsing of its content
Upgrade to Scrapy 2.11.1.
either manually review the response content to discard a ReDos attack or manually define the base tag
By crafting malicious XML content that exploits inefficient regular expression complexity used in the parsing process, an attacker can cause a denial-of-service (DoS) condition.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the default node iterator used by XMLFeedSpider from the regex-based xmliter to the lxml-based xmliter_lxml. It also deprecates xmliter with a ReDoS warning, and backports this to the 1.8 line. For open_in_browser, it replaces the backtracking comment-stripping and head-tag regexes with a plain string-search comment remover and a tighter, single-substitution head pattern, with timing tests for both inputs.

patterns.title: Server-side request forgery in TFIDFRetriever load_local (langchain-community 0.0.26)
patterns.cause: TFIDFRetriever's load_local deserializes local .joblib and .pkl files without an explicit opt-in guard before the fix. Maliciously modified files can execute arbitrary code on the host. The advisory describes remotely exploitable server-side request forgery, while the diff addresses unsafe deserialization; the sources do not explain the connection.
preconditions: The advisory identifies langchain-community 0.0.26 as affected.
The application calls TFIDFRetriever's load_local to load saved retriever files from a local folder.
For the code execution mechanism described by the diff, a maliciously crafted or modified file must be loaded. The sources do not establish how an attacker supplies or modifies that file.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade langchain-community to 0.0.27, which the advisory identifies as addressing the issue. The patched load_local rejects deserialization unless the caller explicitly enables allow_dangerous_deserialization. Enable it only after validating that the files came from a trusted source. Do not load untrusted retriever files. As general hardening, protect trusted files against attacker modification and verify their integrity before loading.
patterns.limitations: The guard requires explicit consent; it does not make deserialization safe or add file-content or provenance validation. Callers that continue loading must explicitly opt in and remain exposed if they load malicious files. The sources do not establish affected versions before 0.0.26 or guarantees for all versions after 0.0.27. They also do not identify the remote entry point, attacker access requirements, SSRF request, or how SSRF relates to the deserialization mechanism.

fixtures.scenario: A service pins langchain-community 0.0.26 and uses TFIDFRetriever load_local in a way that remote users can influence. The service is exposed to server-side request forgery.
The same service is upgraded to langchain-community 0.0.27 or later, and the dependency lock file and deployed image are checked to confirm the old version is gone.

citations.quote: Affected is the function load_local in the library libs/community/langchain_community/retrievers/tfidf.py of the component TFIDFRetriever.
The manipulation leads to server-side request forgery.
Upgrading to version 0.0.27 is able to address this issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the load_local method of TFIDFRetriever so it takes a keyword-only opt-in flag that defaults to false. Unless the caller sets it, the method raises an error before reading the joblib and pickle files, because those formats can run arbitrary code on load. The card's cause (unsafe deserialization of untrusted local files) and its prevention (upgrade, opt in only for trusted files) match this change, even though the CVE title says server-side request forgery.

patterns.title: Stored XSS via attacker-controlled href on anchor elements in Dash apps
patterns.cause: Affected Dash components use URL properties without the sanitization added by the fix. The advisories identify XSS when an adversary controls an anchor's href and the app stores user input that another user reloads. A malicious saved view can execute script in that user's browser. The diff also adds protection to other URL properties, but does not establish that every listed element executes attacker script or does so automatically.
preconditions: The app runs an affected release, including dash before 2.15.0; standalone component package ranges conflict across the advisories.
An attacker can control an anchor's href through user input.
The app provides a mechanism to store that input for a different user to reload.
In the advisory's attack scenario, an authenticated attacker saves a malicious view that another user opens.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade dash to 2.15.0 or later. The fix uses the third-party sanitizeUrl function from @braintree/sanitize-url on href for anchors and dcc.Link, action for forms, formAction for buttons, src for iframes and embeds, and data for objects. dcc.Link also uses the sanitized URL for navigation and fallback text. Components report changed URLs as frontend errors. Tests assert about:blank for supplied javascript URLs, including a newline-obfuscated anchor URL. As general hardening, validate or allow-list URL schemes on the server and keep untrusted stored data from directly setting these properties.
patterns.limitations: The advisories conflict on standalone dash-core-components and dash-html-components ranges, so matching fixed standalone releases are not established. The sanitizer's full scheme policy is not included. Tests check resulting attributes, not script execution, required user interaction, or automatic execution; form action is configured but not asserted. The change adds sanitization only to the listed component properties and does not establish the protection status of other or custom components. General server-side hardening is not a verified mitigation in these sources.

fixtures.scenario: A Dash app lets signed-in users save a view and share it. The saved state sets the href of an anchor tag from user input. The app runs dash 2.14. Another user opens the shared view and the attacker's script runs in that user's session.
The app runs dash 2.15.0 or later with fixed component packages, and saved view data is never used to set an anchor href. A user opening a shared view only sees content the app itself controls.

citations.quote: are vulnerable to Cross-site Scripting (XSS) when the href of the a tag is controlled by an adversary.
This is only exploitable in Dash apps that include some mechanism to store user input to be reloaded by a different user.
versions of the package dash before 2.15.0

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a URL sanitizing library to the generated html components (anchor, form, button, iframe, object, embed) and to the core Link component, so dangerous schemes like javascript are replaced with a blank page URL and a front-end error is reported through the renderer. An integration test confirms the affected properties become a blank page URL.

patterns.title: XSS in djangorestframework via the break_long_headers template filter
patterns.cause: The break_long_headers template filter splits a header value and joins the pieces with line break tags, but the input is not properly sanitized before this step. Untrusted header content can therefore end up in rendered HTML as active markup.
preconditions: The application uses a djangorestframework version before 3.15.2.
A template renders content through the break_long_headers template filter.
The value passed to the filter can be influenced by an attacker, for example a request header value.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade djangorestframework to version 3.15.2 or later. In any custom filter that inserts line break tags into text, neutralize the untrusted input first by escaping it for HTML output, and only then split and join the pieces, so that only the intended break tags are treated as markup. Avoid marking the combined result as safe before the input has been escaped.
patterns.limitations: The sources only name the break_long_headers filter, the improper sanitization before splitting and joining with line break tags, and the fixed version 3.15.2. They do not describe which inputs reach the filter in practice, how exploitation is carried out, or what the exact upstream change is, so the escaping direction above is general guidance rather than a description of the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: An application runs djangorestframework 3.15.1 and renders a page that passes a header value containing markup through the break_long_headers filter. The value is split and joined with line break tags without proper sanitization, so the markup reaches the page unescaped.

An application runs djangorestframework 3.15.2 or later, or uses a custom filter that escapes the header value for HTML before splitting and joining it with line break tags. Markup in the header value is shown as text and not interpreted by the browser.

citations.quote: Versions of the package djangorestframework before 3.15.2 are vulnerable to Cross-site Scripting (XSS) via the break_long_headers template filter

due to improper input sanitization before splitting and joining with
tags.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the break_long_headers filter so the header value is HTML-escaped before it is split on commas and rejoined with line break tags. Previously the raw value was split and joined and then marked safe, so attacker-controlled markup in a long header was rendered as active HTML. Escaping first leaves only the intended break tags as markup, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Unvalidated client-supplied URLs added to proxy target set enable SSRF in gradio
patterns.cause: The advisory attributes SSRF to X-Direct-Url headers on the root and config routes adding arbitrary URLs to the replica_urls set, combined with inadequate safe-URL checks in build_proxy_request. This permits unauthorized proxying and potential access to internal Hugging Face space endpoints. The diff shows that these routes used X-Direct-Url as a fallback when the request scope lacked a root path and overwrote the shared configuration root on qualifying requests. It does not establish that this root alone controlled server-side fetch destinations.
preconditions: An attacker can submit X-Direct-Url headers to the root or config route under the application's applicable access controls.
The header influences trusted proxy destinations as described in the advisory; the shown root calculation uses it only when the request scope has no root path.
The proxy route is accessible to the attacker and build_proxy_request inadequately validates the requested destination.
patterns.prevention: Remove the X-Direct-Url fallback from root calculation. Follow the diff by deriving the root from the request URL and initializing it only when absent from configuration. Generate component file, stream, and proxy URLs during server-side processing and let clients consume those URLs; the diff still constructs upload URLs in the client. Prevent client headers from expanding trusted proxy destinations and validate safe destinations in build_proxy_request, as motivated by the advisory. As general hardening, trust forwarding headers only through a controlled reverse proxy.
patterns.limitations: The diff omits the proxy handler, replica_urls updates, and build_proxy_request, so their validation changes and connection to the shared root cannot be verified. Authentication prerequisites are unspecified; the shown config route has login checks and root configuration is authentication-dependent. Version ranges and exact reachable internal endpoints are unspecified. The diff does not establish arbitrary server-side fetching through file routes or that request-derived roots are inherently trusted. It broadly refactors URL handling across components rather than showing only a minimal security patch.

fixtures.scenario: A client sends a request to the config route with a header naming an internal address. The server adds it to its trusted replica URL set. The client then calls the proxy route with that address, and the server fetches the internal endpoint.

The trusted proxy target set is fixed by server configuration and ignores client headers. A request naming an internal address is rejected when the proxy request is built, because the address is not on the allowlist.

citations.quote: An SSRF vulnerability exists in the gradio-app/gradio due to insufficient validation of user-supplied URLs
allowing the addition of arbitrary URLs for proxying
potential access to internal endpoints within the Hugging Face space

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the use of the client-controlled X-Direct-Url header when computing the app root in the root and config routes. It now derives the root from the request URL and sets it only once in the shared config. It also moves file and proxy URL construction to the server by adding URLs during file caching and prefixing the root on outputs, and it drops the client-side function that assembled these URLs from a root value.

patterns.title: HTML attribute injection through user-controlled keys in the Jinja xmlattr filter
patterns.cause: The xmlattr filter in affected Jinja versions accepts attribute keys that contain spaces. Each space-separated part is then read by the browser as a separate attribute. When keys come from user input, an attacker can inject arbitrary attributes and keys, which bypasses autoescaping and can lead to XSS.
preconditions: The application uses the xmlattr filter on a mapping rendered into HTML or XML.
Attribute keys, not only values, come from user input.
The rendered page is viewed by other users.
A vulnerable Jinja version is in use.
patterns.prevention: Do not let untrusted input choose attribute keys passed to the xmlattr filter. Check each key against a fixed allowlist of known attribute names before rendering, and reject keys with spaces or other unexpected characters. Do not rely on a blacklist of dangerous attributes, since blacklist-based checks may be bypassed. Upgrade Jinja to a release that includes the upstream fix as defense in depth, and keep validating keys anyway.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the fixed Jinja version or describe the exact characters the fix rejects. They do not detail how blacklist checks are bypassed. Attribute values and other contexts are not covered. Accepting user keys is described as an uncommon use of the filter.

fixtures.scenario: A profile page builds an attribute mapping from user-submitted names and values and renders it with the xmlattr filter. A key containing a space adds a second attribute, such as an event handler, which runs for other viewers.
The page accepts only keys from a fixed allowlist, and user input supplies values only. A submitted key with a space or an unknown name is rejected before rendering, so no extra attribute is created.

citations.quote: XML/HTML attributes cannot contain spaces, as each would then be interpreted as a separate attribute.
an application doing so should already be verifying what keys are provided regardless of this fix.
It may also be possible to bypass attribute validation checks if they are blacklist-based.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the xmlattr filter raise a ValueError when any attribute key contains ASCII whitespace, so a key cannot be split into several injected attributes. It was released in 3.1.3 with a regression test, and values are still escaped as before. This matches the card's cause (keys with spaces are accepted) and its prevention (validate keys and upgrade).

patterns.title: Directory traversal in Salt syndic cache directory creation
patterns.cause: Syndic cache directory creation in Salt is vulnerable to a directory traversal attack. The path used to create the cache directory is not confined to its intended location, so a malicious user can cause an arbitrary directory to be created on a Salt master.
preconditions: A Salt master creates syndic cache directories.
A malicious user or attacker can influence the path used for syndic cache directory creation.
The directory creation step does not keep the final path inside the intended cache location.
patterns.prevention: Before creating a cache directory, resolve the final path and confirm it is still inside the intended cache root. Reject any value that would escape that root, such as one containing parent-directory components or path separators. Prefer treating externally supplied identifiers as a single plain name rather than as a path. Upgrade to a Salt release that contains the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources are brief. They do not say which input carries the traversal sequence, which Salt component supplies it, or whether authentication is needed. They do not list affected or fixed versions, and they do not describe how the upstream fix works. The prevention guidance is the general approach for directory traversal, not a description of the upstream change. The sources only describe arbitrary directory creation, not file read or write.

fixtures.scenario: A Salt master builds a syndic cache directory path from a name supplied by a malicious user. The name contains parent-directory components, so the directory is created outside the cache area at a location the attacker chose.

A Salt master builds the syndic cache directory path from a supplied name, resolves the full path, and checks that it stays inside the cache root. A name that would escape the root is rejected and no directory is created.
