For the javascript link vector shown in the test, a user views the Providers page and clicks the rendered link.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 2.9.3 or later; the advisory identifies 2.9.3 as fixing the issue. The fix parses link targets and creates anchors only for http or https schemes. Other matched links are returned as escaped text. As general hardening, apply URL scheme allowlists when building links from untrusted input and install only trusted provider packages.
patterns.limitations: The supplied diff changes provider-description link rendering; it does not establish the safety of other metadata rendering paths. The sources do not specify the exact installation permissions or whether supplying or installing an entire crafted package is necessary. The test checks rendered output, not browser script execution or persistence, so it does not demonstrate a complete stored-XSS exploit. Scheme validation does not establish that an allowed destination is trustworthy.

fixtures.scenario: An Apache Airflow 2.9.2 deployment lets an authenticated user install a provider. That user injects a malicious link during the installation, which is the condition the advisory describes for versions before 2.9.3.
The deployment runs Apache Airflow 2.9.3 or later, the release the advisory names as fixing the malicious link injection during provider installation.

citations.quote: Apache Airflow versions before 2.9.3 have a vulnerability that allows an authenticated attacker to inject a malicious link when installing a provider.
Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.9.3, which fixes this issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the link-building helper in the Providers page description cleaner. It now parses each link target and renders an anchor only when the scheme is http or https. Any other link, such as one using a javascript scheme, is returned as escaped plain text. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Engine-specific SQL functions bypass query authorization in Apache Superset
patterns.cause: Superset's SQL authorization did not check certain engine-specific functions. Special elements in submitted SQL were not properly neutralized, so a user could call functions the authorization logic never inspected and thereby bypass the intended restrictions.
preconditions: The application accepts user-submitted SQL and relies on its own authorization check before running it against a database
The deployment runs Apache Superset earlier than 4.0.2
The backing database exposes engine-specific functions, such as the PostgreSQL ones named in the advisory, that the authorization check does not examine
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Superset 4.0.2 or later. That release introduces a configuration key named DISALLOWED_SQL_FUNCTIONS, which blocks the PostgreSQL functions version, query_to_xml, inet_server_addr, and inet_client_addr. An implementation should treat engine-specific functions as part of the authorization surface, keep a deny list of them per database engine, and extend that list with further functions where more protection is wanted.
patterns.limitations: The sources name only four PostgreSQL functions and do not describe how the bypass works in detail, nor whether other engines are affected. A deny list only covers the functions someone has listed, so it is not a complete guarantee. The sources do not describe the exact checks the fix performs or give advice beyond upgrading and extending the list.

fixtures.scenario: A Superset instance older than 4.0.2 backed by PostgreSQL lets a user submit a query that calls one of the engine-specific functions, such as query_to_xml. The authorization check does not examine the function, so the query is allowed through.

A Superset instance at 4.0.2 or later has DISALLOWED_SQL_FUNCTIONS configured with the default PostgreSQL entries plus any extra functions the operator chose to add, so queries calling those functions are rejected.

citations.quote: certain engine-specific functions are not checked, which allows attackers to bypass Apache Superset's SQL authorization.
This key disallows the use of the following PostgreSQL functions: version, query_to_xml, inet_server_addr, and inet_client_addr.
Users are recommended to upgrade to version 4.0.2, which fixes the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a per-engine deny list setting for SQL functions (PostgreSQL version, query_to_xml, inet_server_addr and inet_client_addr, plus entries for ClickHouse and MySQL). The base engine execute path parses the SQL, searches nested tokens for any listed function name, and raises an error if one is found. This matches the card's prevention of a per-engine deny list of functions the authorization check did not cover. The card's limitation that other engines are unclear is slightly off, since the diff also ships defaults for ClickHouse and MySQL, but the main point is the same.

patterns.title: Unescaped DataStore record data in a table preview view enables XSS
patterns.cause: The Datatables view plugin in CKAN did not properly escape record data coming from the DataStore before showing it, so markup inside a cell could be treated as active content by the browser.
preconditions: CKAN version 2.7.0 or later but earlier than the fixed releases 2.10.5 and 2.11.0
The datatables_view plugin is activated; it is part of CKAN core but not enabled by default
Tabular data containing attacker-controlled values is loaded into the DataStore, for example through DataPusher or XLoader
patterns.prevention: Treat every value read from the DataStore as untrusted text. Escape or encode each record value for the HTML context in which it is rendered, and insert it as plain text rather than markup. Upgrade to CKAN 2.10.5 or 2.11.0 or later. As a stopgap, avoid importing tabular files into the DataStore, especially files from untrusted publishers.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the exact rendering code path, the specific escaping routine used by the fix, or which HTML contexts were affected. The workaround of blocking imports reduces exposure but does not remove the flaw in the plugin. Sites that do not activate datatables_view are described as outside the stated impact.

fixtures.scenario: A site runs CKAN 2.9 with datatables_view active. A publisher uploads a spreadsheet whose cell holds script markup, and it is loaded into the DataStore. A viewer opens the preview and the cell is rendered unescaped.
A site runs CKAN 2.10.5 or later with datatables_view active. The same spreadsheet is imported, but the preview escapes the cell value, so the viewer sees it as literal text and nothing executes.

citations.quote: did not properly escape record data coming from the DataStore, leading to a potential XSS vector.
This vulnerability has been fixed in CKAN 2.10.5 and 2.11.0
Prevent importing of tabular files to the DataStore via DataPusher, XLoader,etc, at least those published from untrusted sources.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the datatables view AJAX endpoint so each record value is HTML-escaped (after conversion to text) before being returned as JSON to the table widget. A test confirms that special characters in a cell come back as entities. This matches the card's cause (unescaped DataStore values) and its prevention (escape values for the HTML context).

patterns.title: HTML injection in the redirect body built by Twisted redirectTo
patterns.cause: The twisted.web.util.redirectTo function builds an HTML body for its HTTP 302 response and inserts the destination URL into it without any output encoding. If an attacker controls all or part of the URL, for example through an open redirect, they can inject HTML into the response, which can lead to reflected cross-site scripting.
preconditions: Application code passes a URL that an attacker can fully or partly control to twisted.web.util.redirectTo
The Twisted version is older than 24.7.0rc1
A browser renders the HTML body of the redirect response; in the reported testing only Firefox did
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Twisted to 24.7.0rc1 or later, where the issue is fixed. Treat the redirect destination as untrusted input. Do not let request data choose the redirect target unless the application has checked it against what it expects. Any HTML that echoes a URL must be output-encoded for the context where the URL is placed, so that attacker-supplied characters stay data and cannot become markup.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so this card does not say how it encodes the URL. The advisory reports that only Firefox rendered the body in its tests, and says nothing about other browser versions. The sources do not say whether other Twisted code paths are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A Twisted web handler reads a url query parameter from the request and passes it unchanged to redirectTo on a version older than 24.7.0rc1. A crafted value ends the link attribute and adds markup that a browser renders in the redirect body.

The deployment runs Twisted 24.7.0rc1 or later, and the handler only redirects to destinations it has checked against what the application expects. Attacker-chosen URL text is never reflected into the redirect body as raw HTML.

citations.quote: The function reflects the destination URL in the HTML body without any output encoding.
All other tested browsers will display an error message to the user and will not render the HTML body.
This vulnerability is fixed in 24.7.0rc1.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes redirectTo HTML-escape the destination URL before placing it in the fallback response body, where it appears in both the meta refresh content and the anchor href. New tests confirm that a normal URL is unchanged and that quotes and angle brackets in a hostile URL become entities. This matches the card's cause (no output encoding of the URL) and its prevention (upgrade, and encode any URL echoed into HTML).

patterns.title: Provider documentation link XSS in Apache Airflow web UI
patterns.cause: Before version 2.10.0, Apache Airflow used a Documentation entry from an installed provider's Project-URL package metadata as a documentation link without checking its URL scheme. A malicious provider author could supply a javascript URI, allowing attacker-controlled script to execute in the user's browser when the user clicked the provider documentation link.
preconditions: Apache Airflow version earlier than 2.10.0 is in use.
A malicious provider with a crafted Documentation Project-URL value is installed on the web server.
A user clicks the provider documentation link in the web UI.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 2.10.0 or later. The fix makes get_doc_url_for_provider parse metadata URLs and accept only http or https URLs with a non-empty network location component. Rejected entries are skipped; the test confirms that a javascript URI results in the default Airflow documentation URL. As general hardening, validate schemes as well as encoding link values, and install providers only from trusted sources.
patterns.limitations: The supplied diff changes provider documentation URL selection; it does not establish protections for other URL rendering paths or show the UI template or exact page placement. A non-empty network location is not full hostname validation. The check permits attacker-chosen http or https destinations, so it does not establish destination trust or prevent links to phishing sites. The sources require an installed malicious provider and a user click but do not establish how the provider gains installation.

fixtures.scenario: An Airflow 2.9 deployment has a third-party provider installed on the web server whose author supplied a hostile documentation link. A user opens the providers page and clicks the link, and the attacker's script runs in the user's browser session.
The deployment runs Airflow 2.10.0 or later, and only providers from trusted sources are installed. Clicking a provider documentation link does not execute injected script.

citations.quote: allows the developer of a malicious provider to execute a cross-site scripting attack when clicking on a provider documentation link
This would require the provider to be installed on the web server and the user to click the provider link.
Users should upgrade to 2.10.0 or later, which fixes this vulnerability.

patch_review.observation: The fix parses the Documentation Project-URL value taken from provider package metadata and only returns it if the scheme is http or https and a host is present. Otherwise the function falls through to the default documentation URL built from the provider name and version. A test confirms a javascript scheme value is replaced by the default link.

patterns.title: Denial of service in Django urlize, urlizetrunc and AdminURLFieldWidget via very large Unicode inputs
patterns.cause: The urlize and urlizetrunc filters processed URL and email candidates without the added length checks, exposing matching and URL quoting paths to very large Unicode inputs and potential denial of service. Regression tests cover long sequences of short Unicode domain labels separated by dots. AdminURLFieldWidget also called smart_urlquote for non-empty values even when URL validation had failed. The sources identify a ReDoS concern but do not isolate the exact expensive operation.
preconditions: Django 5.0 before 5.0.8 or Django 4.2 before 4.2.15 is in use.
Attacker-controlled text reaches urlize, urlizetrunc, or AdminURLFieldWidget.
The supplied input contains a very large number of Unicode characters; tested examples include repeated domain labels following an HTTP prefix, a www prefix, or an email at sign.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Django 5.0.8 or later in the 5.0 series, or 4.2.15 or later in the 4.2 series. The fix limits URL candidates to 2048 characters before either URL regex match, rejects the entire email domain part when it exceeds 63 characters before subsequent checks, and makes AdminURLFieldWidget call smart_urlquote only after successful URL validation. As general hardening, bound untrusted text size and avoid expensive normalization of values already known to be invalid.
patterns.limitations: URL candidates exceeding 2048 characters skip the two URL matching branches, and email domains exceeding 63 characters fail the simple email check, including otherwise legitimate longer values. The diff does not establish protection for other filters or custom code. The sources provide no exact complexity, resource measurements, single-value denial-of-service guarantee, authentication prerequisites, or status of other Django versions. Input limits are general hardening; their effectiveness as a standalone mitigation is not demonstrated.

fixtures.scenario: A site on Django 4.2.14 renders user comments through the urlize filter. An attacker submits a comment with a very large number of Unicode characters, and page rendering becomes a potential denial of service.
The same site runs Django 4.2.15, or a 5.0 deployment runs 5.0.8, so the same comment is handled by the patched urlize filter.

citations.quote: The urlize and urlizetrunc template filters, and the AdminURLFieldWidget widget, are subject to a potential denial-of-service attack
An issue was discovered in Django 5.0 before 5.0.8 and 4.2 before 4.2.15.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a 2048-character cap on a word before the two URL regular expressions are tried in urlize. It also rejects email domain parts longer than 63 characters in the simple email check. In the admin URL widget, the link is now quoted only when the URL was validated, rather than for any non-empty value. All three changes match the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Path traversal in Streamlit static file sharing on Windows
patterns.cause: In Streamlit open source before 1.37.0, the static file handler's validate_absolute_path method resolved the requested path and performed directory and size checks before calling the base class path validator. This ordering allowed filesystem checks before root-containment validation. The advisory identifies a Windows-only path traversal vulnerability when static file sharing is enabled and states that an attacker could leak the password hash of the Windows user running Streamlit.
preconditions: Streamlit open source version earlier than 1.37.0
The app runs on Windows
App static file sharing is enabled
The attacker can reach the app over the network; the advisory's CVSS vector specifies low privileges but does not explain the required access
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Streamlit 1.37.0 or later; the fix was released on Jul 25, 2024. The patch moves the base class validate_absolute_path call ahead of the handler's directory and size checks and returns its saved result afterward. Path resolution still occurs before that call. If upgrading is not possible, disable app static file sharing on Windows. As general hardening, validate root containment before filesystem checks on a requested path.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify the exploit's exact path form or establish that a network share and outbound authentication cause the hash leak. The base class validator's implementation is not shown, and path resolution remains before validation, so the diff does not establish rejection before all filesystem access or containment of every resolved path. The sources do not establish blanket rejection of absolute or network-style paths, or the effectiveness of outbound SMB restrictions or a low-privilege service account.

fixtures.scenario: A Streamlit app version 1.36 runs on a Windows server with static file sharing enabled and is exposed to remote users. An attacker sends a crafted request to the static file route to read files outside the static directory, and obtains the password hash of the Windows account running the app.
The same app runs Streamlit 1.37.0 or later on Windows, or runs on a host where static file sharing is not enabled. The crafted request does not expose files outside the intended static content.

citations.quote: Users of hosted Streamlit app(s) on Windows were vulnerable to a path traversal vulnerability when the static file sharing feature is enabled.
An attacker could utilize the vulnerability to leak the password hash of the Windows user running Streamlit.
We recommend all users upgrade to Version 1.37.0.
The vulnerability only affects Windows.

patch_review.observation: The fix moves the call to the base class containment check (validate_absolute_path in the parent handler) to the start of the static handler's validation, before the directory check and file size check. Paths outside the static root are now rejected with 403 before those filesystem queries run, and the tests were updated to expect 403 for outside paths and directories. This matches the card's cause (filesystem access before root containment) and its prevention (check containment first).

patterns.title: Command injection via unsanitized GitHub context values echoed in a CI workflow
patterns.cause: A functional test workflow echoed GitHub context information, namely the full name of the head repository, the head branch, and the workflow reference, in a command without adequate sanitization. Attacker-influenced values containing special elements could therefore be interpreted as part of the command.
preconditions: A CI workflow builds a command that includes GitHub context values such as the head repository full name, head branch, or workflow reference
Those values can be influenced by someone outside the maintainers, for example through a fork or a branch name
The special elements in those values are not neutralized before the command runs
The workflow runs with access to secrets such as GITHUB_TOKEN, COMMENT_TOKEN, or CHROMATIC_PROJECT_TOKEN
patterns.prevention: Treat every GitHub context value that a contributor can influence as untrusted data. Do not let such values be interpreted as command text. Either avoid echoing them in a command, or neutralize special elements first so they are handled strictly as plain data. Review all workflow steps that print or reuse the head repository name, head branch, and workflow reference.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream remediation, the specific trigger type, or which step was changed. They also do not say whether other workflows are affected. Only versions up to and including @gradio/video@0.6.12 are named as affected. The guidance here is general and not a verified description of the fix.

fixtures.scenario: A workflow step echoes the head repository full name, head branch, and workflow reference directly into a shell command. A contributor picks a branch name with shell special elements, and the runner executes them with secrets available.

The workflow treats the head repository name, head branch, and workflow reference as untrusted data. Special elements are neutralized so a hostile branch name is only printed as text and never executed.

citations.quote: where it echoes the full name of the head repository, the head branch, and the workflow reference without adequate sanitization
allowing for unauthorized modification of the base repository or secrets exfiltration

patch_review.observation: The fix deletes a step in the functional test workflow that echoed the head repository full name, head branch, and workflow reference by interpolating them straight into a shell command. Removing the step eliminates the injection path, which matches the card's cause and its option of not echoing untrusted context values in a command.

patterns.title: Gradio SSRF through unvalidated user-supplied URL fetched by the queue join endpoint
patterns.cause: In gradio 4.21.0, the queue/join endpoint accepts a path value from the user that is expected to be a URL. The save_url_to_cache function uses that value to make an HTTP request from the server without sufficient validation checks. The server therefore fetches whatever destination the client names.
preconditions: A gradio-app/gradio deployment at version 4.21.0, where the issue was discovered, exposes the queue/join endpoint to untrusted clients.
A path value supplied by the user and expected to be a URL reaches save_url_to_cache.
The server makes an HTTP request to that URL without sufficient validation checks.
The server host can reach the local network or the AWS metadata endpoint.
patterns.prevention: Treat every user-supplied URL as untrusted before the server requests it. Validate the destination first, and refuse to fetch anything that points at the local network or at a cloud metadata endpoint. Make the check on the destination the server will actually contact, and reject the request before any outbound connection is made. Upgrade to a gradio release that includes the upstream fix for this issue.
patterns.limitations: The advisories only say that validation checks were insufficient. They do not describe which checks the fix adds, how redirects or DNS resolution are handled, or which gradio versions other than 4.21.0 are affected. The validation direction above is general guidance, not a description of the upstream change. Other code paths that fetch user-supplied URLs are not covered by these sources.

fixtures.scenario: A client sends a request to the queue/join endpoint with a path value that is a URL pointing at an internal host or the AWS metadata endpoint. The server requests it without validation, so an attacker reaches resources that are only available from the server's network position.

A client sends the same request with an internal or metadata URL as the path value. The server validates the destination before making any HTTP request, rejects the request, and makes no outbound connection to the internal target.

citations.quote: A Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability exists in the gradio-app/gradio version 4.21.0,
obtained from the user and expected to be a URL, is used to make an HTTP request without sufficient validation checks
could lead to unauthorized access to the local network or the AWS metadata endpoint

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a safety check, is_safe_url, that runs at the start of both the sync and async URL-to-cache download functions. It allows only http and https, resolves the hostname, and rejects private or multicast addresses. It also stops following redirects automatically, so a redirect cannot lead the server to an internal destination. This matches the card's cause (an unvalidated user URL fetched server-side) and its prevention (validate the destination before any outbound request and refuse local or internal targets).

patterns.title: SSRF through unrestricted resource URLs fetched by CKAN extensions
patterns.cause: CKAN plugins such as XLoader, DataPusher, Resource proxy and ckanext-archiver download the contents of a resource URL to push it to the DataStore, stream it or save a local copy. No check limits which URLs can be requested. A user can therefore create a resource whose URL points somewhere they should not have access to, and the server-side tool fetches it for them.
preconditions: A CKAN deployment runs one or more plugins that download resource URLs server-side, such as XLoader, DataPusher, Resource proxy or ckanext-archiver.
A malicious or unaware user can create or edit a resource and set its URL.
Outbound requests from the CKAN host are not restricted by a proxy, firewall rules or URL validation.
patterns.prevention: Do not let server-side fetchers request arbitrary resource URLs. The sources describe three approaches, which can be combined. First, send plugin downloads through a separate HTTP proxy, such as Squid, that allows or denies IPs and domains, and make the extensions use it through the ckan.download_proxy configuration option. Second, add firewall rules that block access to restricted resources. Third, add custom validators on the resource url field that block or allow certain domains or IPs. Use plugin versions that support ckan.download_proxy. For the Resource proxy plugin, support arrived in CKAN 2.10.5 and 2.11.0.
patterns.limitations: The sources only describe deployment-level workarounds and name no code-level URL filtering. They do not say how redirects, DNS resolution, alternate IP encodings or non-HTTP schemes are handled, so those cases are not covered here. They do not list the exact plugin versions that gain ckan.download_proxy support, beyond saying the latest versions support it and giving the Resource proxy versions. A validator on the url field alone does not protect URLs that are changed or reached by other paths. The sources do not discuss this either way.

fixtures.scenario: A user with permission to create resources sets a resource URL to an internal service address that only the CKAN host can reach. The data pusher or archiver on the CKAN host fetches that URL with no restriction and stores or exposes the response.

The deployment sets ckan.download_proxy to a Squid proxy that allows only approved domains and IPs. Plugins that support the setting send every download through it. A resource URL pointing at an internal address is refused by the proxy, and firewall rules and a url validator add further limits.

citations.quote: All of them use the resource URL, and there are currently no checks to limit what URLs can be requested.
Use custom validators on the resource url field to block/allow certain domains or IPs.
Support for this setting in the Resource Proxy plugin was included in CKAN 2.10.5 and 2.11.0.

patterns.title: Untrusted Markdown HTML enabling DOM Clobbering in JupyterLab and Jupyter Notebook
patterns.cause: Markdown cells and Markdown previews render HTML from untrusted notebook or Markdown content. The HTML sanitizer left the application open to DOM Clobbering, where injected markup interferes with named properties in the page. Script running as the victim can then reach the victim's data and send requests as that user. The sources describe the flaw as HTML injection leading to DOM Clobbering and point to the sanitizer settings as the area that changed. They do not describe the exact markup involved.
preconditions: A vulnerable release is in use: JupyterLab before 3.6.8 or 4.2.5, or Jupyter Notebook before 7.2.2.
The user opens a malicious notebook containing Markdown cells, or opens a malicious Markdown file with the JupyterLab preview feature.
Attacker-controlled Markdown or HTML is rendered into the live page of the application.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a patched release: JupyterLab 3.6.8 or 4.2.5, or Jupyter Notebook 7.2.2, or later. Treat notebook and Markdown content as untrusted input. Rendering it should go through a sanitizer configured so that untrusted markup cannot create named properties that clobber the DOM. The patched versions changed sanitizer settings for this. If an upgrade is not possible in time, the advisory says risk can be reduced by disabling the MathJax extension, the Markdown viewer extension, and the older MathJax 2 extension where it is installed. This costs users math preview and Markdown preview.
patterns.limitations: The sources say there is no workaround for the underlying DOM Clobbering susceptibility. Disabling plugins only reduces risk. The sources do not say which attributes or elements are blocked or how the sanitizer logic changed. The advisory warns the change may break rendering of some Markdown. A sanitizer setting named allowNamedProperties can restore the previous behavior, which would bring back the exposure. Other rendering paths and third-party extensions are not covered by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A user on an unpatched JupyterLab opens a downloaded notebook whose Markdown cell contains crafted HTML. Rendering the cell lets the injected markup clobber named properties in the page, and attacker script then acts with the user's session.

A user on a patched release opens the same notebook. The sanitizer, with its default patched settings, strips the markup that would clobber named properties, so the cell renders without affecting the page. Where Markdown layout is slightly altered, that is the accepted trade-off.

citations.quote: The vulnerability depends on user interaction by opening a malicious notebook with Markdown cells, or Markdown file using JupyterLab preview feature.
JupyterLab v3.6.8, v4.2.5 and Jupyter Notebook v7.2.2 were patched.
There is no workaround for the underlying DOM Clobbering susceptibility.
This change has a potential to break rendering of some markdown.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the HTML sanitizer drop the name and id attributes from untrusted markup by default, across many element types, to block DOM Clobbering. It adds an opt-in setting, allowNamedProperties, that restores the old behavior, and rebuilds the sanitizer options whenever that setting changes. This matches the card's cause, its prevention direction, and its note that the setting brings back the exposure.

patterns.title: Directory containment check bypassed by parent-directory sequences in file paths
patterns.cause: A helper meant to confirm that a file lies inside a given directory (Gradio's is_in_or_equal) could be bypassed by payloads that manipulate file paths with parent-directory sequences. A path that passes the check may therefore point outside the intended directory.
preconditions: The application uses Gradio's is_in_or_equal check for blocklist or directory access validation
Attacker-influenced file paths, for example from file uploads, reach that check
The deployment runs a Gradio version older than 5.0
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Gradio to version 5.0 or later. In your own code, resolve each user-supplied path to a normalized absolute form, with parent-directory sequences collapsed, before any containment check. Compare that resolved path against the resolved allowed directory, and reject malformed paths.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact bypass payloads or how the upstream fix works. They rate exploitation difficulty as high. The workaround guidance is only to sanitize, normalize and resolve paths before the check, and it does not say how complete that is.

fixtures.scenario: An app validates an uploaded file path with the containment helper, passing the raw string. The string contains parent-directory sequences, so the check passes while the path points at a restricted file outside the allowed folder.

The app first resolves the supplied path to a normalized absolute path, then checks containment against the resolved allowed directory. A path with parent-directory sequences that escapes the directory is rejected.

citations.quote: can be bypassed with certain payloads that manipulate file paths using
Attackers could potentially access restricted files if they are able to exploit this flaw, although the difficulty is high.
Ensuring that all file paths are properly resolved and absolute can help mitigate the bypass vulnerabilities

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the path helper used by the containment check (is_in_or_equal) so absolute paths are normalized with parent-directory sequences collapsed before comparison. Previously such paths were returned unnormalized. It also adds a shared safe join helper that rejects traversal for uploads, the file explorer, and static and custom component routes, and adds tests for traversal cases.

patterns.title: pyLoad flashgot download into scripts folder leads to command execution
patterns.cause: pyLoad runs scripts from its scripts folder when events such as a finished download occur. The download folder can be set to a subfolder of that scripts folder, and the flashgot API can then fetch an attacker-chosen file into it. The flashgot access checks rely on the Host and Referer headers, which the requester controls, so they do not restrict who can use the API.
preconditions: The attacker can change pyLoad settings, including the download folder.
The download folder can be set to a subfolder of the pyload scripts folder, such as the one for finished downloads.
Downloaded files are given executable permissions through the permission settings.
The flashgot API is reachable, with Host and Referer headers forged to pass its local-only checks.
patterns.prevention: Do not let download destinations resolve inside the directory that holds event scripts. Canonicalize the configured download path and reject any location under the scripts folder. Do not treat the Host or Referer header as proof that a request is local or trusted; use authentication or a check on the real peer address. Keep downloaded files non-executable and out of any location the application later executes. Upgrade to version 0.5.0b3.dev87 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so the exact validation it applies is unknown. They also do not say whether other writable locations could be abused the same way. The impact described requires access to change settings.

fixtures.scenario: An attacker with settings access points the download folder at a subfolder of the pyload scripts directory, then sends a flashgot request with forged Host and Referer headers to fetch an executable there. The next download-finished event runs it.
The destination is canonicalized and rejected if it lies inside the scripts directory, and flashgot does not trust Host or Referer alone. A fetched file cannot land where event hooks will execute it.

citations.quote: By downloading a executable file to a folder in /scripts and performing the respective action, remote code execution can be achieved
Both of these can be set by an attacker to arbitrary values, thereby bypassing these checks.
Version 0.5.0b3.dev87 fixes this issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix stops the download folder from being placed inside dangerous locations, namely the pyLoad package directory and the user config directory, which holds the scripts folder. It resolves paths with realpath, compares them with a trailing separator, and enforces this at startup and in the set_config_value API instead of only in the web UI save handler, which used a weaker abspath check. A rejected value is ignored at the API and reset to the default folder at startup.

patterns.title: Blind SQL injection through user_id in litellm team update handling
patterns.cause: The get_data helper built a raw SELECT on the user table by joining supplied user ids into an IN list, allowing malicious ids to alter SQL. The advisory reports blind SQL injection through user_id in /team/update, potentially exposing API keys, user information, and tokens. The diff also shows lookup-result handling in user_api_key_auth, but does not establish the request-to-query path. The patched query is a SELECT; the advisory describes a query used for deleting users.
preconditions: The deployment uses affected litellm code with a database; the advisory identifies version 1.27.14.
An attacker can supply a malicious user_id through /team/update, as described by the advisory; required authentication is unspecified.
Attacker-controlled ids reach the multi-user lookup that constructs raw SQL by string joining.
patterns.prevention: Replace SQL string construction in the multi-user lookup with Prisma's find_many method and an IN filter, keeping ids as query data, as the fix does. Update authentication-path result handling to skip null entries and convert returned records to dictionaries before caching or inspecting them. As general hardening, use placeholders with separate parameters wherever raw SQL is necessary and audit other raw-query paths accepting request fields.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish the authentication required, the path from /team/update to the patched lookup, or the affected version range beyond the reported 1.27.14. They do not explain the discrepancy between the advisory's deletion description and the SELECT replaced in the diff. The diff fixes one raw query and adjusts result handling; it does not establish coverage of other raw SQL paths.

fixtures.scenario: A team update request carries a crafted user_id value. The service places that value directly into a raw SQL statement that deletes users, so the attacker's text is interpreted as SQL. Through blind techniques the attacker can infer sensitive data such as API keys, user information and tokens.

A team update request carries the same crafted user_id value. The service keeps the delete statement fixed and supplies user_id only as a bound parameter, so the database treats it as a literal value. The delete matches no user and no other data is exposed.

citations.quote: The vulnerability arises due to the improper handling of the 'user_id' parameter in the raw SQL query used for deleting users.
A blind SQL injection vulnerability exists in the berriai/litellm application, specifically within the '/team/update' process.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the raw SELECT in the multi-user lookup helper, which joined the supplied user ids into an IN list as quoted strings. It replaces it with the Prisma find_many method using an IN filter, so the ids are passed as bound values. The authentication code that consumes the results is also changed to convert each returned ORM object to a dict and to skip empty entries.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS from Jinja2 templates without automatic escaping (OctoPrint login and application key dialogs)
patterns.cause: OctoPrint versions up to and including 1.10.2 rendered pages through a Jinja2 template system that was not configured to enforce automatic escaping. Request-supplied values placed into templates, including those in the login dialog and the standalone application key confirmation dialog, were therefore not reliably escaped. A crafted value could run as script in the victim's browser session.
preconditions: Templates are rendered with a Jinja2 setup that does not enforce automatic escaping, so each output location depends on manual escaping.
Attacker-influenced values, such as those in a specially crafted login link or in parameters sent through the application key workflow, reach a template output location.
A victim is persuaded to open the crafted link, or a malicious app redirects the victim to the standalone application key confirmation dialog.
The victim has access to an OctoPrint instance, so script running in their browser can act on that instance.
patterns.prevention: Enable automatic escaping for the whole template environment, so output is escaped by default and an unescaped location needs an explicit opt-out. Until then, audit each template location that renders request-derived data and escape it individually, starting with the login dialog and the application key confirmation dialog. Treat parameters from the application key workflow as untrusted input. Upgrade to 1.10.3 or later for the two reported dialogs, and to the 1.11.0 line for globally enforced automatic escaping. Plugin authors should opt into automatic escaping during the transition period, because enforcement for third party plugins is planned for 1.13.0 unless they opt out.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not name the exact parameters, template files or escaping calls involved, so this card cannot say which fields were injectable. The 1.10.3 fix escapes only the detected locations, so other unescaped locations may remain until global automatic escaping arrives. Third party plugins stay exposed until they opt in or enforcement begins. The sources do not describe any other defenses, such as a content security policy, and this card does not claim any.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens a crafted login link on an OctoPrint 1.10.2 instance. A value from the link is placed into the login dialog markup without escaping, so attacker-chosen script runs in the user's browser and can change settings or interrupt a print.

The same crafted login link is opened on an instance where the template environment enforces automatic escaping, or where that output location is escaped. The value is shown as inert text, and no script runs.

citations.quote: reflected XSS vulnerabilities through its Jinja2 template system, as this is not configured to enforce automatic escaping
patched in the bugfix release 1.10.3 by individual escaping of the detected locations
switching to globally enforced automatic escaping and thus reducing the attack surface in general

patch_review.observation: The fix adds explicit escaping at the template locations that render request-derived data. These include the login dialog username field, the application key dialog (where the app name is no longer pasted into the request text before rendering), and the user name, theming URLs and reverse proxy test values. It also turns on automatic escaping for the discovery XML template. This is per-location escaping, not a global switch, which matches the card's cause, its note that only detected locations are fixed in 1.10.3, and its advice to enable automatic escaping globally.

patterns.title: Local file inclusion via user-controlled JSON reaching file-caching traversal in gradio
patterns.cause: The JSON component postprocess step parses a user-controlled string as JSON. The result is passed to move_files_to_cache(), which walks any object looking for a dictionary with a path key and copies the named file to a temporary directory. The file can then be fetched through the file endpoint, so an attacker can read arbitrary files on the server.
preconditions: A gradio app (reported in version 4.25) returns a JSON component whose value includes a user-controlled string.
That string is parsed as JSON, so the user decides the keys and values of the resulting object.
The parsed object contains a path key naming a file on the server, and the caching traversal accepts it without validation.
patterns.prevention: Do not let user-controlled data decide which server files get cached or served. Validate input before it reaches the file-moving logic, so a user-supplied structure with a path key is not treated as a file reference. Apply the file-handling traversal only to values the application built itself, not to parsed user strings. Upgrade to a gradio release that includes the upstream fix.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the flaw in version 4.25 and do not give the exact fixed version or the details of the upstream change. They do not say which other components or code paths might reach the same traversal. They do not list what validation rules are sufficient.

fixtures.scenario: An app echoes a user-typed string into a JSON component. The user types a JSON object whose path key names a sensitive server file. The file is copied to the temp directory and the user downloads it via the file endpoint.

An app builds its JSON output from trusted values only. A user-typed string that looks like an object with a path key is shown as plain data and never treated as a file reference, so no server file is copied or exposed.

citations.quote: a user-controlled string is parsed as JSON
the specified file is moved to a temporary directory, making it possible to retrieve it later
The vulnerability can be exploited by an attacker to read files on the remote system

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the JSON component's postprocess return a dedicated opaque JSON wrapper type instead of a plain dict or list. The file-caching traversal therefore no longer treats a user-supplied object with a path key as a file reference, and a test confirms such data is not moved to the cache. The patch also adds a check that file paths in event data lie inside the upload cache folder. This matches the card's cause and its direction of not applying the file traversal to parsed user strings.

patterns.title: File URI scheme check bypassed by omitting the double slashes
patterns.cause: The URL safety check accepts file: as a scheme. The later check that blocks local files only applies when the URL starts with the literal prefix file://. The file URI scheme does not require double slashes, so a URL such as file:/etc/passwd skips the local-file restriction. A webdriver-backed fetch can then read the file and show its contents in the watch preview.
preconditions: The instance has a webdriver (browser-based fetching) enabled.
The ALLOW_FILE_URI setting is false or not defined.
An attacker can create a watch with an attacker-chosen URL and enable webdriver mode for it.
patterns.prevention: Decide whether a URL is a local-file URL from its parsed scheme, not from a string-prefix match on the raw text. Parse the URL with a standard URL parser, normalise the scheme, and apply the local-file policy to every file URI form: no hostname, empty hostname, and with hostname. Run the same decision wherever the URL is validated and wherever the fetcher chooses how to load it, so the two checks cannot disagree. Reject file URIs by default unless local files are explicitly allowed. Upgrade to version 0.47.06 or later, which the advisory says addresses the issue.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so this card gives only the general direction. They do not discuss other bypass forms, such as case variations, other schemes, or redirects. They state that no workarounds are known. The issue is reported only for instances with a webdriver enabled and ALLOW_FILE_URI false or undefined.

fixtures.scenario: An instance has a webdriver enabled and ALLOW_FILE_URI unset. A user creates a watch whose URL is file:/etc/passwd with webdriver mode on. The prefix check for file:// does not match, so the watch is accepted, fetched, and the file contents appear in the preview.

The same instance parses each submitted URL and reads its scheme. The watch URL file:/etc/passwd is recognised as a file URI and rejected because local files are not allowed. The forms file:///etc/passwd and file://host/etc/passwd are rejected the same way.

citations.quote: The issue comes with the fact that the file URI scheme is not required to have double slashes.
It later checks if local files are permitted, but one of the preconditions for the check is that the URL starts with
This issue has been addressed in version 0.47.06 and all users are advised to upgrade.

patch_review.observation: The fix widens the local-file guard in the browser-fetch path so it matches any URL beginning with the file scheme followed by a single slash, not only the double-slash form. It also trims surrounding whitespace before the check. A new test confirms the single-slash form is denied unless ALLOW_FILE_URI is enabled.

patterns.title: SQL injection through an unvalidated api_key value concatenated into a spend logs query in litellm
patterns.cause: The /global/spend/logs endpoint in litellm built an SQL query by concatenating an unvalidated api_key parameter directly into the query text. Special elements in that value were not neutralized, so a caller could change the structure of the SQL command instead of only supplying a value.
preconditions: The application builds an SQL command as text and inserts a request parameter, here api_key, into it by concatenation.
The parameter value is not validated or neutralized before it reaches the SQL command.
An attacker can send the endpoint a request whose api_key value contains malicious data.
patterns.prevention: Never place request-supplied values such as api_key into the SQL command text by concatenation. Keep the command structure fixed and pass user-controlled values to the database separately, so special characters are treated as data and not as SQL syntax. Also validate the expected shape of the value before use. Review every endpoint that filters spend or log data by caller-supplied identifiers for the same pattern.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the actual upstream fix, the affected version range, or which other parameters or endpoints might share the flaw. They say only that the issue affects the latest version at the time of the report. The prevention direction above is the general remedy for the stated cause, not a confirmed description of the patch. The sources also do not say whether authentication limits who can reach the endpoint.

fixtures.scenario: A spend report endpoint receives an api_key query parameter and joins it into the text of a SELECT statement. A caller supplies a value containing SQL special characters and extra clauses, and the database runs the altered statement, exposing or modifying data beyond the intended key.

The same endpoint uses a fixed SELECT statement with a placeholder for the api_key filter and hands the caller's value to the database driver as a separate bound parameter. The same hostile input is matched literally as a key string, finds no rows, and does not change the statement.

citations.quote: The affected code constructs an SQL query by concatenating an unvalidated
The vulnerability arises due to improper neutralization of special elements used in an SQL command.
Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could lead to unauthorized access, data manipulation, exposure of confidential information, and denial of service (DoS).

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the spend logs handler for the global spend logs endpoint so the api_key filter is no longer concatenated into the SQL text. The query now uses a numbered placeholder, and the api_key is passed to the raw query call as a separate bound argument. This matches the card's cause (string concatenation of an unvalidated parameter) and its main prevention (fixed query structure with values passed separately).

patterns.title: Incomplete engine-specific function checks let SQL bypass Superset authorization
patterns.cause: Superset's SQL authorization uses engine-specific disallowed-function sets. The advisory describes a bypass involving missing PostgreSQL functions query_to_xml_and_xmlschema, table_to_xml and table_to_xml_and_xmlschema, following CVE-2024-39887. The diff adds these three functions and database_to_xml to the default PostgreSQL set. It does not establish that database_to_xml independently enables the reported bypass.
preconditions: Apache Superset earlier than version 4.1.0 is deployed.
A PostgreSQL database is accessible through Superset.
The PostgreSQL entry in DISALLOWED_SQL_FUNCTIONS lacks coverage for the functions involved in the reported bypass.
An attacker can submit SQL subject to Superset's authorization check; the configuration comment identifies SQL Lab and Charts as uses of this control.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Superset 4.1.0, which the advisory identifies as fixing the issue. Alternatively, the advisory recommends adding query_to_xml_and_xmlschema, table_to_xml and table_to_xml_and_xmlschema to the PostgreSQL entry in DISALLOWED_SQL_FUNCTIONS. To match the diff's expanded default set, also include database_to_xml. As general hardening, review related function families when a bypass is reported and restrict database account privileges to reduce reliance on this check.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not explain the bypass mechanism, accessible data or exact attacker privileges. They do not establish an independent bypass through database_to_xml or that the advisory's three-function workaround is insufficient. They also do not establish whether other functions or engines are affected, or whether a disallowed-function list alone is sufficient protection.

fixtures.scenario: A Superset instance older than 4.1.0 is connected to PostgreSQL and uses the default disallowed-function set. A user submits a query that calls table_to_xml. The authorization check does not flag the function, so the query passes the check that should have blocked it.

A Superset instance runs version 4.1.0 or later, or an older instance has query_to_xml_and_xmlschema, table_to_xml and table_to_xml_and_xmlschema added to its disallowed-function configuration. A query calling any of them is flagged by the authorization check.

citations.quote: certain engine-specific functions are not checked, which allows attackers to bypass Apache Superset's SQL authorization
This issue is a follow-up to CVE-2024-39887 with additional disallowed PostgreSQL functions now included
Users are recommended to upgrade to version 4.1.0, which fixes the issue or add these Postgres functions to the config set DISALLOWED_SQL_FUNCTIONS.
This issue affects Apache Superset: <4.1.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix extends the default disallowed-function set for PostgreSQL in the Superset configuration. It adds the four XML export functions database_to_xml, query_to_xml_and_xmlschema, table_to_xml and table_to_xml_and_xmlschema, next to the existing entries. SQL calling any of them is now rejected by the authorization check, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Prefix-based file URL blocklist bypassed for local file read in watch URLs
patterns.cause: The application accepted user-supplied watch URLs and tried to block local file access by checking whether the stripped URL began with the file scheme followed by a slash. Variants such as a relative form with dot-dot segments right after the scheme, or a space before the slashes, slipped past this weak check. User input could then reach file paths without adequate validation.
preconditions: The attacker can create a watch with an arbitrary URL
The instance has a webdriver configured
The only guard is a text-prefix check on the URL string
The watch preview returns fetched content to the attacker
patterns.prevention: Do not rely on matching a blocked prefix in the raw URL text. Parse the URL with a real parser, then allow only the web schemes the feature needs and reject everything else, including any form of the file scheme. Apply this check to the parsed result and on every path where a watch URL is accepted or fetched, so odd spacing or relative forms cannot change the outcome. Upgrade to 0.48.05 or later, where this issue is reported fixed.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream fix, so the allow-list and parser guidance is a general direction and not a confirmed account of the patch. They also name only the file scheme and the webdriver-backed preview path, and do not say whether other schemes or fetchers were affected.

fixtures.scenario: A user creates a watch whose URL starts with the file scheme and uses a relative path with dot-dot segments, or has a space before the slashes. The prefix check misses it, and the preview shows the contents of the system password file.
The same watch URLs are parsed first. Only permitted web schemes are accepted, so any file-scheme variant is rejected at creation and no local file content appears in the preview.

citations.quote: Improper input validation in the application can allow attackers to perform local file read (LFR) or path traversal attacks.
The attacker can still bypass this by using:
This vulnerability is fixed in 0.48.05.

patch_review.observation: The fix widens the check in the browser-call path so that any watch URL whose stripped text starts with the file scheme is denied, instead of only those where the scheme is followed by a slash. Tests were added for the double-slash, single-slash and no-slash forms of the file scheme. This matches the card's cause, a prefix check that required a slash after the scheme and so missed variants.

patterns.title: Pickle deserialization of untrusted bytes in FAISS.deserialize_from_bytes (CVE-2024-5998)
patterns.cause: FAISS.deserialize_from_bytes in langchain-community passed serialized bytes directly to pickle without an explicit opt-in guard in the shown implementation. Malicious bytes from an untrusted source could execute arbitrary code, including commands through os.system.
preconditions: The application calls FAISS.deserialize_from_bytes on serialized vector store bytes.
An untrusted party can supply or alter those bytes, for example through an upload, shared store, or download.
The implementation lacks the new guard, or the caller enables deserialization through the allow_dangerous_deserialization flag.
patterns.prevention: Use a release containing the FAISS opt-in guard. The patched method defaults to refusing deserialization and raises ValueError unless the caller enables the allow_dangerous_deserialization flag. Enable it only for data from a trusted source that has not been tampered with, such as bytes the application created and kept protected from modification. Do not enable it for untrusted bytes. The flag acknowledges risk; it does not verify provenance or make pickle safe.
patterns.limitations: Pickle remains in use, so enabling the flag permits the same unsafe deserialization of malicious input. Existing calls without opt-in now raise ValueError even for trusted data. GHSA-f2jm-rw3h-6phg and PYSEC-2026-1514 specify versions before 0.2.4, while the CVE and PYSEC-2024-323 refer to the latest version. The sources do not resolve this conflict or map fixed releases to langchain versus langchain-community. They do not establish whether warnings existed elsewhere, how developers react to the guard, or signature, MAC, or index-rebuilding workflows. The WebResearchRetriever diff concerns a separate SSRF guard.

fixtures.scenario: A web service lets users upload a saved vector store file and passes the uploaded bytes straight to FAISS.deserialize_from_bytes. An attacker uploads a crafted pickle payload that runs a system command on the server when it is loaded.

A service builds its vector store from its own documents, stores the serialized bytes in a location only the service can write, and loads only those bytes. Files from outside parties are never deserialized. They are re-indexed from the source documents instead.

citations.quote: A vulnerability in the FAISS.deserialize_from_bytes function of langchain-ai/langchain allows for pickle deserialization of untrusted data.
This can lead to the execution of arbitrary commands via the os.system function.
The issue affects versions prior to 0.2.4.

patch_review.observation: The FAISS fix adds a keyword-only opt-in flag to deserialize_from_bytes that defaults to false. Without it the method raises an error before the pickle load, and the message warns that pickle data can execute arbitrary code and should only be trusted if the caller created it. The other commit in the diff adds a similar opt-in guard to WebResearchRetriever for SSRF, which is a separate issue and does not affect the card.

patterns.title: Client-chosen api_base sends server-held API key to attacker domain in litellm
patterns.cause: In litellm 1.38.10, users could specify the api_base parameter when calling POST /chat/completions. The application then sent the request to whatever domain api_base named, and that request included the OpenAI API key. The caller, not the operator, controlled the destination of a request that carried a server-side secret.
preconditions: The deployment runs litellm 1.38.10 and exposes POST /chat/completions to users.
The endpoint accepts a user-supplied api_base parameter and uses it as the upstream destination.
The outbound request carries the OpenAI API key held by the server.
patterns.prevention: Do not let a request-supplied value choose the destination of an outbound call that carries server-held credentials. Take the upstream base address from operator-controlled configuration, or accept a user-supplied value only if it matches an operator-defined allowlist of trusted destinations. Treat any per-request override of the destination as untrusted input, and never attach the server's API key to a request sent to an address the operator did not approve.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe only the vulnerable behavior in version 1.38.10. They do not describe the upstream fix, the patched version, or any other affected parameters or endpoints. They do not say whether authentication on the endpoint changes exploitability. The allowlist approach above is a general design direction and not a description of the upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A user sends a chat completions request to the litellm server and sets api_base to a domain they control. The server forwards the request to that domain with the OpenAI API key attached, and the user reads the key from their own server logs.

A user sends a chat completions request that includes an api_base pointing at their own domain. The server ignores or rejects the value because it is not on the operator-approved list, and sends the request only to the configured upstream. The API key never reaches the user's domain.

citations.quote: This request includes the OpenAI API key.
leading to unauthorized access and potential misuse of the API key.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a request-body safety check to the proxy's common authorization checks. It rejects any request that carries an api_base or base_url field, so callers can no longer redirect upstream calls, which carry the server's API key, to a domain they control. This matches the card's cause and its direction of keeping the destination under operator control.

patterns.title: Arbitrary callback names in litellm post_call_rules allow remote code execution
patterns.cause: In litellm 1.40.12, the post_call_rules configuration accepts a callback function. The supplied value is split at the final dot. The last part is treated as the function name, and the remaining part is given a .py extension and imported. Nothing restricts the value to a vetted callback, so an attacker can name a system method such as os.system as the callback. The command then runs when a chat response is processed.
preconditions: litellm 1.40.12 is in use, the version named in the advisory.
The post_call_rules configuration accepts a callback value that an attacker can influence.
The callback value is split at the last dot and resolved to an importable module and function name.
A chat response is processed, which triggers the configured callback.
patterns.prevention: Never turn a configuration string directly into an imported module and callable. Resolve each callback only against an explicit allowlist of operator-approved callback functions, or against a fixed, trusted location that holds only callback code. Reject any value that resolves to a standard library or system function such as os.system. Treat the post_call_rules setting as sensitive, so that untrusted users cannot write or change it.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe only the vulnerable behavior. They do not say how an attacker gains the ability to set post_call_rules, which versions besides 1.40.12 are affected, or exactly how upstream changed the code. The allowlist and access-control directions above are general mitigations, not a description of the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment on litellm 1.40.12 lets a user supply a post_call_rules entry whose value names a system method such as os.system. The value is split at the last dot and resolved, so processing a chat response runs an arbitrary command on the server.

A deployment accepts only callback names from a fixed allowlist of approved functions in operator-controlled code. A value naming os.system is rejected at configuration time, and untrusted users cannot edit post_call_rules, so no arbitrary command runs when a chat response is processed.

citations.quote: The issue exists in the handling of the 'post_call_rules' configuration, where a callback function can be added.
The provided value is split at the final '.' mark, with the last part considered the function name
This allows an attacker to set a system method, such as 'os.system', as a callback

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a security check that get_instance_fn calls on the module portion of the configured callback string before any import or file loading. It rejects module names containing risky modules such as os, subprocess, sys, socket, pickle and builtins, case-insensitively, and raises an import error. This matches the card's cause, which is an unvalidated callback string turned into an import, and its direction of rejecting system-level callbacks. The upstream fix is a denylist rather than the allowlist the card prefers, and the card says as much in its limitations.

patterns.title: Stored XSS through files uploaded in Open WebUI chat
patterns.cause: In open-webui version 0.3.8, the chat file upload feature accepts a file containing attacker-controlled malicious content. When a victim later opens that file through a URL or a shared chat, the content runs as JavaScript in the victim's browser. The uploaded content is therefore treated as active content, not as inert data.
preconditions: The application is open-webui version 0.3.8, the version named in the advisories.
An attacker can upload a file through the chat file upload functionality.
A victim accesses the stored file through a URL or through a shared chat.
patterns.prevention: Treat every uploaded file as untrusted data. When a file is delivered to a user, by direct URL or through a shared chat, make sure its content cannot execute as script in the application's browser context. Neutralize or sanitize attacker-controlled content, or serve it so the browser does not interpret it as active content. Apply this check on every path that returns uploaded content, including shared chat views.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, the exact file types or payloads involved, or which versions after 0.3.8 are fixed. They do not say which delivery mechanism, such as sanitization, response headers or content-type handling, resolves the issue. This card gives only a general direction and should be checked against the vendor's patched release.

fixtures.scenario: A user uploads a file with embedded script content in a chat and shares the chat. A second user opens the file through its URL or the shared chat, and the script runs in that user's browser session.

A user uploads the same file and shares the chat. When the second user opens the file through its URL or the shared chat, the content is handled as untrusted data and does not run as script in the application's context.

citations.quote: A Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability exists in the chat file upload functionality of open-webui/open-webui version 0.3.8.
when accessed by a victim through a URL or shared chat, executes JavaScript in the victim's browser

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the file content endpoint in the files router so the stored file is returned with a header that marks it as an attachment. The browser then downloads the file instead of rendering it inline, so uploaded HTML or script content no longer runs in the application's origin. This matches the card's cause (uploaded content treated as active content) and its prevention direction of serving the file so the browser does not interpret it as active content.

patterns.title: Prompt injection in GraphCypherQAChain leading to database injection
patterns.cause: Prompt injection in GraphCypherQAChain can induce unintended database operations within the connection's permissions. The advisories describe unauthorized creation, updates and deletion of nodes and relationships, sensitive-data extraction, cross-tenant access, integrity damage and denial of service through data deletion. The diff adds mandatory risk acknowledgement and credential-scoping warnings to this class and ten other graph QA chains; it does not add query filtering.
preconditions: The application uses GraphCypherQAChain; the advisories report version 0.2.5 in langchain and langchain-community.
An attacker can influence prompt text processed by the chain.
The database connection permits the reads or mutations needed for the unauthorized outcome.
patterns.prevention: Use an update containing the shown constructor gate, which rejects construction of the modified chains unless the dangerous-requests opt-in is explicitly true. Opt in only after understanding the risks and taking precautions. Restrict database credentials to necessary permissions, as the upstream warning directs. As general hardening, treat prompts as untrusted, enforce authorization and tenant isolation in the database layer, and use read-only, user-scoped access where appropriate. The opt-in acknowledges risk; it does not filter queries or enforce credential scope.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish the full affected version range or the fixed release number. The advisories identify GraphCypherQAChain; applying the same gate to sibling chains does not establish identical CVE exposure. The diff does not show the full query execution path or prove that earlier documentation lacked warnings. It adds acknowledgement rather than query validation, leaving dangerous operations possible with sufficient permissions after opt-in. Existing construction calls without opt-in now fail, but claims about how users will respond are unsupported.

fixtures.scenario: A multi-tenant app passes end-user questions to GraphCypherQAChain using one shared, full-privilege database account. A crafted prompt makes the chain delete nodes or read another tenant's data.
The app passes end-user questions to the chain through a database account limited to read-only access on the current tenant's data. A crafted prompt cannot modify data or reach other tenants.

citations.quote: A vulnerability in the GraphCypherQAChain class of langchain-ai/langchain version 0.2.5 allows for SQL injection through prompt injection.
Attackers can create, update, or delete nodes and relationships without proper authorization, extract sensitive data, disrupt services

patch_review.observation: The diff adds a required opt-in flag, defaulting to false, to ArangoGraphQAChain, GraphCypherQAChain, FalkorDBQAChain, GremlinQAChain, HugeGraphQAChain, KuzuQAChain, NebulaGraphQAChain, the two Neptune chains, OntotextGraphDBQAChain and GraphSparqlQAChain. Each constructor now raises an error unless the caller sets the flag to true, and the docstring warns to narrowly scope database credentials. No query validation is added, and tests are updated to pass the flag.

patterns.title: Local file read in MLflow dbfs handling when only the URL path is validated
patterns.cause: The non-local model version source validator repeatedly URL-decodes the source but checks only the parsed path for traversal. The regression test shows an encoded question mark moving subsequent parent-directory segments into the query, outside that path check. The advisory reports that, in MLflow 2.15.1 with dbfs configured, used, and mounted locally, direct concatenation of the URL into a file-protocol location enables arbitrary local file reads (CWE-22, CWE-29).
preconditions: MLflow 2.15.1 is the affected version identified by the advisory; the broader affected range is unspecified.
The dbfs service is configured, in use, and mounted to a local directory.
A supplied non-local model version source reaches the validator; the regression test uses a dbfs source with an encoded question mark before slash-separated parent-directory segments.
For the reported file read, the dbfs URL is subsequently concatenated into a file-protocol location and read locally.
patterns.prevention: After repeated URL decoding is complete, reject sources containing an exact parent-directory segment anywhere in the full source when split on forward slashes, including outside the parsed path. Preserve the existing null-character check on the parsed path. The regression test requires model version creation to reject the encoded-question-mark dbfs source with HTTP 400 and an invalid-source error. As general hardening, confirm that the final resolved local location remains inside the intended artifact root before reading.
patterns.limitations: The diff adds a targeted check for exact parent-directory segments separated by forward slashes; it does not add scheme or host restrictions or final artifact-root containment. It does not establish whether other encodings or path tricks bypass existing validation. The test verifies request rejection, not an end-to-end local file read. The supplied sources do not show the downstream URL-to-file conversion, authentication requirements, fixed release, or affected versions beyond the advisory's named 2.15.1.

fixtures.scenario: A dbfs service is mounted to a local directory. A URL is joined into a file protocol string and only its path is checked. Query or parameter parts are left unchecked, so a crafted URL reads an arbitrary local file.

The same mounted dbfs service validates every URL component, including query and parameters. It rejects unexpected parts. It also confirms the resolved local location stays inside the mounted directory before any read.

citations.quote: only the path part of the URL is checked, while parts such as query and parameters are not handled
The vulnerability is triggered if the user has configured the dbfs service, and during usage, the service is mounted to a local directory.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check in the non-local source validator so that the whole fully decoded source string is split on slashes and rejected if any segment is a parent-directory reference. Previously only the parsed URL path was inspected, so an encoded question mark could move the parent-directory segments into the query part and past the check. The added test uses a dbfs source with an encoded question mark followed by many parent-directory segments and expects a 400 response.

patterns.title: Unvalidated user-supplied model file path allows directory traversal in MLflow Tracking Server
patterns.cause: The advisory attributes directory traversal to insufficient validation of user-supplied model file paths before file operations, allowing remote code execution as the service account. The diff adds validation of the caller-supplied source in the model version creation endpoint. It does not establish which crafted paths bypassed existing checks or whether exploitation involves reads, writes, or both.
preconditions: An attacker can reach the affected MLflow Tracking Server remotely; the advisory states authentication is not required.
The attacker supplies a model file path that reaches file operations without adequate validation. The patched endpoint accepts a caller-supplied source.
patterns.prevention: Use a release containing the change and configure MLFLOW_CREATE_MODEL_VERSION_SOURCE_VALIDATION_REGEX to allow only intended sources. When both the source and configured pattern are nonempty, the model version creation handler uses regular expression search and rejects a nonmatching source with an invalid-parameter error before the existing source-validation branches. This also precedes the prompt-specific validation exemption. Existing validation remains in place. As general hardening, anchor the pattern and restrict allowed schemes and locations to deployment needs. The test demonstrates rejecting an S3 source and accepting a proxied MLflow artifact source.
patterns.limitations: The setting defaults to unset; an unset or empty pattern adds no restriction, and an empty source skips this new check. This alone does not prove exploitability in every deployment. Search can match a substring unless the pattern constrains it; protection depends on the configured pattern. The diff adds this check only to the shown endpoint and does not establish coverage of all model creation paths. The test restricts the URI scheme, not a specific storage root. No canonical path containment check is added. The sources give no affected or fixed version ranges, exact malicious source, downstream file operations, or explanation of the code-execution chain.

fixtures.scenario: A remote, unauthenticated client sends a model creation request whose model file path contains parent-directory segments. The server uses it directly in file operations, so files are written or read outside the intended model storage location.

The same request is received, but the server validates the supplied path, resolves it, and finds it falls outside the allowed model storage root. The request is rejected and no file operation occurs outside that root.

citations.quote: The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied path prior to using it in file operations.
Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.
An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the service account.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds an optional operator-set regular expression setting, read from an environment variable and off by default. The model version creation handler rejects any non-empty source that does not match it, with an invalid-parameter error, before the existing source validation runs. This matches the card's cause, its allowlist prevention, and its opt-in limitation.

patterns.title: ReDoS in GPT-NeoX-Japanese subword tokenizer regular expressions
patterns.cause: The SubWordJapaneseTokenizer class in the GPT-NeoX-Japanese tokenization module uses a regular expression with exponential complexity on certain inputs. When specially crafted text is processed, the regex engine performs excessive backtracking, consuming high CPU time.
preconditions: The application uses the GPT-NeoX-Japanese tokenizer from the transformers library, specifically the SubWordJapaneseTokenizer class.
The installed transformers version is affected (the advisory names v4.48.1 as affected).
Untrusted or attacker-influenced text reaches the tokenizer, so specially crafted input can trigger the vulnerable regular expression.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to a transformers release that includes the upstream fix for this tokenizer.
