preconditions: vLLM versions 0.6.5 through 0.8.4 with the V0 engine
The PyNcclPipe KV cache transfer integration is in use
The TCPStore port is reachable from hosts outside the intended private network
The attacker can join the communication domain and send a serialized object to the receiving node
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to vLLM 0.8.5 or later, where the TCPStore socket is limited to the private interface that was configured. When building similar services, bind the listening socket explicitly to the intended private interface instead of treating the supplied IP address as a client-side hint, and confirm the real bind address. Keep the KV transfer port on a secured private network as the vLLM security documentation requires.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the fix as restricting the TCPStore socket to the configured interface. They do not say the deserialization of peer data was changed, so a peer that can reach the port may still be trusted to send serialized objects. Only the PyNcclPipe integration with the V0 engine is described as affected. PyTorch judged the all-interface listening behavior intentional. The sources give no further detail on the fix beyond the binding workaround.

fixtures.scenario: A node runs PyNcclPipe KV transfer on the V0 engine, vLLM 0.6.5 to 0.8.4, with kv-ip set to a private address. The TCPStore still listens on all interfaces, so any reachable host can send a serialized object that the node deserializes.

A node runs vLLM 0.8.5 or later, where the TCPStore socket is bound to the configured private interface, and the network is restricted per vLLM security guidance, so untrusted hosts cannot reach the control port.

citations.quote: Attackers can exploit this by sending malicious serialized data to gain server control privileges.
The intention was that this interface should only be exposed to a private network using the IP address specified by the
The IP address given was only used as a client-side address to use.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the group creator on rank 0 open its own listening socket bound to the configured host and port, then hands that socket to the TCPStore through a listen file descriptor. This replaces the default all-interface listening, so the store is reachable only on the intended private interface. The pickle-based receive path is left unchanged, which matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS via label_config in Label Studio upload-example endpoint
patterns.cause: The upload_example_using_config view accepted POST requests, read label_config, validated it, generated sample task data, and returned JSON-serialized data through HttpResponse without explicitly specifying a JSON content type. The advisory demonstrates that attacker-controlled markup reflected through this response can execute in the victim's browser. The view had no login_required decorator, but this alone does not establish the absence of authentication or CSRF controls elsewhere. The upstream fix removes the view and its route.
preconditions: A Label Studio version prior to 1.18.0 is running with the upload-example route available.
A crafted POST to /projects/upload-example/ reaches the vulnerable view and its response is rendered by the victim's browser.
The attacker induces the victim to submit a crafted label_config value; the advisory demonstrates an auto-submitting form.
The crafted configuration passes validation and carries executable markup into the returned sample task data.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to 1.18.0 or later. The supplied upstream fix removes upload_example_using_config, its URL registration and URL inventory entry, the playground_replacements helper, and the associated sample-task tests. This eliminates the vulnerable endpoint. As general hardening for any retained equivalent, use an explicitly typed JSON response, prevent content-type sniffing, and handle user-controlled content safely for its output context; these measures are not the patch shown.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish deployment-wide authentication or CSRF behavior, nor show actual response headers. They do not fully trace which generated task fields carry the payload. The diff does not cover other label_config processing paths. Clients relying on the removed endpoint lose that functionality. HttpOnly session cookies prevent direct script access to those cookies, but do not prevent unauthorized actions through XSS; the broader advisories list session hijacking without explaining a mechanism.

fixtures.scenario: A page on an attacker site auto-submits a form to the upload-example endpoint with a label_config value holding script markup. The server reflects it in a response built from the sample task data, and the victim's browser runs it.

The same crafted label_config is submitted. The response is explicitly typed as JSON and values are encoded, so the browser never interprets the input as markup. The deployment runs release 1.18.0 or later.

citations.quote: The vulnerability is specifically located in line 57, where HttpResponse is used.
A vulnerability in versions prior to 1.18.0 allows an attacker to inject a malicious script into the context of a web page
Version 1.18.0 contains a patch for the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix deletes the unauthenticated upload-example view, which took a label_config form value, built a sample task from it and returned it as a default HTML HttpResponse. It also removes the URL route, the URL listing entry and the tests for that endpoint. The card's cause and its remove-the-endpoint prevention match this.

patterns.title: Internal-only upload form inputs let clients make the server move arbitrary host files
patterns.cause: The central file upload processor trusted form inputs meant only for internal use. A crafted HTTP request to an upload endpoint could supply them, so the server treated an arbitrary host file as a freshly uploaded temporary file and moved it into the upload folder, where it could be downloaded.
preconditions: Attacker holds an account with the FILE_UPLOAD permission
OctoPrint version 1.11.1 or earlier, or a third-party plugin upload endpoint built on the same upload processor
The target file is readable by the OctoPrint process
patterns.prevention: In the central upload processing component, strip every internal-only form input from incoming requests before any handler sees them, so only values the server itself generates can identify a temporary uploaded file. Do not let client-supplied fields decide which file on disk is moved. Upgrade to version 1.11.2 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say how the internal form inputs are named or validated, so this card gives no detail on the fix mechanics. Third-party plugin endpoints might be affected, but the sources do not say which ones or how to check them. The sources also give no detail on how the moved file is later served.

fixtures.scenario: A user with FILE_UPLOAD sends a crafted multipart request to an upload endpoint with an internal-only field naming a config file path. The server moves that file into the upload folder, and the user downloads it.
The same crafted request is sent, but the upload processor first removes all internal-only form inputs. Only server-created temporary files are handled, and the named host file stays in place.

citations.quote: A specially crafted HTTP Request to an affected upload endpoint that contains some form inputs only supposed to be used internally
The fix removes any internal-only form inputs from incoming requests in the central file upload processor component.
allows an attacker with the FILE_UPLOAD permission to exfiltrate files from the host that OctoPrint has read access to

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the multipart upload handler in the Tornado utilities. When a request part finishes, any part whose name ends with one of the server's internal suffixes is thrown away, and its file handle is closed. Client-supplied fields can therefore no longer pose as server-generated temporary-file path entries, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Catastrophic backtracking in the vLLM pythonic tool call parser regex
patterns.cause: The pythonic tool parser uses a complex tool call detection pattern with nested quantifiers, optional groups and inner repetitions through the standard library regular expression engine. Crafted near-matching input can cause catastrophic backtracking, exponential CPU consumption and denial of service. The upstream change replaces that engine with the third-party regex package in the parser and many other modules, leaving the detection pattern unchanged. The advisory reports improvement from exponential to quadratic time.
preconditions: vLLM version 0.6.4 up to but excluding 0.9.0 is in use.
The pythonic tool parser handles function call text.
An attacker can cause crafted text to reach the tool call detection pattern through an API or interface.
The vulnerable pattern is evaluated using the standard library regular expression engine.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to vLLM 0.9.0, which the advisories identify as patched, or a release confirmed to include the fix. The patch switches parser imports to the regex package and adds it to build requirements; ensure that dependency is available. As general hardening, avoid nested unbounded repetitions over overlapping sub-patterns, prefer unambiguous patterns, structural parsing or a linear-time matcher where suitable, cap input length, and test runtime with near-matching inputs of increasing length.
patterns.limitations: The advisory reports quadratic behavior after the change and warns that the regex may remain problematic; the diff does not establish a universal worst-case bound. It leaves the pattern's ambiguity intact and adds no timeout, input length limit or pattern simplification. Import changes in other modules do not establish that their patterns were exploitable. The supplied sources do not show the exact input path, establish that the matched text must be model output, or verify behavior in every later release.

fixtures.scenario: A server runs vLLM 0.8.x with the pythonic tool parser. A client sends model-bound text with many repeated, almost-valid call fragments. The nested-quantifier regex backtracks exponentially and one request pins a CPU.

A server runs vLLM 0.9.0 or later. The same crafted text is parsed with the patched pattern, which has far lower worst-case cost, and the team keeps testing long near-matching inputs because quadratic cost may remain.

citations.quote: The pattern contains multiple nested quantifiers, optional groups, and inner repetitions which make it vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking.
this regex may still be problematic. It has gone from exponential time complexity, O(2^N), to O(N^2).
the associated KV cache (used for model inference and typically stored in GPU memory) is not released in a timely manner.

patch_review.observation: The diff replaces the standard library regular expression module with the third-party regex package in the pythonic tool parser and many other modules, and adds regex as a build requirement. The pattern in the parser is not edited, and no timeout, length cap or pattern simplification is added, which matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: urllib3 redirect settings are ignored under Pyodide in browsers and Node.js
patterns.cause: When urllib3 runs in a Pyodide runtime, it uses the JavaScript Fetch API or XMLHttpRequest. The retries and redirect parameters are ignored there, and the runtime decides redirect behavior. Code that turns redirects off or limits them through urllib3 therefore gets no such control.
preconditions: urllib3 version 2.2.0 or later and before 2.5.0
Code runs in a Pyodide runtime, in a browser or in Node.js
The application relies on urllib3 retries or redirect settings to limit or disable redirects, for example to mitigate SSRF or open redirect
patterns.prevention: In Node.js, upgrade to a patched urllib3 release; the CVE record says 2.5.0 patched the issue. In browsers, urllib3 has no suitable way to control redirects, so do not treat its redirect or retries settings as a safeguard there. Expect the default browser redirect behavior and do not rely on disabled redirects as an SSRF or open redirect mitigation in that environment.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch works in Node.js, so this card does not either. Browsers have no remediation: XMLHttpRequest offers no redirect control, and the Fetch API returns opaque redirect responses without data when redirects are handled manually. The sources give no other mitigation for browser use. Environments outside Pyodide are not discussed.

fixtures.scenario: An app runs urllib3 2.4.0 under Pyodide and sets redirect to false to block redirects to internal hosts. The runtime ignores the setting and follows redirects itself, so the SSRF mitigation does not work.
An app in Node.js runs urllib3 2.5.0 or later. In browsers, it does not assume urllib3 settings stop redirects and accepts the default browser redirect behavior.

citations.quote: Starting in version 2.2.0 and prior to 2.5.0, urllib3 does not control redirects in browsers and Node.js.
the retries and redirect parameters are ignored with Pyodide; the runtime itself determines redirect behavior.
Redirects are often used to exploit SSRF vulnerabilities.
Expect default browser behavior for redirects.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a Node.js check in the Pyodide fetch code and, only there, sets the Fetch redirect mode to manual so urllib3 handles redirects itself. This makes the retries and redirect settings take effect in Node.js, and the new test confirms it. Browsers are left unchanged and the test skips them, which matches the card's cause, its upgrade advice for Node.js, and its warning about browsers.

patterns.title: Catastrophic regex backtracking in TensorFlow-to-PyTorch weight name conversion in Transformers
patterns.cause: The convert_tf_weight_name_to_pt_weight_name() function converts TensorFlow weight names to PyTorch format using a regular expression. The pattern matches a run of non-slash characters, then a triple underscore, then another run of non-slash characters. Crafted input strings can trigger catastrophic backtracking in this pattern and cause excessive CPU consumption.
preconditions: The application uses a Transformers version up to 4.51.3.
The application runs TensorFlow-to-PyTorch model conversion, which reaches the weight name conversion function.
An attacker can influence the weight name strings that the function processes.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Transformers to version 4.53.0 or later, which the advisories list as the fixed release. Until then, treat weight names from untrusted sources as potentially crafted. Avoid running TensorFlow-to-PyTorch conversion on such input inside a shared service where CPU exhaustion would cause service disruption. In general, name-parsing patterns should not allow backtracking blowup on attacker-controlled strings.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the code change in the fix, the exact input shapes that trigger the slowdown, or how an attacker would deliver crafted names in practice. They also do not describe workarounds other than upgrading. The impact is described only as service disruption and resource exhaustion, with no further detail on exposed API surfaces.

fixtures.scenario: A service running Transformers 4.51.3 accepts uploaded TensorFlow checkpoints and converts them to PyTorch. An uploaded checkpoint contains a weight name crafted to cause catastrophic backtracking, so the conversion worker uses excessive CPU and other requests are delayed or fail.
The same service runs Transformers 4.53.0 or later. The same crafted weight name goes through the conversion step without catastrophic backtracking, and the worker stays responsive.

citations.quote: can be exploited to cause excessive CPU consumption through crafted input strings due to catastrophic backtracking
The vulnerability affects versions up to 4.51.3 and is fixed in version 4.53.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a guard in convert_tf_weight_name_to_pt_weight_name() before the regex substitution. It rejects names that are very long and contain the triple underscore separator, or that contain too many such separators, by raising a ValueError. This limits the input that could trigger catastrophic backtracking in the pattern, which matches the card's cause.

patterns.title: Unfiltered filter-error text in changedetection.io watch overview enables XSS
patterns.cause: Filter errors could carry HTML from watch configuration into the watch overview. The overview template marked the string returned by compile_error_texts as safe, bypassing automatic escaping and allowing XSS (CWE-79). In the branch without an application context, wrapping errors in Markup and then converting them to strings did not escape their contents. The regression test demonstrates the include-filter path.
preconditions: changedetection.io is running a version earlier than 0.50.4.
A watch filter produces an error containing malicious markup; the regression test uses an include-filter value containing HTML and script.
The affected error text is rendered in the watch overview viewed by a user.
The overview treats the error text as trusted HTML instead of escaping it.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to changedetection.io 0.50.4 or later. Remove the safe marking from the watch overview so template auto-escaping applies. In compile_error_texts, explicitly escape both the last error and the last notification error in the branch without an application context, using render_fully_escaped. Keep regression coverage that submits markup through an include-filter field and verifies escaped text, with no literal script element, in the overview response, plus a unit test for the escaping helper.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish required authentication or permissions, all inputs that can influence errors, or the safety of other rendering paths. The diff retains HTML construction in the application-context branch; removing the overview's safe marking escapes the returned string there. The regression tests check response text and helper output, not browser execution. They demonstrate one include-filter case, not every filter or error type.

fixtures.scenario: A deployment running a version before 0.50.4 has a watch whose filter fails. The resulting error text is shown in the watch overview without being filtered, so markup or script content in that text can run in the browser of the user viewing the overview.

A deployment runs version 0.50.4 or later. When a watch filter fails, the error text is filtered before it appears in the watch overview, so it is shown as inert text and does not run in the viewer's browser.

citations.quote: errors in filters from website page change detection watches were not being filtered resulting in a cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability
XSS - Errors in filters from website page change detection watches were not being filtered.
This issue has been patched in version 0.50.4

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the safe marking from the error text in the watch overview template. It also changes the plain-text branch of the error builder in the watch model, which used to wrap the last fetch error and last notification error as trusted markup, so that both are fully HTML-escaped by a new helper in the safe rendering module. A regression test stores a script-bearing include filter and confirms the overview page shows it as escaped text.

patterns.title: SSRF through unvalidated gateway_path in MLflow gateway_proxy_handler
patterns.cause: In MLflow before 3.1.0, gateway_proxy_handler lacks gateway_path validation. The advisory classifies the result as server-side request forgery (CWE-918) via this handler.
preconditions: The deployment runs an MLflow version earlier than 3.1.0.
The gateway_proxy_handler code path is reachable.
A gateway_path value reaches the handler without being validated.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to MLflow 3.1.0 or later, which is the version the advisories give as the boundary for this flaw. In any similar proxy handler, treat gateway_path as untrusted input and validate it before it influences an outbound request. Prefer a strict allowlist of expected gateway paths and reject anything else.
patterns.limitations: The sources only state that gateway_path validation is missing before 3.1.0. They do not say how the path is used to build the outbound request, what input forms are abusive, or what the upstream validation checks. They also do not say which deployments expose the handler or whether authentication is required. The allowlist approach is a general direction, not a description of the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: An MLflow server older than 3.1.0 exposes gateway_proxy_handler. It accepts a caller-supplied gateway_path and applies no validation to it before handling the request.
An MLflow server at version 3.1.0 or later handles the request. Any custom proxy code of the same kind checks gateway_path against an allowlist of expected values and rejects everything else.

citations.quote: gateway_proxy_handler in MLflow before 3.1.0 lacks gateway_path validation.
gateway_proxy_handler in MLflow before 3.1.0 lacks gateway_path validation.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a validation step for the gateway path in the gateway proxy handler, run before the outbound request is built from the configured target address and the user-supplied path. For GET requests only the endpoints listing path is accepted. For POST requests only a path shaped like gateway, one name segment, then invocations is accepted. Anything else is rejected with an invalid-parameter error, and tests cover the rejected paths.

patterns.title: Unescaped user input rendered through NiceGUI ui.html() or HTML-mode ui.chat_message leads to XSS
patterns.cause: Before NiceGUI 3.0.0, ui.html and ui.chat_message with HTML text enabled rendered content as raw markup without enforced sanitization or an explicit sanitization choice. Unescaped, untrusted content could therefore execute JavaScript in the victim's browser, as demonstrated by an image with an error handler.
preconditions: The application uses NiceGUI 2.24.2 or earlier, as identified by the advisory, or the patched behavior with sanitization disabled or ineffective.
Untrusted content, such as user input or model-generated output, reaches ui.html or ui.chat_message with HTML text enabled.
The content contains executable markup that is not neutralized by escaping or effective sanitization before rendering.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to NiceGUI 3.0.0, identified as fixed by the advisory. The patch requires an explicit sanitization choice for ui.html and HTML-mode ui.chat_message; omission raises an error. For untrusted HTML, supply an effective sanitizer; the project recommends the sanitize method of Sanitizer from html-sanitizer, and the tests show it blocks the demonstrated payload. Disable sanitization only for trusted content, such as controlled SVG or documentation markup. When HTML is unnecessary, use ui.label for text or leave chat HTML mode off, which escapes message text. Escaping untrusted values is also supported by the advisory. As general hardening, review disabled sanitization and verify content trust.
patterns.limitations: The patch requires a choice, not effective sanitization: disabling it or supplying an ineffective callable can leave executable markup intact. Mechanically disabling sanitization during migration does not protect untrusted content. Protection depends on the supplied sanitizer; the tests do not establish comprehensive filtering guarantees. The shown enforcement changes concern ui.html and HTML-mode ui.chat_message. The diff does not change ui.add_head_html or ui.add_body_html or establish other components' security. It does not establish behavior across all later 3.x releases. The advisory labels this reflected XSS; stored cases are not discussed.

fixtures.scenario: A page has a text input whose change handler takes the typed value and renders it with ui.html() as-is. A user types markup containing an image element with an error handler that runs script. The browser inserts it into the DOM and runs the script in the user's session.

The same page escapes the typed value as HTML text before giving it to ui.html(), or never passes the typed value to ui.html() at all. Markup typed by the user appears as visible characters and no script runs. The application is also upgraded to NiceGUI 3.0.0 or later.

citations.quote: Versions 2.24.2 and below are at risk for Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) when developers render unescaped user input into the DOM using ui.html().
Applications that do not pass untrusted input into ui.html() are not affected.
the library does not enforce any HTML or JavaScript sanitization
This issue is fixed in version 3.0.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the HTML element require a sanitize choice, either a sanitizing function or an explicit False, and applies it whenever content is set or changed. The chat message component raises a ValueError if HTML mode is on and no sanitize choice is given, and escapes text otherwise. Internal uses, examples and docs were updated to pass False or a real sanitizer, which matches the card's cause, prevention and limitations.

patterns.title: Roundup XSS via URL and tracker template interaction (CVE-2025-53865)
patterns.cause: In Roundup before 2.5.0, XSS can occur through interactions between URLs and issue tracker templates; the advisories name devel and responsive. The diff addresses unsafe dynamic output in page titles, headings, edit-collision messages and username headers. It changes rendering of item IDs, titles, names, usernames, designators, some tracker names and the website tracker assignee display, using TAL content or explicit escaping. These changes indicate an output-escaping weakness, but do not establish that every changed value is attacker-controlled.
preconditions: The deployment runs Roundup older than 2.5.0.
A vulnerable template rendering path is used. The advisories identify devel and responsive; the diff also changes classic, minimal and the website issues tracker.
Attacker-influenced input must reach vulnerable output viewed by a victim. The sources do not establish the exact URL, controllable fields or required permissions.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Roundup to 2.5.0 or later and incorporate the relevant template fixes. Follow the targeted changes from TAL replace to TAL content for affected dynamic output, including named parts in translated blocks. For username headers, the fix retains TAL replace and uses the plain accessor with escaping enabled. Do not infer that TAL replace always bypasses escaping. As general hardening, compare customized or copied templates with the fixed versions and apply corresponding escaping changes where applicable.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not identify the exact exploit URL, prove that designators originate from it, or specify attacker permissions and control over each changed field. Changes to classic, minimal and the website tracker do not independently establish their exploitability or version ranges. The diff does not show the template engine implementation, upgrade behavior for local templates, or whether other template constructs and custom code remain unsafe. This card uses both the advisory text and the diff.

fixtures.scenario: A tracker runs Roundup 2.4.x with the responsive template. An attacker sends a user a crafted link to the tracker, and the interaction between the URL and the template lets script run in the user's browser session.

The same tracker runs Roundup 2.5.0 or later with the updated devel or responsive template. Any customized template copies have been compared against the updated ones, so a crafted link does not lead to script execution.

citations.quote: In Roundup before 2.5.0, XSS can occur via interaction between URLs and issue tracker templates (devel and responsive).

patch_review.observation: The fix changes shipped tracker templates (classic, devel, responsive, minimal and the website issues tracker) so that item ids, titles, names, designators and the tracker name are printed with the TAL content statement instead of the replace statement, which skipped escaping. It also changes the username shown in the devel and responsive page headers to use an escaping plain accessor. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Unsafe dynamic evaluation of CAPTCHA responses in pyLoad web UI script
patterns.cause: The interactive CAPTCHA userscript executes message-supplied script through direct eval after JSON parsing, object and action checks, and signature verification. Direct eval exposes the message handler's local scope, including the parsed request and signature object, to that script. The advisory reports XSS allowing browser code execution, session hijacking and credential theft, but the diff does not establish how attacker-controlled CAPTCHA responses become accepted signed scripts.
preconditions: A deployed interactive CAPTCHA userscript uses the vulnerable direct eval path. The CVE record identifies 0.5.0b3.dev89 as including the patch.
A message passes the existing parsing and activation checks, contains a script, and passes signature verification before execution.
The advisory describes remote exploitation without authentication or user interaction; the supplied material does not demonstrate the attacker-to-signed-script delivery path.
patterns.prevention: Apply the upstream change replacing direct eval with a Function constructor whose body explicitly uses strict mode and receives request and gpyload as parameters. This removes implicit access to the handler's local scope while retaining signature verification. The constructed function can still access global objects and the supplied objects. As general hardening, minimize exposed objects, validate message origins and structure, and prefer declarative data handled by fixed code where delivered scripts are unnecessary.
patterns.limitations: Dynamic execution remains and still depends on signature verification and trusted signed code. The Function constructor is not a sandbox: window and document remain accessible, and request is explicitly passed. The patch adds no origin checks or additional input validation; basic message checks already existed. No signature bypass or complete path from the advisory's CAPTCHA POST to this execution site is shown. The advisory's onCaptchaResult example differs from the patched handler. Backend code execution is claimed conditionally but is not demonstrated by this browser-side diff. The advisory names 0.4.20 in reproduction steps, while the CVE names a fix in the 0.5.0 beta line; a precise affected range is not established.

fixtures.scenario: A CAPTCHA response field is submitted containing a short piece of script text that reads the page cookies. The client-side result handler passes the text straight to the JavaScript eval() function, so the script runs in the browser session with no check on its content.

The same response text is received, but the handler treats it only as an opaque string. It is checked against the expected CAPTCHA answer format, rejected when it does not match, and never passed to eval() or any other code execution facility, so the script text has no effect.

citations.quote: allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code in the client browser and potentially the backend server.
No sanitization or validation is performed on this input
Commit 909e5c97885237530d1264cfceb5555870eb9546, the patch for the issue, is included in version 0.5.0b3.dev89.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces direct eval of the signed CAPTCHA script code with a function built through the Function constructor in strict mode. The code now runs in global scope and receives only the request and the helper object as parameters, so it can no longer see the message handler's local variables such as the signature objects. The signature check stays, and no origin or structure validation is added. The rest of the diff is a version bump and a style cleanup that swaps var for let and const.

patterns.title: Path traversal through uploaded filename in pyLoad json/upload endpoint
patterns.cause: The /json/upload endpoint joins the configured storage folder with a prefix and the client-supplied filename of each uploaded file, then saves the file there. The filename is neither sanitized nor validated, so parent-directory sequences in it move the write location outside the intended upload directory.
preconditions: The attacker holds a valid authenticated session on the pyLoad web interface.
The attacker sends a multipart upload to the json/upload endpoint with a crafted filename containing parent-directory sequences.
The filename is appended to the storage folder path without validation before the file is saved.
The target location is writable by the pyLoad process.
patterns.prevention: Never treat a client-supplied filename as a trusted path component. Validate or sanitize the filename so it cannot contain directory separators or parent-directory sequences. Then resolve the final destination path, for example with os.path.realpath(), and confirm it remains inside the intended storage folder before saving. Reject the upload if the check fails. Upgrade to pyload-ng 0.5.0b3.dev90 or later, where the issue is reported as fixed.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so the validation approach above is general guidance rather than a statement of what the patch does. The CVE names version 0.5.0b3.dev89 as affected, while the advisory proof of concept refers to version 0.4.20, and the sources do not reconcile this. The sources give no information on other endpoints or on other ways filenames reach the filesystem.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user uploads a file whose multipart filename has several parent-directory sequences followed by a system path. The server joins it to the storage folder and saves it, writing outside the upload directory.

An authenticated user uploads a file with the same crafted filename. The server reduces it to a safe name or rejects it, and checks that the resolved path is inside the storage folder, so nothing is written elsewhere.

citations.quote: By manipulating the filename of an uploaded file, an attacker can traverse out of the intended upload directory
an authenticated path traversal vulnerability exists in the /json/upload endpoint of pyLoad.
This is fixed in version 0.5.0b3.dev90.

patch_review.observation: The fix passes the client-supplied upload filename through werkzeug's secure_filename before joining it with the storage folder and temporary prefix, so directory separators and parent-directory sequences can no longer move the write location. The card's cause (unsanitized filename joined into the storage path) and its prevention (sanitize the filename, then confirm the destination stays inside the storage folder) match this change. The patched code sits in the package-adding handler of the JSON blueprint rather than a function named for upload, but it is the same upload-saving logic.

patterns.title: SSRF via URL-based file upload fields in BentoML multipart and JSON handlers
patterns.cause: BentoML request deserializers automatically download files from user-supplied URLs for file-type parameters. The multipart path performs no validation. The JSON path checks only the URL scheme. Neither blocks internal network addresses, localhost, or cloud metadata endpoints, so an unauthenticated client can make the server issue arbitrary HTTP requests.
preconditions: BentoML 1.4.0 up to but not including 1.4.19
A service endpoint with a file-type parameter such as a filesystem path or image type
A client can send a multipart form field or JSON body containing a URL instead of file content
The server can reach internal services, localhost, or a cloud metadata endpoint
patterns.prevention: Treat every user-supplied URL as untrusted before the server fetches it. Apply the same validation in both the multipart and JSON paths. Go beyond a scheme check: use allowlist-style validation and reject targets in internal or private network ranges, localhost, and cloud metadata endpoints. Upgrade to 1.4.19 or later, which contains the patch.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch validates URLs. They do not say how redirects, DNS rebinding, or alternate IP encodings are handled, or whether the remote URL download feature can be disabled by configuration. Validate those cases separately.

fixtures.scenario: A service exposes an endpoint taking a file-type parameter. An unauthenticated client submits a multipart field whose value is a link-local cloud metadata URL. The server fetches it with no address validation.

The same endpoint checks the submitted URL against an allowlist and rejects internal, private, localhost, and metadata destinations in both the multipart and JSON paths. The server never issues the request.

citations.quote: neither path restricts access to internal networks, cloud metadata endpoints, or localhost services.
automatically download files from user-provided URLs without validating whether those URLs point to internal network addresses, cloud metadata endpoints, or other restricted resources.
should be enhanced to include allowlist validation rather than just scheme checking.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a new URL safety check that requires an http or https scheme, rejects localhost and the cloud metadata address, and resolves hostnames to reject private, loopback and link-local addresses. It is applied in both the body-URL download path and the multipart file-field helper, which previously had no validation. The card's cause and prevention match this, including the need to block internal ranges, localhost and metadata endpoints in both paths.

patterns.title: Stored XSS from insufficient sanitization in CKAN markdown_extract helper
patterns.cause: The helpers.markdown_extract() function did not sufficiently sanitize user-provided input before wrapping it in an HTML literal element. Markup in stored text, such as a resource description, could therefore reach rendered pages as active HTML.
preconditions: CKAN version prior to 2.10.9 (2.10 line) or prior to 2.11.4 (2.11 line)
User-provided data on dataset, resource, organization or group pages is rendered through markdown_extract
An extension page that uses the same helper also exposes the issue
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to CKAN 2.10.9, CKAN 2.11.4 or later. In custom code and extensions that call this helper, treat user-provided text as untrusted. Do not wrap it in an HTML literal (marked-safe) element until it has been sanitized or escaped.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact change made to the helper, any workaround short of upgrading, or what write access an attacker needs to store the malicious text. Only the pages named in the advisory are confirmed as affected.

fixtures.scenario: A user able to edit a resource stores a description containing HTML markup. A vulnerable CKAN version renders it through markdown_extract and wraps it as an HTML literal without sufficient sanitization, so the markup reaches other visitors.
The same description is rendered on CKAN 2.10.9 or 2.11.4 or later, where the helper sanitizes input before wrapping it, so the stored text does not become active markup on the page.

citations.quote: did not perform sufficient sanitization of input data before wrapping in an HTML literal element
This helper is used to render user-provided data on dataset, resource, organization or group pages
This vulnerability has been fixed in CKAN 2.10.9 and 2.11.4

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces a naive regular expression that stripped HTML tags from the markdown output in markdown_extract with a call to the bleach-based cleaner in strip mode. The same weak regex is also removed from render_markdown, which already used bleach. This confirms the cause was insufficient sanitization before the result was marked as a safe literal.

patterns.title: Path traversal in pyLoad CNL addcrypted endpoint via the package parameter
patterns.cause: The addcrypted endpoint of the CNL blueprint builds a file path from the request-supplied package value and writes the submitted content to it. The path is not reliably confined to the designated storage directory, so an unauthenticated caller can write arbitrary files outside it. The advisory shows only simple character stripping on the package value before the path is built.
preconditions: pyload-ng version 0.5.0b3.dev89 or below
The addcrypted endpoint is reachable by an unauthenticated attacker
The attacker-controlled package value is used to build the output file path
The pyLoad process can write to the target location, for example system files when running as root
patterns.prevention: Do not let a request value decide where a file is written. After building the output path, resolve it to its final absolute form, for example with os.path.realpath(), and confirm it still lies inside the intended download directory before opening it. Reject the request otherwise. Do not rely on removing a few characters from the name. Upgrading to 0.5.0b3.dev90 or later addresses the issue.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the actual upstream fix, so this card gives only a general direction. They are also inconsistent: the quoted code strips slashes, backslashes and colons from the package value, yet the proof of concept uses dot-dot and slash sequences. The sources do not explain this gap, so the exact exploit mechanics are unclear. They do not describe authentication or deployment hardening.

fixtures.scenario: An unauthenticated client posts to the addcrypted endpoint with a package value meant to point at a cron directory and a crafted content field. The server joins the value to the download directory and writes the file outside it, which can lead to code execution as root.
The same request arrives. The server builds the target path, resolves it to a final absolute path, and sees that it is not inside the download directory. It rejects the request and writes no file.

citations.quote: suffers from an unsafe path construction vulnerability, allowing unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files outside the designated storage directory
overwrite critical system files, including cron jobs and systemd services
This issue is fixed in version 0.5.0b3.dev90.

patch_review.observation: The fix keeps the character stripping on the package name but then normalizes the joined path, makes it absolute, and checks that it lies under the configured storage folder, including the trailing separator. If the check fails, the endpoint returns a 400 error and never opens the file. This matches the card's cause (a request value controls the write location) and its prevention (confine the final path to the download directory and reject otherwise, not rely on stripping characters).

patterns.title: SQL injection through string-built IN clause in pyLoad link info update
patterns.cause: In pyLoad before 0.5.0b3.dev91, the add_links value submitted to the add_package JSON endpoint travels through the info thread and file manager to the database layer's link info update routine. That routine joins the submitted URLs into one string and inserts it directly into the text of a SELECT statement with an IN list. A quote character in a submitted link therefore ends the string literal and lets the attacker add their own SQL.
preconditions: Attacker-controlled text reaches the add_links parameter of the add_package endpoint (the published proof of concept sends it with session cookies).
The submitted link strings flow unchanged into the database layer's link info update routine.
That routine builds an IN list by joining the URL values into the SQL text instead of binding them as parameters.
patterns.prevention: Never place user-supplied values, including URLs, into SQL text by joining or formatting strings. Build the IN list from one bound-parameter placeholder per URL, and pass the URL values separately to the database driver's execute call. The same routine already binds its UPDATE statement values with question-mark placeholders, so the SELECT should follow the same pattern. Treat data that arrives through background threads and manager layers as untrusted, because it can originate from an HTTP request. Review other places that format SQL from lists of values.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say what privileges are needed to call the endpoint. The proof of concept only shows that a session cookie is sent. They do not name the database engine or say which injected statements run, so the full impact is unconfirmed beyond data modification or deletion. They also do not describe the upstream patch beyond the fixed version number, and this card does not assess other SQL construction sites in the project.

fixtures.scenario: A user submits a package whose add_links field contains a URL with an embedded single quote followed by extra SQL. The database layer joins the URLs into a quoted list inside the SELECT text, so the extra SQL is parsed as part of the statement instead of being treated as a URL.

A user submits the same package with the same quote-containing URL. The database layer builds a statement with one placeholder per URL and passes the URLs as separate bound values. The quote is treated as part of the URL text, no extra SQL runs, and the lookup simply finds no matching row.

citations.quote: the parameter add_links in API /json/add_package is vulnerable to SQL Injection.
statuses is constructed from data, and data is the value of the add_links parameter entered by the user through /json/add_packge.
data is list of tuples (name, size, status, url)

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the link info update routine in the file database. Instead of joining the URLs into the SELECT text, it builds one bound placeholder per URL and passes the URL list to the driver separately. This matches the card's cause (string-built IN clause) and its prevention (bound parameters, as the UPDATE statement already does).

patterns.title: Command injection through uploaded filenames used in OctoPrint system event handler commands
patterns.cause: OctoPrint system event handlers substituted placeholder values, including file names, paths, and event payload fields, into command strings without escaping and executed them through a shell. Filename sanitization allowed characters such as semicolons, so an authenticated attacker could upload a specially named file and execute arbitrary commands when a configured handler incorporated that filename and its event fired.
preconditions: OctoPrint version 1.11.2 or earlier is running.
The attacker is authenticated and can upload a file with a chosen filename.
A system event handler is configured to include the uploaded filename through a filename-based placeholder in its command.
The corresponding event is triggered after the upload.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to the fixed version, 1.11.3. SystemEventSubscription applies shlex.quote to each placeholder value before substitution when shell execution is enabled. Filename sanitization now removes semicolons, pipes, ampersands, question marks, dollar signs, asterisks, angle brackets, and ASCII characters outside Python's string.printable set before either normal or universal sanitization. Until patched, disable system event handlers using filename placeholders, or enable universally safe filenames and restart OctoPrint, then vet existing uploads and delete suspicious files. The advisory also recommends avoiding hostile network exposure and vetting instance access.
patterns.limitations: The diff adds a shell option but retains shell execution by default. Disabling it leaves placeholders unescaped in a formatted command string; it does not construct separate arguments or establish safe execution across platforms and command templates. The sources do not establish attacker control of arbitrary payload fields. No existing-file renaming is shown; manual review is part of the filename-setting workaround. The advisory reports no impact without system handlers incorporating uploaded filenames. Configured commands remain trusted; the fix does not validate their intent. Network and access restrictions are mitigations, not the underlying fix.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user uploads a file whose name contains a semicolon followed by a shell command. An administrator has an event handler that runs a system command with a filename placeholder, and the event fires after the upload. The attacker's command runs on the host.

The same upload is attempted on an instance that is upgraded to 1.11.3 or later, or that enforces safe filenames, or that has no enabled event handler passing filename placeholders to system commands. The crafted name is not interpreted as a command.

citations.quote: allows an authenticated attacker to upload a file under a specially crafted filename that will allow arbitrary command execution
If no event handlers executing system commands with uploaded filenames as parameters have been configured, this vulnerability does not have an impact.
then vet the existing uploads and make sure to delete any suspicious looking files
The vulnerability is patched in version 1.11.3.

patch_review.observation: The fix moves event handling into subscription classes. System subscriptions now quote every placeholder value for the shell when shell mode is on, and add a configurable shell option with a deprecation warning that the default will later become no shell. Filename sanitization now removes separators, pipes, ampersands, glob and redirection characters, the dollar sign, and control characters in both normal and strict modes. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Stored XSS from unsanitized blog post titles in the Mezzanine admin displayable links endpoint
patterns.cause: The displayable_links_js function in the Mezzanine admin includes blog post titles in JSON responses served from the admin displayable_links.js endpoint without properly sanitizing them. A script payload stored in a title is therefore delivered to an admin's browser and can execute there.
preconditions: Mezzanine version earlier than 6.1.1 is in use.
An authenticated admin user can create or edit a blog post and set a malicious JavaScript payload in the title field.
A second admin user is tricked into following a direct link to the admin displayable_links.js endpoint.
patterns.prevention: Treat every stored title as untrusted data when building the displayable links response. Sanitize or encode titles for the context in which the response is delivered, so that a title can never be interpreted as script by the browser. Apply this at the point where titles are placed into the response, not only when they are saved. Upgrade Mezzanine to version 6.1.1 or later, which is the first version not described as affected.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact escaping method, the response content type, or how the browser comes to execute the payload. They do not say whether content types other than blog posts, or fields other than the title, are affected. They do not describe the fix beyond the fixed version number. The attack needs an authenticated admin to plant the payload and another admin to follow the link, so the real-world impact depends on how many admin accounts exist and how far they are trusted.

fixtures.scenario: An admin creates a blog post whose title contains a script payload. A second admin opens a direct link to the admin displayable_links.js endpoint. The title is emitted into the response without proper sanitization, and the script runs in the second admin's browser session.

The same blog post title is stored, but the displayable links response neutralizes the title for its output context. When the second admin opens the direct link, the title is shown only as inert text and no script runs.

citations.quote: fails to properly sanitize blog post titles before including them in JSON responses served via
An authenticated admin user can create a blog post with a malicious JavaScript payload in the title field

patch_review.observation: The fix HTML-escapes each displayable's title inside the displayable_links_js view, at the point where titles are put into the links response. This matches the card's cause (unsanitized stored titles in that endpoint) and its prevention (encode titles when building the response, and upgrade).

patterns.title: ReDoS in Transformers EnglishNormalizer number normalization on long digit strings
patterns.cause: The normalize_numbers method of the CLVP EnglishNormalizer processes numeric strings with regular expressions. The original pound and dollar patterns contain overlapping repetitions of digits and separators followed by digits. The decimal and ordinal patterns allow backtracking through a digit run when the required continuation fails. The advisory reports that crafted long digit sequences cause excessive CPU consumption, potentially disrupting services or exhausting resources (CWE-1333).
preconditions: The application uses Transformers version 4.52.4 or earlier, according to the advisory.
Attacker-controlled text reaches the normalize_numbers method of EnglishNormalizer, such as during text-to-speech preprocessing or number normalization.
The attacker can supply crafted input containing long sequences of digits.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Transformers to version 4.53.0 or later, identified by the advisory as fixed. The fix replaces the trailing digit repetition in the pound and dollar patterns with a single digit and makes the leading digit runs in decimal and ordinal patterns possessive, preventing backtracking within those runs. It uses the standard re module on Python 3.11 and later and the regex package on older Python versions, where that dependency must be available. For similar normalizers, avoid overlapping adjacent repetitions. As general defense in depth, cap input length before regex processing.
patterns.limitations: The diffs cover CLVP number normalization, not other normalizers or library regexes. The release boundary comes from the advisory. Neither source supplies input thresholds, timings, or an exact worst-case complexity analysis. Possessive runs prevent internal backtracking but do not establish immediate failure of the entire search or linear runtime. The sources do not require every exploit input to fail a full pattern match. Input length limits are general hardening, not part of the upstream fix.

fixtures.scenario: A text-to-speech API runs Transformers 4.52.4 and passes user-submitted text to the normalize_numbers() method of the EnglishNormalizer class. A request containing a very long run of digits drives CPU usage up and delays or blocks other requests.
The same API runs Transformers 4.53.0 or later. A request with a very long run of digits is normalized without the excessive CPU consumption described for the affected versions.

citations.quote: crafted input strings containing long sequences of digits, leading to excessive CPU consumption
This vulnerability affects versions up to 4.52.4 and is fixed in version 4.53.0.
potentially causing service disruption, resource exhaustion, and API vulnerabilities

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the number normalization step in the CLVP English normalizer. It removes the redundant trailing digit quantifier in the pound and dollar patterns and makes the leading digit runs in the decimal and ordinal patterns possessive. It also imports the regex package on Python older than 3.11, since the standard re module only gains possessive quantifier support in 3.11. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS from unvalidated parameters in pyLoad CNL and captcha endpoints
patterns.cause: The advisories report insufficient validation of CNL and captcha inputs allowing content injection and browser-side JavaScript execution. The diff shows two narrower weaknesses: addcrypted derived a filename from a request-supplied package name using limited character removal, and the interactive captcha userscript processed messages without checking their origin. A storage-directory containment check and script signature verification already existed; the diff does not establish directory escape or arbitrary unsigned script execution.
preconditions: An affected pyLoad version earlier than 0.5.0b3.dev91 is running with the relevant web UI or CNL functionality accessible.
For the CNL filename issue, a crafted package name reaches addcrypted through an HTTP form request.
For the captcha message issue, an attacker-controlled page can send messages to the window running the userscript; script execution still requires successful signature verification.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to 0.5.0b3.dev91 or later. In addcrypted, sanitize the package name with Werkzeug's secure_filename function, construct an absolute destination path, and retain the existing storage-directory containment check. In the captcha userscript, reject incoming messages whose origins are not explicitly trusted before parsing or processing them. Set the trusted origins to the intended parent origins for the deployment.
patterns.limitations: The advisories demonstrate XSS through the jk parameter in addcrypted2, but the supplied diff changes addcrypted filename handling and captcha message-origin checks, without showing how these address that example or reflected output encoding. Other CNL handlers and the server-side captcha endpoint are not shown as changed. The allowlist contains only https://pyload.net, with comments directing customization; other legitimate parent origins would be rejected. Authentication requirements and a complete exploit chain for the changed code are not established.

fixtures.scenario: A CNL endpoint receives a query parameter containing script-like text and places it in the response unchanged. A victim who opens a crafted link runs the attacker's script inside the Web UI session.
The same endpoint checks the parameter against its expected format, rejects non-conforming input, and encodes any value placed in the response, so the text is never executed as script.

citations.quote: The application did not consistently enforce input validation or encoding, making it possible for an attacker to craft malicious requests.
user-supplied parameters from HTTP requests were not adequately validated or sanitized before being passed into the application logic and response generation.
Version 0.5.0b3.dev91 contains a patch for the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the manual character stripping of the package name in the CNL addcrypted handler with a standard filename sanitizer. It resolves the final path to an absolute form and rejects anything outside the storage folder. It also makes the interactive captcha userscript ignore cross-window messages whose origin is not in a trusted allowlist. The card describes both changes correctly and notes that no output-encoding change appears in the diff.

patterns.title: Hardlink-based path traversal in the llama-index ObsidianReader
patterns.cause: The load_data() method of ObsidianReader has path restrictions whose security checks fail to differentiate between real files and hardlinks. A hardlink inside the read location can therefore point to a sensitive file elsewhere on the system, and the check does not catch it.
preconditions: The application uses ObsidianReader from a vulnerable release, before llama-index-readers-obsidian 0.5.2 (reported against llama-index 0.12.27).
The application calls load_data() on a directory that an attacker can influence.
A hardlink in that directory refers to a sensitive file outside the intended location, such as /etc/passwd.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to llama-index-readers-obsidian 0.5.2 or later, where the issue is resolved. In your own file-reading code, do not assume a path check on the file name is enough, because a hardlink looks like a real file. Make the containment check treat hardlinks explicitly, and restrict what readers can access.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the fix works, so this card cannot say which check was added. They do not say whether other readers or other link types such as symlinks are affected. They give the fixed version as 0.5.2 but do not explain the version numbering between llama-index and the reader package.

fixtures.scenario: An application points ObsidianReader load_data() at a vault directory where an attacker placed a hardlink to /etc/passwd. The path check treats it as a normal vault file, and the contents of the sensitive file are read.
The application uses llama-index-readers-obsidian 0.5.2 or later, so the same hardlink placed in the vault is covered by the fixed release instead of being treated as an ordinary in-vault file.

citations.quote: allows for hardlink-based path traversal
the security checks fail to differentiate between real files and hardlinks
This issue is resolved in llama-index-readers-obsidian version 0.5.2.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that reads the file's link count and, inside load_data(), skips and warns about any file with more than one hard link before the existing path-prefix containment check runs. This matches the card's cause, that the resolved-path check cannot tell a hardlink from a real file, and its prevention, which is to handle hardlinks explicitly. The package version is bumped to 0.5.2, as the card states.

patterns.title: Unchecked sparse tensor loading from user prompt embeddings enables out-of-bounds write
patterns.cause: The Completions API deserializes user-supplied prompt embeddings with torch.load and calls to_dense without sufficient sparse tensor validation. Since PyTorch 2.8.0, sparse integrity checks are disabled by default, allowing crafted tensors to trigger an out-of-bounds write, a crash, or potentially server code execution. The prompt embedding option already defaulted to off, but load_prompt_embeds did not enforce it. The diff also adds multimodal embedding gates and warns that incorrect embedding shapes can crash the engine.
preconditions: vLLM 0.10.2 up to but not including 0.11.1, as specified by the CVE advisory.
An attacker can submit crafted serialized prompt embeddings to the affected Completions API; the advisory states that any user with access can exploit it.
PyTorch 2.8.0 or later with sparse tensor invariant checks left disabled.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to vLLM 0.11.1 or later, identified by the CVE advisory as patched. Enforce the existing enable-prompt-embeds option in load_prompt_embeds before deserialization. Keep the new enable-mm-embeds option off by default and enforce it in both image embedding chat parsers and for embedding items in the multimodal processor. Reject disabled embedding inputs with an explanatory error. Enable either feature only for trusted users. The advisory also calls for explicitly enabling sparse invariant validation during loading through the torch.sparse.check_sparse_tensor_invariants context manager; the supplied diff does not show that validation.
patterns.limitations: The shown gates restrict access to embedding paths; they do not validate enabled inputs, and incorrect shapes can still crash the engine. No sparse invariant check is added in this diff, so it does not establish whether validation exists elsewhere or that enabled inputs are safe. The sources do not establish the same out-of-bounds write through chat or multimodal embeddings. RCE remains potential. The diff shows ValueError rejection but does not establish the HTTP response status.

fixtures.scenario: A server on vLLM 0.10.2 with PyTorch 2.8.0 receives a base64 prompt embedding holding a crafted sparse tensor. It is loaded with torch.load(), passes the dtype check, and to_dense() performs an out-of-bounds write.

A server on vLLM 0.11.1 receives the same crafted sparse tensor. Sparse invariant validation is enforced before densifying, so the malformed tensor is rejected with an error and the process keeps running.

citations.quote: Due to a change introduced in PyTorch 2.8.0, sparse tensor integrity checks are disabled by default.
maliciously crafted tensors can bypass internal bounds checks and trigger an out-of-bounds memory write during the call to to_dense().
this needs to be enabled explicitly using the

patch_review.observation: The fix adds an opt-in gate: the prompt embeddings loader now rejects input unless the enable-prompt-embeds option is set. A new enable-mm-embeds option, off by default, is also enforced in the chat parser for image embeddings and in the multimodal processor for embedding items. Docs warn that wrong embedding shapes can crash the engine and that these flags are for trusted users only. The diff adds no sparse tensor invariant check, which the card correctly says.

patterns.title: Stored XSS via unvalidated watch URL scheme in the update API
patterns.cause: Inconsistent watch URL checks allowed stored XSS through API updates. The advisory describes a missing update check; the diff's baseline already has a weak scheme-prefix check shared with forms and datastore insertion. That check removed the source marker anywhere and did not render templates before validation. Create and import handlers used generic URL syntax validation locally. An attacker could store a malicious watch URL, and a user clicking its link in Preview could execute attacker script in the application origin.
preconditions: The attacker can update a watch through the API; the advisory demonstrates a request with an API key.
The update accepts an unsafe URL, either replacing an existing watch URL or following creation and retrieval of a harmless page.
A user opens Preview and clicks the malicious link.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to 0.50.34, identified by the advisories as fixed. Use the shared is_safe_valid_url routine across forms, API creation and updates, imports, and datastore insertion. Strip the source marker only at the start, render templates and reject rendering errors, reject literal angle brackets, normalize query encoding, then check the configured scheme pattern. The default permits HTTP, HTTPS and FTP, adding file URLs when enabled. Apply syntax validation to non-file URLs, respecting the simple-host setting. Repeat validation in the Watch link property before and after formatting, returning DISABLED on failure, and guard the current-diff link in the base template.
patterns.limitations: The advisory and diff describe different pre-fix update checks; their relationship is not established here. SAFE_PROTOCOL_REGEX can override the default scheme pattern, so file exclusion is not unconditional. File URLs bypass generic syntax validation. No stored-data cleanup is shown. The Preview template and its escaping behavior are not shown, although the base-template link guard is. Disabled file-form tests do not establish rejection of those forms, and one rejected unsafe template query does not establish rejection of template queries generally. Compatibility impact is not established.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated API client updates an existing watch and sets its URL to a javascript: scheme value. The server stores it without any protocol check. A user later opens Preview and clicks the link, and the script runs in the application's origin.

The same update request is sent through the API, but the server applies the shared protocol check first. It rejects the javascript: URL with a validation error and leaves the stored URL unchanged. An ordinary http or https URL is accepted through both the UI and the API.

citations.quote: When instead the Watch API is used, this check is not performed resulting in unsafe URLs added as Watch.
Watch protocol is not permitted by SAFE_PROTOCOL_REGEX or incorrect URL format
When the user clicks on *Preview* and then on the malicious link, the JavaScript malicious code is executed.
Version 0.50.34 fixes the issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the old loose scheme-prefix check with one shared validator that is used by the web form, API create, API update, import, datastore insertion, the link property and the template helper. The validator strips the source marker only at the start, renders template markup before checking, rejects angle brackets, allows file access only when explicitly enabled, and then runs URL syntax validation. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: HTML and script injection through printer-generated Action Command popups in OctoPrint
patterns.cause: Text sent by the printer for Action Command notification and prompt popups can contain arbitrary HTML and JavaScript. In OctoPrint 1.11.3 and earlier, this text is not neutralized before it appears in the web interface, so the markup is injected into the page.
preconditions: OctoPrint version 1.11.3 or earlier is in use
Action Command notification popups or prompt dialogs are enabled
A victim is convinced to print a specially crafted file that makes the printer emit the malicious text
The victim has an active OctoPrint session in the browser
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to OctoPrint 1.11.4 or later, where the issue is fixed. In your own code, treat any text that originates from the printer as untrusted data. Show it in popups as plain text and never as markup. If you cannot upgrade, an administrator can disable Action Command notification popups and set prompt dialog support to Never. Print only files from trusted sources, ideally sliced with your own slicer.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the code change in 1.11.4, so the exact escaping or sanitizing approach is not covered here. Disabling popups is a workaround and does not remove the underlying flaw. Trusting file sources reduces exposure but is not a technical control. Other OctoPrint versions or output paths are not addressed by the sources.

fixtures.scenario: A printer running a crafted file sends an action command notification whose text contains HTML and script markup. The web UI puts that text into the popup as markup, so the script runs in the logged-in user's session.
The same crafted file sends markup in the notification text. The UI shows it as literal text in the popup, so no script runs. The instance is also upgraded to 1.11.4 or later.

citations.quote: allows injection of arbitrary HTML and JavaScript into Action Command notification and prompt popups generated by the printer.
An attacker who successfully convinces a victim to print a specially crafted file could exploit this issue
It is also strongly recommended to ensure that files being printed originate from trusted sources
This issue is fixed in version 1.11.4.

patch_review.observation: The fix applies HTML escaping on the client side to printer-supplied text before it is shown. In the Action Command notification plugin it escapes the notification message. In the Action Command prompt plugin it escapes the prompt message and each button label. This matches the card's cause (printer text injected unescaped into the page) and its prevention (treat printer text as untrusted and show it as plain text).

patterns.title: Stored DOM XSS from unsanitised prompt body inserted as rich text via innerHTML
patterns.cause: When rich text insertion is enabled, the prompt body is converted by a markdown parser and assigned to the innerHTML property of a temporary element with no sanitisation. The markdown parser does not sanitise content, so attacker-supplied HTML and event handler attributes reach the DOM and run as script.
preconditions: The attacker has permission to create prompts, which low-privilege users do not have by default.
The victim has the Insert Prompt as Rich Text preference enabled; it is off by default.
The victim runs the slash command that inserts the attacker's prompt into the chat input.
Open WebUI is version 0.6.34 or below.
patterns.prevention: Treat the prompt body as untrusted. Sanitise the HTML produced from it with an HTML sanitiser such as DOMPurify before it is assigned to innerHTML or otherwise parsed into the DOM. Do not rely on the markdown parser or its character handling as a defence, because the advisory shows quote limits can be bypassed by building strings from character codes. Upgrade to version 0.6.35 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail, so this card does not claim which sanitiser settings it uses. They do not say whether other DOM sinks in the application are affected. The remediation text names DOMPurify only as a suggestion. Users with the rich text setting disabled are described as unaffected.

fixtures.scenario: A user with prompt-creation rights saves a prompt body containing an image tag with an error handler. A victim with rich text insertion enabled runs the slash command, and the body is assigned to innerHTML unsanitised, so script runs.

The same prompt body is passed through an HTML sanitiser such as DOMPurify before being assigned to innerHTML, so the event handler attribute is removed and no script runs when the victim inserts the prompt.

citations.quote: the prompt body is assigned to the DOM sink .innerHtml without sanitisation
Sanitise the user controlled HTML with DOMPurify before assigning it to
The setting is off by default. Users with this setting disabled are unaffected.
This issue is fixed in version 0.6.35.

patch_review.observation: The fix passes the HTML produced by the markdown parser through DOMPurify's sanitize step before it is placed into the temporary element in the rich text prompt insertion path. This removes attacker-supplied script-capable markup such as event handler attributes. It matches the card's cause (unsanitised parser output reaching innerHTML) and its prevention (sanitise with DOMPurify before parsing into the DOM).

patterns.title: Unvalidated user-supplied URL fetched by server-side web loader (SSRF)
patterns.cause: The web processing endpoint of Open WebUI passes the user-supplied URL straight to its content loaders, which fetch it from the server. No check is made on the destination, so any authenticated user can make the server send HTTP requests to arbitrary URLs and read the returned content.
preconditions: The attacker holds any valid authenticated account; no special role is needed
The server accepts a user-supplied URL and fetches it through a web loader
No validation of scheme, destination address, or domain is applied before the fetch
For credential theft, the server runs where an internal or cloud metadata endpoint is reachable
patterns.prevention: Treat every user-supplied URL as untrusted before any loader fetches it. Restrict the allowed protocols to the web schemes the feature needs, and reject file and other non-web schemes. Resolve the host and refuse loopback, private (RFC1918), link-local and cloud metadata addresses. Where practical, require the destination to match a domain allowlist. Apply these checks in the shared fetch path so every loader is covered, including the video loader. Upgrade to a release that contains the vendor fix, which the CVE record lists as 0.6.37.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the 0.6.37 fix works, so this card gives general direction only. They do not address redirects, DNS rebinding, or alternate IP encodings, and these need separate handling. They also do not say which of the listed checks the vendor applied.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user posts the cloud metadata endpoint URL to the web processing endpoint. The server fetches it and returns the content, exposing cloud credentials.

A user submits a web URL for retrieval. The server checks the scheme, rejects loopback, private and metadata addresses or requires an allowlisted domain, and only then fetches the page. A request for the metadata address is refused.

citations.quote: allows any authenticated user to force the server to make HTTP requests to arbitrary URLs
Both loaders fetch the user-supplied URL without validation
Cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254, fd00:ec2::254)
This vulnerability is fixed in 0.6.37.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes URL validation allow only http and https schemes, and adds a default blocklist of cloud metadata addresses and hostnames that can be extended through an environment setting. It applies the same filter logic to resolved IP addresses of search results, and raises an error when every supplied URL is blocked, so the loader never fetches unvetted destinations.

patterns.title: ReDoS in MarianTokenizer remove_language_code() via malformed language code patterns
patterns.cause: The remove_language_code() method of MarianTokenizer in the Hugging Face Transformers library relies on inefficient regex processing. Crafted input strings containing malformed language code patterns can make it consume excessive CPU, which can lead to denial of service.
preconditions: The application uses Hugging Face Transformers version 4.52.4, the version named as affected.
The application uses MarianTokenizer, and remove_language_code() runs on strings that an attacker can influence.
The attacker can supply input containing malformed language code patterns.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Transformers to version 4.53.0 or later, where the issue is reported as fixed. In any tokenizer or text-handling code, avoid inefficient regex processing of untrusted strings, especially when matching language code patterns. Prefer matching approaches whose running time does not blow up on malformed input.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the vulnerable regex, the exact trigger string, or how the fix changed the implementation, so no specific code-level remedy is given here. They name only 4.52.4 as affected and 4.53.0 as fixed, so the status of other earlier versions is not stated. They give no guidance on mitigations short of upgrading, such as input length limits or timeouts.

fixtures.scenario: A translation service runs Transformers 4.52.4 and passes user-submitted text through MarianTokenizer, where remove_language_code() handles it. An attacker sends strings with malformed language code patterns, and a worker spends excessive CPU on each request, degrading service for other users.

The same service runs Transformers 4.53.0 or later. The same crafted strings with malformed language code patterns no longer cause excessive CPU consumption in remove_language_code(), and request handling stays responsive.

citations.quote: This vulnerability is present in version 4.52.4 and has been fixed in version 4.53.0.
The issue arises from inefficient regex processing, which can be exploited by crafted input strings containing malformed language code patterns

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the regular expression used by the language code remover in MarianTokenizer, which could backtrack heavily on crafted input with a start marker but no matching end marker. It now uses plain string prefix and search operations to split off a leading language code, so the cost stays linear. The card's cause (inefficient regex handling of malformed language codes) and its direction of avoiding backtracking-prone matching agree with this.
