fixtures.scenario: A user uploads a ZIP to the backup restore endpoint with an entry whose path climbs out of the datastore directory toward the Flask secret key file. Bulk extraction writes the attacker content outside the directory.

The same ZIP is uploaded, but each entry's resolved destination is checked against the datastore directory before extraction. The escaping entry causes the restore to be rejected and nothing is written outside the directory.

citations.quote: The application uses zipfile.extractall() without validating entry paths, allowing ../ sequences to escape the extraction directory.
Prior to version 0.54.4, a Zip Slip vulnerability in the backup restore functionality allows arbitrary file overwrite via path traversal in uploaded ZIP archives.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the bulk extraction in the restore import routine with a per-entry loop. Each entry's destination is resolved to a real path and the whole archive is rejected with an error if any entry falls outside the extraction directory. This matches the card's cause and prevention. The patch also adds hardening the card does not mention: an uncompressed-size limit, an upload-size limit, UUID-only top-level directories, removal of the session secret file from backups, and a stricter download path check.

patterns.title: Reflected XSS in NLTK WordNet Browser lookup route from unescaped word
patterns.cause: In nltk.app.wordnet_app, the lookup_ route decodes URL state into a word value and, when no results are found, inserts that word directly into the HTML body. The search route escapes its input, but the lookup_ route does not, so a crafted URL injects HTML or JavaScript into the response page.
preconditions: The nltk.app.wordnet_app WordNet Browser server is running (versions 3.9.3 and prior).
A request to a lookup_ URL carries an attacker-chosen word, which the URL state decoder accepts.
The word is placed into the HTML response without escaping, as on the not-found message path.
A user opens the attacker-supplied link in a browser.
patterns.prevention: Treat every value decoded from the URL as untrusted. Apply HTML escaping, for example html.escape(), to the word at the point where it is written into the page, on every route and branch. Do not rely on one route escaping while another does not. Prefer one shared output-encoding step for all user-derived text, and re-check the decoded value rather than trusting its origin.
patterns.limitations: The sources name the not-found message as the confirmed sink and do not list other places where the word may be rendered. They do not describe the exact upstream change, nor how the pickle-based URL state decoding should be hardened. The fix is stated only to be in a commit. The sources also note that the server listens on all interfaces by default, but give no guidance on changing that.

fixtures.scenario: A user opens a lookup_ link whose encoded word is a script tag. The word has no dictionary match, so the not-found message embeds the raw word and the browser runs the script.
The same lookup_ link is opened, but the word is HTML-escaped before the not-found message is built. The browser shows the tag as plain text and runs no script.

citations.quote: This impacts users running the local WordNet Browser server and can lead to script execution in the browser origin of that application.
accepts attacker-controlled base64-encoded pickle data for the URL state.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the not-found branch of the page_from_reference function so the word decoded from the URL is HTML-escaped before it is placed in the response body. This matches the card's cause (an unescaped word in the not-found message on the lookup route) and its prevention (escape the decoded value where it is written into the page).

patterns.title: NLTK downloader path traversal via unvalidated index subdir and id
patterns.cause: The NLTK downloader builds local file and directory paths from the subdir and id attributes of a remote XML index without validating them. A malicious index can supply values with parent-directory sequences such as ../, so the path escapes the download directory.
preconditions: NLTK version 3.9.3 or earlier is in use
The downloader is pointed at a remote XML index server that an attacker controls
A download is requested for a package whose index entry carries malicious subdir or id values
patterns.prevention: Treat the subdir and id values from a remote index as untrusted input. Reject absolute paths and parent-directory sequences. Before creating any directory or opening any file for writing, resolve the final target path and confirm it stays inside the configured download directory. Apply the same check to both directory creation and file writing.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream commit implements its fix, so this card gives only the general direction. They do not say whether other index attributes, symlinks, or archive extraction need extra checks. Only versions 3.9.3 and prior are named as affected.

fixtures.scenario: A downloader uses an attacker-controlled index. A package entry has a subdir with many ../ segments pointing to a system temp location. Downloading it creates directories and writes a file outside the download directory.

The downloader resolves the target path for each index entry and checks it lies inside the download directory. An entry whose subdir contains ../ and escapes the directory is rejected before any directory or file is created.

citations.quote: which can lead to arbitrary directory creation, arbitrary file creation, and arbitrary file overwrite.
Can create arbitrary directories outside the download directory
Create directories at arbitrary locations in the file system

patch_review.observation: The fix rejects package subdir values that are absolute or contain parent-directory components, and rejects id values containing path separators or parent-directory sequences, when a package object is built from the remote index. It also adds a containment check in the package download routine that resolves the final target path and aborts with an error if it falls outside the download directory. This matches the card's cause (unvalidated index values) and its prevention (reject traversal input and confirm the resolved path stays inside the download directory).

patterns.title: Unrestricted class import when deserializing serialized DAGs in Airflow
patterns.cause: The deserialize method of BaseSerialization allowed unrestricted use of the import_string helper on class paths taken from the serialized DAG. A DAG author controls that data, so a class path they embedded was imported and used by the Scheduler or API Server. This is unsafe deserialization (CWE-502).
preconditions: The Scheduler or API Server loads a serialized DAG that contains attacker-controlled class paths.
The attacker can author or submit DAGs, for example by embedding a malicious trigger in a DAG.
The deployment runs a version of apache-airflow older than 3.3.0.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade apache-airflow to 3.3.0 or later. Do not let class paths read from serialized data be imported without an explicit check. Resolve them only against a fixed allowlist of expected classes. Where DAG-author trust is limited, set the allowed_deserialization_classes option in the core configuration section to a narrow allowlist. Keep DAG-author code out of the Scheduler and API Server processes, since the security boundary requires that it never run there.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say which versions before 3.3.0 are affected, which serialized fields or trigger types carry the class path, or how the upstream change works. They describe the allowlist configuration only as defense-in-depth, not as a full fix. They do not say whether other deserialization paths need the same protection.

fixtures.scenario: A DAG author submits a DAG whose serialized form embeds a trigger with an attacker-chosen class path. The Scheduler or API Server loads it, the class path is imported without restriction, and the attacker gains remote code execution in that process.

The deployment runs apache-airflow 3.3.0 or later, and the allowed_deserialization_classes option holds a narrow allowlist. A serialized DAG that names a class outside the allowlist is not turned into an imported class in the Scheduler or API Server.

citations.quote: a DAG author could embed a malicious trigger into a DAG to gain remote code execution on the API Server / Scheduler process
crossing the Airflow security boundary that DAG-author code must never execute in those processes.
3.3.0 or later. As a defense-in-depth mitigation, deployments where DAG-author trust is limited can restrict the

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the base-trigger type from BaseSerialization, so its deserialize method no longer imports a class by path and instantiates it with kwargs taken from serialized data. It also stops decoding trigger kwargs and next-method kwargs when a serialized DAG is loaded, keeping them as raw encoded data. The scheduler then stringifies the encoding keys when it stores them. This matches the card's cause of unrestricted class import from DAG-author-controlled serialized data.

patterns.title: Validate request paths before resolving them to avoid UNC-based SSRF on Windows
patterns.cause: Attacker-supplied filesystem paths were resolved with os.path.realpath() or Path.resolve() before sufficient validation, including in the ComponentRequestHandler. On Windows, a UNC path made this resolution start an outbound SMB connection, which could send NTLMv2 credentials of the account running the Streamlit process.
preconditions: Streamlit Open Source version earlier than 1.54.0
The server runs on a Windows host
Component endpoints are reachable by untrusted parties, with no authentication needed
The server can open outbound SMB connections on port 445
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Streamlit 1.54.0 or later. In your own code that handles request-derived paths, validate the untrusted path before passing it to any resolving call such as os.path.realpath() or Path.resolve(), and reject values that point to remote network locations. As defense in depth, restrict NTLM, disable outbound NTLM authentication, require SMB signing, or block NTLM authentication to remote servers.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not give the exact validation rules used in the fix, so this card does not specify them. They state only that the issue affects Windows. NTLM hardening reduces the impact of credential relay or hash exposure but does not remove the unvalidated path handling. Residual risk depends on the organization's authentication configuration and network posture.

fixtures.scenario: A Streamlit server older than 1.54.0 on Windows exposes component endpoints to an untrusted network. A GET request appends an attacker-controlled SMB host to the URI path, and the server resolves it as a filesystem path before validating it.

The server runs Streamlit 1.54.0 or later. Any request-derived path is validated and rejected if it targets a remote network location before os.path.realpath() or Path.resolve() is called, so no outbound SMB connection starts.

citations.quote: The vulnerability arises from improper validation of attacker-supplied filesystem paths.
can cause the Streamlit server to initiate outbound SMB connections over port 445
Streamlit Open Source versions prior to 1.54.0 running on Windows hosts.
Organizations that enforce NTLM restrictions, disable outbound NTLM authentication, require SMB signing, or block NTLM authentication to remote servers

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a shared check, run before any call that resolves a path, that rejects UNC paths, drive-qualified paths, rooted or absolute paths, traversal segments and null bytes. It is applied in the safe-path builder used by the component handlers, in the app static file handler, in the static routes, and in a new Starlette middleware. Rejected requests now get a 400 response. This matches the card's cause (resolving untrusted paths before validation, which lets Windows open an SMB connection) and its prevention (validate first, reject remote locations).

patterns.title: Unsafe deserialization of XCom values through legacy serialization keys in the Airflow webserver
patterns.cause: The public XCom creation request model lacked a check for reserved serialization metadata in user-supplied values. The advisory identifies a legacy type/var marker bypass that lets a Dag Author craft an XCom payload causing arbitrary code execution in the webserver context, where that role normally cannot execute code. The fix blocks current class name, version, data, schema id and cache keys, plus legacy type, source and var keys. This blocked set does not establish that every listed key independently triggers object reconstruction.
preconditions: The attacker is a Dag Author able to craft XCom payloads.
For the creation path addressed by the diff, a crafted value reaches the public XCom creation request model without the new reserved-key validation.
The payload contains serialization metadata in a dictionary, potentially nested within dictionaries, lists or tuples, and reaches unsafe deserialization in the webserver context.
The deployment uses an affected Airflow release; the supplied sources do not enumerate the affected version range.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Apache Airflow 3.2.0, which the advisory identifies as resolving the issue. The fix recursively checks XCom creation values through dictionaries, lists and tuples, rejecting dictionaries containing any reserved current or legacy serialization key. Added API tests expect HTTP 422 for representative current, legacy and nested markers. Shared serialization constants supply the validator's forbidden-key set and the SDK deserializer's marker definitions, reducing drift. As general hardening, validate untrusted values at storage entry points and reject attempts to impersonate internal serialization metadata.
patterns.limitations: The diff shows validation on XCom creation values, but does not establish coverage for updates, execution API writes or existing stored entries, nor that those paths are vulnerable. It leaves legacy deserialization behavior unchanged apart from moving constants. The full deserialization call chain and exploitable object types are not shown. The sources neither establish exploitability for other API users nor enumerate affected releases below 3.2.0. Recursive traversal is shown, but unlimited nesting is not guaranteed. The advisory rates severity Low because Dag Authors are already highly trusted.

fixtures.scenario: A Dag Author on a pre-3.2.0 deployment stores an XCom value that uses the legacy serialization keys. When the webserver's XCom API handles that value, it deserializes it in the webserver process and arbitrary code runs there.
The deployment runs Apache Airflow 3.2.0 or later. The same crafted XCom value with legacy serialization keys does not lead to code execution in the webserver context.

citations.quote: Unsafe Deserialization via Legacy Serialization Keys (__type/__var) Bypass in XCom API
could craft XCom payload causing the webserver to execute arbitrary code
Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Airflow 3.2.0, which resolves this issue.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a validator on the XCom create request body. It walks the submitted value through nested dictionaries, lists and tuples and rejects it with a validation error if any reserved serialization key appears. The reserved set covers the five current-format keys and the three legacy keys (type, source, var). The constants move into a new shared serialization package so the deserializer and the check use one list. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Stored XSS from unsafely parsed MLmodel YAML artifacts shown in the MLflow web UI
patterns.cause: MLflow has stored XSS caused by unsafe parsing of YAML-based MLmodel artifacts in its web UI. An authenticated attacker can upload a malicious MLmodel file whose payload executes when another user views the artifact, potentially enabling session hijacking or operations on the victim's behalf. The diff replaces the YAML load function with safeLoad in ShowArtifactLoggedModelView and useValidateLoggedModelSignature.
preconditions: The attacker is authenticated and can upload a malicious MLmodel artifact.
Another user views the malicious artifact in the MLflow web UI.
The deployment uses MLflow 3.10.1 or earlier, as stated in the advisory.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to an MLflow release containing the upstream fix, which replaces load with safeLoad when parsing artifact YAML in ShowArtifactLoggedModelView and useValidateLoggedModelSignature. As general hardening, review other artifact YAML parsing paths for equivalent unsafe parsing and handle parsed values as untrusted data, using appropriate escaping or sanitization if strings are rendered as markup.
patterns.limitations: The diff shows two changed parsing call sites but does not establish their coverage of all artifact YAML handling. Neither source specifies the payload, exact tag or schema behavior, or complete execution chain. They do not establish that script executes during parsing itself or that signature validation alone triggers exploitation. The sources do not identify a fixed release version or establish that every affected version uses identical parsing code.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user uploads an MLmodel file whose YAML content carries a script payload. A second user opens the artifact in the MLflow UI, and the payload runs in that user's browser session.
The same MLmodel file is uploaded, but the UI shows its parsed content only as plain text. Opening the artifact does not execute anything in the viewer's browser.

citations.quote: MLflow is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) caused by unsafe parsing of YAML-based MLmodel artifacts in its web interface
An authenticated attacker can upload a malicious MLmodel file containing a payload that executes when another user views the artifact in the UI.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the unrestricted YAML load call with the safe-schema loader at two front-end call sites: the logged model artifact view and the logged model signature validation hook. This stops crafted MLmodel YAML from building non-plain values such as functions during parsing, which matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: SSRF through unvalidated download link submission in pyload-ng
patterns.cause: The package submission endpoint passes user-supplied links straight to the download engine. The engine accepts any URL scheme and requests arbitrary destinations, including internal addresses and cloud metadata endpoints, without validating the destination.
preconditions: The attacker holds a valid pyLoad account of any role, ADMIN or USER.
The application fetches user-supplied URLs through its download engine with no destination validation.
The host can reach internal network services or a cloud metadata endpoint such as 169.254.169.254.
patterns.prevention: Validate every submitted link before the download engine starts a request. Allow only the http and https schemes. Check the destination host and reject private address ranges (RFC 1918), link-local addresses, and known cloud metadata endpoints. Enforce this check in the download path, not only in the web endpoint, so all entry points are covered.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no detail on the actual patch in version 0.5.0b3.dev97, so its exact behavior is unknown. They do not discuss redirects, DNS resolution tricks, or IPv6 and alternate address encodings. The remediation list is advisory, and a name-based blocklist alone may be incomplete. Affected versions beyond 0.5.0 are described only as potentially earlier.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated user submits a package whose link points to the link-local cloud metadata address on a cloud-hosted pyLoad server. The download engine fetches it and saves the metadata, including keys, as a downloadable file.
The same submission is rejected before any request is made, because the destination is link-local. A link to a public http or https host is accepted. A link using a non-http scheme is also rejected.

citations.quote: PyLoad's download engine accepts arbitrary URLs without validation, enabling Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks.
Block requests to private IP ranges (RFC 1918, link-local addresses)
Whitelist allowed URL schemes (http/https only)

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a check in the downloader plugin base download method. It parses the hostname from the download URL, resolves it to IP addresses, and fails the download if any address is not globally routable, which blocks private, loopback, link-local and metadata destinations. This is the same destination validation in the download path that the card recommends. The diff does not show scheme restriction or redirect handling, but the card's main cause and prevention still match.

patterns.title: SSRF through unvalidated file URLs in the vLLM batch runner
patterns.cause: The batch runner's download_bytes_from_url function fetched attacker-controlled HTTP or HTTPS URLs from the file_url field of batch transcription and translation requests without destination validation. It did not apply the media allowlist used elsewhere or validate redirect targets, allowing requests to reachable internal services or metadata endpoints. The fix also addresses parser differences, including backslash-before-@ confusion, by checking a urllib3-parsed hostname and passing that parser's normalized URL to aiohttp.
preconditions: vLLM version from 0.16.0 up to but not including 0.19.0.
An actor can control the batch input JSON read by the batch runner.
Batch requests use the audio transcription or translation endpoints with an attacker-controlled HTTP or HTTPS file_url.
To target internal services or cloud metadata endpoints, those destinations must be reachable from the vLLM host.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to vLLM 0.19.0 or later. Pass the configured allowed media domains through the transcription and translation wrappers into download_bytes_from_url. When a list is supplied, parse the URL with urllib3, reject hostnames absent from the list, and pass the normalized URL to aiohttp to avoid parser discrepancies. An empty list denies all HTTP and HTTPS destinations; an unset list permits any host for backward compatibility, so configure the list to enforce destination restrictions. Control redirects through the media redirect setting and disable them to prevent redirects from leaving allowed domains.
patterns.limitations: The hostname restriction applies only when an allowlist is supplied. An unset list permits any host; an empty list denies all HTTP and HTTPS URLs. Unlisted private or metadata IP literals are rejected, but the shown check adds no IP-range, resolved-address, or DNS-rebinding protection for allowed hosts, and no port or path restrictions. If redirects are enabled, the shown code does not re-check their targets against the allowlist. The supplied sources do not establish the redirect setting's default or require explicit operator opt-in. Data URLs are intentionally exempt from domain restrictions.

fixtures.scenario: A batch input line sets the file_url of a transcription request to an internal metadata address. The batch runner fetches that URL from the server and returns or reports the result, with no host check.

The batch runner checks the file_url host against a configured allowlist, including redirect targets, before fetching. A line pointing at an internal address is rejected, and an approved audio host is fetched.

citations.quote: allows any actor who can control batch input JSON to make the vLLM batch runner issue arbitrary HTTP/HTTPS requests from the server
This is a classic SSRF pattern: a server-side component makes arbitrary HTTP requests to a URL string taken from untrusted input.
does not reuse this allowlist or any equivalent validation, even though it also fetches user-provided URLs.
This vulnerability is fixed in 0.19.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix passes the configured allowed media domains into the batch download function used by the transcription and translation wrappers. For http and https URLs it checks the hostname against the list, treats an empty list as deny-all, and fetches the URL in the normalized form from the urllib3 parser to close the backslash-before-@ parser mismatch with aiohttp. It also makes redirect following depend on the media redirect environment setting. When no list is configured, behavior is unchanged, and data URLs are exempt.

patterns.title: Arbitrary code execution from loading untrusted files with aiohttp CookieJar.load()
patterns.cause: The advisory identifies aiohttp releases before 3.14.0 as affected. Before the fix, CookieJar.save stored cookies as pickle and CookieJar.load used unrestricted pickle deserialization. A crafted attacker-controlled file could invoke arbitrary callables during reconstruction, allowing arbitrary code execution (CWE-502). The fix writes JSON and restricts global resolution in the legacy pickle fallback to an allow-list of cookie types and supporting containers.
preconditions: The application uses an aiohttp release prior to 3.14.0.
The application calls CookieJar.load on a file path.
An attacker can control, replace or supply the content of that file.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade aiohttp to 3.14.0 or later. CookieJar.save then writes JSON; CookieJar.load tries JSON first and falls back to restricted pickle loading on JSON decoding, Unicode decoding or value errors. The fallback rejects globals outside its allow-list. As general hardening, load only trusted cookie files, prefer data-only persistence formats, and re-save trusted legacy cookies as JSON after upgrading to avoid pickle loading for those files. The advisory suggests sanitizing attacker-controlled files before loading on older releases, but provides no procedure.
patterns.limitations: Legacy pickle support remains. The diff tests rejection of several code-execution payloads, but does not establish blanket safety for arbitrary files or compare the restriction with removing pickle entirely. The JSON loader expects a particular structure; malformed input may raise errors or trigger fallback. The sources do not define or validate sanitization. They say most applications load the user's own data and are unlikely to be affected. CookieJar.load is the named vulnerable API; the sources do not establish whether other aiohttp APIs are affected.

fixtures.scenario: A service running an aiohttp version older than 3.14.0 lets users upload a cookie file and passes the uploaded file to CookieJar.load(), so an attacker can supply a crafted file.
A service running aiohttp 3.14.0 or later loads with CookieJar.load() only a cookie file that the same application previously saved for the same user, and does not accept cookie files from outside.

citations.quote: AIOHTTP is Vulnerable to Deserialization of Untrusted Data
Version 3.14.0 patches the issue.
a workaround on older releases would be to sanitize the files before loading.
Most applications using this function will be doing so with the user's own data, so this is unlikely to affect many applications.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the cookie jar's save method to write JSON and its load method to try JSON first, which is pure data. If the file is not valid JSON, load falls back to a restricted unpickler that raises an error for any class outside a small cookie-related allow-list. This matches the card's cause (unrestricted pickle loading) and its prevention. The 3.14.0 version number is not visible in the diff, but nothing in the diff contradicts it.

patterns.title: SSRF filter bypass through automatic HTTP redirects in a download manager
patterns.cause: The SSRF check validated only the hostname of the initial download URL. The HTTP client was configured to follow redirects automatically, up to 10 hops, so redirect targets were never checked against the filter. An attacker-controlled public server could therefore redirect the client to an internal address.
preconditions: The application checks that a user-supplied URL resolves to a global address, but only for the initial URL.
The HTTP client (pycurl here) follows redirects automatically, with no per-hop validation.
An authenticated user with ADD permission can submit a URL that points to a server they control.
patterns.prevention: Apply the same address validation to every redirect hop, not only the first URL. One direction is to turn off automatic redirect following and follow redirects manually, validating each target before the next request. Another is to restrict the allowed redirect protocols to HTTP and HTTPS and add a callback that checks the destination IPs before the client follows. Treat loopback, private and link-local addresses, including cloud metadata endpoints, as blocked at every hop.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, so the two directions above come from the advisory's suggestions and are not confirmed as what was shipped. They do not discuss DNS rebinding between the check and the connection, or how redirect hostnames should be resolved. The reported affected range is 0.5.0b3.dev96 and earlier.

fixtures.scenario: A user with ADD permission submits a link on a public attacker host. The host passes the address check, then answers with a redirect to a cloud metadata address. The client follows it without validation and saves the response to storage.

The same link is submitted. The public host passes the check and answers with a redirect to a metadata address. The redirect target is validated before it is followed, is rejected as non-global, and no request reaches the internal address.

citations.quote: Redirect targets are never validated against the SSRF filter.
An authenticated user with ADD permission can bypass the SSRF fix by submitting a URL that redirects to an internal address.
Disable automatic redirect following and validate each redirect target

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the one-time hostname check on the initial download URL. In its place it registers a pre-request callback on the HTTP client that checks the actual connected IP address before every request, including each redirect hop, and aborts the transfer if that address is not global. A failed check is reported as a refusal to download from an internal host.

patterns.title: Admin-only guard skipped for plugin config lets non-admin users set an executable path
patterns.cause: The admin-only check for security-critical settings is applied only to core config options, not to plugin config options. The AntiVirus plugin stores an executable path in its config and passes it directly to a process-spawning call, so a non-admin user with SETTINGS permission can change it and gain code execution.
preconditions: The attacker is an authenticated non-admin user with SETTINGS permission
Plugin config values can be written through the settings API without an admin check
A plugin reads an executable path from its config and passes it directly to a process-spawning call
The plugin is enabled and its scan step runs, for example when a download completes
patterns.prevention: Apply the same admin-only authorization to plugin config writes as to core config writes. Treat every plugin option that controls an executable or path as admin-only. Also validate that the configured executable is a known antivirus binary before it is launched, rather than trusting the stored value.
patterns.limitations: The sources name only the AntiVirus executable and argument options and say any plugin option controlling executables or paths should be protected. They do not list other affected plugins or the final upstream fix. Affected versions are stated as 0.5.0b3.dev96 and earlier. A separate storage folder file-read issue is mentioned in the advisory but not covered here.

fixtures.scenario: A non-admin user with SETTINGS permission sets the AntiVirus executable option to a shell through the settings API, enables the plugin, then adds a download. When it finishes, the scan launches the chosen program.
The same non-admin request to change the AntiVirus executable option is rejected with a permission error. Only an admin can set it, and the value must be a validated known antivirus binary.

citations.quote: this protection is only applied to core config options, not to plugin config options.
The AntiVirus plugin stores an executable path (avfile) in its config, which is passed directly to subprocess.Popen().
A non-admin user with SETTINGS permission can change this path to achieve remote code execution.

patch_review.observation: The fix computes the caller's admin status once at the start of the config-write function and adds an admin-only list for plugin options (the AntiVirus executable path and arguments), enforced in the plugin branch, which previously had no check. It also adds the storage folder to the core admin-only list. This matches the card's cause (admin guard applied only to core options) and its main prevention (admin-only writes for executable-controlling plugin options).

patterns.title: Writable download folder redirected into a pickle-backed session store
patterns.cause: The storage_folder setting could be changed by a non-admin user. Its path check only blocked PKGDIR and userdir. Downloads could therefore be written into the Flask filesystem session directory, whose files are deserialized with pickle when a request carries the matching session cookie.
preconditions: A non-admin user holds both SETTINGS and ADD permissions.
The storage_folder option is missing from the admin-only options set, and the path check denies only PKGDIR and userdir.
Flask is configured with filesystem sessions, whose files are deserialized with pickle.
Session file names are predictable from the session id, so a downloaded file can be given a chosen session file name.
patterns.prevention: Make storage_folder an admin-only option. Do not rely on a short denylist of directories for download destinations. After resolving the path with realpath, also reject destinations that fall inside directories the application reads and deserializes on its own, such as the session store, the template bytecode cache and the temp directory. Check that the names in the admin-only set match the real option names, so that no entry is dead code.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream commit, so the exact approach it took is unknown. Directory locations vary by deployment, and the session path given is the standard Docker one. The sources do not cover other writable paths beyond those named, or any change to how the session store deserializes data.

fixtures.scenario: A user with SETTINGS and ADD permissions sets the download folder to the Flask session directory, which lies outside PKGDIR and userdir. They add a download named like a predictable session file. A later request with that cookie deserializes it.

The download folder setting is admin-only, so a user with SETTINGS and ADD permissions cannot change it. Destinations that overlap the session store or other auto-consumed directories are also rejected after path resolution.

citations.quote: The storage_folder option is not in this set and passes the existing path restriction because the Flask session directory is outside both PKGDIR and userdir.
plant a malicious pickle payload as a predictable session file, and trigger arbitrary code execution when any HTTP request arrives with the corresponding session cookie
or extend the path check to block writing to auto-consumed temporary directories (Flask session store, Jinja bytecode cache, pyload temp directory)

patch_review.observation: The fix adds the general storage_folder option to the set of core options that only an admin may change, so a non-admin with SETTINGS permission can no longer redirect the download folder. It also restructures the role check so it is computed once, and it adds admin-only protection for the AntiVirus plugin file and argument options and a few other sensitive core options.

patterns.title: Backslash filenames bypass upload name sanitization on Windows in NiceGUI
patterns.cause: Upload filenames were sanitized by taking the name component with PurePosixPath, which only treats forward slashes as separators. A filename with backslashes passes through unchanged. On Windows, path construction then reads those backslashes as directory separators, so the result can leave the intended upload directory.
preconditions: The application runs on Windows; Linux and macOS treat backslashes as literal filename characters.
The application builds a filesystem path from the uploaded file's name, a pattern shown in NiceGUI's bundled examples.
The NiceGUI version is earlier than 3.10.0.
An attacker can supply the upload filename, for example with backslash-separated parent-directory segments.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade NiceGUI to 3.10.0 or later. In application code, do not trust the client-supplied filename as a path component. Sanitize with the rules of the platform that will use the name, so that both forward slashes and backslashes count as separators. Better still, store uploads under a server-generated name and keep the original name only as metadata. After building the destination path, confirm it still lies inside the intended upload directory before writing.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so this card does not say how 3.10.0 changes the sanitization. They also do not say whether other separator forms or special Windows path forms are affected. They only discuss the backslash case on Windows.

fixtures.scenario: A Windows NiceGUI app older than 3.10.0 joins its uploads folder with the uploaded file's name. An attacker uploads a file whose name has backslash-separated parent-directory segments, and the file is written outside the uploads folder.

The app runs NiceGUI 3.10.0 or later, stores uploads under a generated name, and checks that the final destination is inside the uploads folder. The same backslash filename cannot place a file elsewhere.

citations.quote: Linux and macOS are not affected, as they treat backslashes as literal filename characters.
Applications that construct file paths using file.name (a pattern demonstrated in NiceGUI's bundled examples) are vulnerable to arbitrary file write on Windows.
This vulnerability is fixed in 3.10.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix drops the POSIX-only name extraction for upload filenames and adds a helper that strips everything up to the last forward slash and then up to the last backslash. Backslash-separated traversal names therefore reduce to a bare file name on every platform. Tests cover forward-slash, backslash and mixed separators, as well as empty and missing names. This matches the card's cause and its prevention advice to treat both separator types as path separators.

patterns.title: Mako TemplateLookup path traversal via double-slash URI prefix
patterns.cause: Two code paths strip leading slashes inconsistently. TemplateLookup.get_template() removes all leading slashes and finds the file, while Template initialization removes only one. The remaining leading slash changes how the path is normalized, so the parent-directory check passes and a file outside the template directories is read and rendered.
preconditions: Mako version earlier than 1.3.11 is in use
Untrusted input is passed directly to TemplateLookup.get_template()
The URI begins with two slashes followed by parent-directory segments
The target file is readable by the process
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Mako to 1.3.11 or later. Any implementation that validates template paths should handle leading slashes the same way in every step, so the path that is looked up is the path that is checked. Do not pass raw user input to the template lookup. Map user input to an allowlist of known template names, and reject URIs containing parent-directory segments or extra leading slashes.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the inconsistency and the 1.3.11 fix only at a high level. They do not list other affected entry points or every unsafe URI form. The advisory says HTTP exploitation is mitigated in Python's BaseHTTPRequestHandler, but other HTTP servers may be affected. Exposure depends on the application passing untrusted input to the lookup.

fixtures.scenario: A web handler passes a user-supplied path straight to TemplateLookup.get_template(). A request whose path starts with two slashes and then climbs out with parent-directory segments returns a system file as rendered template output.
The handler maps the request to a fixed allowlist of template names and rejects unknown names. Mako 1.3.11 or later is installed, so a double-slash prefix cannot bypass the traversal check.

citations.quote: The root cause is an inconsistency between two slash-stripping implementations.
Any file readable by the process can be returned as rendered template content when an application passes untrusted input directly to TemplateLookup.get_template().
This vulnerability is fixed in 1.3.11.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the path check in Template initialization so it strips all leading slashes from the URI instead of just one, matching what the template lookup already does. Previously a URI with a double-slash prefix kept a leading slash through normalization, so the check for a path escaping the root was skipped. Tests now confirm that single, double and triple slash prefixes with parent-directory segments are all rejected.

patterns.title: Open redirect via unsupported response_type in Authlib authorization endpoint
patterns.cause: When a request used an unsupported response_type, the authorization server copied the raw redirect_uri from the request into the error object before any client was resolved and before any redirect URI validation. The error rendering step then returned a 302 redirect to that URI whenever it was set. An unvalidated, attacker-supplied URL therefore became the redirect target.
preconditions: The application runs Authlib's OAuth 2.0 authorization server and exposes the documented authorization endpoint flow.
The request uses an unsupported response_type and carries an attacker-controlled redirect_uri.
The affected version is earlier than 1.6.10 (1.6 line) or 1.7.1 (1.7 line).
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Authlib to 1.6.10 or 1.7.1 or later. In any authorization server implementation, never place a redirect_uri taken from the request into an error response or redirect until a client has been resolved and the URI has been checked against that client's registered redirect URIs. When no client or validated URI exists, return a direct error response instead of a redirect. Add a test that sends an unsupported response_type with an external redirect_uri and expects no Location header.
patterns.limitations: The sources state that the issue is fixed in 1.6.10 and 1.7.1 but do not describe how the fix works, so the exact validation order in patched releases is not covered here. The advisory reproduces the issue with the Flask and Django integrations. Other error types or code paths are not discussed in the sources.

fixtures.scenario: An authorization endpoint receives a request with an unsupported response_type, an unknown client, and a redirect_uri pointing to an external attacker site. The server answers with a 302 to that site, carrying the error and state parameters.
The same request, with no redirect_uri validated against a client, produces a direct error response with status 400 and no Location header, as seen in the advisory when redirect_uri is omitted.

citations.quote: The vulnerable behavior happens before client lookup and before any redirect URI validation.
If redirect_uri is set, Authlib automatically returns a redirect response to that URI
This vulnerability is fixed in 1.6.10 and 1.7.1.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the unsupported response_type path in the authorization server so it no longer copies the request redirect_uri into the error. It now looks up the client and only sets a redirect target when the requested URI passes that client's registered redirect URI check, or falls back to the client's default URI when none was requested. Otherwise no redirect is used, and the added Flask regression test expects a 400 response with no Location header.

patterns.title: Ray Data Arrow extension types unpickle Parquet schema metadata, enabling code execution
patterns.cause: Ray Data registers custom Arrow extension types globally in PyArrow. When a Parquet file declares one of these types, PyArrow calls the type's deserialize hook on the field metadata bytes. Ray passed those bytes straight to cloudpickle.loads(), so attacker-controlled bytes ran as code during schema parsing, before any row data was read.
preconditions: The process uses Ray Data, which registers the tensor extension types globally in PyArrow.
The process reads a Parquet file, through Ray Data or through pyarrow or pandas readers.
An attacker can place a crafted Parquet file where a Ray Data pipeline reads it, with a column using one of the ray.data tensor extension type names.
The Ray version is one that contains the vulnerable deserialization path.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Ray to version 2.55.0 or later, which the advisories list as patched. Until then, do not read Parquet files from untrusted sources in any process that has imported Ray Data. More generally, an extension type deserializer must never hand file-supplied metadata bytes to a pickle-style loader. Treat Parquet schema metadata as untrusted input.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch changes deserialization, so this card gives no fix mechanism. The advisories disagree on the affected range: one says 2.49.0 through 2.54.0, while the CVE record says 2.54.0 up to but not including 2.55.0. Verify the exact range for your build. The sources do not cover mitigations other than upgrading.

fixtures.scenario: A pipeline on a vulnerable Ray version reads Parquet files from a shared upload folder. An attacker drops a file whose schema declares a ray.data tensor extension type with malicious metadata bytes. Opening the file runs attacker code during schema parsing.

The same pipeline runs on Ray 2.55.0 or later, and Parquet files come only from trusted producers. A file declaring a tensor extension type with unexpected metadata does not lead to unpickling of attacker bytes.

citations.quote: Ray's implementation passes these bytes directly to cloudpickle.loads(), achieving arbitrary code execution during schema parsing, before any row data is read.
The extension types are registered globally in PyArrow, so all Parquet reads in the process are affected
The attacker must place a crafted Parquet file where a Ray Data pipeline reads it.
This issue has been patched in version 2.55.0.

patterns.title: GitPython unsafe-option check bypassed by underscore-form kwargs
patterns.cause: GitPython checks the raw Python kwarg names against its list of unsafe Git options before those names are converted into command-line flags. The unsafe-option check runs before the dashified flag form is produced. The upload_pack and receive_pack kwargs therefore pass the check, then become the dangerous upload-pack and receive-pack flags, which let git run an attacker-chosen helper command.
preconditions: GitPython version 3.1.30 up to, but not including, 3.1.47 is in use
An application passes attacker-influenced kwargs into Repo.clone_from(), Remote.fetch(), Remote.pull(), or Remote.push()
The allow_unsafe_options setting is left at its default of False, so the application relies on the built-in guard for protection
patterns.prevention: Upgrade GitPython to 3.1.47 or later. Do not forward untrusted dictionaries of extra Git options into these calls as kwargs. Any unsafe-option validation must compare option names in the same normalized, dashified form that is later passed to git, so that underscore and hyphen spellings are treated identically. Do not treat a passing guard as proof that a kwarg is safe.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail, so how 3.1.47 normalizes names is not stated here. They say that not every unsafe option is affected, for example exec is already rejected, but they do not list every option or spelling that might still bypass a check. Only the four named APIs are covered, and the sources do not describe any other entry points.

fixtures.scenario: A service forwards a user-supplied options dict to Remote.fetch() on GitPython 3.1.40. The dict has an upload_pack key naming a helper program. The guard does not reject it, and the helper runs as the service account.
The same service runs GitPython 3.1.47 or later, or never forwards user-supplied keys to these calls. The underscore-form upload_pack key no longer bypasses the guard or never reaches git.

citations.quote: Because the unsafe-option check runs before this normalization, underscore-form kwargs bypass the safety check even though they become the exact dangerous Git flags
From version 3.1.30 to before version 3.1.47
This issue has been patched in version 3.1.47.

patterns.title: PyPI Extension Manager allow-list not enforced for installs in JupyterLab before 4.5.7
patterns.cause: The allow-list of extensions that can be installed from the PyPI Extension Manager was not correctly enforced in JupyterLab 4.0.0 through 4.5.6. The manager was not contained to packages listed on the default PyPI index. The advisory title describes a discrepancy between the API and GUI policy, which let third-party extensions be installed through a direct POST request.
preconditions: JupyterLab version is between 4.0.0 and 4.5.6, or an application such as Notebook v7+ depends on such a version.
The default PyPI Extension Manager is enabled.
The operator relies on the extension allow-list to stop users from installing packages, for example because kernels and terminals are disabled or delegated to remote hosts.
The attacker is an authenticated user, such as a student in a shared JupyterHub or a user in a multi-tenant deployment.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade jupyterlab to 4.5.7 or later, including in applications that depend on it, such as Notebook v7+. Where upgrading is not yet possible, switch to the read-only extension manager so the server cannot install extensions. An implementation should enforce the install policy on the server for every install request, not only in the GUI. It should also confine the PyPI manager to packages from the default PyPI index and not trust the client to have applied the allow-list. Do not treat a PyPI proxy with allow-listed packages as a substitute for this enforcement.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the 4.5.7 patch enforces the allow-list, the exact request format, or which checks were added, so this card gives only the direction. The advisory notes that multi-tenant deployments not configured for untrusted users are outside the intended security model. The read-only workaround disables extension installation entirely.

fixtures.scenario: A JupyterLab 4.5.6 server has the PyPI Extension Manager enabled and an allow-list set. Terminals are disabled. An authenticated user sends an install request directly to the server for a package outside the allow-list, and it is accepted.
The server runs JupyterLab 4.5.7 or later, or uses the read-only extension manager. The same direct install request for a package outside the allow-list does not result in an installation.

citations.quote: The PyPI Extension Manager was not contained to packages listed on the default PyPI index.
Switch to read-only extension manager
configuration of a PyPI proxy with allow-listed packages is not sufficient to protect from this vulnerability.

patterns.title: GitPython clone validates multi_options before shlex.split rewrites them
patterns.cause: The clone routine checks the unsafe-option list against the original multi_options entries, but passes git the result of joining those entries and re-splitting them with shlex.split. The check compares the start of each entry, so one string beginning with a safe option can hide a config option that only becomes its own token after the split.
preconditions: GitPython earlier than 3.1.47 is in use
User-controlled text reaches multi_options in clone_from, clone, or Submodule.update (via clone_multi_options)
Git honors the smuggled config option during the clone and runs hooks from the attacker-chosen directory
patterns.prevention: Run the unsafe-option check on the exact final argument list that will be handed to git, after any joining and splitting, not on the pre-transformation input. Upgrade GitPython to 3.1.47 or later. Keep untrusted text out of multi_options where possible.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream patch works or list every option that could be smuggled this way. They describe the check as a prefix comparison and name only the config option for hooks. Whether other call paths are affected is not stated beyond Submodule.update.

fixtures.scenario: An app passes a user string to a clone call's multi_options: a safe branch option followed by a config option that sets the hooks path. The check sees only the safe prefix. After splitting, the config becomes its own token and git runs attacker hooks.
Validation runs on the exact tokens passed to git, after splitting, so a config option embedded in a longer string is rejected before the clone starts. GitPython is also upgraded to 3.1.47 or later.

citations.quote: passes validation (starts with --branch), but after split becomes
Git applies the config and executes attacker hooks during clone.
Same class as CVE-2023-40267.
This issue has been patched in version 3.1.47.

patterns.title: XCom PATCH endpoint bypassed reserved-key validation and enabled deserialization RCE on the triggerer
patterns.cause: The XCom create request model rejected reserved serialization metadata keys inside user-provided values, but the update (PATCH) model lacked that validation. An authenticated user with XCom write permission on a Dag could plant a crafted value. The advisory reports remote code execution on the triggerer when the affected task next deferred. This bypassed the incomplete fix for CVE-2026-33858, which covered only the POST/set path.
preconditions: An authenticated UI or API user has XCom write permission on a Dag.
The user can submit a crafted value through the XCom PATCH endpoint without the added validation.
The affected task defers to the triggerer, which deserializes the planted value.
The deployment lacks the PATCH-path fix.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade apache-airflow to 3.2.2 or later, including deployments already upgraded for CVE-2026-33858. The fix extracts the existing recursive reserved-key validation into a shared helper and applies it to the value fields of both create and update request models. It checks dictionaries and traverses nested dictionaries, lists and tuples, rejecting forbidden serialization metadata keys with a validation error. As general hardening, restrict XCom write permission to trusted users.
patterns.limitations: The advisory describes reserved XCom entry names such as return_value, but the diff validates keys inside the value payload, not the entry name; this discrepancy remains unresolved. The diff does not change the deserializer or establish validation coverage for other write paths, including task code or the execution API. The sources do not establish the exact exploit payload, how metadata controls deserialization, or a complete affected-version range.

fixtures.scenario: A user with XCom write permission on a deferring Dag sends a PATCH request to the XCom endpoint that sets the reserved key return_value to a crafted serialized payload. The next deferral makes the triggerer deserialize it as code.
The same PATCH request to an upgraded deployment (3.2.2 or later) is rejected because reserved keys are validated on every write path, and XCom write permission is limited to trusted users.

citations.quote: combined, this allowed RCE on the triggerer when the affected task next deferred.
the PATCH path was not covered.
The endpoint also accepted serialized payload shapes the triggerer's deserializer treats as code

patch_review.observation: The fix moves the recursive reserved-key check into a shared helper function and applies it as a field validator on both the XCom create body and the XCom update body. Previously only the create body rejected nested dicts and lists containing reserved deserialization metadata keys, so the PATCH path accepted them. A test now confirms the update endpoint returns a validation error for such values.

patterns.title: Config-supplied internal attention field triggers remote code download and execution in transformers
patterns.cause: Model configuration attributes are deserialized without filtering, and internal fields are not sanitized. A crafted config file can set the internal attention implementation field to an attacker-controlled Hub repository ID. The library then downloads kernels from that repository and runs them without a sandbox, bypassing the trust_remote_code safeguard.
preconditions: Running a transformers version earlier than 5.3.0
Loading a model through the standard from_pretrained path, such as with AutoModelForCausalLM
The model configuration file comes from a source the attacker controls or can influence
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to transformers 5.3.0 or later. In code that loads configurations, treat every field in a loaded config file as untrusted input. Internal fields such as the internal attention implementation attribute should be dropped or rejected when they come from a file rather than being applied. A value read from a config must never select a remote repository whose code gets downloaded and executed. Executing downloaded code should require an explicit, visible opt-in and should not run with the full privileges of the host user.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, the full list of internal fields affected, or any workaround for versions before 5.3.0. They also do not say how the kernel download step is gated after the fix. Treat the upgrade as the confirmed mitigation and review other config fields that influence code loading.

fixtures.scenario: A service on transformers 4.x loads a model from a third-party repository. Its config file sets the internal attention implementation field to an attacker's Hub repository ID. Loading the model fetches and runs the attacker's code.

The service runs transformers 5.3.0 or later. It loads the same third-party model, and the internal attention field in the config file does not cause code from another repository to be downloaded or executed.

citations.quote: This issue arises due to unfiltered deserialization of configuration attributes, insufficient sanitization of internal fields, and unsandboxed execution of downloaded kernels.
Users are advised to upgrade to version 5.3.0 or later to mitigate this issue.
is invisible to the victim, and exploits the standard documented usage pattern, making it particularly severe.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the configuration constructor skip the two internal implementation fields (attention and experts) when they arrive through loaded config data, so only the public field can set them. It also tightens the kernel-detection helper so that Hub kernel identifiers are accepted only from the kernels-community organization, and any other repository is skipped with a warning. Together these stop a crafted config from pointing the library at an attacker-controlled repository whose code would be downloaded and run.

patterns.title: Backslash traversal in Mako TemplateLookup on Windows
patterns.cause: Mako normalizes template URIs with posixpath, which treats a backslash as an ordinary character, but checks and opens files with os.path, which on Windows treats a backslash as a separator. Parent-directory segments written with backslashes pass the traversal check and are then resolved by the file existence check.
preconditions: The application runs on Windows.
A Mako version before 1.3.12 is used.
User-controlled template names or include paths reach TemplateLookup.get_template().
The target file is readable by the application process.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Mako 1.3.12 or later. Before any path operation, convert backslashes in the URI to forward slashes so that every normalization and validation step sees the same separators. Avoid passing untrusted input directly as template names, and prefer an allow-list of known template names.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream code change, only the direction of normalizing backslashes early. They do not state whether other platforms are affected, though the described mismatch is specific to Windows. If a targeted file contains template syntax, it may be parsed and executed as a template, but the sources give no further detail.

fixtures.scenario: A Windows web app passes a request parameter straight to the template lookup. A name made of backslash-separated parent-directory segments plus a filename loads a file outside the template directory.

The same app runs Mako 1.3.12 or later, converts backslashes in the name to forward slashes before any path handling, and so rejects the parent-directory segments or keeps the lookup inside the template directory.

citations.quote: The primary impact is local file disclosure.
The fix should normalize backslashes to forward slashes early in the URI processing pipeline, before any path operations, to ensure consistent behavior across platforms.
This vulnerability is fixed in 1.3.12.

patch_review.observation: The fix converts backslashes to forward slashes in the URI inside TemplateLookup.get_template, before the leading-slash strip and directory joining, and again in Template initialization before the normalization and the check for escaping the root. This makes every step see the same separators, so backslash-written parent-directory segments are now rejected. The new tests cover backslash traversal with and without a leading backslash or forward slash.

patterns.title: Stored XSS in nbconvert HTML handlers from a missing sandbox CSP directive
patterns.cause: The nbconvert HTTP handlers in jupyter_server serve HTML rendered from user-authored notebooks under the Jupyter origin. Their Content-Security-Policy has no sandbox directive. nbconvert.HTMLExporter does not sanitize by default, so an HTML payload in a display_data output is served as active content in the Jupyter origin.
preconditions: The nbconvert file or post handlers in a jupyter_server release before 2.20 render a notebook to HTML
The notebook contains attacker-authored HTML in a display_data output
The HTML exporter is used with its default non-sanitizing behavior
An authenticated user opens the nbconvert HTML URL for that notebook
patterns.prevention: Do not serve exported notebook HTML under the main application origin without isolation. Make sure the Content-Security-Policy on the nbconvert handler responses includes a sandbox directive, so notebook-supplied markup is not treated as the Jupyter origin. Upgrade jupyter_server to 2.20 or later, which contains the fix. Where editing the installed package is impractical, the advisory describes a configuration-level workaround that adds the same sandbox directive to these two handlers.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not say exactly which sandbox flags the fix uses beyond the advisory workaround, and they do not describe what a sandboxed page can still do. They do not say whether sanitizing the exported HTML is an alternative or an additional fix. Only the file and post handlers of the nbconvert endpoint are named as affected.

fixtures.scenario: An attacker shares a notebook whose display_data output holds an HTML payload. A signed-in user opens the nbconvert HTML URL for it, and the response has no sandbox directive, so the payload runs in the Jupyter origin with cookie and API access.

The same notebook is opened through the nbconvert HTML URL, but the response Content-Security-Policy includes a sandbox directive, so the payload is not treated as the Jupyter origin and does not get its cookie or API authority.

citations.quote: render user-authored notebook HTML under the Jupyter origin without a sandbox directive in their Content-Security-Policy
a notebook carrying an HTML payload in a display_data output triggers stored XSS with cookie access, full /api/* authority, and kernel RCE.
This vulnerability is fixed in 2.20.

patch_review.observation: The fix overrides the Content-Security-Policy for both the nbconvert file handler and the nbconvert post handler. It appends a sandbox directive that allows scripts, so any script in exported notebook HTML runs in a unique origin and cannot reach the Jupyter server. A new server setting, on by default, controls this behavior, and tests check the header for both handlers.

patterns.title: Unescaped figclass and figwidth options in Mistune Figure directive allow attribute injection XSS
patterns.cause: The render_figure() function in the image directive module of Mistune concatenates the figclass and figwidth options directly into HTML attributes without escaping. These values bypass the inline renderer, so they are not protected by the renderer's escape setting. Other attributes in the same file (src, alt, style) were escaped, but these two were missed.
preconditions: Mistune version 3.2.0 or earlier is in use
The Figure directive from the image directives module is enabled when rendering Markdown
Untrusted users can supply figclass or figwidth option values in Markdown input
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Mistune 3.2.1, which contains a patch. In general, any value placed into an HTML attribute by a directive renderer should be escaped for attribute context before concatenation, and this should be applied consistently to every option the directive emits, not only some of them. Do not rely on the HTMLRenderer escape setting to cover directive options, because those values do not pass through the inline renderer.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact escaping routine used in the patch, nor whether other directives have similar gaps. They also do not say whether figclass or figwidth values are validated against an allowlist. Only versions up to 3.2.0 are stated as affected, and 3.2.1 is the only version stated as patched.

fixtures.scenario: An app renders user Markdown with HTMLRenderer escape enabled and the Figure directive on. An attacker supplies a figclass value that closes the attribute and adds an event handler, which appears unescaped in the output.
The app runs Mistune 3.2.1 or later. The same figclass and figwidth values are escaped, so the injected characters stay inside the attribute value and no new attribute or script is created.

citations.quote: the `render_figure()` function concatenates `figclass` and `figwidth` options directly into HTML attributes without escaping
This allows attribute injection and XSS even when HTMLRenderer(escape=True) is used, because these values bypass the inline renderer.
Version 3.2.1 contains a patch.

patch_review.observation: The fix applies the shared text-escaping helper to the figclass and figwidth values in the figure renderer, which matches the card's cause and prevention. The same commit also escapes the class option in the admonition directive and the text in the block error renderer, so the card's note about other directives is incomplete but its main point holds.

patterns.title: Unescaped heading IDs in mistune table-of-contents links allow HTML injection
patterns.cause: The table-of-contents renderer render_toc_ul() in mistune before 3.2.1 inserts the heading id into an anchor href and the heading text into the link label through a plain format string. It applies no HTML escaping to either value, so a crafted id can close the href attribute and inject arbitrary tags, including script blocks, into the rendered TOC.
preconditions: The application uses the mistune TOC plugin and renders its output with render_toc_ul().
Heading IDs are derived from user-supplied heading text, for example through a custom heading_id callback that returns raw text as the slug.
The mistune version is older than 3.2.1.
The TOC output is placed into a page viewed by other users.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mistune to 3.2.1 or later. Treat every heading id and label as untrusted when building TOC markup. Escape the id for use inside an attribute value and escape the label for HTML text before inserting either into an anchor. Prefer generated slugs restricted to a safe character set, or the default sequential identifiers, over raw heading text. Review the TOC rendering path separately from the body renderer, because it can be trusted implicitly.
patterns.limitations: The sources conflict on the label. The CVE text says neither id nor text is escaped, while the advisory observes that the label is already escaped by the inline renderer before it reaches the TOC list and that the id is the exploitable value. The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, and they do not cover other plugins or renderers beyond the TOC and heading id path. Escaping alone is not shown to be a complete defense for every output context.

fixtures.scenario: A documentation site registers a heading_id callback that returns the raw heading text as the anchor id. A contributor submits a heading whose text closes the href attribute and adds a script tag. The TOC renderer pastes it unescaped, and the script runs for every reader.
The site runs mistune 3.2.1 or later, or keeps the default sequential IDs. The same malicious heading yields an anchor whose id and label are inert text, so no extra tag or script appears in the TOC.

citations.quote: with no HTML escaping applied to either value.
injecting arbitrary HTML tags including <script> blocks directly into the rendered TOC.
When heading IDs are derived from user-supplied heading text (the standard use-case for readable slug anchors)
This vulnerability is fixed in 3.2.1.

patch_review.observation: The fix imports the existing escape helper and applies it to the heading id when render_toc_ul() builds each anchor href in the table of contents. The link label is left unchanged, so the id is the value being fixed. This matches the card's main point that an unescaped id can break out of the href attribute.

patterns.title: Blind SSRF via user-supplied MCP SSE and streamable-http connection URLs and headers
patterns.cause: When MCP is enabled, the connection endpoint accepts a client-supplied url and headers dictionary with no scheme check, private-address filtering or allowlist. The handler passes them straight to the MCP SDK's SSE and streamable-http clients, which make outbound requests from the server.
preconditions: The MCP feature is enabled in the Chainlit configuration (disabled by default since 2.7.0)
The MCP connection endpoint is reachable by any client that can open a session, with no authentication required
User-controlled url and headers are passed to the outbound MCP client without an allowlist
patterns.prevention: Never let clients choose outbound destinations freely. Keep MCP off unless needed. If user-supplied SSE or streamable-http connections are required, make them opt-in with a non-empty allowlist and default deny. Accept only http or https, and match scheme, host, port and path prefix. Reject dot segments, encoded separators, double encoding, backslashes and non-ASCII path characters. Strip sensitive headers (Cookie, Host, forwarding, proxy credentials) from client headers. Do not follow redirects, and re-check every outgoing request, including endpoints announced by the remote server, against the grant. Require authentication on the endpoint and restrict network egress.
patterns.limitations: The sources say the allowlist is hostname-based, so a DNS name resolving to a loopback, link-local or metadata address is not rejected; resolve-then-pin validation was deferred. Without a registered auth callback the endpoint stays anonymous, so any allowlisted URL can still be driven. Header filtering is a denylist, and Authorization is still forwarded. The sources do not give implementation details beyond these behaviors.

fixtures.scenario: MCP is enabled with no auth. An anonymous client posts a streamable-http connection request with a loopback URL and a forged Authorization header, and the server sends that request.
User-supplied connections are off by default. When enabled, only allowlisted http or https URLs pass, redirects are refused, Cookie and Host are stripped, and a loopback URL is rejected.

citations.quote: An unauthenticated attacker can force the Chainlit server to make outbound HTTP requests to arbitrary URLs
HTTP redirects are no longer followed on MCP transports.
Every outgoing transport request is now re-checked against the connection's grant, not just the initial URL.
There is no private-IP or IP-literal blocking.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes client-chosen outbound destinations for MCP. Developer-configured named servers replace the old per-transport sections, and user-supplied SSE or streamable-http URLs become opt-in behind a default-deny allowlist. The allowlist matches scheme, host, port and path prefix, and rejects dot segments, encoded separators, double encoding, backslashes and non-ASCII paths. Restricted headers are stripped, redirects are disabled, and every outgoing request is re-checked against the grant, including endpoints the remote server announces.

patterns.title: Blind SSRF through unescaped user input in PDF export HTML
patterns.cause: The PDF export builds an HTML document from user-controlled fields and passes it to an HTML-to-PDF renderer. User input is interpreted as HTML, so an attacker can inject an image tag whose source URL the server then fetches.
preconditions: An endpoint accepts user-supplied fields such as the title or message content and uses them to build an HTML document for PDF generation.
The fields are inserted into the HTML template without escaping.
The PDF renderer fetches remote resources referenced by image tags, and the server can reach internal or external hosts.
patterns.prevention: Treat every user-controlled field that flows into the PDF HTML template (title, message content, role, model name and formatted date) as plain text. HTML-escape these values with a standard escaping routine before placing them in the template, so injected markup is rendered as literal characters and never parsed as tags. Upgrade to Open WebUI 0.5.11 or later. Do not rely on blocking a list of dangerous tags such as scripts, iframes and objects, because an image tag still triggered a request.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe only the escaping fix and the affected version range. They do not say whether the renderer can be restricted from fetching remote resources, whether egress filtering would help, or whether other tags or attributes could cause requests. The report was tested on version 0.5.4, and no way to read responses was found, so the impact is blind requests and timing-based enumeration.

fixtures.scenario: A user sends a PDF export request whose title field holds an image tag pointing at an external host. The server puts it in the HTML template, the renderer fetches the URL, and the attacker receives a callback.
The same request is received, but the title, message content, role and model fields are HTML-escaped before templating. The tag is rendered as literal text and no outbound request occurs.

citations.quote: In the PDF export, user inputs are interpreted as HTML and embedded into the PDF.
However, an image tag can be used to force a server-side request (SSRF)
During the available testing time, no method was found to read the responses (Blind SSRF).
This vulnerability is fixed in 0.5.11.

patch_review.observation: The fix imports an HTML escaping routine and applies it to the chat title, message role, message content, model name and formatted date before they are placed into the HTML template used for PDF generation. This stops injected markup such as image tags from being parsed, which removes the server-side request the renderer would otherwise make. The card's cause and prevention match this change.

patterns.title: Scheduler imports arbitrary class paths from DAG-author-controlled deadline reference state
patterns.cause: The scheduler-side decoder for custom deadline references imported and instantiated whatever class path appeared in serialized state supplied by a DAG author. No allowlist or plugin-registry gate limited which classes could be loaded, and the instantiated class received a live database session.
preconditions: A DAG author can get code or serialized DAG state to the scheduler, which is the default on single-host deployments where the DAG bundle is importable from the scheduler process
The serialized deadline reference names a module path chosen by the DAG author
The deployment treats DAG-author code as less trusted than the scheduler process
patterns.prevention: Do not resolve class paths from serialized DAG state by importing them dynamically. Before any import or instantiation, check the requested class against an explicit allowlist or a registry of registered plugins, and reject anything else. Do not hand privileged resources such as a database session to classes that were not vetted. Upgrade apache-airflow to 3.2.2 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, the affected version range below 3.2.2, or whether other decoders share the pattern. The issue only matters where DAG authors are less trusted than the scheduler. Running DAG code on a single host with a shared importable bundle is a default, so this is not a rare configuration.

fixtures.scenario: A DAG author serializes a custom deadline reference naming a module path they control. The scheduler imports that path and instantiates the class with a live database session attached.
The scheduler checks the class path in a serialized deadline reference against an allowlist or plugin registry first. An unregistered path is rejected, and no import or instantiation occurs.

citations.quote: imported and dispatched arbitrary class paths drawn from DAG-author-controlled serialized state without an allowlist or plugin-registry gate
instantiate that class with a live SQLAlchemy session attached
Affects deployments where DAG-author code is less trusted than the scheduler process.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the unrestricted dynamic import of the class path found in serialized custom deadline reference state with a lookup in a registry of classes that plugins declare through a new deadline references attribute. Unregistered class paths are rejected with an error before any class is loaded or instantiated. This matches the card's cause (no allowlist or registry gate on imported classes) and its prevention (check against a registry of registered plugins and reject everything else).

patterns.title: Pygments AdlLexer ReDoS from inefficient GUID-matching regular expression
