patterns.cause: The AdlLexer in pygments/lexers/archetype.py uses a regular expression for GUID matching whose complexity is inefficient. Crafted input can make the lexer consume excessive CPU time, which is a regular expression denial of service (CWE-1333, CWE-400).
preconditions: The application uses a pygments release before 2.20.0 (the CVE record says versions up to 2.19.2).
Text is processed with AdlLexer, for example when highlighting ADL (Archetype Definition Language) content.
An attacker with local access can supply or influence the text being lexed.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade pygments to 2.20.0 or later. Where an upgrade is not possible, avoid running AdlLexer on input from untrusted sources, or bound the CPU time spent on highlighting by using a timeout or a separate worker process. When writing lexers, make GUID-matching patterns match in time that stays reasonable as the input grows, and test them against long near-miss inputs.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the vulnerable pattern, the triggering input shape, or the timing impact, so those details are not covered here. They describe the attack as possible only with local access. The advisories also say the project had not responded, yet they name 2.20.0 as the version before which pygments is affected. Check the release notes to confirm the fix. This card does not describe the exact upstream change.

fixtures.scenario: A local tool built on pygments 2.19.2 highlights ADL files with AdlLexer. A local user submits a crafted file containing GUID-like text, and the lexer spends excessive CPU time on it, stalling the tool.
The same tool runs pygments 2.20.0 or later. If the tool must handle files from less trusted users, it also runs highlighting under a time limit, so a slow input cannot stall the whole service.

citations.quote: Pygments has Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) due to Inefficient Regex for GUID Matching
A security flaw has been discovered in pygments before 2.20.0.
The manipulation results in inefficient regular expression complexity.
The attack is only possible with local access.

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the GUID pattern in AdlLexer, which repeated a group of alternating digit or hex-letter choices (overlapping alternatives that cause heavy backtracking), with a single hex character class and bounded repeat counts. It also puts upper bounds on the identifier-part repeats in the archetype id pattern of the shared AtomsLexer base. This matches the card's cause (an inefficient GUID regex in AdlLexer) and its prevention (upgrade, and write patterns that stay efficient).

patterns.title: Encoded dot segments escape WsgiDAV filesystem share root via prefix-based containment check
patterns.cause: In WsgiDAV 4.3.3 and prior, the filesystem provider joins the share root with the request path parts, normalizes the result, and then checks containment with a plain string prefix comparison. A string prefix test is not path-boundary aware, so a sibling directory whose name merely begins with the root path string passes the check. An encoded parent-directory segment in the request path, forwarded by the server layer to PATH_INFO, can resolve into such a sibling.
preconditions: The deployment uses a filesystem-backed WsgiDAV share.
The attacker can send WebDAV requests the share accepts, either anonymously or as an authenticated WebDAV user.
A sibling path exists whose absolute path starts with the configured root path string, for example a share root and a neighboring directory sharing that prefix.
The WsgiDAV process has operating system permissions for the path outside the share.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade WsgiDAV to version 4.3.4 or later. In similar code, decide containment on whole path components after the candidate path is fully resolved, not with a string prefix comparison, so a sibling directory sharing a name prefix with the root is rejected. Do not rely on the server layer to strip encoded dot segments, since the WSGI layer may pass them through as parent-directory segments. Also run the WebDAV process with least privilege on the filesystem.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the flaw and the fixed version but not the details of the upstream change, so the exact fix is not described here. The local proof used the wsgiref server; behavior with other WSGI servers is not stated. Impact depends on the deployment and on the permissions of the WsgiDAV process. This is not an authentication bypass, and only the filesystem provider is described as affected.

fixtures.scenario: The share root is /tmp/share and a sibling directory /tmp/share_evil exists. A request path with an encoded parent segment resolves to the sibling, and a plain string prefix check accepts it, so reads, writes and deletes reach outside the share.
Same layout, but containment is checked on whole path components after resolution, so the sibling directory is rejected. The deployment also runs WsgiDAV 4.3.4, the fixed release.

citations.quote: This is not path-boundary aware.
The WSGI/server layer forwards the encoded dot segment to WsgiDAV's PATH_INFO.
The issue is fixed with version 4.3.4.

patch_review.observation: The fix changes the containment check in the filesystem provider's path-resolution method. Both the share root and the resolved file path now get a trailing separator before the prefix comparison, so a sibling directory whose name merely begins with the root string is rejected. This matches the card's cause (a prefix check that ignores path boundaries) and its prevention (compare whole path components).

patterns.title: PyJWKClient fetches JWKS from any URL scheme urllib supports, including file, ftp and data
patterns.cause: PyJWKClient passes its uri argument directly to urllib.request.urlopen(). The default opener in the Python standard library registers handlers for HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, file and data URLs. Before PyJWT 2.13.0 there was no documented option to restrict which schemes the client would fetch. If an application lets an attacker influence the JWKS URL, for example from the jku header of a token, a configuration file or an OAuth flow parameter, the client can be pointed at local files or other non-HTTP resources.
preconditions: The application runs PyJWT older than 2.13.0 and uses PyJWKClient to fetch a key set.
The URL given to PyJWKClient is influenced by an attacker, such as one taken from a token header, a configuration file or an OAuth parameter.
No scheme check is done by the application before the URL reaches PyJWKClient.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to PyJWT 2.13.0 or later, which the advisories list as the fixed version. Independently of the library version, do not take the JWKS location from the unverified token header or other untrusted input. Use a fixed, operator-configured URL, or check the URL against a trusted list of issuers before creating the client. Before any fetch, parse the URL and reject any scheme other than the ones you intend to use. Prefer HTTPS only, and refuse file, ftp, data and URLs with no scheme. Reject the URL before a request is built, not after the response arrives.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how 2.13.0 implements its fix, so the exact option names and defaults should be taken from the release notes. The advisory notes that the library does not directly return non-HTTP(S) content to the attacker. The key-forgery chain also needs further application flaws, such as attacker write access to a filesystem path and untrusted jku derivation, which the library fix does not address. The sources do not discuss restricting which hosts an allowed HTTP or HTTPS URL may reach, so a scheme check alone does not cover that concern.

fixtures.scenario: A service reads the jku value from an incoming token header and builds a PyJWKClient with it, without any check. An attacker supplies a file URL or an ftp URL as the jku, and the client attempts to fetch it using the default urllib handlers.

A service configures the JWKS URL once as a trusted HTTPS address and ignores any jku value in token headers. It also verifies that the scheme is HTTPS before creating the client and runs PyJWT 2.13.0 or later. A token that names a file, ftp or data location never reaches the fetch layer.

citations.quote: PyJWKClient passes its uri argument directly to urllib.request.urlopen() which uses Python stdlib's default OpenerDirector registering HTTPHandler, HTTPSHandler, FTPHandler, FileHandler, and DataHandler.
There is currently no documented option to restrict which schemes PyJWKClient will fetch.
the attacker can cause PyJWKClient to read arbitrary local files via file:// (SSRF on local filesystem)
requires additional application-layer flaws (attacker write access to a filesystem path, untrusted jku derivation) that this fix does not address.

patterns.title: Resolve static file paths without letting Windows UNC paths trigger outbound SMB
patterns.cause: On Windows, StaticFiles joins the requested path onto the served directory and calls os.path.realpath before the containment check. A UNC path is absolute, so the join discards the served directory. Resolving the bare UNC path opens an outbound SMB connection and sends NTLM authentication before the path is rejected with a 404.
preconditions: The application runs on Windows and serves files with StaticFiles, directly or through a framework built on Starlette such as FastAPI.
StaticFiles uses its default setting that does not follow symlinks, which resolves paths with os.path.realpath.
Starlette is version 1.0.1 or earlier.
The host can make outbound SMB connections on port 445, and the endpoint accepts requests from untrusted clients.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Starlette to 1.1.0 or later. In general, never pass an untrusted, possibly absolute or UNC path to a resolver that performs I/O, such as os.path.realpath, before confirming it stays inside the served directory. Where an upgrade is not possible, serve static files from a dedicated web server such as nginx or IIS, or block outbound SMB on port 445 from the application host.
patterns.limitations: The sources say the issue is fixed in 1.1.0 but do not describe how the fix works, so the exact validation approach is not covered here. Blocking port 445 stops the credential leak but does not change how paths are resolved. The sources also note that response timing can reveal which internal hosts are reachable over SMB, and they do not say whether the SMB block alone stops that.

fixtures.scenario: A Windows service runs an unauthenticated StaticFiles mount with default settings on Starlette 1.0.1. A client requests a UNC path naming a host it controls. The server connects out over SMB and leaks its NTLMv2 hash, while the client only sees a 404.

The same Windows service runs Starlette 1.1.0 or later, or serves static files through nginx or IIS, or blocks outbound port 445. A UNC-style request yields a 404 and no credentials reach an outside host.

citations.quote: can cause os.path.realpath to initiate an outbound SMB connection before the path is rejected
Blocking outbound SMB (port 445) from the application host prevents the credential disclosure even if a UNC path is resolved.
The issue is fixed in 1.1.0.
POSIX systems are not affected.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds an early check in the StaticFiles path lookup function that rejects any requested path starting with a forward slash or backslash, returning no result before the path is joined to the served directory or resolved. This stops absolute and UNC paths from replacing the served directory and reaching realpath, which is what caused the outbound SMB connection. Tests cover a POSIX absolute path and a UNC-style path.

patterns.title: Gradio FileExplorer preprocess path traversal escapes root_dir
patterns.cause: The FileExplorer preprocess() method combines client-supplied path segments with the configured root directory using os.path.join. Segments with traversal sequences or absolute paths cause the root_dir prefix to be discarded, so paths outside the root reach callbacks.
preconditions: Gradio before 6.16.0 is in use
An app exposes the FileExplorer component with a configured root_dir
An attacker can submit crafted path segments to the component; no authentication is needed
patterns.prevention: Upgrade Gradio to 6.16.0 or later. When building file paths from client-supplied segments, do not assume that joining them to a root keeps the result under that root. Reject or neutralize traversal sequences and absolute path segments, and confirm the final resolved path is still inside the configured root before passing it to application callbacks.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, so the exact validation it performs is unknown. They do not cover symlinks, platform-specific path forms, or any version other than the stated fixed release. The impact is described only as arbitrary file read or exposure of sensitive files.

fixtures.scenario: An app uses FileExplorer with root_dir set to a project folder. A client submits a path segment that is absolute or contains parent-directory sequences, and the callback receives a path outside the folder.
The same app runs Gradio 6.16.0 or later. A client submits an absolute or traversal-style segment, and the path is not allowed to resolve outside root_dir, so no outside file reaches the callback.

citations.quote: allows unauthenticated attackers to escape the configured root directory by supplying path segments containing directory traversal sequences or absolute paths
Attackers can provide crafted path segments that cause os.path.join to discard the root_dir prefix entirely

patch_review.observation: The fix replaces the direct combination of client-supplied path segments with the root directory in the FileExplorer preprocess method, for both single and multiple selection, with a call to a safe-join helper. Tests show that absolute segments and parent-directory segments now raise InvalidPathError, while legitimate in-root selections still resolve normally. This matches the card's cause (joining discards the root prefix) and its prevention (reject out-of-root paths and verify containment).

patterns.title: Unvalidated JSONP callback reflected into script responses by oauthlib RevocationEndpoint
patterns.cause: The RevocationEndpoint offered an optional JSONP mode. When enabled, it took the callback request parameter from the query string or body and placed it unmodified in success and error response bodies. Because the value was never checked as a legal function name, an attacker could inject arbitrary script text. A page that loaded the response as a script would run that text in its own origin.
preconditions: The RevocationEndpoint has JSONP explicitly enabled; it is disabled by default.
The callback value reaches a success or error response without validation.
A browser page loads the revocation response as trusted JSONP.
An attacker can influence the callback value that the page sends.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to oauthlib 4.0.0, identified as fixed by the CVE advisory. The fix removes the JSONP constructor option and callback wrapping: the shown OAuth2 error path returns JSON, and success returns an empty body. Both prepare_token_revocation_request helpers drop the explicit callback argument and put generated parameters in the request body; the PR diff also rejects the callback keyword with TypeError. Use CORS for cross-origin browser access. If retaining JSONP in a separate implementation, the advisory recommends full-string validation of legal identifiers, optionally dot-separated, rejecting or ignoring invalid callbacks on both paths, and serving a JavaScript content type.
patterns.limitations: JSONP removal breaks integrations relying on it. Passing the removed constructor option fails; the PR diff explicitly rejects callback keywords in the helpers, but does not guarantee rejection of every former positional callback argument. Callback parameters no longer affect response wrapping; the diff does not establish that all request processing ignores them. The CVE advisory reports versions from 0.6.1 before 4.0.0 as affected and 4.0.0 as fixed; the diffs alone do not identify a release. Browser impact requires trusted JSONP consumption and attacker influence, and occurs in the including page's origin. The supplied changes do not assess other endpoints or establish response formats for every exception path.

fixtures.scenario: A revocation endpoint with JSONP turned on receives a request whose callback value is a JavaScript statement followed by a comment marker. The response body begins with that statement, and a page loading it as a script runs it.

The same endpoint receives callback values that are plain dotted function names and returns them wrapping the data. A value containing parentheses, quotes, or comment markers is ignored or rejected, so no attacker code appears in the body.

citations.quote: The callback can come from the query string or request body and is used without restricting it to a legal JavaScript function name.
The feature is disabled by default, so only deployments that explicitly enable JSONP are affected.
This is the standard mitigation used by jQuery, Express.js, Google APIs, and other major JSONP implementations.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes JSONP support from the revocation endpoint. The constructor loses its JSONP option, and the error and success responses no longer wrap or prefix the request-supplied callback value, so they return plain JSON and an empty body. The client-side request builders also drop the callback argument, and the follow-up change makes them raise a TypeError if a caller still passes one.

patterns.title: Strip internal update headers from client requests before proxy forwards to object servers
patterns.cause: Gatekeeper excluded account, container and object sysmeta, object transient sysmeta, and x-backend header prefixes, but omitted legacy internal update headers. Client-supplied container and delete-at host and device headers could pass through the proxy to object-servers, allowing an authenticated user with write access to redirect container update requests to an attacker-controlled server. The fix also filters account, container and delete-at partition headers, account host and device headers, delete-at container, and container root db state.
preconditions: OpenStack Swift is older than 2.37.2.
The attacker is an authenticated user with write access.
Client-supplied internal update headers reach object-servers through the proxy.
Object-servers use the injected headers to redirect container update requests.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to Swift 2.37.2 or later. Treat internal update headers as server-controlled metadata. Extend gatekeeper's inbound exclusions with exact-name matching for account, container and delete-at host, device and partition headers, plus delete-at container and container root db state, so client-supplied copies are removed. Retain the existing exclusions. As general hardening, prevent client headers from controlling internal backend destinations and review new internal header names for equivalent filtering.
patterns.limitations: The diff implements filtering in gatekeeper but does not establish its required pipeline position or protection for entry points that bypass it. The advisory establishes exploitation by authenticated users with write access through object-servers; the broader header filter does not establish exploitable account or container request paths for every added header. Future internal headers outside the exclusion patterns are not covered by these additions. The sources provide no configuration-only mitigation or method for detecting past exploitation.

fixtures.scenario: A user with write access sends an object PUT that includes X-Container-Host and X-Container-Device pointing at a server they control. The proxy forwards the headers, and the object-server sends its container update to that server.

The same PUT carries forged internal update headers. The proxy drops them and sets its own values, so the object-server sends container updates only to the real container servers and nothing reaches the attacker.

citations.quote: proxy-server does not strip internal update headers (X-Container-Host, X-Container-Device, X-Delete-At-Host, X-Delete-At-Device) from client requests before forwarding them to object-servers.
An authenticated user with write access can inject these headers to redirect container update requests to an attacker-controlled server

patch_review.observation: The fix extends the gatekeeper middleware's inbound exclusion list with exact-match patterns for the legacy update headers that predate the x-backend naming. These are the account, container and delete-at host, device and partition headers, plus the delete-at container and container root db state headers. Client-supplied copies are now stripped at the proxy edge, so a client can no longer steer where backend servers send their update requests. This matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Path traversal via crafted trace ID in MLflow FileStore trace creation
patterns.cause: The FileStore tracking backend uses a client-supplied trace ID when deciding where to write trace files. A trace ID containing traversal sequences, submitted to the POST /api/3.0/mlflow/traces endpoint, makes FileStore.start_trace() write trace_info.yaml, request metadata and tag files outside the intended experiment trace directory.
preconditions: MLflow 3.17.1 or earlier is running
The FileStore tracking backend is in use (the default before MLflow 3.7.0, opt-in from 3.7.0 onward)
The attacker can reach the trace creation endpoint, and no authentication is needed
The server process has filesystem permission on the target location, since writes are bounded by those permissions
patterns.prevention: Treat the trace ID as untrusted input and never let it act as a path. Accept only a plain identifier, and reject separators, parent-directory sequences and absolute paths. Before creating any file, build the destination path, resolve it fully (for example with os.path.realpath()), and confirm it is still inside the experiment trace directory. Refuse the request if it is not. Apply the same check to every file written for a trace, including the info file, request metadata and tags. Where possible, run the server with a filesystem account that can write only to the tracking store, and prefer a non-FileStore backend, since the default moved to SQLite in 3.7.0.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix, so the exact validation rules it uses are unknown. They also do not say whether other FileStore entry points or other backends accept unsafe identifiers. The sources describe the written content as attacker-controlled metadata, not fully arbitrary file content, and the impact depends on which files the server account can write. Whether authentication or a network boundary mitigates the issue in a given deployment is not covered beyond the statement that attackers are unauthenticated.

fixtures.scenario: A server on MLflow 3.17.1 with FileStore enabled receives an unauthenticated POST to the traces endpoint. The trace ID contains parent-directory sequences, and the trace info, metadata and tag files are created outside the experiment trace directory.

The same request arrives, but the trace ID is rejected because it is not a plain identifier, or because the fully resolved destination falls outside the experiment trace directory. No file is written outside that directory.

citations.quote: allows unauthenticated attackers to control filesystem paths by submitting a crafted trace ID containing traversal sequences to the POST /api/3.0/mlflow/traces endpoint
write trace_info.yaml, request_metadata, and tag files with attacker-controlled metadata outside the intended experiment trace directory, subject to the server process's filesystem permissions
FileStore is the default tracking backend before MLflow 3.7.0 and opt-in thereafter

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a validation step that requires a trace ID to be a single path component. It rejects empty values, separators, absolute paths, dot and dot-dot names, and names ending in spaces or periods, which Windows would normalize. It runs this check in the trace creation path before any directory is made, and also in the trace deletion path. A follow-up change also rejects URI-special and control characters in new trace IDs and validates assessment IDs the same way.

patterns.title: Decode-after-check path traversal in nltk.data.load() via percent-encoded segments
patterns.cause: The unsafe-path regex check in nltk/data.py runs on the raw resource string. The path is built later from url2pathname(), which decodes percent sequences. Encoded slashes and dots are invisible to the check but become real path separators and traversal segments in the final filesystem path.
preconditions: Attacker-controlled input reaches nltk.data.load()
The resource uses the nltk: URL scheme
The installed NLTK version is earlier than 3.10.0-rc1
patterns.prevention: Run every unsafe-path check on the same decoded form that is used to build the final filesystem path, never on the raw string. Reject absolute paths and parent-directory segments that appear only after decoding. Upgrade to NLTK 3.10.0-rc1 or later. Avoid passing untrusted resource identifiers to nltk.data.load().
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the upstream fix works, so this card does not say what it checks. They do not say whether other URL schemes or other NLTK functions are affected. The proof of concept notes a default enforcement setting that is off, but the sources do not explain its effect in detail.

fixtures.scenario: A web app passes a user-supplied resource name into nltk.data.load(). The name uses the nltk: scheme with percent-encoded slashes pointing at /etc/passwd. The raw-string check sees no traversal, then decoding yields a real path and the file is read.
The app validates the decoded resource name before building any path and rejects absolute paths and parent segments. Encoded payloads are refused, and the deployment runs NLTK 3.10.0-rc1 or later.

citations.quote: The unsafe-path regex check is performed before url2pathname() decodes the %xx sequences
encoded variants such as %2fetc%2fpasswd, %2e%2e%2f..., and ..%2f..%2f slip past the regex
This vulnerability is fixed in 3.10.0-rc1.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that URL-decodes the resource string once and applies the same unsafe-path pattern to the decoded form. It rejects the string when decoding reveals absolute paths, drive letters, backslashes or parent-directory segments that the raw check missed. The helper is called from the no-protocol rejection, the nltk: scheme branch of URL normalization, and find(), so encoded payloads fail before url2pathname() turns them into real paths.

patterns.title: Path confinement gaps in LangChain file search and config loaders
patterns.cause: Several components validate a starting directory but not the search pattern or the resolved target of matched files. Loaders accept path fields without confining them to a trusted base or rejecting symlink targets. Path-prefix checks compare plain strings without a path-segment boundary, so a sibling path sharing the prefix is accepted.
preconditions: An agent exposes file-search middleware over a directory, or a loader reads prompt or chain/agent configuration.
Path values, search patterns, or workspace contents are influenced by an untrusted source, including an LLM acting on untrusted input.
The installed LangChain version is older than 1.3.9.
patterns.prevention: Canonicalize each candidate path, resolving symlinks, and verify the real path stays inside the configured root before reading or returning it. Normalize search patterns so they cannot escape the root. Make loaders confine resolved path fields to a trusted base and reject symlink escapes unless the caller opts in to dangerous loading. Enforce a path-segment boundary in prefix checks. Upgrade to 1.3.9 or later. Also confine file tools to a dedicated, sandboxed directory.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe the affected behavior and the mitigation only in general terms. They do not name specific classes or functions, and they do not detail the exact changes in the fix. The mitigation text is written in future tense. The sources report no evidence of exploitation in the wild.

fixtures.scenario: An agent with file search rooted at a project folder receives a glob pattern from an LLM reading untrusted content. The pattern, or a symlink in the workspace, resolves to a file outside the root and its contents are returned.

The same agent normalizes the pattern, resolves each match to its real path, and returns it only if inside the root. A sibling directory sharing the root name prefix is rejected by a segment-boundary check.

citations.quote: a file-search agent middleware that validates a starting directory but not the search pattern or the resolved target of matched files
verify the resolved real path remains within the configured root before reading or returning it
path-prefix checks will enforce a path-segment boundary
This vulnerability is fixed in 1.3.9.

patch_review.observation: The fix confines the file search middleware to its root. It rejects glob patterns that are absolute or contain parent-directory segments, and it resolves each matched path, including in both grep paths, to drop files that symlinks point outside the root. The Python grep fallback also stops following symlinked directories. Separately, the Anthropic tools middleware replaces raw string prefix checks with a path-segment boundary check, so a sibling directory such as one sharing a prefix with the allowed directory is rejected. The loader confinement part of the card is not visible in this diff, but the file-search and prefix-boundary parts match the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: SQL injection via URL record key in the WsgiDAV sample MySQL provider
patterns.cause: The sample MySQLBrowserProvider builds SQL by string concatenation. The record key parsed from the request URL is placed directly into WHERE clauses with no escaping, so a single quote in the key breaks out of the quoted literal and the rest runs as SQL. The table name is checked against the real table list, but the key is not.
preconditions: The sample MySQLBrowserProvider is explicitly enabled and mapped to a share; it is not enabled by default
WsgiDAV is a version prior to 4.3.5
An attacker can reach the share with a normal GET request, and read shares are often published without authentication
The record key from the URL path is used to build the SQL query
patterns.prevention: Never concatenate URL-derived values such as the record key into SQL text. Keep the data separate from the query structure, for example by using the database driver's parameter binding, and keep validating identifiers such as table names against a known list. Upgrade to WsgiDAV 4.3.5 or later, or do not enable the sample provider. Run the database account with the fewest privileges possible to limit the impact.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the code change in 4.3.5, so the exact fix mechanism is not stated here. They say only the sample provider is affected, not the default filesystem provider. They also mention an unrelated md5 bug and a numeric-type check typo, which are not the core finding. Impact depends on the privileges of the configured MySQL account.

fixtures.scenario: An administrator enables the sample MySQLBrowserProvider on an anonymous read share. A GET to a path under /db/users/ whose key contains a single quote and an extra condition breaks out of the literal, and the status code reveals whether the condition matched.

The same request with a quote in the key is handled with the key kept as plain data, separate from the SQL text, so it only fails to match a record and returns 404. Deployments on 4.3.5 or later, or without the sample provider, are also not affected.

citations.quote: the record key from the request URL goes straight into the WHERE clause with no escaping
The table name is validated against the real table list, but the key is dropped directly into the query.
This issue is fixed in version 4.3.5.

patch_review.observation: The fix passes the record key to the database driver as a bound parameter instead of concatenating it into the query, which closes the injection through the URL key. It also adds a helper that escapes identifiers (database, table and field names) and removes the numeric versus string branching that built unquoted or quoted literals by hand. The card's cause and its parameter-binding prevention match this.

patterns.title: Unbounded regex compilation for structured outputs lets one request hang an inference worker
patterns.cause: The structured_outputs.regex request parameter passes a user-supplied regular expression straight to the grammar compiler backends with no compilation timeout. The xgrammar backend has no guard at all. The outlines backend only rejects structural issues such as lookarounds and backreferences and does no complexity analysis, so nested quantifier patterns pass and cause exponential state-space expansion.
preconditions: The server accepts the structured_outputs.regex parameter from untrusted clients
The xgrammar or outlines backend compiles the supplied pattern
The vLLM version is earlier than 0.24.0
No compilation deadline or pattern complexity check is applied before compilation
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to vLLM 0.24.0 or later. In an implementation, run grammar compilation for user-supplied patterns under a hard deadline of a few seconds so a slow compile fails the request instead of occupying the worker. Also add a complexity check before compilation that rejects nested quantifier patterns, because structural validation alone does not detect exponential blow-up. Treat both the xgrammar and outlines paths as needing these controls.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the upstream fix in detail, so the exact timeout value, the complexity rules and whether a timed-out compilation is actually cancelled are not established here. The advisory suggests a thread with a deadline, which may bound the request without necessarily freeing the underlying work. A complexity check aimed at nested quantifiers may not cover every pattern that causes state-space growth. Other backends or parameters are not discussed.

fixtures.scenario: A client sends a completion request whose structured_outputs.regex value is a pattern with nested quantifiers. The server hands it to the grammar compiler with no deadline and no complexity check, and the worker stays busy compiling.

The same request is checked for nested quantifier patterns before compilation and is rejected. Any pattern that is accepted is compiled under a short deadline, so a slow compile fails that one request and the worker stays available.

citations.quote: a single request containing an adversarial regex to hang an inference worker indefinitely and deny service
performs no complexity analysis, so a pattern with nested quantifiers passes all checks
provides zero protection against exponential DFA state-space explosion

patch_review.observation: The fix adds a helper that runs regex compilation in a worker thread and fails the request with a value error if it exceeds a configurable deadline, with a default of 5 seconds and 0 to disable. It is applied to the xgrammar compile and validation paths and to the outlines index build. The diff adds no pattern complexity check, and a timed-out thread is only abandoned, not truly stopped, so the card's main cause and timeout-based prevention match, and its complexity check is extra advice beyond the fix.

patterns.title: Windows image viewer command injection through an unescaped file path in Pillow
patterns.cause: In Pillow before 12.3.0, the Windows viewer's get_command() built a cmd.exe command string by embedding a file path directly, with no escaping. The string was then run through subprocess.Popen with shell mode enabled. Shell metacharacters in the path, such as a double quote that closes the wrapping quotes followed by an ampersand, let an attacker append arbitrary cmd.exe commands. The macOS and Linux viewers quote the same path, so only the Windows path was exposed.
preconditions: Pillow earlier than 12.3.0 is running on Windows and uses the Windows viewer class
An attacker can influence the file path passed to the viewer command builder
The path is embedded in a command string that cmd.exe interprets through a shell
patterns.prevention: Do not build a shell command string from a file path. Pass the viewer program and the path as separate arguments without a shell, or apply correct cmd.exe-aware escaping to every place the path is embedded. A quoting helper written for POSIX shells does not automatically fit cmd.exe. Treat any path that contains quote or command-separator characters as untrusted. Upgrade Pillow to 12.3.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream change, so this card cannot say which escaping or argument-passing approach it uses. They also do not say how an attacker gets a hostile path into normal Pillow use. The proof of concept calls get_command() directly with a crafted path, so real exposure depends on how the application chooses file names. Only the Windows viewer is described as affected.

fixtures.scenario: On Windows with Pillow before 12.3.0, an app passes a user-influenced file name containing a double quote and an ampersand to the Windows viewer command builder. The command string is run with shell mode enabled, so cmd.exe runs the injected command.

On Windows with Pillow 12.3.0 or later, or a wrapper that launches the viewer without a shell, the same hostile file name stays a single path. The metacharacters are not interpreted, and no extra command runs.

citations.quote: WindowsViewer.get_command() constructed a cmd.exe shell command by directly embedding a file path into an f-string without escaping
allowing shell metacharacters in the file path to inject arbitrary cmd.exe commands.
This issue is fixed in version 12.3.0.

patch_review.observation: The upstream changes make the Windows viewer's command builder reject file names containing a double quote and escape percent signs so cmd.exe cannot expand them. The viewer's show_file method also stops running a shell command and opens the file with the OS file-open call, then removes the temporary file later through a shared helper. This matches the card's cause (an unescaped path inside a shell command string) and its prevention (avoid the shell or escape for cmd.exe). The card does not mention percent-sign expansion, but that is a secondary detail.

patterns.title: Missing sparse tensor validation in vLLM prompt embeddings enables DoS and memory corruption
patterns.cause: PyTorch disables sparse tensor invariant checks by default. vLLM did not validate sparse tensors in multimodal embeddings processing, so crafted embedding requests with negative or out-of-bounds indices were accepted. The earlier fix for CVE-2025-62164 only disabled prompt embeds by default and left this root cause in place.
preconditions: vLLM version at or above 0.10.2 and below 0.13.0
The prompt-embeds feature is enabled
An attacker can submit embedding requests containing sparse tensors
patterns.prevention: Validate every client-supplied sparse tensor before use. Confirm that indices are valid, non-negative and within the bounds of the declared shape, and do not rely on PyTorch to check them, since its invariant checks are off by default. Reject malformed input with an error. Treat turning the feature off by default as a mitigation only, not a fix. Run a release that includes the validation change.
patterns.limitations: The sources give no proof of concept and do not name the exact validation calls. They do not describe the performance cost of the checks. They describe the fix only as a pending change, so they do not confirm which release first contains it beyond the stated affected range. The memory corruption outcome is described only as a potential.

fixtures.scenario: An affected vLLM server has prompt embeds enabled and accepts an embedding request whose sparse tensor holds negative or out-of-range indices. No invariant check runs, so the process crashes or exhausts resources.
The server checks that sparse tensor indices are non-negative and within the declared bounds before using the tensor. It rejects a malformed embedding request with an error instead of processing it.

citations.quote: Because PyTorch disables sparse tensor invariant checks by default, an attacker can submit crafted embedding requests with malformed (negative or out-of-bounds) tensor indices
vLLM is adding the sparse tensor validation to ensure indices are valid, non-negative, and within bounds.
The fix only disables prompt embeds by default rather than addressing the root cause

patch_review.observation: The fix turns on PyTorch's sparse tensor invariant checking around loading and densifying client-supplied tensors in the prompt embeds loader and the image and audio embedding loaders. Malicious sparse tensors with out-of-bounds or negative indices are now rejected with an error instead of causing out-of-bounds writes during conversion to dense form. This matches the card's cause (checks off by default, no validation) and its prevention (validate sparse tensors and reject malformed input).

patterns.title: Default WebDataset decoder deserializes pickle and torch payloads from untrusted tar archives
patterns.cause: The default decoder of the WebDataset reader in Ray routes tar members by file extension. Members ending in pkl or pickle are passed to pickle.loads(), and members ending in pt or pth are passed to torch.load() with weights_only set to False. Both calls deserialize attacker-controlled bytes without validation. The reader enables this decoder by default, so a crafted archive runs code in the Ray process that reads it.
preconditions: Ray version earlier than 2.56.0 is in use
read_webdataset() is called with the default decoder setting
An attacker can supply or modify the tar archive, for example via a shared bucket, an HTTP URL, or a public hub
The archive contains members with pkl, pickle, pt, or pth extensions
patterns.prevention: Do not deserialize archive members with general-purpose object loaders by default. Make pickle and unrestricted torch loading an explicit opt-in that is documented as safe only for trusted sources, or remove those branches from the default decoder so callers supply their own decoder. Until upgraded, pass no decoder or a custom decoder that handles only known-safe formats and rejects pickle-style members. Only read archives from sources you trust. Upgrade Ray to 2.56.0 or later.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact change shipped in 2.56.0. The two patch options come from the reporter's suggestion, not a confirmed fix. A custom decoder is only as safe as its own logic. The sources do not say whether other Ray readers have similar behavior.

fixtures.scenario: A pipeline calls the WebDataset reader with the default decoder on a tar shard from a shared bucket. One member has a pkl extension and holds a crafted payload, which runs inside the Ray worker that decodes the sample.
The pipeline passes no decoder, or a custom decoder that handles only text and image members and rejects pkl and pt members. The same shard is read, but its crafted payload is never deserialized.

citations.quote: The _default_decoder() function in webdataset_datasource.py unconditionally calls pickle.loads() on tar entries with .pkl/.pickle extensions
No flags, no opt-in, no environment variable.
and require callers to provide their own decoder when working with .pkl/.pt samples.

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the default WebDataset decoder refuse pickle and pt/pth members, raising an error that tells the caller to supply a custom decoder or explicitly opt in through an environment variable meant for trusted sources. A custom decoder bypasses the guard. This matches the card's cause (unrestricted object deserialization of attacker-controlled tar members by default) and its opt-in prevention. The card's limitations note about the exact shipped change is outdated, but that does not affect the cause or prevention.

patterns.title: Unrestricted class import when deserializing exception nodes in Airflow serialized Dags
patterns.cause: The deserializer rebuilt Airflow and builtin exception nodes by calling import_string with names derived from the serialized blob, then invoking the result with arguments from that blob. The Airflow branch accepted an unrestricted name; the builtin branch prefixed the supplied name with builtins but did not restrict the callable. A Dag author could therefore cause arbitrary callable execution, including builtin functions.
preconditions: A Dag author can place a crafted value in an operator executor_config that reaches the exception-node deserializer.
The Scheduler reconstructs the serialized Dag in its normal loop without a request, or the API server deserializes it during an authenticated Dag read, such as a details request.
The deployment lacks the exception-branch fix. No non-default configuration is required.
patterns.prevention: Resolve exception nodes without importing blob-selected names. For Airflow nodes, split the name into module and attribute, consult only already loaded modules, and read the module namespace directly to avoid lazy deprecation hooks that can import. Require a class deriving from AirflowException, otherwise raise DeserializationError. For builtin nodes, allow only KeyError and AttributeError, the exceptions the encoder emits, and reject other names. The advisory recommends apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later; the diff shows these stricter checks rather than merely a BaseException check. Deployments updated only for CVE-2026-33264 must upgrade again because that fix covered the trigger branch, a separate sink.
patterns.limitations: Airflow exception names whose modules are not loaded are rejected; subclasses outside Airflow remain supported when resolvable, as do the tested legacy module names. User-defined subclasses of builtin exceptions still do not round-trip through the builtin branch; this predates the fix. Accepted AirflowException constructors still receive blob-supplied arguments, so constructor side effects remain possible, although no exploitable constructor is established here. The diff covers only exception-node branches and does not establish protection for other branches. The sources do not describe mitigations for deployments unable to upgrade.

fixtures.scenario: A Dag author sets an executor_config value whose exception node names a process-running or eval-style callable. When the Scheduler or API server reconstructs the Dag, it imports and calls that callable with attacker-chosen arguments.

The same executor_config value is rejected at deserialization because the imported object is not a subclass of BaseException. A genuine exception class name still deserializes normally, and the Scheduler and API server run no Dag-author code.

citations.quote: so a Dag author could place a value there that causes an arbitrary callable to be imported and invoked
with no restriction on what could be imported.
deployments that upgraded in response to that advisory are still affected through the exception branch and must upgrade again
Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the generic import of a class name taken from the serialized blob in the exception-node branch. Airflow exception nodes are now resolved only from modules already loaded, by reading the module namespace directly, and are accepted only if the result is an AirflowException subclass, otherwise a deserialization error is raised. Builtin exception nodes are mapped through a fixed allow-list of KeyError and AttributeError, and everything else is rejected.

patterns.title: Overlapping quantifiers in skill-mention regexes cause quadratic backtracking
patterns.cause: Open WebUI parsed skill-mention tags (a dollar-prefixed id with an optional pipe-separated label inside angle brackets) with two regular expressions whose id and label parts could match the same characters. When the input had the opener but no closing angle bracket, the engine retried every split point between the two parts, so work grew quadratically with input length. The patterns ran synchronously on the asyncio event loop for every chat completion, with no feature gate.
preconditions: Open WebUI version 0.9.2 up to, but not including, 0.10.0
Text reaches the mention-parsing code containing the mention opener followed by a long run with no closing angle bracket
The deployment runs a single worker, which is the default, so a blocked event loop stalls all users
patterns.prevention: Write mention patterns so adjacent quantified parts cannot match the same characters. Make the optional label a single optional group that starts with its own delimiter, so the id part and label part are unambiguous and matching stays linear. Check any pattern with consecutive quantifiers for overlapping character classes. Test patterns against long inputs that start a tag but never close it, and confirm that well-formed mentions still produce the same captures and output.
patterns.limitations: The sources describe only these two patterns and the 0.10.0 fix. They give no guidance on input size limits, running regex work off the event loop, or auditing other patterns in the codebase. Exploit cost varies by version: 0.9.2 to 0.9.5 needed a large input, while 0.9.6 needed only a small one.

fixtures.scenario: A chat message or retrieved RAG chunk contains the two-character mention opener followed by tens of thousands of characters and no closing angle bracket, on a single-worker instance running version 0.9.2 to 0.9.6.

The same oversized input is scanned by a mention pattern whose optional label part cannot overlap the id part, so the scan stays linear and returns quickly, and well-formed mentions still yield the same captures.

citations.quote: parsed <$skillId|label> skill mentions with overlapping quantifiers, allowing an authenticated chat message containing <$ without a closing > to trigger quadratic backtracking
Polynomial, not exponential, but more than enough to hang a single worker on a ~100 KB input.
Both patterns become linear; captures and substituted output are unchanged on well-formed

patch_review.observation: The fix rewrites both skill-mention regexes (the detection pattern and the stripping pattern in the strip function) so the optional label becomes one optional group that begins with the pipe delimiter. Before, the id part and the label part could both match non-pipe characters, so an unclosed tag forced the engine to try every split point. Now the split is unambiguous and matching stays linear, which is what the card describes.

patterns.title: Reserved-key guard skipped for JSON string literals in Airflow XCom deserialization
patterns.cause: The reserved-key validator used for API XCom creation and updates walked dictionaries, lists and tuples but ignored strings. A JSON string literal containing reserved serialization keys could be stored verbatim and re-parsed into a dictionary or list on a read with deserialization enabled. The advisory identifies the read endpoint passing this payload to BaseXCom.deserialize_value without the reserved-key guard, allowing arbitrary classes in the airflow namespace to be instantiated on the API server (CWE-502). The diff closes the string-handling gap in submission validation.
preconditions: An authenticated API user has XCom write-and-read access on an affected installation.
The submitted XCom value is a string that decodes as JSON to an object or list carrying reserved serialization keys.
The XCom entry is subsequently read with deserialization enabled.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade apache-airflow to 3.3.1 or later, as advised. The fix extends _check_forbidden_xcom_keys to parse strings as JSON and recursively inspect decoded dictionaries and lists for reserved keys, including nested structures. Tests cover rejection through both create and update endpoints. Validation must inspect these decoded structures rather than only the outer payload shape. As general hardening, restrict XCom write access to trusted users and avoid server-side deserialization of values that untrusted principals can write.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not establish the complete affected version range or the validator's coverage across other endpoints and write paths, including task execution. The diff shows no added read-time revalidation or cleanup of stored entries; it does not establish how existing entries are otherwise handled. Strings that are invalid JSON or decode to scalars are not rejected by this reserved-key check. Benign JSON object and array strings also remain accepted.

fixtures.scenario: A user with XCom write and read access stores a JSON string literal containing reserved serialization keys, then requests that entry with the deserialize option on. The server skips the reserved-key guard and instantiates an airflow class.

The same user stores the same string literal on a patched server. The reserved-key check runs on string literals too, so the read with deserialization is rejected and no class is instantiated on the API server.

citations.quote: An authenticated user who can write an XCom value and then read it back with
Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow 3.3.1 or later, which rejects reserved XCom serialization keys submitted as JSON string literals.

patch_review.observation: The fix extends the reserved-key check used on XCom create and update requests so that string values are parsed as JSON. If a string decodes to an object or list, that structure is checked recursively for reserved serialization keys. Strings that are not valid JSON or that decode to scalars are still accepted, and the added tests cover both the create and patch paths.

patterns.title: Request-supplied OIDC file references in LiteLLM connection tests allow local file read
patterns.cause: The /health/test_connection endpoint resolved request-supplied environment and OIDC file references in litellm_params. The OIDC file provider opened supplied paths without a directory restriction, allowing privileged callers to cause local file reads subject to the proxy process's filesystem permissions. Supported per-request callback parameters also resolved environment references through the secret resolver.
preconditions: LiteLLM proxy runs a version prior to 1.83.10-stable.
The caller is a proxy administrator or another privileged caller permitted to test model connections.
Request-supplied litellm_params contain an oidc/file/ reference that reaches file resolution.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to 1.83.10-stable or later. The patch rejects os.environ/ prefixes in string values throughout request-supplied litellm_params, including nested dictionaries and lists, before merging server configuration. It drops supported callback parameters containing os.environ/ from direct arguments and metadata. Configure those values server-side. OIDC file paths must be absolute; paths and allowed directories are normalized with realpath before containment checks. Defaults are /var/run/secrets and /run/secrets; LITELLM_OIDC_ALLOWED_CREDENTIAL_DIRS replaces them with an operator-supplied list for other token locations. Restrict connection-test access to trusted administrators.
patterns.limitations: OIDC file reads remain available within allowed directories, including for server-side configuration. Other secret-provider implementations are unchanged in the supplied diff; request validation specifically targets os.environ/ references, not every secret-reference form. The sources do not establish that an environment reference is required for exploitation, whether file contents are returned to the caller, or equivalent file-read exploitability through callback parameters. The advisory classifies this as defense in depth requiring privileged access, rather than a cross-tenant privilege bypass; that does not establish negligible impact.

fixtures.scenario: An administrator-level caller sends a connection-test request to a proxy older than 1.83.10-stable. The model parameters include an oidc/file/ reference pointing at a local file, and the proxy resolves the reference and reads that file from its own filesystem.

The proxy runs 1.83.10-stable or later, and access to the connection-test endpoint is restricted to trusted administrators. A request carrying an oidc/file/ reference in its parameters does not cause the proxy to read an arbitrary local file.

citations.quote: Because exploitation requires privileged proxy access, this is treated as a defense-in-depth issue rather than a cross-tenant privilege bypass.
Prior to 1.83.10-stable, LiteLLM's /health/test_connection endpoint resolved request-supplied environment and OIDC file references in litellm_params
read files from the local filesystem via an oidc/file/ reference

patch_review.observation: The fix stops request-supplied environment references from being resolved. The connection-test endpoint now rejects them with a 400 error, and per-request callback parameters drop them with a warning. It also confines the OIDC file provider to an allowlist of credential directories: paths must be absolute, symlinks and dot segments are resolved first, and a containment check follows. The default directories are the standard container secret mounts, and operators can extend the list through an environment setting.

patterns.title: Path traversal in LiteLLM Skills ZIP archive extraction
patterns.cause: Skills archive extraction did not sufficiently validate file paths from uploaded skill ZIP archives. Entries with path traversal sequences could therefore be written outside the intended extraction or staging directory.
preconditions: LiteLLM is running a version earlier than 1.83.7-stable.
The caller is authenticated and can reach the Skills upload route, for example through LLM API routes or a key whose allowed_routes includes /v1/skills, anthropic_routes, or llm_api_routes.
The caller uploads a crafted skill ZIP archive containing path traversal entries.
The skill is processed for execution, which triggers extraction of the entries.
patterns.prevention: Validate every entry path from an uploaded archive so that each extracted file stays inside the intended extraction or staging directory, and reject any entry that would land outside it. Upgrade to 1.83.7-stable or later. If upgrading is not possible, block POST /v1/skills at the reverse proxy or API gateway and restrict Skills API access to trusted users only.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact validation the fix applies, nor which entry forms (such as dot-dot sequences, absolute paths or symlinks) were exploited. Impact beyond arbitrary file write, including code execution, depends on deployment configuration and writable paths. The workarounds reduce exposure but do not fix the extraction logic.

fixtures.scenario: A key allowed to call /v1/skills uploads a skill ZIP whose entries use traversal sequences. When the skill is processed on a LiteLLM version before 1.83.7-stable, a file is written outside the staging directory.
The same upload is handled on 1.83.7-stable or later, or POST /v1/skills is blocked at the gateway, so no entry is written outside the intended extraction directory.

citations.quote: did not sufficiently validate file paths from uploaded skill ZIP archives
those entries could be written outside the intended extraction/staging directory.
This issue is fixed in version 1.83.7-stable.

patch_review.observation: The fix adds path checks in two places. When skill files are read from the ZIP, extract_all_files normalizes each entry path and skips any that start with a parent-directory component or are absolute. When the sandbox executor stages files into a temporary directory, it resolves each target path and skips any that fall outside that directory. This matches the card's cause (unvalidated archive entry paths written outside the staging directory) and its prevention (confine every entry to the intended directory and reject the rest).

patterns.title: SSRF in LiteLLM Proxy via api_base nested in user_config
patterns.cause: The request body guard is_request_body_safe rejected top-level api_base and base_url but did not inspect or reject user_config. Because user_config is used to build the outbound router, a caller could nest a destination there and bypass the check.
preconditions: LiteLLM Proxy version 1.83.8 or earlier is running
The caller holds a valid virtual key
The caller can send a user_config object in the request body
The proxy can reach internal or external hosts the caller cannot reach directly
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to LiteLLM 1.83.9 or later. In general, apply destination-parameter checks to every request field that can feed outbound routing, including nested objects such as user_config, not only the top-level keys. Do not let caller-supplied configuration choose the host the server contacts.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how the patch works internally. They do not say whether other nested fields can carry a destination, nor whether host allowlisting or network egress controls are in place. Exploitation requires a valid virtual key, so unauthenticated callers are not covered.

fixtures.scenario: An authenticated caller sends a request whose user_config object contains an api_base pointing at an internal host. The guard checks only top-level keys, so the proxy contacts that host for the caller.
The same request is rejected because the nested api_base inside user_config is inspected like a top-level one, or the proxy runs version 1.83.9 or later.

citations.quote: user_config constructs the outbound router, the nested destination redirects a server-side request to an internal or external host selected by the caller
which blocks top-level api_base and base_url but previously did not inspect or reject user_config
Exploitation requires a valid virtual key.

patch_review.observation: The relevant change extends the banned parameter list in the request body safety check (is_request_body_safe) so that user_config is rejected from caller-supplied bodies, alongside api_base and base_url. This closes the bypass where a destination was nested inside user_config. The rest of the diff (an internal-call context variable, stripping internal keys and spoofable auth metadata, formatting) is related hardening and does not change the SSRF fix.

patterns.title: Quadratic-time scanning in mistune strikethrough, mark and insert plugins
patterns.cause: In mistune's formatting plugin, the strikethrough, mark and insert parsers search forward for a closing marker from each potential opening marker. The old regex rejects a closing pair followed by another character of the same marker type. In long runs of adjacent closed pairs, this rejects nearby closes and repeatedly scans toward the end of the input, causing quadratic work and possible CPU exhaustion.
preconditions: The application renders attacker-controlled Markdown with mistune earlier than 3.3.0.
The strikethrough, mark, or insert plugin is enabled; the advisory states that the default configuration does not enable them.
A long run of adjacent closed tilde, equals-sign, or caret marker pairs around a character reaches the formatting parser.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mistune to 3.3.0 or later. The upstream fix replaces the closing regex search with a string-search helper that accepts a close followed by another full marker pair, subject to preceding-character and escape checks. This allows nearby closes in the reported payload to end the scan. Disabling the affected plugins removes this parsing path. As general hardening, cap untrusted Markdown size and rendering time. For similar parsers, avoid closing conditions that force repeated long scans from successive opening markers.
patterns.limitations: The diff adds neither failed-position memoization nor a delimiter stack or marker cap. The advisory suggests the latter two alternatives, but the supplied patch does not establish their effectiveness or prove linear behavior for every marker layout. Its regression test checks 3,000 repeated pairs per plugin against a 0.5-second limit. Timings depend on the environment; the advisory's 8 KB description conflicts with its 40,000-byte example. No safe input-size threshold is supplied, and absence of size or time limits is not required for the parsing weakness.

fixtures.scenario: A comment service renders untrusted Markdown with mistune before 3.3.0 and the strikethrough plugin on. An anonymous user posts about 40 KB of closed tilde pairs around one letter, and one request keeps a worker busy for seconds.
The same service runs mistune 3.3.0 or later, or caps input size and render time. The same repeated-marker payload is rejected or parsed in time roughly proportional to its length.

citations.quote: a run of closed tilde, equals-sign, or caret marker pairs around a character causes quadratic work in src/mistune/plugins/formatting.py
This issue is fixed in version 3.3.0.
The minimal fix is to cap the number of simultaneously-tracked unmatched markers, treating extras as literal text.
The bounded regex on each individual scan does not bound the parser-level repetition.

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the close-marker regexes, which rejected a close followed by another marker character and so scanned to the end of the input from each opener. It adds a helper that uses plain string search and accepts a close followed by a full marker pair. It also keeps the checks for the preceding character and for escaping, so repeated closed pairs now end at the first valid close. A regression test covers the repeated-pair payload for all three plugins.

patterns.title: Percent-encoded javascript scheme bypasses Mistune safe_url() link filtering
patterns.cause: HTMLRenderer.safe_url() checks the lowercased URL prefix against harmful protocols without first URL-decoding the input. A scheme written with a percent-encoded colon is therefore not recognized as javascript. The browser later decodes the URL, so script runs when the user interacts with the link.
preconditions: The application renders attacker-controlled Markdown to HTML with a Mistune version before 3.3.0.
The application relies on the built-in safe_url() protection and adds no separate URL sanitization.
A victim opens the rendered HTML in a browser and interacts with the link.
patterns.prevention: Evaluate the URL scheme on the decoded form of the URL, so percent-encoded characters in the scheme cannot hide a harmful protocol from the check. Upgrade to Mistune 3.3.0 or later, which is reported as fixed. Until then, add application-level URL sanitization that decodes before checking.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe how version 3.3.0 changes the check. They do not say whether other encodings, such as double encoding or entity encoding, are handled. They also do not state whether image URLs and link URLs are covered identically beyond a brief mention of both.

fixtures.scenario: A comment system renders user Markdown with Mistune 3.2.0. An attacker posts a link whose target starts with the word javascript followed by a percent-encoded colon. The filter misses it, and a viewer who clicks it runs script.
The same system runs Mistune 3.3.0 or later. The same link target is neutralized, or the check decodes the URL before testing the scheme, so clicking the link does not run script.

citations.quote: However, the input URL is not URL-decoded before this check.
When rendered in a browser, the URL is decoded, resulting in execution of arbitrary JavaScript upon user interaction.
Prior to 3.3.0, HTMLRenderer.safe_url() does not block percent-encoded javascript URIs, allowing attacker-supplied Markdown links or images to bypass URL protections

patch_review.observation: The fix makes the safe URL check percent-decode the URL, repeating up to three times to catch double encoding, before lowercasing and comparing it against the harmful protocol list. It also adds several more blocked schemes, and tests cover encoded javascript and data schemes for links, reference definitions and images. This matches the card's cause (no decoding before the scheme check) and its prevention (check the decoded form).

patterns.title: Path traversal in mistune Include directive when reading markdown files
patterns.cause: In versions before 3.3.0, Include.parse() joins a user-supplied include path to the directory of the source markdown file and normalizes it. It never checks that the result stays inside an intended directory. Traversal sequences such as parent-directory segments can therefore point at files outside that location.
preconditions: The application uses mistune before version 3.3.0.
The Include directive is enabled, for example through the RST directive plugin.
Markdown files are processed with md.read(), so include paths are resolved relative to the source file.
The markdown content, and therefore the include path, can be influenced by an untrusted party.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade to mistune 3.3.0 or later. In any code that resolves include paths, convert the final path to its resolved form, for example with os.path.realpath(). Compare it against a trusted base directory and refuse to open it if it falls outside. Do this check before opening the file. If untrusted markdown is processed, consider leaving the Include directive disabled.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact upstream fix or how it treats symbolic links. They do not say which base directory the fix enforces, or whether other directives or code paths are affected. Impact depends on how the feature is used and which files the process can read.

fixtures.scenario: A markdown file contains an include directive whose path climbs several parent directories to reach a file outside the content folder. It is processed with md.read() on mistune before 3.3.0, and the outside file is read.

The same markdown file is processed on a version with the fix, or with path validation. The resolved include path falls outside the allowed directory, so the request is rejected and the file is not opened.

citations.quote: Include.parse() joins and normalizes user-supplied include paths without verifying that the result remains within the intended markdown directory
Validate the resolved path and ensure it remains within an allowed directory before opening the file.
This issue is fixed in version 3.3.0.

patch_review.observation: The fix resolves both the source file and the include target to their real paths, rejects absolute include paths, and refuses any target that is not under the source file's directory, returning an error block instead. It also adds circular-include detection and escapes included text on output, which are secondary hardening. The card's cause (no containment check after joining and normalizing) and its prevention (resolve the path, compare to a trusted base directory, refuse before opening) match the main fix.

patterns.title: Quadratic emphasis parsing in mistune inline parser on long runs of strong-emphasis pairs
patterns.cause: The inline parser treats every opening run of one to three asterisks as a possible start and scans forward for a matching close marker from each one. Each scan is bounded per call, but the scan is repeated from every potential start position. A long input of many well-formed double-asterisk or triple-asterisk pairs therefore costs quadratic work, even in the default configuration with no plugins.
preconditions: The application uses a mistune version prior to 3.3.0 to render markdown.
The markdown comes from an untrusted party, such as a network user who needs no authentication.
The input contains a long sequence of well-formed double-asterisk or triple-asterisk emphasis pairs around a character.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mistune to 3.3.0 or later, which the advisories list as the fixed version. When writing or reviewing an inline parser, do not rescan forward to the end of the input from every opening marker. Process delimiters in a single pass with a delimiter stack, as CommonMark reference implementations do, so each marker is handled a bounded number of times. The advisory also suggests, as a weaker alternative, capping how many unmatched opening markers are tracked at once and treating the rest as literal text. Add a regression test that renders a very large run of emphasis pairs and checks that it finishes quickly.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe what the 3.3.0 change actually does, so this card does not claim a specific upstream approach. The cap on open markers is only a suggestion in the advisory, and its effect on rendering of real documents is not verified here. The reported timings come from one PoC on one machine and version, and the sources give no safe input size limit. Related bracket and formatting-plugin denial-of-service reports are mentioned but not detailed.

fixtures.scenario: A comment service renders user markdown with default mistune before 3.3.0. An attacker posts about 40 KB made of thousands of short strong-emphasis pairs, and one request keeps a worker busy for several seconds.
The service runs mistune 3.3.0 or later. The same large input of repeated emphasis pairs renders in time roughly proportional to its size, and a regression test guards this.

citations.quote: long sequences of well-formed double-asterisk or triple-asterisk emphasis pairs around a character cause quadratic work
Each scan is bounded per call, but the parser invokes the scan from every potential start position.
The CommonMark reference parser handles emphasis in linear time using a delimiter-stack algorithm

patch_review.observation: The fix removes the per-opener forward regex search for a closing marker. The emphasis rule now only emits the marker as plain text, and a finalize step at the end of inline parsing resolves emphasis in one pass over a delimiter list, using a lower-bound table for openers as in the CommonMark reference algorithm. The same commit also reworks link bracket matching, link href and title parsing, and block-level parsing, but the emphasis change matches the card's cause and prevention.

patterns.title: Attribute injection XSS via unescaped class option in mistune Admonition directive
patterns.cause: The render_admonition() function in the Admonition directive concatenates the user-supplied class option directly into the HTML class attribute without escaping. The option comes from raw user input, so it can break out of the attribute and inject new attributes or script.
preconditions: The application uses a mistune version prior to 3.2.1
The Admonition directive is enabled in the Markdown renderer
Untrusted users can author Markdown containing the class option on an admonition
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mistune to version 3.2.1 or later. In an implementation, treat the class option as untrusted input and escape it for the HTML attribute context before placing it in the class attribute, or validate it against a strict allowlist of class names. Do not assume that enabling escape mode on the HTML renderer covers directive options, because it does not.
patterns.limitations: The sources do not describe the exact fix, the full set of directives or options that may be affected, or which characters are accepted in the class option. They state only that the directive name is validated against a whitelist. Whether other directives handle options safely is not covered.

fixtures.scenario: A site renders user Markdown with an old mistune and the Admonition directive. An author supplies a class option containing a quote that closes the attribute and adds an event handler, and it appears in the output HTML despite escape mode.

The site runs mistune 3.2.1 or later, so the class option is escaped before it enters the class attribute. A quote in the option cannot close the attribute, and no injected attribute or script reaches the page.

citations.quote: concatenates the `:class:` option directly into the HTML class attribute without escaping
This allows attribute injection and XSS even when `HTMLRenderer(escape=True)` is used.
This issue is fixed in version 3.2.1.

patch_review.observation: The fix escapes the user-supplied class option in the admonition renderer before it is added to the HTML class attribute, which matches the card's cause and prevention. The same commit also escapes the figure directive's class and width options and the error block text, so the weakness reaches beyond the admonition directive. The card's limitations note already leaves other directives open.

patterns.title: Quadratic parse time from many reference-link definitions in mistune
patterns.cause: For each reference-link definition, parse_ref_link searched forward for a blank line to bound optional title parsing. With many consecutive definitions and no blank lines, these repeated searches scanned the remaining input, producing quadratic work and possible CPU exhaustion. The diff fixes this repeated regex scan; it does not substantiate the advisory's explanation about revisiting stored definitions.
preconditions: The application uses a mistune version before 3.3.0, according to the advisories; the reported reproduction used 3.2.1.
The application renders attacker-supplied Markdown. The advisory reports that the default create_markdown configuration is sufficient, with no plugins required.
The attacker can supply many repeated or distinct reference-link definitions consecutively without blank lines, as in the reported attack pattern.
patterns.prevention: Upgrade mistune to 3.3.0 or later, where the advisories report the issue fixed. The fix collects blank-line positions in source order, caches them in the parser environment for the current source string object, and uses binary search for each next-blank-line query. It rebuilds the cache when the source object changes. This avoids repeated forward regex scans while that cache remains reusable.
patterns.limitations: Cache reuse requires the same source string object and a retained environment cache entry. The diff addresses this scan, without establishing the complexity of every parser path. The advisory reports linear patched timing; the added regression test asserts that 3,000 distinct definitions parse in under 0.5 seconds, but supplied material includes no test execution result. Neither establishes a universal timing guarantee. Input size limits and timeouts are general hardening, not measures validated by these sources.

fixtures.scenario: An application renders attacker-supplied Markdown with default mistune create_markdown() on a version before 3.3.0. A document of thousands of short repeated reference definitions followed by one reference link pegs the CPU for seconds.

The same application runs mistune 3.3.0 or later. The same document of repeated definitions is parsed in time that grows linearly with the number of definitions, so doubling the input roughly doubles the time.

citations.quote: Prior to 3.3.0, a Markdown document containing many repeated or distinct reference-link definitions causes quadratic work
Doubling input quadruples time.
